en: The Abhidharmadīpa, together with the Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti commentary.
First Chapter.
First Chapter. Om, may there be well-being! Homage to the Omniscient One, who demonstrated to humans and gods the path that leads to the pacification of the causes of suffering.
In this context, since a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is accepted, the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) is the primary element.
Thus it has been said: "I am the knower of the path, of the path... and so forth in detail.
What is meant by this is that he is the one who has shown the path to gods and humans.
However, if one considers the collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), then all four noble truths possess equal primacy.
Thus it has been said: "O monks, regarding these dharmas unheard of before, the eye of dharma arose [with the thought], 'This is the truth of suffering,'" and so forth in detail.
What this means is that he is the one who revealed the four noble truths to gods and humans.
In that regard, the truth of suffering is of one kind by virtue of its nature as actualization;
thus it has been said: "Monks, the actualization of existence is indeed suffering. Alternatively, it consists of eight types, beginning with birth, which constitute the result.
Or else, they are the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).

Alternatively, there are five factors pertaining to the past and two factors pertaining to the future; these, taken together, constitute seven factors. The truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) is of one kind, because it is specified as craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
It is twofold because it consists of karma and afflictions;
or it has five members because it comprises the members belonging to the prior and subsequent ends [of existence];
or it consists of the five aggregates of clinging which function as the cause.
The truth of cessation is of one kind because it is the cessation of birth without further rebirth;
or it is of two kinds due to the distinction between the abandonment of the two truths,
or due to the distinction between the realm with remainder and the realm without remainder.
Alternatively, it is of three kinds through the distinction of the realms of abandonment (*prahāṇa*), detachment (*virāga*), and cessation (*nirodha*);
or it is of four kinds through the distinction of the four fruits;
and the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) is of one kind, as it is designated by right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

Alternatively, it is of two kinds, distinguished by being either with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*), or by the distinction between the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

It is of three kinds, distinguished by the aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Or it is of four kinds, distinguished by the stages such as the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and so forth.
Or [they are four] because of the distinction in the modes of practice,
since they exist as the eight factors beginning with right view.

Thus the Blessed One demonstrated that these four noble truths are to be fully known, abandoned, realized, and cultivated, for the sake of humans and gods who are capable of seeing those truths and for whom they have arisen.
Therefore, because they are intended as the ones to whom the act of showing the path is directed, the fourth case is used to denote them as the recipients:
"Having prostrated to that Buddha who knows the true path, I shall compose the treatise *Abhidharmadīpa*. (Abhidh-d 1)

Regarding the word "that" (*tam*): that which is grasped by the injunction of the pronoun *ya-* as delimited by specific qualifiers is touched upon by the pronoun *tat*, through its connection with the preceding *ya-* which refers back to what was previously mentioned.
Furthermore, it is a "good path" (*satpatha*), meaning both "existent" (*sat*) and "path" (*panthāḥ*). Alternatively, it is the "path of the virtuous" (*satām panthāḥ*).

"One who knows the true path" (*satpathajña*) means one who knows that true path as "know this to be the true path. "Having prostrated to that knower of the true path" means having honored him through the actions of body, speech, and mind.

"Buddha": although [the term] is delimited by specific qualifiers, it is designated by the name "Buddha"—which has a directly perceived referent—for the sake of the practice of individuals who follow the Buddha.

Here, the conventional usage of the word *buddha* occurs when the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *budh* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), with the intention that the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Alternatively, since all roots meaning "to know" (*jñāna*) also mean "to go" (*gati*), the rule for the suffix *kta* applies to the reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*).
Furthermore, since *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compound formations are characterized by denotation (*abhidhāna*), there is no objection [to their application here].
This usage "Buddha" is observed in the world as being employed in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*);
for example, upon the cessation of sleep, upon the awakening to objects, and upon the removal of ignorance, one says, "Devadatta has awakened (*vibuddha*)", or "has become enlightened (*prabuddha*)".

In this way, the Blessed One is also called "Awakened," "Fully Awakened," and "Thoroughly Awakened" because of his departure from the sleep of ignorance and his realization of all objects of knowledge.

Or, just as a lotus is said to be "awakened," "fully awakened," and "thoroughly awakened" by its own nature through a particular stage of ripening, so too the Blessed One is "awakened," "fully awakened," and "thoroughly awakened" due to the ripening of the excellence of qualities such as wisdom.
And because it is the usage of all refined persons (*śiṣṭa*); for the usage of refined persons is observed here,
as stated by Vyāsa:
“Having understood this, one becomes a Buddha; what other characteristic of a Buddha could there be?
Therefore, one should show disregard for the objections of the unrefined.
Here, moreover, in the first half of the verse, the two forms of fearlessness that accomplish the welfare of others have been demonstrated.
In the third foot, two forms of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) that manifest the perfection of one's own welfare are revealed;
for one whose outflows (*āsrava*) have not been exhausted is not capable of proclaiming the path.
Nor is one who is not perfectly awakened able to fully awaken to all phenomena.
Furthermore, how is it that these [entities], such as the self imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas, being non-existent, are neither eternal nor non-eternal?
Non-existence has already been demonstrated previously.
Furthermore, the *pradhāna* of the Sāṃkhya school is not eternal.
Why? Because of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*).
If the [guṇas] such as *sattva* were unchanging, it would follow that there is an absence of manifestation;
furthermore, because of the transformation of those [manifestations], the primal nature (*prakṛti*) would itself be subject to change, since it is non-different from them.
If the qualities such as *sattva* and the others do not undergo change through the process of decrease or increase,
then nothing manifest could arise from them.
But if they do undergo change, [then it follows that they are impermanent].
In that case, they would follow as being impermanent.
If it is argued that there is no fault because this occurs through the power of karma, we reply to this as follows.
Karma does not belong to the individual because it is a commonality;

for if, for every person, karmas—whether performed intentionally or unintentionally—resided in the Pradhāna, then the postulation of a common Pradhāna would result in futility. Furthermore, the impurities consist of the nature of the knower and the manifest.
In the first case, there would be an absence of liberation; in the second, there would be other afflictions as well.
If those actions were of the nature of the person (*puruṣa*), then it would follow that liberation is impossible;
for if the person is eternal, it would entail the eternity of action.
Furthermore, by the word "and" (*ca*), defects such as the person being the agent [of action] are also implied.
"In the second [position], there are other disturbances as well.

These faults follow in the view that [the self] is essentially the primary element (*pradhāna*), and other disturbances also arise because of the commonality [of these defects], leading to the undesirable consequences of experiencing the results of actions not committed and the impossibility of liberation.
Therefore, it is established that only the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) things taught by the Omniscient One are eternal.
The eight categories of phenomena have been explained: five are conditioned and three are unconditioned.
All of this is comprised of nothing other than the conditioned and the unconditioned.

And this is established by way of the classification of the bases (*āyatana*) and the elements (*dhātu*). There are indeed twelve bases, beginning with the eye and ending with the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
There are eighteen elements (*dhātu*):
the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, and so on, up to the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
Regarding these, first:
The aggregate of form consists of the ten bases and elements beginning with the eye;
the three aggregates designated as "dharmas" consist of non-informative matter and the three eternal [factors].
"Furthermore, there are the seven consciousness-elements, which are designated as 'mind' (manas).
What, then, is the meaning of "base" (āyatana) and "element" (dhātu)? This is explained as follows:
For an *āyatana* is defined as a door of arrival (*āyadvāra*), and a *dhātu* is defined as a lineage (*gotra*). // Abhidh-d_5 //
This is what is meant: they are called *āyatanas* because they extend (*tanvanti*) this net consisting of mind and mental factors;

since the seven mind-elements and the four formless aggregates extend from these—which consist of the four conditions—or since they bring about their own arising, they are therefore *āyatanas*. The meaning of "element" (*dhātu*), however, is the sense of a lineage (*gotra*).
This is what is meant: within the single mountain of the body, there are eighteen lineages of the Dharma (*dharmagotra*).
Here, the acquisitions (*prāpti*) that serve as substitutes for the two eternal [factors] exist as the lineages (*gotra*).
And space is the support for the forms belonging to all the elements; therefore, it too exists here.
Alternatively, its status as a "constituent" (*dhātu*) is due to its maintaining its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Now, why are twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen constituents (*dhātu*) explained separately?
[Objection: "But surely this is already understood from the mention of either one [of the two]. [Reply: To this it is said:

"The Sage taught the twelve bases (āyatana) because they conform to the nature of yoga and so forth, and he taught the eighteen elements (dhātu) for the sake of abandoning the notion of the unity of consciousness and the other [mental factors]. (Abhidharmakośa 1.17)
For when the aggregates (*skandha*) are being observed, reflections of objects that are not to be known by an omniscient one appear before the yogin.

Furthermore, among the elements (*dhātu*), the reflections of the seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) are difficult to discern due to their similarity [to the other elements]. Moreover, the establishment of the elements and aggregates within the context of the sense-bases (*āyatana*) is easily characterized because the reasons for it have already been stated; thus, the teaching on the elements is presented.
Beyond that is the designation of the aggregates (*skandha*).
As it has been said: "Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises;
from the coming together of these three, contact occurs."
“Feeling and volition are co-emergent.
Therefore, the sense-bases are the source of the elements, and the elements are the source of the aggregates.
"He taught eighteen elements in order to eliminate the notion of the unity of consciousness and so forth.
For when the seven consciousness-elements are taught, they dispel the grasping at the unity of consciousness and they also dispel the grasping at a single, solid self.
The Vaibhāṣikas, moreover, say: "The teaching on the bases (āyatana) is for those confused about form; the teaching on the aggregates (skandha) is for those confused about mind and mental factors;
the teaching on the elements (dhātu) is for those confused about both form and mind."
The teaching on the aggregates (skandha) is for those of sharp faculties; the teaching on the sense bases (āyatana) is for those of medium faculties;
the teaching on the elements (dhātu) is for those of dull faculties.
Thus, it has been stated concisely for those who do not delight in prolixity.
Alternatively: "Or rather, he spoke of eighteen elements (*dhātu*) for the sake of abandoning the cognition of the unity of consciousness and so forth.
Indeed, those who have determined the unity of consciousness...

He taught the eighteen elements (dhātus) for the purpose of dispelling the notion of "mine" regarding the mind (manas), whether in its function as volition or in its identity with form and consciousness.
But what is this mind-element (manodhātu) that is distinct from the six groups of consciousness? Indeed, it is not something other at all. What then?
Since the six [senses] are mutually dependent, that which is their cause is indeed the mind (*manas*).

With respect to its activity of apprehending its own object and with respect to its power to produce another consciousness and so forth, a single consciousness is designated in three ways—as "mind" (*manas*), "thought" (*citta*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Thus, there is a designation by means of past or future names even for what is present, whether it be future or past.
This being the case, the Abhidharma treatise—"The eighteen elements belong to the three time periods"—is also brought into conformity.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra: "That which is called 'mind' (citta) or 'intellect' (manas)," and so forth.
By explaining it in this manner, you [assert that] the instrument, the intellect (manas), is eternal, while the self (ātman), the agent, is impermanent.
Thus it is prohibited.
Now, why is that very [element] not stated to be the support for all five, beginning with visual consciousness? To this we reply:
Because the five [sensory consciousnesses] have as their basis both that which possesses form and that which is formless, they are designated as "possessing form."

"Because the eye and the other [faculties] are not common [to all]. Now, as for what was stated— "together with their associations and together with their aggregates"— it is explained what these two, "aggregate" (*saṃgraha*) and "association" (*saṃprayoga*), are.
The inclusion of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) by way of their own nature is traditionally taught.
It should be understood that the inclusion of moments, atoms, classes, and numbers occurs individually according to what is appropriate. Why?
Because they are eternally inseparable from their own nature.
Therefore, there is the inclusion within the nature of substance (*dravyātmasaṃgraha*).
For the cause of the word "existent" (*sat*) is existence (*sattā*), which is the state of being; this is the meaning of the base form (*prakṛtyartha*).
The inclusion within the nature of substance is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*).
Alternatively, "existence" (sattā) may consist of the reality of ritual treatment or respectful service;
however, the existence [posited] by the Vaiśeṣikas is neither of these two, because it is a distinct entity (arthāntara). Indeed, a distinct entity cannot be established as its own self.
Furthermore, because it would follow that [the cause] is independent,
and because it contradicts etymological derivation;
for existence is not produced by a pot.

Because there is an absence of obscuration and because its permanence is accepted, it also falls away from its etymological definition: that they "exist" (*santi*) due to their connection with existence (*sattā*).
It might be argued that, like garlands and the like, they either possess existence or possess activity.
This "inclusion" (saṃgraha) that has been explained regarding the bases of sympathy (saṃgrahavastu) and so forth should be understood as secondary because it occurs only occasionally, not as primary.
However, association (saṃprayoga) is the state of equality between the mind and mental factors.
"They are engaged with a common focal object by way of five [factors]" means that only the mind and mental factors are associated, and no other phenomena are.

Now, as for those phenomena mentioned in other sūtras under the names of aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu)—do they fall within these very categories, or not? To this it is said:
Those designated by those names which are spoken of in other sūtras are included within these very [categories].
One who is proficient in the principles of the treatises should speak, having considered the specific characteristic with their intellect.

In that regard, first, among the five aggregates such as the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), the aggregate of ethical discipline is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
while the remaining four are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Furthermore,

because the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their intrinsic nature, they are subsumed under the sense-base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) among the eight [remaining] sense-bases.
But together with their attendants, they are comprised within the spheres of mind and mental objects (*manodharmāyatana*), because they have the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The final two *kṛtsnāyatanas* are comprised within the spheres of mind and mental objects, because they have the nature of four aggregates.
Among the elements as well, there are six elements;
of these, four belong to the tangible element,
and the fifth belongs to the visible-form element.
The sixth [consciousness] is associated with seven mental elements.
The mutual inclusion of the aggregates (skandha) and so forth should be understood according to their respective natures.
It should be known that the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is included within the ten bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu) that possess form.

Furthermore, all three aggregates are included, as appropriate, within the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana) and the element of mental objects (dharmadhātu), by means of their respective portions.
But for the final one, the sense-base of the mind, it is by means of the seven mental elements.
Now, why is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) not included among the aggregates (*skandha*)? We reply:
because they do not fall [into] the time-periods (*adhvan*) and so forth, there is no inclusion of permanent things within the aggregates. (Abhidharmadīpa 10)
By the word "etcetera," it is meant that [the self] is also devoid of activity and is dissociated from the characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas).
The inclusion of even the eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma should be understood as occurring precisely within these [five] entrances, because they lead one onto the true path.
Indeed, there are eighty thousand descents by which those to be trained are led onto the true path.
What, then, is the measure of each one of them? We reply:
regarding this, the views of the teachers differ. Some say that the measure of a *dharmaskandha* is a single discourse on [one of] the truths and so forth.
A "dharma-aggregate" (dharmaskandha) is a discourse on each individual topic, such as the truths, meditations, concentrations, attainments, liberations, dependent origination, and the aggregates.
According to the Teacher [the Buddha], a dharma-aggregate is that which serves as an antidote to specific behavioral tendencies such as passion and so forth;
however, according to others, its true nature is held by some to be speech, while by others it is held to be names.

For those for whom the Buddha’s word has speech as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the eighty thousand aggregates of dharma (*dharmaskandha*) are subsumed under a portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). For those, however, for whom it has name (*nāman*) as its intrinsic nature, they are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

But this is the traditional teaching (*āgama*): while the Blessed One was living, the Buddha’s word had both speech and name as its intrinsic nature, according to the principle of the secondary and the primary.
But for one who has attained final nirvāṇa, it consists solely of the nature of name and not of the nature of speech,
because the Lord of Sages possesses a voice like that of Brahmā.
Because it is impossible for worldly speech to possess similarity to that [ultimate reality].
Furthermore, why are these six elements mentioned separately? Because these six elements are considered the fundamental basis for the designation of a sentient being (*sattvaprajñapti*).
Because it is taught that through its various divisions, the conceit "I am" (asmimāna) is brought to cessation.
For these six elements are, at the time of entry into the womb, the fundamental basis for the designation of the substance of a sentient being.

How so? Because this physical mass called "body" is supported by the earth element, characterized by hardness, which is a preponderance of the activity of the other primary elements—a collection of bones, sinews, nails, teeth, hair, and so forth; and it is moistened and cohered by the water element, characterized by fluidity and moisture, consisting of phlegm, blood, and the like, which likewise coheres the other primary elements.

The moisture and foul odors are ripened by the fire element through its nature of heat; the accumulation of food-essence, bodily constituents, feces, urine, phlegm, and bile is circulated by the wind element through its nature of propulsion;
and the activities of entering and exiting—such as the intake and discharge of food and drink—are produced by the space element through the openings of the mouth, nose, ears, and so forth.

By means of the consciousness-element (*vijñānadhātu*), characterized by the apprehension of objects, there arises and is produced the movement of the major and minor limbs presided over by the activity of the wind-element (*vāyudhātu*); this is metaphorically designated as the "substantial entity of a sentient being" (*maulaṃ sattvadravyam*).

Indeed, in this context, the sense-faculties such as the eye are included under the term "elements" (*bhūta*), while the mental factors (*caitasika*) are included under the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); thus, the elements and the mind are mentioned because of their predominance.
For what purpose, then, are only these six elements taught?
Because through their differentiation, "the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna) ceases.
How so? Through the analysis of the six elements, the view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi) is eliminated.
Through the elimination of that [view], there is the uprooting of the conceit "I am."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because it is nourished by the view of a self-identity" (*satkāyadṛṣṭipuṣṭatvāt*), it is indeed only the afflicted consciousness (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*) [that is meant].
The consciousness element (vijñānadhātu) is intended [here]. Why?
Because it is the basis for what is to be seen at birth;
since these six elements constitute the support for birth, therefore [the consciousness element is intended].
"Only the afflicted consciousness"—this is what should be understood here.
But what is this space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) that is different from space (*ākāśa*) itself? To this it is said:
The element of space is distinct from [mere] space, because it is included within the sphere of visible form.
For space (*ākāśa*) is comprised within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and is eternal;

however, the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) is visible, comprised within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), and consists of the specific colors of light and darkness, appearing as a distinct form manifested through apertures such as windows. Furthermore, that...
Space is indeed the cause proximate to the element of space;
this [space] is the cause of the primary elements, those [elements] are the cause of derived matter, and that [derived matter] is the cause of the mind. (Abhidh-d 15)
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Earth rests upon water; water rests upon wind;
wind rests upon space."
"But space, because of its permanence, is self-established.
If indeed space is self-established, why then was it said: "Space is perceived when there is light"? We reply:
This is not a fault,
because the locus is made known by means of that which is contained within it.
Indeed, for every conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*) that acquires form and activity, space (*gagana*) is the locus.
Alternatively, the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is what is expressed here by the word "space.
For that Brahmin questioner possesses the perception of space within that very space-element; it is for this reason it was said: "When there is light, it is discerned.
And yet, space itself is not discerned when there is light.
Because it is non-demonstrable,
this space-element is the nearest support for the primary elements,
whereas those [elements] are the support for the derived matter born from them.
That too belongs to consciousness;
consciousness [belongs] to the mental factors (*caitasika*) and the dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*).
Therefore, space is the foundation of the three worlds.
In the absence of that [space], the three worlds would be without foundation and without support, and thus could not be perceived.
Therefore, it is established that space, and not Nārāyaṇa, is the cause of the origin and dissolution of the world. This point is concluded.
Now it must be stated:
what is the sequence of the six internal elements (*dhātu*)? We reply:
that which functions through direct perception (*pratyakṣavṛtti*), and that which apprehends its object even before reaching it.
Even further than that, there is an object which is more distant and more subtle than the other.
Indeed, the five [faculties] beginning with the eye were previously stated to function through direct contact (*pratyakṣavṛtti*).
Among those, two were previously stated to grasp their objects without reaching them (*aprāptagrāhin*).
Of those two as well, if—
The meaning of "faster" has been explained previously.
However, regarding those [cognitions] that grasp what is reached, that which is more acute than the other is what was explained previously as being "faster."
In the commentary *Vimāṣāprabhā* on the *Abhidharmadīpa*, this is the second quarter of the first chapter.
The third quarter of the first chapter.
This must now be discussed.
Regarding these eighteen elements (dhātu), how many are with demonstration (sanidarśana) and how many are without demonstration (anidarśana)?
How many are with resistance (sapratigha) and how many are without resistance (apratigha)?
How many are determinate and how many are indeterminate?
It is for this reason that the following is set forth.
The first object is "with demonstration" (*sanidarśana*): the object of the first, the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), which is called the form-element (*rūpadhātu*),
is "with demonstration," because it is indicated together with a demonstration.
Or, it is "with demonstration" (sanidarśana) because a demonstration related to it exists.
The ten material elements are characterized by resistance.
Excluding the seven mental elements and the dharma-element, the other ten material elements are "the ten with resistance.
Resistance (*pratigha*) means obstruction (*pratighāta*).
And that [resistance] is threefold:
resistance as obstruction (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*), resistance regarding the object (*viṣaya-pratighāta*), and resistance regarding the focal point (*ālambana-pratighāta*).
Among these, resistance as obstruction is the prevention of another's arising in one's own location.
That [resistance], however, belongs only to those phenomena that are material, possess configuration, consist of atoms, and are designated by direction and location—

just as a hand is struck by a hand, or a stone by a stone. Furthermore, there is resistance regarding objects (*viṣayapratighāta*), which is the obstruction of the sense faculties, such as the eye, toward their respective objects, such as visible form.

That which has a function characterized by conjunction (*sannipātalakṣaṇā*) and designated as activity (*kāritra*) is obstructed with respect to that [object], because it does not function toward anything other than that.
Furthermore, objective obstruction (*ālambanapratighāta*) is the obstruction of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) regarding their own respective objects.
What, then, is the distinction between the object-field (*viṣaya*) and the focal point (*ālambana*)?
That in which a [cognition] exercises its activity is its object-field;
that which is grasped by the mind and mental factors is the focal point.
In this context, the ten [bases] possess resistance (*sapratighatva*) by way of resistance as obstruction (*āvaraṇapratighāta*), because they obstruct one another.

Is it the case that "those dharmas which possess resistance by way of resistance to objects (*viṣayapratighāta*) also possess it by way of resistance as obstruction"? This is a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*).
The first category consists of the seven consciousness-elements and that portion of the dharma-element which is associated [with them].
The second consists of the five objects.
The third consists of the five sense-faculties.
The fourth [category] is a portion of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) excluding the associated factors (saṃprayuktaka).

Regarding the statement, "Those which are with resistance (sapratigha) by way of resistance toward an object (viṣayapratighāta) are also [with resistance] by way of resistance toward an objective support (ālambanapratighāta)," this is the "converse" (paścātpādaka): first, those which are with resistance by way of resistance toward an objective support would necessarily also be with resistance by way of resistance toward an object.
The five sense-faculties are characterized by resistance with respect to their objects, not by resistance with respect to their focal objects; for in that regard,
it is possible for others to create an obstruction to the mind as it seeks to arise.
"That which possesses resistance (sapratigha) is to be known as such; by the opposite, it is held to be non-resistant (apratigha).
Thus says the Venerable Kumāralāta.
Those with resistance have been explained.
The wholesome and so forth are designated [by their respective names];
elsewhere, with the exception of form and sound, those very same [factors] are considered indeterminate.
These same ten are neutral, excluding the elements of visible form and sound;
for those two are of three types: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
The remaining seven mental elements (cittadhātu) and the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) are each of three kinds.
The associated [condition] is of three kinds, the dissociated is [of one kind], and the unconditioned is [of one kind].
According to the treatise, some are of three kinds and some are of one kind; this should be understood according to what is possible.
What, then, is the meaning of "wholesome" (*kuśala*)?
The meaning of "wholesome" is the meaning of "trained," like one who is skilled (*pravīṇa*).
It should be understood as being illustrative with respect to the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*).
In the same way, the unwholesome is also [unexplained]; however, the intention is that the indeterminate is called "indeterminate" because it is not explained in terms of either side.
How many are associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and how many, up to, are dissociated from it? This is now undertaken:
here, all [of them]...
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all eighteen [elements] are present;
in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are fourteen,
excluding the elements of taste (*rasa*) and odor (*gandha*) along with their corresponding consciousnesses.
Excluding the elements of odor, taste, and their respective consciousness-elements, in the formless realm there are the last three.
The first and the last are traditionally taught [as the two extremes].
There is also an addition stating that "the ends" [are included].

In this way, the final [elements]—the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*)—exist likewise in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
How many are with outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)?
The last three mentioned immediately above are both with and without outflows; among them, those that are with outflows are comprised within the truths of suffering and its origin.
The untainted [phenomena], however, are comprised within the truth of the path and the unconditioned.
The remaining [elements], however, are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Fifteen elements are with outflows because they are associated with the outflows, are intermingled with them, and serve as their constituent parts.

The author of the Kośa, however, says: "They are *sāsrava* because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhere (*anuśayana*) to them. This is incorrect; it is not so, because he has failed to fully understand the etymological meaning of *anuśaya*.
First, there is a lack of thorough understanding of the etymological definitions.
They are "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) because the latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere to them;
they are not merely "with outflows" (sāsrava), nor are they as far as the "floods" (ogha).
For the outflows (*āsrava*) are so called because they flow from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, causing the continuum of consciousness to flow and flowing themselves;
the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), however, lie dormant (*anuśerate*);
the afflictions (*kleśa*) defile (*kliśnanti*).
The knots tie together;
the fetters bind;
the floods carry away.
Thus, by way of their own respective functions, these etymological designations apply to these categories; this method of explanation is the superior one.

Furthermore, if the meaning of *anuśaya* were "nourishment," then since an increase in nourishment is observed in false views and the like when they take the Path or Nirvāṇa as their objects, it would follow that even Nirvāṇa and the Path possess outflows (*sāsrava*), just like form and the other aggregates. This point has been settled.
"How many are with vitarka? How many are with vicāra? and so forth.
"The first five possess objects; three [of those] are with upacara; [all] three are of three kinds."
Among the elements that possess objects, those which are the first five are with vitarka and with vicāra;
"the last three are of three kinds," meaning those which are the final three are of three types.
They are with applied thought and sustained thought; those with only sustained thought and no applied thought;
and those with neither sustained thought nor applied thought.
In the desire realm and in the first dhyāna, applied thought (vitarka) does not enter into these three modes;
it is indeed without applied thought and consists of sustained thought (vicāra) alone.

Here it is asked: If the five bodies of consciousness (pañcavijñānakāya) possess both applied thought (savitarka) and sustained thought (savicāra), how then are they said to be non-conceptual (avikalpa)? We reply: They have their own objects as their quality; those whose quality is their own object are "quality-objects" (guṇasvārtha). For these—
Because they are free from recollection and lack conceptual determination,
they are called "non-conceptual.
For these two are the primary types of conceptualization, having as their objects the phenomena belonging to the three times.

For yogins, mindfulness (*smṛti*)—which consists in the examination of actions performed and left undone—is primary for the protection of the mind. However, that which has the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), known as discernment (*pravicaya*, *vibhajana*), exercises primacy regarding the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, as well as the relationship between causes and effects, and so forth. In this context, however, mindfulness belongs to the mental level (*manobhūmi*); the former is mindfulness, while the second is the discerning wisdom (*dhī*). *Abhidharmadīpa 20*
The term "belonging to the mental level" (*manobhaumī*) continues [to apply here].
The activity of the five groups of consciousness is like a man who is congenitally deaf looking at forms;
furthermore, in that regard, there is mindfulness—both concentrated and unconcentrated—which is the conceptualization of recollection (*anusmṛtivikalpa*).
Because they are equal in their verbalization of the object;
however, wisdom that is not in meditative equipoise is the conceptualization of investigative discernment, since wisdom in equipoise lacks the discernment of specific modes.
And because it functions solely as a mere secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇa) previously determined.
Now, among these six groups of consciousness, which consciousness is conceptualized by how many [factors]?
This is being clarified:
in the realm of desire, the fivefold consciousness is conceptualized by one [factor].
By means of the conceptualization of intrinsic nature;
other than that, the mental consciousness in the realm of desire is conceptual by means of all three.
And in the first dhyāna, there is also that which is not concentrated.
For in the first dhyāna, that mental consciousness which is not concentrated consists of only three [mental activities];
however, that which is concentrated and undistracted consists of only two, having excluded the conceptualization of investigation (*abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa*).
By one [element], there is that which has the eye, ear, and body as its basis.
Furthermore, the consciousness that has the eye, ear, and body as its basis in the first dhyāna exists by means of that one [element] alone;
above that, it is engaged with two.
In the second and subsequent dhyānas, it is distracted by two [factors];
it is concentrated by one alone.
By means of the conceptualization of recollection alone;
thus it continues up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
This must now be explained:
in what case does which of the six types of consciousness become discriminative regarding the wholesome and so forth? This thicket of the Abhidharma is now set forth.
For one whose seeds of the wholesome have been severed,
there is no wholesome consciousness involving conceptualization, except for that which pertains to rebirth-linking.
In this case, for one whose roots of merit have been severed, there exists no wholesome visual consciousness produced by the power of the five material sense-faculties as its basis,
except through the reconnection of those roots of merit;
[this applies to] the fool who is free from passion for the desires and is not subject to falling away.
In both ways, there is no unwholesome [state] for one who is of the nature of non-retrogression; neither the seeing-consciousness nor the mental-consciousness [is unwholesome].
Furthermore, for a Noble One, the defiled [consciousness] is not supreme.
Furthermore, for a noble one, there exists no afflicted, conceptual consciousness that takes a higher level as its object.
Furthermore,
there is no non-afflicted neutral [state] that conceptualizes a higher level,
nor is there any unobscured-neutral state that conceptualizes a higher level.
Furthermore, that which is afflicted and conceptual does not have a lower stage as its object.
Furthermore, there is no afflicted consciousness that takes a lower stage as its object and is conceptual.
Here, for the noble one, there are three types; here, the two—the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—are both the visual consciousness and the conceptual mental consciousness.
For one who possesses passion and is virtuous—
that is, for an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who has not yet abandoned passion but whose roots of merit are not severed— there are three types [of minds] and two [types of acquisition].
However, in the second and subsequent [moments], there is neither the virtuous nor the afflicted that can be seen.
"Consciousness exists."
This must now be explained:

if there is no eternal self and no eternal quality belonging to it, and if the formative forces (saṃskāra) that serve as the cause of memory do not exist, and if consciousnesses perish at every moment and have not established a mutual convention with one another, how is an object previously experienced remembered?
That is now explained:
although this argument has already been answered, nevertheless, this [explanation] is undertaken in accordance with the treatise.

Due to application, the proximity of its constituent factors, and the homogeneity of the mental continuum, memory arises in the mind with respect to an object previously experienced by consciousness. (Abhidharmadīpa 27)

Memory arises with respect to objects such as forms previously experienced by a prior consciousness, due to the presence of auxiliary causes— namely, the proficiency of the knowledge resulting from past vows, its continuity, its constant operation, and its lack of dependence on other factors— and which are favorable to the mental continuum.
If it is argued that its production occurs through the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), we say no.

The conjunction of the self and the mind is impossible because mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) are as unestablished as a hare's horn; for these impressions cannot logically belong to this eternal self.

Furthermore, the conjunction with impressions is untenable both because [the self] would have to pervade the entire body and because of the fault inherent in the admission that it exists only in a specific location.

Therefore, it is rightly said that memory arises from the application [of the sense organs], the proximity of the factors [of recollection], and so forth, having as its object the ultimate conventional reality (*paramārtha-saṃvṛtti*).
Due to the opposite of this—namely, dullness and being overwhelmed by the disease of the afflictions—forgetfulness arises regarding things previously known. (Abhidharmadīpa 28)
This is now investigated:
by which [type of consciousness] is that which was experienced by the fivefold consciousness—such as that to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśanaheya)—remembered?
This is now set forth.

That which has been seen by a mind of two, three, four, or five types is remembered by those same minds and by others; however, in the destruction of the vision of obstacles, one does not remember what was seen by another.

Indeed, all [mental states] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and so forth, being of five types, remember what has been experienced in succession. However, there is this restriction here: "One does not [remember] another's [object] at the time of the destruction of the vision of the obstructions. For that which is experienced by what is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path is not remembered by another, because memory is restricted to its specific object.
However, the remaining three types are not prohibited because they have a mixed object of focus.
The meaning is that whatever is experienced by one of the five consciousnesses is also remembered by another,
namely, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Indeed, by that [same principle], it is also [established] for others.
Furthermore, that which has been experienced by the mental consciousness is also remembered by all six [consciousnesses].
Now, regarding the twelve types of consciousness: what is their meaning, by whom are they experienced, and by how many are they remembered?
There are twelve consciousnesses:
the four belonging to the desire realm, beginning with the wholesome (*kuśala*).
There are three belonging to the form realm (rūpāvacara), excluding the unwholesome;
likewise, there are these same three belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara),
as well as those of the learner (śaikṣa) and the one beyond learning (aśaikṣa).
Mindfulness associated with that [consciousness] is likewise of twelve kinds.

In that regard, what was experienced by what? That which was experienced by any of the twelve is remembered by all twelve. That which was experienced by wholesome [states] of the desire realm is remembered by the twelve kinds [of mindfulness].

In the same way, one remembers what was experienced through unwholesome [action] and through that which is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) by means of eight kinds [of mindfulness]. In the case of the desire realm (kāmāvacara), it is by means of all [eight kinds].

By means of a mind belonging to the form or formless realms— excluding the obscured-unspecified and the unobscured-unspecified— and by means of the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), one likewise [remembers] by means of an unobscured-unspecified mind. One remembers everything experienced by a wholesome mind of the form realm through all [of these aforementioned minds].

That which is experienced as obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) belonging to the desire realm is experienced by ten [minds], excluding the obscured-unspecified and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) of the desire realm.

That which is experienced as unobscured-unspecified belonging to that same realm is experienced by ten [minds], excluding the obscured-unspecified and the unobscured-unspecified of the formless realm.
That which is experienced as wholesome (*kuśala*) belonging to the formless realm is experienced by ten [minds], excluding the obscured-unspecified and the unobscured-unspecified of the desire realm.
That which has been experienced by a defiled-neutral [mind] is [retained] by nine [minds], excluding the defiled-neutral and the non-defiled-neutral minds of the desire realm,
as well as the non-defiled-neutral mind of the form realm;
thus it is also [retained] by the non-defiled-neutral [mind].

That which is experienced by a learner (*śaikṣa*) is [perceived] by eleven [minds], except for the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind of the desire realm; likewise for that experienced by one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This summary meaning is demonstrated by the following verses:
"The mind experienced here as twofold-unspecified is twelvefold."
Because it is free from both form and the formless, that [knowledge] is remembered as being attained by means of exactly eight [knowledges].

In the desire realm, that which has been experienced by the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is remembered by eight [minds], excluding the two obscured minds belonging to the form and formless realms. Likewise, that which has been experienced by the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) is remembered by the unobscured-unspecified mind.

But that which is remembered by means of the obscured-unwholesome and the wholesome states pertaining to the form and formless realms—respectively, excluding the two unwholesome states pertaining to the desire realm—is remembered by ten [mental factors]. (Abhidharmadīpa 32)
Excluding the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) of the desire realm (kāmāvacara),

that which is seen by the unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) in the form realm (rūpa) is remembered again by other [minds], excluding the two types of unspecified [minds] in the formless realm (ārūpya).

Indeed, that which has been experienced in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) by the unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) mind is remembered by ten [minds], excluding the unspecified minds of the formless realm (ārūpya).
The knowledge of the neutral states of the formless realm is known by nine [minds];
that [knowledge] excludes the two neutral states belonging to the desire realm and likewise the non-obscured-neutral state belonging to the form realm.
This introductory section is concluded;
let the subject at hand be discussed.

Regarding these eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many have an object (*sālambana*), how many are without an object (*anālambana*), how many are appropriated (*upātta*), how many are unappropriated (*anupātta*), and how many are accumulated (*saṃcita*)?
This is now undertaken: "The seven called mind (*citta*) have objects, as does that which is called mental factors (*dharma*) when it is associated (*saṃprayuktaka*)."
The phrase "having an object" (sālambanā) continues [to apply here].
However, the remaining ones are without an object (anālambana), because they do not grasp an objective domain.
Those seven mind-elements (cittadhātu) that were mentioned together with half of the dharma-element, being formless, are not appropriated along with sound; other than these,
the nine [elements] are of two kinds.
Those which ascend the continuum— namely, the present eyes and so forth, as well as the forms and so forth that are inseparable from them— are appropriated; the rest, however, are non-appropriated,
because they lack sentience and because they are not included within the personal existence (*anātmabhāva*).
It is established that those remaining external things, which exist apart from the continuum of the body-faculty, are non-appropriated.
How many are the primary elements (bhūta) and how many are the derivative elements (bhautika)?
Regarding this, it is said:
"The tangible is of two kinds."

In this context, there are the four primary elements and the sevenfold derivative matter beginning with heaviness; these nine derivative matters, together with their corresponding factors, constitute "those nine derivative matters.
Together with the portion of the dharma-element known as non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), they constitute "those nine derivative matters."
Thus, how many are material? Ten are material because they possess parts;
the remaining ones, such as the visual consciousness element and so forth, are immaterial.
Those same ten, when accumulated, [constitute a "great"]. // Abhidh-d_36 //
The meaning is "aggregates of atoms.
Excluding those same eight—the eye-consciousness element and so forth—the remaining ten are accumulated (*saṃcita*).
How many are the cutters? How many are the things to be cut? How many are the burners? How many are the things to be burned?
How many are the weighers? How many are the things to be weighed?
Regarding this, it is said here:
Form, odor, taste, and tangibility are considered to consist of that which cuts and that which is cut;
they are also the burners and the weighed, or rather, they are the burned and the weighed. (Abhidh-d 37)
The word "or" (*vā*) signifies an alternative view:
for some, it is the fire element alone that is burned, and weight alone that is weighed.
How many are born of maturation (*vipākaja*)? How many are accumulative (*aupacayika*)?
The five consisting of the material sense-faculties have the nature of both maturation and accumulation.
Because their birth is dependent upon the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*), the five [faculties] such as the eye do not exist as outflowing (*naiṣyandika*).

Because for one who has died, there is no outflow (niṣyanda) distinct from that which is born of maturation (vipākaja). In this context, "born of maturation" means produced from a cause of maturation;
the middle term is elided, as in the case of "ox-cart" (goratha).

The seven mind-elements and the dharma-element are formless and not accumulative; however, they do exist as outflows (*naiṣyandika*) and as results of maturation (*vipākaja*), because they arise through the power of homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*).
The remaining [elements] are of three kinds.
The four [objects] beginning with visible form in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) are of three types; those that coexist with the body-faculty (kāyendriya) are of three kinds.
The external [objects] are of two types.
Sound is of two types. (Abhidh-d 38)
The scriptural authority is that sound is not born of maturation;
the reasoning is also that it proceeds from volition.
Now this is said:

Is one who is endowed with the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) and acquires such an endowment also endowed with the eye-consciousness-element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu)? Or is one who is endowed with the eye-consciousness-element also endowed with the eye-element? He replied:
There is no single certainty here; for the eye and its perception may be acquired either separately or together.
One first acquires the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu), but not the eye-consciousness-element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu).
One who gradually acquires the eye-faculty in the desire realm,
or one who dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the second or higher meditative absorptions,
may possess the eye-consciousness element but not the eye-element.
One born in the second or higher dhyānas who does not bring eye-consciousness into manifestation;
one who, having passed away from there, is being reborn in a lower realm;
and one who, having passed away from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), is being reborn both in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and in the Brahma-world.
Excluding these two modes:
is one who is endowed with the eye-element also endowed with the eye-consciousness-element? There are four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
The first [case] refers to one born in the second or higher dhyānas who is not bringing eye-consciousness into manifestation.
The second refers to one in the desire realm who has neither obtained nor lost the eye-faculty.
The third refers to one in the desire realm who has obtained and not lost the eye-faculty, as well as one born in the first dhyāna or born in the second or higher dhyānas, while actually seeing.
The fourth [alternative] is: setting aside these aspects.
This has been explained. Now let us return to the subject at hand.
How many are internal and how many are external? It should be known that twelve are internal.

The five sense-faculties and the seven mental elements constitute the self, because they are the basis for the notion of "I. As it is said: "By means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains heaven."
The external [objects] consist of the six sense-fields.
How many are to be abandoned by seeing, how many are to be abandoned by cultivation, and how many are not to be abandoned?
This is now undertaken:
the last three are of three kinds.
The mind element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*) are of three types:
those that accompany the eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and their acquisitions (*prāpti*) are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*);
the remainder are to be exhausted through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Those which are with outflows are [to be abandoned],
whereas those which are without outflows are not to be abandoned because they are faultless.
There is no form to be abandoned by seeing, nor is there any that is non-defiled or non-conceptual.
If it is argued that this refers to the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), we say no; for that state is unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*),
since even those who have severed their roots of virtue and those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*) still possess it.

Furthermore, the bodily and vocal actions belonging to the miserable realms (*āpāyika*), which have matter (*rūpa*) as their intrinsic nature, are also merely abandoned—not yet eliminated—because they are in opposition to the Noble Path. Therefore, both [types of action] are not to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), because there is no misconception regarding the Truths, and because it would entail the consequence that one would still be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) during the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*). Moreover, the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) are non-conceptual; they too are not to be abandoned by seeing.

How many are "homogeneous" (sabhāga) and how many are "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga)? Only that which is called the *dharmadhātu* is exclusively homogeneous; the remaining [elements] are known to be of both kinds.
Excluding the *dharmadhātu*, the other elements are of two types.
They are both homogeneous (sabhāga) and partially homogeneous (tatsabhāga).

What, then, is the meaning of "homogeneous" (sabhāga), and what is the meaning of "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga)? That which is homogeneous is so called because it participates in its own activity; that which is partially homogeneous is considered equal [to it] in that respect. (Abhidharmadīpa 41)
That which performs its own function is called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
That which is devoid of its own function is designated as "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) because it possesses only a resemblance to that [function].
In this context, the homogeneous is of three kinds.
It is to be designated according to the distinction of its own activity across the time-periods (*adhvan*);
likewise, its counterpart (*tatsabhāga*) is to be designated as being devoid of such activity.
The Kashmiris maintain that the fourth [type] consists of those factors whose nature is non-arising (*anutpattidharmaka*).
How many are views (*dṛṣṭi*) and how many are not views?
The eye and a ninefold portion of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are called views. First of all, the eye is recognized as "view" even in common worldly usage.
Within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as well, there is a portion whose nature is "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), consisting of eight types characterized by afflicted and non-afflicted wisdom (*prajñā*).
The remainder, however, is not view.
Wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses is not view, because it lacks investigative judgment (*anitīraṇa*).
For views are analytical because they depend upon investigation;
however, that [non-conceptual wisdom] is non-conceptual and has an insentient nature.
This which has been stated is far too little.
It should be added that [the view] associated with the abandonment of the level of mental consciousness and so forth is not [right] view.
But how do these wisdoms see? This is now being revealed:
Just as the eye perceives the visible object during nights with clouds or without clouds, and during days with clouds or without clouds.
In the same way, those who possess both afflicted and non-afflicted vision, as well as those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), perceive it accordingly.
Just as forms are seen during a cloudy night when the moon and the circle of stars are mostly veiled by a film of darkness, so do the five afflicted views perceive the knowable.
But just as forms are seen during a three-watch night that is free from dust and veiled by the silken rays of the moon,
so does the mundane right view perceive.
Just as forms are seen on a day when the sun’s rays are shrouded by a mass of clouds and do not shine forth, so does the vision of one in training (śaikṣa) see.

But just as on a day when the accumulation of darkness has been dispelled by the rays of the sun, which have become tawny from being sprinkled with the liquid essence of refined gold, the eye of a sighted person like Devadatta perceives form;
in that same way, the wisdom-eye (prajñācakṣus) of the Buddhas and Arhats—being free from the cataracts of the film of ignorance, afflictions, and secondary afflictions—beholds the knowable.
In the *Abhidharmadīpa*, in the commentary known as the *Vibhāṣāprabhā*, this is the third quarter of the first chapter.
The fourth section of the first chapter says:
As it was stated— that the eye is vision and that wisdom (*prajñā*) of eight kinds is "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Now, does consciousness see, or does it not see?
If it sees, then the ten dharmas would have the nature of vision (*dṛṣṭi*).
If, on the other hand, it does not see, then the position of the Dārṣṭāntikas is abandoned.
The gods will grasp this if they consider it something that ought to be grasped.
As for what was said—that ten factors would result in having the nature of vision—we shall later provide a refutation of the notion that consciousness possesses primary vision.
However, this must be stated:
Among the eye, visual consciousness, wisdom, and their causal complex, which one sees?
If you ask why there is this doubt,
it is because faults are observed in every case.
If the eye sees, up to the body touching, then it follows that there would be the simultaneous enjoyment of all objects.
Alternatively, if visual consciousness sees, then who is it that cognizes?
And why does it not see even what is obstructed?
Is it because of its non-obstructive nature?
If you say that wisdom (*prajñā*) sees, then since wisdom also exists in auditory consciousness and so forth, it would follow that those too possess the capacity for seeing.

If you say that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of the eye and other factors sees, then that complex itself does not exist as something distinct from its constituent parts, because it lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and independent activity (*kriyā*).

Furthermore, each individual component of the causal complex, such as the eye and so forth, lacks the power and activity of seeing— just like a hundred blind men— and is therefore non-existent [as a producer].
This is because it would follow that every causal complex could produce every effect,
as there would be no distinction between them.
If it is argued that consciousness arises as mere activity depending on the totality of causes and conditions, we say no;
for if there were an agent of production, independence with respect to the act of production would be untenable, just as in the case of [the agent of] destruction and so forth.
Because causes and conditions are dependent, established in their own nature, and devoid of self, they lack the capacity to effect a state of selflessness.
Furthermore, in the absence of an object of cognition, consciousness cannot arise, just as there can be no burning without something to be burned.
Furthermore, in the absence of dependence on the activity of consciousness, that [consciousness] would also be absent, like a painting on a wall.

If birth and destruction were the properties (*dharma*) of the substratum (*dharmin*), there would be the occurrence of one of two contradictions, or the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that destruction has a cause of its own kind (*sajāti*).
If it is argued that the persistence of a certain genus (*jāti*) is the seed [of that destruction], we say no.

Because it is impossible for [the mind] to be a seed when wholesome, unwholesome, and other types of minds have ceased, and because this involves abandoning the position of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) while accepting the fault of the Sāṃkhya doctrine;
for according to them as well, everything arises from a single, independent seed called *pradhāna*.
If it is argued that [the seed] depends on other causes for its capacity or incapacity, we say no;

for that would entail the fault of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*). Furthermore, if one accepts that the seed possesses all the constituent parts of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it would follow that there is a diversity of the nature of the effect and so forth.
Therefore, a faultless position must be stated;
that is now undertaken:
"The eye sees; consciousness cognizes its own object-domain."
Because one involves observation and the other perception, there is a very great distinction between the two.
For the substance of the eye has the nature of a seer;
when its power is awakened through the acquisition of the totality of causes and conditions, there arises merely the activity of seeing form.

Furthermore, the difference between the substance and the activity should be understood from their respective natures as that which is established and that which is being accomplished, and from their designations as independent and dependent.
In that regard, the eye—possessing form and action—is presided over by consciousness and initiates the activity of seeing;
it is not devoid of consciousness.
Just as visual consciousness cognizes through an activity presided over by observation, [so too does the eye].

Not only that, but by the power of mutual assistance through a continuous succession, these two—when supported by other conditions such as a lamp and so forth—attain their functional activity simultaneously upon a single object.

However, he who, disregarding this, imagines as follows: "The effect, which is consciousness, does not coexist at the same time with its causes, namely the eye and the visible form, which have arisen previously."
Thus, because there would be no direct experience of objects for him, it follows that inference and scripture would be impossible.
Furthermore, if there were no cognition of experience, it follows that mental consciousness and memory would not arise, as their objective domain would be absent;
this is also because there would be no recollection of specific objects.

Therefore, consciousness—having obtained its stability through a fixed basis and object, and having its activity produced by the convergence of a collection of auxiliary causes—directly perceives the object.
At that very same time, the eye observes and the lamp illuminates.

These factors—the consciousness, the eye, the form, and so forth—whose potencies have been awakened by their own causal complex, simultaneously assume their respective excellent functions, designated as the representation of the object, observation, and illumination.
Thus, this is the logical principle:
therefore, even though other conditions are present, because the eye is predominant in the act of seeing, it alone is said to "see directly."

Or, for example, just as Devadatta, when cooking is underway despite the presence of the pot, water, fire, rice, and so forth, is said to "cook" because he has acquired the capacity for his own actions— placing [the pot] on the stove, pouring in the water, putting in the rice, stirring with the ladle, rinsing, and draining— and because Devadatta has attained sovereignty over others through the coordination of the instruments;
yet, when it concerns the rice grains...
When moisture or cooking is intended, the designation occurs based on the predominance of water or fire, such that one says "water moistens" or "fire cooks.
Therefore, when the causal complex is present and vision is occurring, it is said that "the eye sees" due to its predominance.
If it is asked, "In what sense is there predominance? [the answer follows].
Because there is a superiority of vision when there is a superiority of that [organ].

For, while the visual consciousness of the first dhyāna is equal [to those of the higher stages], a superiority of vision is observed in the second dhyāna and so forth due to the superiority of the eye.
Therefore, it is correct to say: "The eye sees; the organ of sight sees; but with respect to the mind, the activity of wisdom is metaphorically designated as 'seeing with the mind'."
In this regard, what was stated by the author of the *Kośa*: "What is this? Is space being chewed?
For when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, the metaphorical designation 'it is seen' occurs.
In that case, who is it that sees?"
Therefore, in this matter, the Venerable One is denying the activity of the constituent parts of the causal complex;
by marking himself with the stigma of confusion regarding the Abhidharma, he demonstrates that he is facing a fall into the abyss of irrational emptiness.
Furthermore, does one see with even a single eye, or indeed with both?
There is no fixed rule here, because:
Is the effect of consciousness produced by one eye or by both?
Thus [is explained] the case of the consciousness that perceives two moons and so forth.
Do they grasp their objects by reaching them, or do they grasp them without reaching them? To this it is said:
"The mind, the eye, and the ear grasp their objects without reaching them; the other three [senses] are otherwise."
The meaning is that the faculties of the nose, tongue, and body grasp their objects through direct contact.
On this point, the follower of Kaṇāda observes:
the sense faculties do not apprehend what they have not reached;
for the eye sees by means of a ray that has gone forth.
The ear, however, being all-pervading, hears everything only after reaching it; with reference to that, this is said:
"Those [faculties] which grasp what is not reached are established because they perceive both the distant and the near."
For in the same amount of time that Devadatta sees the lines on the palm of his own hand, he likewise sees the crescent moon;
yet this is not the nature of those who possess motion.
For those who possess motion, such as Devadatta and others, travel a long distance in a long time and a near distance quickly. [This is] not so.
Because that is established by way of analogy with a lamp.
If it is argued that this is due to the power of a lamp or similar objects—
just as, for instance, in the same amount of time that a lamp manifests a form that is very near, it likewise manifests one that is very far away.
Regarding that, the rebuttal is:
"It is not equal, because it arises from that. (Abhidharmadīpa 46)
If the lamp were to move, this same fault would follow there as well;
furthermore, because specific degrees of heat are observed at the beginning, middle, and end of its radiance, its unity is not established.
Furthermore, since the production of material atoms occurs simultaneously by depending upon the light of all lamps together, this fault does not apply to that case.
If it is argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence [of seeing everything], it is not so, because we observe magnets and the like.
If the eye perceives without reaching its object, why does it not see Brahmā in the world of Brahmā?
To this, the following is said:
It is not so, because that [attraction] is established like a magnet;
for just as, although the power of attraction is equal even when not in contact, an eastern magnet does not attract iron situated to the north, so it is in this case.
In this regard, however, Vindhyavāsin maintains that the sense faculties are omnipresent.
To him, this is said:
"If it is argued that there is no fault because they are omnipresent, it is not so, because of the impossibility [of their functioning], as in the case of sesame oil. (Abhidharmadīpa 47)
For what sane person would say that oil exists pervasively within sesame seeds?
Likewise, what person of unclouded mind would imagine that the sense organs exist outside their respective bases, such as the mouth, eyes, and ears?
This must be explained.

Regarding the body in which one dwells while seeing forms with the eye: are that body, the eye, the forms, and the visual consciousness all of the same level, or can they also belong to different levels?
There is no fixed rule for all of them.
In that regard, first, for one born in the desire realm who sees their own forms with their own eye, everything belongs to their own level.
For that same person, when seeing their own forms with the eye of dhyāna, the body and the forms belong to their own level, while the two [the eye and the consciousness] come from the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, those forms also belong to that [first dhyāna] level.
For one observing with the eye of the second dhyāna, the body and visible forms belong to its own level,
the eye belongs to the second dhyāna, and the consciousness belongs to the first.
For one seeing the levels of the first dhyāna, consciousness and form belong to the first dhyāna;
the body belongs to the desire realm (kāmāvacara);
and the eye belongs to the second dhyāna.

For one seeing forms belonging to the level of the second dhyāna with eyes belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, the eye and the form belong to the level of the second dhyāna, the body belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), and the consciousness [arises] from the first dhyāna.
In the same way, it should be understood for one seeing forms belonging to that level or to lower levels with eyes belonging to the level of the third or fourth dhyāna.
For one born in the first dhyāna who sees forms of his own level with his own eyes, everything belongs to his own level.
For one seeing forms belonging to a lower level, the triad [of body, consciousness, and contact] belongs to its own level, while the forms belong to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).

For one seeing forms of its own level with the eye of the second dhyāna, the triad belongs to its own level; for one seeing forms of the realm of desire with that same eye, the body and consciousness belong to their own level [the first dhyāna], while the eye belongs to the second dhyāna.

Regarding forms belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*): for one seeing forms of the second dhyāna stage with an eye of the second dhyāna stage, the eye and the forms belong to that stage, while the rest belong to one's own stage. This should be applied accordingly to the eyes of the third dhyāna and so forth.

For one born in the second dhyāna or higher, who sees forms belonging to their own or another level with the eyes of their own or another level, it should be understood according to the possibilities as follows.
This [sequence] is fixed:
for above the eye there is neither body nor form, nor is there mind born of the sense-faculties;
however, the object of the eye and the eye itself are entirely present for the consciousness and for the body.
The body, the eye, and visible forms belong to five levels; visual consciousness belongs to two levels—those with vitarka and vicāra.
In this regard, the eye belongs to the same level as the body or to a higher level, but never to a lower level.
Visible form becomes the object of that eye belonging to a certain level or to a lower level, but never to a higher level.
In this way, visual consciousness does not manifest in relation to a lower eye;
however, for this visual consciousness, visible form becomes its object from all sides.
Likewise, both visible form and visual consciousness exist in relation to the body from all sides. Thus it is.
Above the ear there is neither body nor sound, nor one's own mind;
however, there is the resonance of consciousness, and those two [body and sound] exist for the body on all sides.
Furthermore, for the three beginning with the nose, all three cognitions of their own objects— namely, the body, odor, and so forth— are exclusively of their own level.
This is an exception to the general rule:
consciousness of the body is also [restricted] to the lower level;
the body and the tangible object belong only to its own level.
However, for some, body-consciousness belongs to a lower level,
as in the case of those born in the second dhyāna or above;
the mental faculty (manas), on the other hand, is indeterminate.
Because the body exists everywhere at the times of meditative attainment and rebirth,
and because it has as its object all phenomena that are liberated from the paths of the three periods of time.
But for what purpose is this composition of such a vast work undertaken when it serves only a minor purpose? The author of the *Kośa* replies: "For no fruit [of this work] is perceived here.
To him, this fruit is now shown.
In that regard, indeed,
the manifold forms of the yogi are demonstrated.
This is indeed the manifold nature of yogins: having taken up a body from one source, an eye from another, a form from another, and consciousness from another, they see.

Having manifested various bodies and traveled by means of the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) that moves with the speed of mind, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, perform the work of a Buddha for those to be trained (*vineya*) among other world-systems according to their wish.

Having seen forms and heard sounds with the divine eye and ear, they manifest many bodies belonging to the five realms of existence simultaneously as they desire, and perform the work of training beings within the various realms of the many destinies.
"They perform [these actions].
This incidental discussion is concluded.
This must now be explained:
what is the specific distinction between the aggregates (*skandha*) and the aggregates of appropriation (*upādānaskandha*)? To this it is said:
the aggregates are subsumed under three truths, because...
Those aggregates which are designated as "clinging" (upādāna), whether they be with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava),
should be known as exclusively "with outflows" because of their functioning as companions to those [outflows] and other such reasons.
The phrase "by means of causes" is to be supplied as an ellipsis in the sentence.
Therefore, the aggregates of appropriation (*upādānaskandha*) are comprised within the two truths;
however, since the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) does not possess the characteristics of an aggregate, it should be understood as being distinct from the characteristics of an aggregate.
Terms such as "time-period" (*adhvan*) and so forth are synonyms for the aggregates (*skandha*);
"conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta*) and "bases of discourse" (*kathāvastu*) and so forth are synonyms for the elements (*dharma*) and so forth,
which exist as entities (*vastu*).
Existence, entity, phenomenon, substance, sphere, and element—these and others such as these are [the names of the conditioned].
However, those which are designated as "with outflows" (sāsrava) are spoken of by the names of "suffering" (duḥkha) and so forth.
The world is designated by such names as "suffering," "existence," and "origination."
Now, why is it that although the eyes, ears, and noses exist as pairs, they constitute a single element (*dhātu*)?
This is now undertaken: "The status of being a single element arises from the unity of their own nature, their objects, and their functions."

Even though the eye and so forth exist as pairs, because these three [factors]— the organ, the object, and consciousness— are of a single nature, have a single sphere of activity, and perform a single function, their status as a single dominant influence (*ekādhipatya*) and their status as a single element (*ekadhātu*) are established despite their twofold occurrence.
Their arising as two is due to the power of the threefold karma.

But as for those who say, "The arising of the two [sexual organs] is for the sake of beauty," it follows that the arising of elephantiasis, goiters, and so forth would be for the sake of extreme beauty.
This must now be explained:

when the causal complex of the eye and so forth is present and visual consciousness arises, why is it called "eye-consciousness," "ear-consciousness," and so on? To this, the following response is given:
