Due to its unique excellence, its sovereignty, and its being internal,
cognition is distinguished by those [causes], even though there are many causes.
A distinction in consciousness is observed due to the distinction among the sense faculties, such as the eye;
and the sovereignty of the eye and the other faculties is observed through four reasons,
and they are considered internal because they are the specific causes.

Here he asks: Now, if all entities (*padārtha*) possess the nature of substance (*dravyasvabhāva*), why is it said that *nirvāṇa* alone is a substance in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), since it is the *dharmadhātu* itself that, through its connection with that [nirvāṇa], is designated as "possessing substance"?
And why, given that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), are only the last three elements (*dhātu*) said to be momentary?
Both of these points are now demonstrated.
Because it is eternal and wholesome, Nirvana is truly a substantial entity;
since it is a substance consisting of the core essence, the single dharma called Nirvana is considered to possess substantial reality.
The first stainless mind is designated as a "moment" (kṣaṇa) due to its rarity;
because of that wondrous moment, these final three are called "momentary" (kṣaṇika).
Furthermore, do these [faculties], such as the eye and so forth, grasp an object that is equal [in size] to themselves, or rather one that is smaller or larger?
This is now being explained:
The nose, the tongue, and the body—these three are taught to have a fixed correspondence between their objects and what they grasp;
for the two, namely the eye and the ear, there is no such fixed rule.

Furthermore, is the support (*āśraya*) of these [consciousnesses], such as visual consciousness and the rest, exclusively simultaneous, or is it also past? To this it is said: the support of the last one is past.
The support of the active mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is always past;
that of the five [sensory consciousnesses] is also simultaneous with them.
Because of the word "also" (*ca*) in the phrase "also together with those [five consciousnesses] and the past," regarding the five groups of consciousness,
a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) is thus undertaken:
Are those factors which are the supports of consciousness also their immediate antecedents (*samanantara*)?
The question involves four alternatives:
the eye and so forth are exclusively bases;
feeling and so forth are exclusively immediate antecedents.
Both [refers to] consciousness that has ceased immediately prior;
neither [refers to] anything other than these aforementioned modes.
Now, this very essence of the Abhidharma, which has transcended the range of the memory of the author of the *Kośa*, must be stated.
Furthermore, among these eighteen elements (*dhātu*), depending upon which basis (*niśraya*) is the cessation of which element effected by the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*)?
Indeed, it is by depending upon either the "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*) stage or the four bases (*niśraya*).
The visual element (cakṣurdhātu) is ceased by means of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga).
Indeed, the untainted path exists in nine stages,
whereas the eye-element belongs to five stages.
In that regard, for a noble one liberated by wisdom who has not attained dhyāna, the eye-element ceases based upon the threshold concentration (anāgamya).

Because that which consists of the knowledge of cessation and the path is the antidote to the three realms, for one who has attained the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), it further relies upon four supports, since the intermediate absorption is included by means of the first [support].
However, the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*) ceases by relying on the *anāgamya* [concentration],
because for one who has not attained the dhyānas, it ceases therein;
the mind-element (*manodhātu*) [ceases] either by relying on the *anāgamya* or on the seven supports.
The four dhyānas and the three formless attainments, because they belong to the triple world.

The same applies to the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) and the first dhyāna; it is said that "the one designated as eye-consciousness ceases," because [the practitioner] has entered into the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the desire realm or the first dhyāna.
One should explain [the elements] according to their application, due to the manifold nature of the dharmadhātu.

Indeed, some part of the *dharmadhātu* belongs exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), such as the [afflictions] beginning with hostility (*pratigha*). Some belongs to both the desire realm and the first dhyāna, such as the [mental factors] beginning with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). Some belongs to both the desire realm and the first and second dhyānas, such as joy (*prīti*).
Some exist in the desire realm and in the first two dhyānas, such as the faculty of pleasure;
some exist in all three realms, such as the life-faculty and others.
Therefore, it is said that they should be designated according to their respective application.
"In this same way, one should point out other elements as well, according to their respective application, by means of this very principle already stated."
Now this other point must be stated:
when an ordinary person thoroughly understands the eye-element as belonging to the realm of form, from which element does he then attain detachment,
and how many latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to which realms does he abandon?
And which fetters does he abandon by exhausting them? That is now revealed:
the ordinary person, thoroughly understanding the eye-element as belonging to the realm of form...
One attains detachment from the entire realm consisting of form.
Therefore, from that element, he abandons thirty-one latent dispositions;
yet at that time, he does not eliminate even a single fetter.
For while there is a demarcation of realms for the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), there is none for the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
One attains detachment from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and abandons three latent dispositions—
namely, those called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)— which are included within the realm of form.
At that time, the noble one completely exhausts the fetters, not leaving anything remaining.
Which three latent dispositions (anuśaya) does the noble one abandon—namely those called attachment to existence, pride, and ignorance?
Since the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned by cultivation are not delimited by the realms, he abandons nothing of that [category] at that time.
But by thoroughly understanding the element of eye-consciousness, and that very [element],
one necessarily becomes detached from the Brahma-world.
But at that time, that ordinary person (pṛthagjana), while fully understanding the odor-element and what is called the taste-element, does not exhaust any fetter (saṃyojana).
One attains detachment from the realm of desire, for one certainly abandons even the latent proclivities;
at that time, one casts off the thirty-six fetters along with the three bonds.

One abandons the thirty-six proclivities belonging to the desire realm, as well as the three fetters: the fetter of aversion, and the fetters of envy and avarice. An ordinary person, however, does not fully understand the elements of odor and taste.

The noble one, however, effects detachment from the realm of desire; he also fully understands the four latent tendencies known as aversion, sensual lust, pride, and ignorance, which are to be abandoned by cultivation.
And it also consumes the triad.
It is called the fetter of repugnance, envy, and avarice.
Fully understanding the mind-element, one becomes detached from the formless realms;
the term "noble one" continues to apply here, and he abandons three underlying tendencies.
Likewise, it completely exhausts the triad known as passion, pride, and ignorance.
This very [point].
Indeed, by fully understanding that very joy, he abandons it;
he attains detachment from the Ābhāsvara realm, yet he does not destroy the outflows (āsravas).
Because that [pleasure] does not exist above it,
the yogi, fully understanding that pleasure, abandons it both here and there;
he attains detachment from the Śubhakṛtsna realm, yet he does not destroy the afflictions.
Because the faculty of pleasure does not exist above the third dhyāna, one does not abandon the afflictions of the entire realm [of form].
This section concerning the purpose has been concluded. Let the subject at hand be discussed.
Now, among these elements (*dhātu*), which ones and how many are cognizable by consciousness?

That is now commenced: the five qualities known as form and so forth, which are the constituents (*dhātu*), are cognizable by two types of consciousness; that is, they are cognizable by the eye-consciousness and so forth, as well as by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The remaining ones are to be cognized by the mental consciousness.
How many are causes and how many are not causes?
That is explained:
all things, whether perishable or imperishable, are causes.
For all phenomena have the nature of causal conditions;
however, their perishability should be considered according to the specific circumstances.
How many have the nature of faculties (*indriya*), and how many do not have the nature of faculties? That is now being revealed:
Except for half of the dharma-element, the six external [objects] do not have the nature of sense-faculties.
By implication, all internal elements (*dhātu*) are established.

As for the external ones, they consist of the five [objects]—form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibility—and half of the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*); these do not have the nature of sense faculties (*indriya*), with the exception of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and the five beginning with pleasure (*sukha*).
This concludes the first chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.
The second chapter, first quarter:
[This concerns] the entire section on the faculties (indriya-parvan), which consists of twenty-two types.
The dharmas, beginning with their etymological definitions (nirvacana) and so forth, will be explained in brief.

Indeed, the faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) constitute the entire aggregate of faculties; it is neither more nor less than this.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "There are twenty-two faculties. Which are the twenty-two?
They are the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, and so on, up to the faculty of one who has already known."
The various classifications of that aggregate of faculties—such as their etymologies, sequence, elements, stages, and so forth—will be briefly explained.
Furthermore, are the twenty-two faculties [distinguished] by substance or by name?
This is explained as follows:
by name there are twenty-two, but by substance they are seventeen.
Because there is no other duality apart from the effect, nor the triad of nine [factors] beginning with pleasure.
For it is a certain portion of the body-faculty itself that receives the designation "female faculty" or "male faculty," because it serves as the basis for a specific afflicted consciousness.

Furthermore, among the nine faculties beginning with faith, the three designations— such as the "faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and so forth— are applied to their respective triads when they are present together.
Others, however, observe: "Because the characteristics [indicated by] the name do not exist, yet that name is meaningful;
therefore, even though it applies to three groups, its meaning is sought by others. (Abhidh-d 74)
Indeed, that which is the characteristic of conventional truth does not exist for them [the noble ones], because those terms function by way of activity and human agency,
like the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*);
since the name is meaningful, it is indeed possessed of an object, and thus it is called by that name.
The female and male faculties are also distinct from the body faculty because they are causes for specific cognitions; due to their particular predominance,
these two are distinguished from the body faculty just as the eye faculty and others are.
For just as the eye and other [faculties] are distinguished from the body-faculty because they produce specific cognitions and because of their specific predominance, so it is with these two as well.
What, then, is the meaning of "sense-object" (indriyārtha)? This is now undertaken: the wise declare that the meaning of "sense-object" is "the object of sovereignty.
Over which objects, then, does which [sense] have sovereignty?

We, for our part, observe that among the five [faculties] beginning with the eye, there is a predominant influence (*ādhipatya*)— meaning an unequal observation of even and uneven paths— in the fivefold activity of illuminating their respective objects.
But for four [of these], it applies to two meanings each.
The life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the female faculty, and the male faculty each have two functions.
Among these, first, the life-faculty has the functions of connecting one to the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) and maintaining it;
the mind-faculty likewise has the functions of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*).

As it has been said: "Through the defilement of the mind, sentient beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, they are purified" (Jaini_46). Or [it refers] to the mastery over the connection to renewed existence and its persistence. Regarding the connection to renewed existence first, as it has been said: "At that time, one of two minds becomes manifest for the gandharva—either accompanied by attachment or accompanied by aversion."
Or:
"Likewise, Ānanda, if consciousness were not to descend into the mother's womb... Regarding the conformity to mastery, it is said in detail: "By the mind this world is led," and so forth.
The female and male faculties also exercise sovereignty over the production of sentient beings and their differentiation.
First, regarding the production of sentient beings,
it is because that production is for the most part dependent upon them.
Even regarding the conceptualization of sentient beings, [the Lord acts] by virtue of that [conceptualization];
for among the beings of the first eon, there is a diversity of conceptual distinctions such as the movements, voices, and behaviors of women and men.
Others know his sovereignty to consist in the perception of his own objective domain and so forth.
The ancient masters, however, say: "Each of the five [faculties], beginning with the eye, possesses sovereignty over four purposes.
First, regarding the beauty of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*): because those who are blind or deaf possess an unattractive form.
Second, regarding the maintenance of the personal existence..."
Because of the avoidance of sense objects upon seeing and hearing,

and because they serve as the uncommon causes for the arising of visual and auditory consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors, as well as for the acts of seeing forms and hearing sounds.
However, for the nose, tongue, and body, [their function] is as before:
for the adornment of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) and for the maintenance of the personal existence, because one partakes of solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) by means of them.
The rest is as before.
Furthermore, regarding the four faculties—the female, male, life, and mind faculties—they function with respect to two objects each.
First, concerning the female and male faculties: they function with respect to the differentiation of sentient beings and the distinction among sentient beings.
The distinction of sentient beings refers to "woman" and "man.
The distinction of conceptual construction also includes [differences in] physical form, speech, movement, and so forth, as previously described;
or it refers to the distinction between affliction and purification.
For those devoid of that [life-faculty], there is no such thing as restraint (*saṃvara*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), and so forth;
however, for those who possess it, there is the attainment of the fruit of restraint.
The same applies to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the mind-faculty (*manaindriya*) regarding their two respective functions, as previously explained.
Others who consider themselves wise say that [the object] exists only in the cognition of its own form.
The authors of the *Kośa* and others, however, say: "The sovereignty of the five [faculties], beginning with the eye, lies precisely in the apprehension of their own respective objects.
This is merely a partial adoption of the Vaibhāṣika position;
herein there is nothing that represents the author of the *Kośa*’s own unique perspective.
The Vaibhāṣikas themselves have stated that it is the apprehension of its own object.
For according to the Dārṣṭāntika, everything is imperceptible;
because the five groups of consciousness have past objects as their domain, at the very time when the eye and visible form exist, the consciousness is non-existent.
When consciousness exists, the eye and visible form do not exist;
furthermore, in the absence of the persistence of the moment of consciousness, the apprehension of its own object is impossible.

Regarding the arising of afflictions and the attainment of qualities such as faith, the five faculties beginning with pleasure also exercise sovereignty over the arising of afflictions such as attachment.
As it has been said: "Conditioned by feeling is craving."
“Attachment underlies pleasant feeling,” and so forth.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣikas say that the eight [faculties] beginning with faith possess sovereignty over the arising of all virtuous qualities,
whereas [the others] are associated with defiled feelings.
For it has been said: "In pleasant feeling, attachment lies latent," and so forth.
Regarding purification, there are the five beginning with faith, because by means of them one suppresses the afflictions and gives rise to the Path.

As it has been said: "The noble disciple, endowed with the arrow of faith, endowed with the gatekeepers of strength, steadfastness, and mindfulness, with a concentrated mind, is liberated; he cuts through all fetters with the weapon of wisdom."
And so forth.

As for the three faculties beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya), they exercise sovereignty over the successive stages [of the path] and over nirvāṇa.
What, then, is the sequence of these faculties? We reply:
the sequence is according to [the order of] result, defilement, equipment, and purification. (Abhidh-d 78)

First, the fruit of prior karma consists of eight [factors], because they are born of maturation (*vipāka*); therefore, they were mentioned first. When that maturation exists, there are the five factors consisting of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth, as well as the provisions for the path (*mārgasaṃbhāra*) beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
Purification is by means of the three untainted [paths].
Why, then, are exactly twenty-two [faculties] taught as they have been proclaimed, neither more nor fewer?
That is explained:
because they [account for] the designation of sentient beings, the diversity of sentient beings, sustenance, and the arising of afflictions.
The means to the path and the attainment of the fruit are considered their state of being faculties (indriyatā).
Indeed, the designation "sentient being" (sattva) applies to the six faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the mind.
For this constitutes the fundamental substance of a sentient being.
The diversity of sentient beings is established by two [faculties]: the female and male faculties.
Fortitude is by means of the life-faculty;
the arising of afflictions is by means of the five sensations;
and the means for the path is by means of faith and the other [faculties].
The attainment of the fruit is by means of the last three;
for this reason, their status as faculties is recognized.
There are fourteen [faculties] because they are the basis for contact, its arising, its support, and its enjoyment;
the other eight are faculties because they are the causes of heaven and liberation.
In that regard, the basis of contact consists of the six sense faculties, beginning with the eye;
manifestation occurs through the female and male faculties;
and the support is provided by the life-faculty.
Enjoyment consists of the five sensations;
thus, fourteen [faculties] have been mentioned so far.
The five beginning with faith are the causes for rebirth in heaven.
The causes of liberation are three, beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya); therefore, there are exactly this many.

If the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) is "sovereignty," why do desire (*chanda*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—which belong to the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*)—not have the status of faculties despite possessing sovereignty?

For it has been said by the Blessed One: "All phenomena are rooted in desire, born of contact, and have their manifestation through attention. Furthermore, the sovereignty of perception and volition over both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) has indeed already been stated, as has that of wholesome volition.
In this way, the afflictions also possess sovereignty in setting in motion the causes of saṃsāra;
yet, why do they not constitute faculties (*indriya*) with respect to the preeminence of nirvāṇa?
To this, it is said:

The Sage did not declare desire to be a faculty because it is subordinate to the factor of energy; nor contact, because it nourishes feeling; nor perception, because it is overcome by wisdom. (Abhidharmadīpa 81)
For zeal (*chanda*) is the desire to act, and it is a constituent part of vigor (*vīrya*);
however, vigor is directly connected with actual performance. That very [vigor] is what is called a faculty (*indriya*).
Contact (*sparśa*) also has its capacity exhausted for producing that [feeling], as it is said: "Feeling is conditioned by contact.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) too is for the most part fallen into worldly convention.
Because she has been overcome by wisdom whose single flavor is the ultimate truth, she is not called a sense-faculty.
Regarding faith and the other [faculties], as well as the [five] knowledges, the fault lies in their purity or the arising of defilement;
because of their predominance, mental attention (manaskāra) is not designated as a faculty.

Indeed, proper mental attention (yoniśo-manasikāra) accompanies faith and the other [faculties], while improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manasikāra) accompanies feeling and the others when they are associated with passion and so forth; therefore, that [improper attention] is also not a faculty.
Because it conforms to esteem (*saṃbhāvanā*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is also not a faculty;
since resolve also assists faith, it is not a faculty.
Volition [is not the cause] because of the uncertainty regarding the production of a result at a later time.
Furthermore, since the fruit of volition indeed occurs at a later time, its potency does not manifest when that fruit is absent.
Even the world, observing the non-destruction of the existence of that fruit, is confused;
some say the fruit is causeless, some say it is created by Īśvara, and some say it has causes such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
Because the fruit of volition (*cetanā*) is unmanifest,
even though the Blessed One knows its sovereignty and it is the cause of the three worlds, volition was not established among the sense-faculties.
Moreover, among the great universal wholesome factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*),
this [faith] is not non-negligence because it arises from vigor, nor is it shame because it restrains audacity.
Neither equanimity nor non-greed [are present], because they are overwhelmed by vigor and faith.
First of all, heedfulness stands in the place of a treasurer for energy;
it acquires wholesome qualities through energy and protects those already present.
Modesty, moreover, is the rival of fearlessness, like a modest young bride.
Whence does it [equanimity] have sovereignty?
Even equanimity is overcome by faith,
and since non-attachment is opposed to vigor, it is not a faculty.
Pliancy is not [a faculty] because of the intensity of feeling, and it is not an outflow because it is irreproachable.
Indeed, pliancy is overwhelmed by the predominance of the activity of feeling;
thus, it too is not a faculty.
However, because unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*) are also to be censured, they are not *āsravas*, just as a king of the Caṇḍālas is not [considered a true king].
Even for those factors dissociated from mind, such as birth and so forth, there is no sovereignty because they exist for the sake of another;
for dharmas such as birth are dependent on others like servants— how, then, could they possess mastery?
Because it is devoid of activity, there is no cessation.
Since even nirvāṇa is inactive and lacks a fruit, whereas dharmas that possess activity are fruitful and endowed with sovereignty, the Blessed One did not establish nirvāṇa as a faculty (*indriya*).
There is nothing here to be added, nor anything to be removed.
Now, the definition of the faculties (indriya) must be stated.
Among them, that of the eye and the others has already been explained.
That of the life-faculty, faith, and so forth will be explained when the associated (saṃprayukta) and dissociated (viprayukta) factors are being discussed.
Now, however, suffering and the others are being explained:
"Suffering is the affliction of the body, while mental distress is that of the mind.
The term "affliction" carries over [from the previous definition].
Happiness and mental well-being are bodily and mental satisfaction.
"Sāta" is a synonym for exhilaration (*prahlādana*). Due to its preeminence, mental *sāta* is sometimes designated as "pleasure" (*sukha*). (Abhidharmadīpa 87)
In the third dhyāna, mental agreeable feeling (*mānasaṃ sātam*) is designated as "pleasure" (*sukha*) by the Blessed One because it surpasses the pleasure of the five sense faculties.

Mental joy (*saumanasya*), however, has gladness (*prīti*) as its intrinsic nature, and since that does not exist in the third dhyāna, it is simply called "pleasure" there. This [pleasure] belonging to that level is thus indicated.
The faculty that is free from passion (*anīrajas*) and so forth is to be understood as existing in six stages.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) exists in six stages:
in the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), and in the intermediate meditation (*dhyānāntarika*).
The others, however, are to be seen as pure faculties belonging to the nine stages.

The faculty of final knowledge (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) exist in nine stages: namely, in these same six [lower] stages and in the first three formless stages (*ārūpyabhūmi*).
Now, which are the twenty-two faculties, and which are to be abandoned? To illustrate: the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is to be abandoned in two ways.
The three mental feelings are of three kinds:

the mind-faculty (*manas*), pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or are not to be abandoned (*aheya*).
The eight faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the life-faculty, as well as the faculty of suffering, are to be abandoned through cultivation;
five are of two kinds.
Faith and the other [faculties] are both to be abandoned by cultivation and not to be abandoned,
because they are both with-outflows and without-outflows;
however, this is not the case for the [remaining] three.
The three untainted [factors] are indeed not to be abandoned, because they are free from fault.
If, then, faith and the other [faculties] are of two kinds— both to be abandoned and not to be abandoned— because they are both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava),
while only these three are without-outflows,
how then is this Sūtra to be interpreted?
As for what was said by the Blessed One: “One in whom these five faculties are entirely and in every way absent, I declare him to be an outsider, standing on the side of the ordinary worldlings”—
this does not prove [the point], because it refers specifically to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) context.

This was indeed said with reference to the untainted (anāsrava) states, because the Blessed One, having established the classification of noble persons (āryapudgala), said: "He for whom these [exist]. Furthermore, the ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is of two kinds.
The internal one has not severed the roots of virtue, while the external one has severed the roots of virtue.
With reference to him, it was said: "I declare the external one to be situated on the side of ordinary worldlings."

Or, because of the expression "in every way, all [of them]," the intended meaning is: "one for whom even the worldly [faculties] do not exist. The term "external" refers to that which does not belong to the followers of the Śākya-son (Buddhists), being situated on the side of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and thus situated as an adversary to the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
For otherwise, he would have said: "One who does not possess these five faculties, I call him one situated on the side of ordinary worldlings."

For it has been said: “There are beings in the world who are born in the world and grow old in the world—those with sharp faculties, those with medium faculties, and those with dull faculties”—even before the Wheel of Dharma had been set in motion.

Furthermore, it was said: “As long as I did not know, as they really are, the arising and the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these five faculties, so long did I not claim to have awakened from this world with its gods,” and so forth.
And this is not the method of investigation for untainted (anāsrava) phenomena;
rather, we cite this scripture here: "There are these three signs of faith in one who has faith," and so forth.
How does this serve as a proof?
For if faith were absent, there would be no desire to see the Noble Ones,
no desire to hear the True Dharma,
and no desire to dwell within the household with a mind free from stinginess.

Furthermore, that ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who lacks these faculties is in every respect an external ordinary person, due to the deficiency of the causal conditions that serve as the basis for wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-upaniṣaddhetu*).
Therefore, it is established that they are "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
The classification of types has been explained;
now the acquisition must be discussed.
How many faculties are first acquired as maturation (vipāka) in which realm?
This is now begun:
"In the desire realm, two types of maturation are first obtained by those born in succession.
In the desire realm, by those born in succession—namely, the egg-born, the womb-born, and the moisture-born—the first two faculties are obtained.
The body-faculty and the life-faculty—
these two first arise as results of maturation (*vipākaja*) within that drop of semen and blood; however,
because they are afflicted, the mind-faculty and the equanimity-faculty are not maturation.
Others have six, seven, or eight;
those born by spontaneous generation (aupapāduka), however, have six:
the five beginning with the eye-faculty and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
If they are without sexual organs, they are like those of the first aeon;
furthermore, if they possess one sexual organ, they are like the gods and so forth;
or if they possess both sexual organs, they are like those in the miserable realms.
Thus it is first in the desire realm;
furthermore, in the form realm, six faculties are initially acquired as maturation.
The five beginning with the eye-faculty and the life-faculty; however, the last [of these] is the life-faculty alone.
In the formless realm, the life-faculty is obtained as a maturation. Thus, acquisition has been explained.
Relinquishment (tyāga) must be explained;
it is now being revealed:
for those who are dying, three [faculties] are ceased at the end.
Vitality, mind,
and equanimity; however, there are eight in the intermediate [dhyāna].
For those dying in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), eight [faculties] cease:
those three [mental faculties] and the five beginning with the eye.
In the desire realm, there are ten, eight, nine, four, or five wholesome [minds].
By those with both sexual organs, ten are ceased—
namely, those eight plus the female and male organs;
by those with one sexual organ, nine are ceased.
With those lacking the secondary sexual characteristics, eight [faculties] cease.
This rule applies specifically to simultaneous death;
however, for those dying gradually, four faculties are ceased: the body faculty, the life faculty, the mind faculty, and the equanimity faculty.
For there is no separate cessation of these [faculties].
And this rule is to be understood as applying to death with a defiled or neutral mind;
however, when the mind is wholesome, faith and the other four are added, making five in all cases.
Thus, there are eight in the formless realms and thirteen in the form realms;
in this manner, they are to be counted in detail.
In the *Abhidharmadīpa*, in the commentary known as the *Vibhāṣāprabhā*, this is the first quarter of the second chapter.
In the second chapter, second section,
since all the properties of the sense organs are being investigated in the context of the discussion on the senses, he asks:
Now, among these wholesome faculties (*kuśalendriya*), by which faculty is which fruit of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) attained?
This is now set forth:
"The attainment of the first and the last is by nine; that of the two middle ones is by seven or eight."

This garland consisting of four fruits has the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) as its first [fruit] and arhatship (*arhattva*) as its last, with the fruits of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and non-returner (*anāgāmin*) in between.
Regarding that, the attainment of the first and last fruits is by means of nine faculties.

First, concerning the fruit of stream-entry: it is attained by the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and by the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*). Of these two, one [faculty] belongs to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
The second [moment] is to be understood as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*):

by the first [moment], there is the severance of the possession of the afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*), and by the second, there is the drawing forth of the possession of dissociation (*visaṃyogaprāpti*). This is also [accomplished] by means of the mind (*manas*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Furthermore, the possession of arhatship is by means of the faculties beginning with faith, excluding the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), as well as the mind-faculty (manaindriya) and any one of the faculties of pleasure (sukha), mental joy (saumanasya), or equanimity (upekṣā).
And in the two intermediate cases, it is by seven or eight [faculties].

Furthermore, regarding the fruits of the once-returner and the non-returner, [the attainment occurs] "by seven, eight, or nine," due to the word "and" (*ca*). Among these, first, if one who follows the gradual path attains the fruit of the once-returner,
and does so by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), its attainment is by means of seven [faculties].
By means of the five beginning with faith, and by means of the faculties of mind and equanimity.
Now, by means of the supramundane path, it consists of eight [faculties], with the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) as the eighth.
Now, if one who is already largely free from passion attains [it], [it consists of nine].
The fruit of non-returning is attained by those same nine [paths] by which the fruit of stream-entry is attained,
provided that one attains it through the gradual sequence and by means of the mundane path.
For that [fruit], it is by seven [faculties], just as in the case of the fruit of once-returning.
Now, if it is by means of the supramundane [path],
for that [fruit] it is likewise by eight.
Now, when one who is free from passion attains [the fruit],
it is by means of nine faculties, just as in the case of the fruit of stream-entry;
however, due to the distinction of the basis (niśraya), there occurs any one of the faculties of pleasure, mental joy, or equanimity.
Even when this practitioner of the gradual path enters dhyāna by means of the mundane path during the ninth path of liberation,
he still attains the fruit of non-returning through eight faculties;
for him, in that ninth path of liberation, mental joy (*saumanasya*) constitutes the eighth faculty.
In the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*), however, there is only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*);
for its attainment always occurs through both [the faculties of equanimity and mental pleasure].
Now, if one enters by means of the supramundane [path],...
In that case, with nine [faculties], the faculty of knowledge (ājñendriya) becomes the ninth.
If that is so, how is it that the Abhidharma states, "The fruit of arhatship [is attained] by eleven [faculties]," while here it is said, "Its attainment is by nine"?
There is no fault here, because—
The attainment of the final fruit is by means of eleven [faculties], due to its abandonment.
Having fallen away from it again and again, this arhat liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) regains it by relying on a specific meditative support:
sometimes relying on the third dhyāna,
sometimes on the second, or sometimes on the first.
Sometimes it is the fourth [dhyāna] or the anāgamya;
therefore, because of the occurrence of the three feelings therein, it is said to be associated with eleven [mental factors].

Now, among these three realms—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm—which realm is fully understood by means of a path that takes which realm or level as its object? That is now being revealed:
"The full understanding of one's own realm occurs through a path that views its own specific counter-factors. (Abhidh-d 93)
And thorough knowledge occurs through the untainted path that views its own opposites.

In this regard, thorough knowledge of the three realms occurs by means of viewing one's own realm— taking suffering and its origin as objects— and by means of viewing its own opposites— taking cessation and the path as objects.

However, through the contaminated path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*)— which is comprised of the realization of the lower stage by having that lower stage as its object, and which is comprised of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) by taking the immediately higher stage as its object— the full comprehension (*parijñāna*) of the lower stage occurs;
for the paths of uninterrupted transition have the lower stage as their object, whereas those called paths of liberation have the higher stage as their object.
However, because both types of untainted [factors] have a single level as their objective domain, [they are so classified].

Now, by how many faculties is there full comprehension (*parijñāna*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and by how many is there full comprehension of the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*)? This is now being explained:
The full comprehension of the desire realm is generally held to be by means of seven [factors];
however, it is stated to be by means of eight factors when including both those with outflows and those without outflows.
First, regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): full comprehension (*parijñāna*)—meaning abandonment—occurs through seven faculties with outflows (*sāsrava*):
the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), as well as the mental faculty (*manas*) and the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*).

The inclusion of "mostly" (*prāyas*) is because, for some practitioners whose intention is directed toward meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), there may also be [comprehension] by means of the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) upon entering the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*).
With the eight untainted faculties:
with these same seven and the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*); and, according to the general statement, with the ninth, the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*).
The full comprehension of the realm of form is held to be achieved by ten faculties:
by the five beginning with faith,
and by the mental faculty.
With the three feelings,
and with the faculty of having known (ājñendriya) due to the distinction of its basis.
The full comprehension of the final element is said to be by means of eleven [knowledges].
Through the ten faculties as previously described and through the faculty of one who has already known,

there are two types of full comprehension for that [defilement]: the first is accompanied by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), and the second is associated with the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*).
Now this must be explained: who is endowed with how many faculties?
In this regard, first, there is this rule:
all sentient beings dwelling in the three realms are endowed with equanimity, life, and the mental faculty.
All sentient beings are endowed with these three:
skin, femininity, and the sexual organs.
In the desire realm, the sentient beings of the desire realm possess these—the body, the male organ, the female organ, and those previously mentioned.
Those possessing form [are known] by means of the eye and so forth.
Indeed, material beings [possess] the three beginning with the eye, as well as equanimity, life-force, and mind.
Indeed, one who possesses desire experiences it through suffering, and one who is attached to it through mental distress.

One who has not yet abandoned desire in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) is endowed with both suffering and mental distress. However, one born in the higher realms experiences it through pleasure; likewise, a noble one (ārya) experiences it through the "wholesome" (śubha) in the lower stages.
The noble one born in the higher realms—that is, born in the form and formless realms—is endowed with happiness.
Those born in the Śubhakṛtsna, Parīttaśubha, and Apramāṇaśubha heavens are endowed with both the untainted (anāsrava) and the afflicted and non-afflicted (kliṣṭa-akliṣṭa) [happiness].
Those born in the Ābhāsvara realms and those born in the lower realms are both endowed with joy, which arises from the lips of light;
he is pure and rooted in virtue.
One whose roots of merit are not severed is endowed with all five wholesome faculties beginning with faith.
Those established on the path of liberation are endowed with two faculties belonging to those in training (śaikṣa).
Those established on the paths of seeing and cultivation are endowed with two faculties belonging to those in training.
The one beyond training, the Arhat, proceeds upon his own path.
Now, by way of rule, who is endowed with how many faculties?
This is demonstrated as follows:
One who is possessed of equanimity, life, and mind is necessarily endowed with three.
It is by means of these three alone;
for one is not endowed with them in the absence of any one of the others.
Regarding the remaining [faculties], there is no fixed rule.
In that regard, first, one born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is not endowed with the seven [faculties] beginning with the eye.
Furthermore, in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), those by whom these have not been acquired or have been lost [are likewise not endowed].
And ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) born in the fourth dhyāna or above are not endowed with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
Ordinary beings born in the third dhyāna and above possess mental joy;
those born in the realms of form or formlessness possess the faculty of pleasure; and those who have abandoned desire for the realm of sensuality possess mental grief.
Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are not endowed with the three untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties, nor with faith and the others when they are non-virtuous; however,
one who possesses bodily pleasure is endowed with four.
Whoever possesses the body-faculty (kāyendriya) necessarily possesses four [faculties]: those three [previously mentioned] and the body-faculty itself.
Whoever possesses the pleasure-faculty (sukhendriya) also possesses four: those same three beginning with equanimity (upekṣā), and the pleasure-faculty itself.
One who possesses the eye-faculty likewise possesses five.
By virtue of the word "also" (*api*), it should be understood that [the faculties] are to be known through the sense-faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Whoever possesses the eye-faculty necessarily possesses five: the faculties of equanimity (*upekṣā*), life (*jīvita*), mind (*manas*), and form (*rūpa*), as well as the eye-faculty itself.
One endowed with the female faculty (strīndriya) and so forth is endowed with eight: those seven [previously mentioned] faculties and the female faculty.

By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), it should be understood that the male faculty (puruṣendriya), the faculty of mental distress (daurmanasya), and the faculties of faith (śraddhā) and the others are included.
One who possesses that [faculty] also possesses eight faculties individually: those seven, plus the male faculty as the eighth;
and these—the body, life, mind, and the four feelings—plus the faculty of mental grief.
One who possesses those five beginning with faith, as well as equanimity, vitality, and the mental faculty, is endowed with seven.
However, one who possesses suffering is endowed with seven:
namely, one who possesses suffering is endowed with the body, vitality, the mental faculty, and the four faculties of sensation, excluding the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasya*).
For one who is free from passion for that [realm], it does not exist;
however, one who is endowed with the final two [faculties] is necessarily endowed with eleven.
Each [of these] is associated with pleasure, mental joy, equanimity, life, mind, faith, and so forth, as well as with the faculty of one who has known (ājñendriya).

Likewise, it is associated with the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) and with those [others]. One who possesses the first [faculty] possesses seven; one who possesses the others possesses six. *Abhidharmadīpa* 100.

However, one who is endowed with the first untainted faculty necessarily possesses thirteen: the mind-faculty, the life-faculty, the body-faculty, the four feelings, the [five] beginning with faith, and that [first untainted faculty] itself.
Now, with how many [mental factors] at most, and with how many, are they endowed? This is explained:
Even those born in the three continents or in the hells, and even those fixed in falsehood (*mithyātva-niyata*), are endowed with as many as nineteen and as few as eight. (Abhidharmadīpa 101)
Those in the intermediate state, hungry ghosts, animals, and those who follow through faith are endowed with either thirteen or nineteen [faculties].
With the thirteen minimal factors—namely, the five [faculties] beginning with faith, plus vitality, mind, and equanimity;
however, for a hell-being whose seeds of merit have been severed, there are the five [faculties] beginning with the eye, one gender faculty, the five sensations, vitality, and mind.
For animals, there is no such severance.
Whoever cuts off [the roots of goodness] here will inevitably go to Avīci;
therefore, in that hell, faith and the other [roots] do not exist.
There are the five [faculties], such as the eye, and the five Vedas.
There is one gender faculty, the life faculty, and the mind faculty; thus, there are thirteen.
Furthermore, ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and so forth possess nineteen faculties, excluding the three untainted (*anāsrava*) ones.
Noble ones (*ārya*), however—such as those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*)—possess exactly nineteen, excluding the two untainted faculties and one gender faculty.
Those who are fixed in rightness and those who are liberated through faith are endowed with eleven [faculties], or with ten, or with nine.
In this context, "those fixed in rightness" means the noble ones (*āryas*).
They possess five faculties beginning with faith, the mind faculty, the life faculty, three feelings, and one untainted (*anāsrava*) faculty.
Furthermore, when all [faculties] are present, they possess nineteen: excluding one gender faculty and two untainted faculties.
The Arhats known as those liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta), the body-witnesses (kāyasākṣin), and those called both [liberated by wisdom and by mind],
possess either eleven faculties or eighteen faculties.

At the minimum, it consists of eleven: the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), the six [mental factors]—pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), life-force (*jīvita*), and mind (*manas*)—and one untainted (*anāsrava*) faculty.
At the maximum, however, it consists of eighteen, excluding the two untainted faculties, the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasya*), and one of the sexual organs (*vyañjana*).
The gods of the desire realm die after a short time— ten [eons] plus seven more—
excluding the three untainted [faculties] and the faculty of mental grief.
If an ordinary person dwelling there attains detachment, he becomes a divine seer (*devarṣi*).
Having excluded one faculty, he is endowed with the remaining seventeen;
these same nineteen are joined with many faculties. (Abhidh-d 105)
Excluding two untainted [paths] and one phoneme,
for here too the truths are seen.
However, those born in the two dhyānas possess all [mental factors] with a minimum of fifteen, plus five more.
For ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) born in the first and second dhyānas— excluding suffering, mental distress, the two genders, and the three untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties— they possess fifteen.
The Śubhakṛtsna gods are endowed with ten [mental factors] plus four.
In the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) possesses fourteen [mental factors], excluding mental pleasure (saumanasya).
Indeed, those in the Bṛhatphala heaven are endowed with only thirteen, being extremely few;
in the Bṛhatphala heaven, for an ordinary person, excluding pleasure (sukha), there are the thirteen previously mentioned factors, beginning with suffering (duḥkha).
But these [five] are endowed with all sixteen faculties.
If they are noble ones (ārya), they possess the two untainted states of pleasure and mental ease; thus, there are sixteen [mental factors].
The formless realms are attained through eight, ten, or nine [faculties], depending on whether they are few or many.
Through the "few," which are eight, the ordinary person attains the eight [formless attainments]. These are considered "few."
The five beginning with faith, life, mind, and equanimity—
by means of these eleven, a noble one is endowed.
[It is associated] with five [faculties], beginning with faith;
with two, namely pleasure and mental joy, which are untainted (anāsrava); and with four, namely the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, and the equanimity-faculty, together with one that is untainted.
Sentient beings, including the gods and Kauravas, are endowed with thirteen [faculties].
With the five beginning with faith, the five beginning with pleasure,
and the three consisting of body, mind, and life-force.
One who is devoid of virtue is endowed with eight, or with ten—that is, three more—or with all the fewest, eight:
namely, the five beginning with pleasure (*sukha*), plus the body, life, and mind. One whose roots of virtue are severed is "devoid of virtue" (*niḥśubha*); he is possessed of at least these eight.
However, according to the most extensive [calculation], it consists of thirteen as previously stated—the eight beginning with the eye, the four [objects], and one gender-characteristic;
those with both genders have twenty, while those with the minimum have only one.
One with both sexual organs possesses thirteen: the few [faculties] beginning with pleasure, the body, life, and mind, and the five beginning with faith.

There is no fixed rule regarding the eyes and so forth, because they may be either unobtained or lost. However, one who possesses the maximum number of faculties has nineteen, excluding the three immaculate ones.
This *Matsyaka-grantha-samudra* is completed.

The detailed classification of the faculties (*indriya*) as they occur in the demonstration of the distinctions among the realms (*dhātu*) and destinies (*gati*) has been explained. Now, however, it is to be investigated.
Are these conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) such that they have distinct intrinsic natures (svabhāva) and thus have distinct arisings, or are there some that necessarily arise together?
He says: "There are."

In brief, there are these five categories of phenomena (*dharmajāti*): form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Among these, the unconditioned neither arises nor passes away.
However, for material phenomena (*rūpin dharma*), this is the fixed rule:
An external atom is inseparable from seven substances;
in the realm of desire, it is increased by one in the body and increased by two in the sense organs such as the eye.

Indeed, the atom (*paramāṇu*) is designated as the ultimate limit of the analysis of the accumulation of the appropriation of subtle material formations (*rūpasaṃskāra*). It exists inseparably from seven substances: either from the four primary elements (*bhūta*) and three derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*), or from three primary elements and four derived forms. This [atom] exists as something inseparable. However, the author of the *Aṣṭaskandhaka* says: "The atom is the most subtle aggregate of matter."
Therefore, a form distinct from the aggregate must be stated;
if that [atom] does not exist, then the aggregate also does not exist.
Consequently, it is established that "the most subtle form is the atom (paramāṇu)."
That which is accompanied by the body-faculty is associated with eight; that which is accompanied by the eye-faculty and so forth is associated with nine.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu) as well, it should be understood in this same way, with the exception of the two—odor and taste.
When it exists externally in the realm of form, it is inseparable from five substances, excluding odor and taste;
however, when it accompanies the body, it is inseparable from six, namely the seven [substances] beginning with the eye.
Furthermore, when that aggregate arises accompanied by sound,
then in all the aforementioned cases, sound must be counted as an additional element.

Here, moreover, the great elements (mahābhūtas) are intended to be four distinct substantial entities (dravyajāti), because they possess primacy as the basis for the existence of all derived matter (upādāyarūpa).

However, because the four derivative material elements serve as the basis for the designation of substances such as a jar, they are counted within the enumeration of the sense-bases (*āyatana*); thus, due to a failure to understand what was intended [by the author], there is no room for objection.
Furthermore, in the case of formless states,
it continues that the mind arises inseparably together with the mental factors.
But the conditioned [phenomena] exist by way of their own specific characteristics.
For it should be understood that all conditioned phenomena arise together with their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) as well as [the four characteristics] such as birth (jāti).
In the Abhidharmadīpa, in the commentary known as the Vibhāṣāprabhā, this is the second quarter of the second chapter.
In the third section of the second chapter,
that which was stated— that mental factors arise simultaneously— should now be explained.
What, then, are those mental factors? They are of five categories: the universal mental factors (*mahābhauma*), the wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśalamahābhauma*), and so forth.
The universal mental factors of affliction, the universal mental factors of unwholesomeness, and the limited universal mental factors of affliction.
Because this mental ground (*cittabhūmi*) is great for them, they are called "great-grounded" (*mahābhauma*). "Ground" (*bhūmi*) means "range" (*gati*);
in this manner, the analysis of the compound should be applied everywhere.

In that regard, first the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) are pointed out: "The ten universal factors are sensation, perception, volition, mindfulness, desire, contact, resolve, wisdom, concentration, and attention. (Abhidh-d 112)
These ten dharmas are present in their entirety throughout every mental stage, whether belonging to the three realms or being untainted (*anāsrava*).
Among them, feeling (*vedanā*) is the threefold experience, such as pleasure and so forth;
"threefold sensation" (*saṃvedita*) is its synonym.

Feeling (*vedanā*) is said to be the source of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); it is a specific state of body and mind born from the conjunction of object, sense faculty, and consciousness—whether the object be desirable, undesirable, or neither—and it consists of that which refreshes, that which afflicts, or that which is distinct from both.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the cognition of the unity of the sign, the name, and the object; it is the source of discursive thought (*vitarka*).
Volition (*cetanā*) is the mental formation (*abhisaṃskāra*) of the mind.

Mindfulness is of the nature of mental activity; it is the mind’s verbalization of an object, characterized by the non-forgetting of actions already performed, those yet to be performed, and those currently being performed. Zeal is the desire to act, which serves as a factor of vigor.

Contact (*sparśa*) is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) characterized by vitality; it is the mind's touching of an object born from the coming together of the sense-object, the sense-faculty, and consciousness.
Resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is the mind’s conviction regarding an object, which has the alternative name "desire" (*ruci*), and is characterized by the mind not shrinking back from its object.
*dhī* (wisdom) is discernment (*prajñā*), whose intrinsic nature consists in the discernment of the collection of phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth.
*Samādhi* is one-pointedness of mind, characterized by the stability of the mind.
*Manaskāra* is the mental application of the mind, having as its essential form the recollection of what was previously experienced and so forth.

Indeed, the distinction between the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) is subtle and difficult to discern. Even among material plants that possess many tastes, the specific difference in taste, though perceivable by the sense organs, is difficult to discern;
how much more so, then, for the formless phenomena (*dharma*) consisting of the mind and mental factors, which exist as a single complex (*kalāpa*) and are accessible only to the intellect?
But that [reality] is to be inferred by the wise through the nature of causes and effects.
Those factors that exist on the great ground of the wholesome are called the "wholesome universal mental factors" (*kuśalamahābhūmika*).

They are, moreover, remembered as ten: faith, conscientiousness, heedfulness, pliancy, shame, dread of blame, the roots [of the wholesome], vigor, and non-harming. These are known as the factors belonging to the wholesome ground.
In this context, faith (*śraddhā*) is the clarity of the mind, characterized by a conviction that seeks out the qualities of those who possess them;
it dispels the turbidity of the mind.
Just as a water-clearing gem, when cast into a lake, removes all turbidity and produces clarity, so too is the gem of faith born within the lake of the mind.
Heedfulness (*apramāda*) means the cultivation of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-bhāvanā*), which signifies being attentive to them.
Serenity (*prasrabdhi*) is the serviceability of the mind (*citta-karmaṇyatā*); there is also serenity of the body (*kāya-prasrabdhi*).
It receives the designation "limb of awakening" (bodhyaṅga) because it is favorable to that [awakening],
just as with joy (prīti).
For the Blessed One has stated that both joy itself and those factors conducive to joy constitute the limb of awakening called joy.
Right view, right resolve, and right effort are called the aggregate of wisdom because they are conducive to wisdom.
Similarly, bodily pliancy and mental pliancy are designated by that same term [the aggregate of concentration] because they bring about the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Equanimity is the evenness of mind, the non-exertion of the mind, and the inclination toward the signless equanimity that is free from the exertion of conditioned signs.
*Hrī* is regard for oneself;
it is shame regarding the performance of what should not be done.
*Apatrāpya*, however, is regard for others.
However, the two roots of goodness are non-attachment and non-hatred;
since non-delusion has the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), it is mentioned among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and is therefore not counted here.
Vigor (*vīrya*) is the enthusiasm for the arising of wholesome dharmas and the cessation of unwholesome ones.

The meaning is the upward elevation of a mind submerged in saṃsāra. Non-violence is the non-affliction of sentient beings. Thus have been explained the great wholesome mental factors (kuśalamahābhauma).
Stiffness, negligence, lack of faith, laziness, delusion, and restlessness—
these six are present in the afflicted mind.
Styāna is the unserviceability of body and mind.
Pramāda is the non-cultivation of wholesome dharmas;
it is a dharma that stands as the opposite of cultivation.
Lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) is the absence of clarity in the mind;
it means mental turbidity.
It consists of a lack of conviction regarding virtues and those possessed of virtue, as well as a lack of aspiration for them.
Laziness (*kausīdya*) is the lack of enthusiasm in the mind.
Delusion (*mūḍhi*) consists in a lack of clarity that imitates ignorance (*avidyā*).
Restlessness (*auddhatya*) is the lack of tranquility in the mind.
The six universal mental factors of affliction have been explained.
However, in the Abhidharma, ten are recited: "lack of faith, laziness, ... [and so forth]."
loss of mindfulness, distraction of the mind,
and ignorance.
Lack of clear comprehension, improper mental attention, and false resolve.
"Restlessness and heedlessness.
Among these, forgetfulness, distraction, lack of clear comprehension, improper mental attention, and false resolve are recited among the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
Because both the afflicted and non-afflicted [mental factors] have mindfulness and so forth as their intrinsic nature, they are not counted separately here;
therefore, there are only six universal ground-factors of affliction (*kleśamahābhauma*).
However, in the case of the unwholesome, there are two: lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).

In an unwholesome mind, however, there are two factors— lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)— which constitute the two great universal unwholesome mental states (*akuśalamahābhaumika*).
Among these, lack of shame is the factor that is the opposite of shame (*hrī*),
and lack of dread is the opposite of dread (*apatrāpya*).

According to others, shamelessness (*ahrī*) is the lack of shame regarding oneself when committing an improper act, while lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) is the lack of shame regarding others; thus,
these two are designated as the universal mental factors of limited defilement (*parīttakleśamahābhūmika*).
Deceit, guile, intoxication, anger, harmfulness, envy, malice, subtle resentment, and stinginess—these ten are the ground of the minor afflictions. *Abhidharmadīpa* 115.
For these afflictions are associated only with ignorance that is to be abandoned by cultivation, which belongs exclusively to the mental level.
Their specific characteristics, however, will be explained in the fifth chapter during the investigation of the secondary afflictions (upakleśa).
How, then, is it known that the mental factors (*caitasika*) are entities distinct from the mind?
For if one maintains that the mind itself is designated by such names as "feeling" (*vedanā*) and so forth, then the Buddha’s sūtra is accorded with reason.
As the Blessed One said: "O monks, this person consists of six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*). In this context, only the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) was spoken of.
Therefore, the Venerable Buddhadeva maintains that mental factors (*caitasika*) are not entities distinct [from consciousness].
In response to him, this is stated:
Just as earth and so forth are substances through their association with qualities such as blue;
The mind is likewise distinguished by various terms through its association with mental factors (*caitta*).
For just as the earth element or the water element is distinguished by derived matter such as color, taste, and odor—
as in "blue stones," "blue water," "sweet grapes," "sweet dates," or "sweeter than sweet molasses"— so too is the mind characterized by happiness.
The mind is distinguished by its association with mental factors (caitasika-dharma) through such terms as "afflicted," "concentrated," "energetic," "lazy," "deluded," "attached," and "hating.
If it is argued that this is incorrect because [the distinction] would be equivalent to what is yet to be proven, we say no.
Because the answer has already been stated;
for it was stated here [in the previous discussion] that the answer lies in the investigation into the difference between the primary elements (bhūta) and their derivatives (bhautika).
Therefore, since specific cognitions are not without cause, it is established that mental factors (caitasika) are distinct [from the primary elements].
Furthermore, the distinctness of mind and mental factors is as follows:
Just as the diversity between the primary elements and their derivatives is established by their own nature, function, and form,
so too should the separateness of mind and mental factors be understood.
Just as there is indeed a difference between the primary elements and derived matter due to the distinction in their intrinsic natures and the distinction in their activities,
so too should the difference between the mind and mental factors be understood from the distinction in their intrinsic natures and activities.
Just as a transformation is perceived in water due to its connection with something related to it,
so too should the modification of the mind be observed due to its association with that which is associated with it.

Just as a transformation is indeed observed in water due to contact with substances such as fire, myrobalan, molasses, salt, and so forth— [resulting in it being perceived as] hot, sour, astringent, sweet, or salty— in the same way, due to contact with mental factors (*caitasika*), the mind also becomes happy, suffering, serene, elated, luminous, or darkened.
Furthermore, their distinctness is stated in the Sūtra: "Perception and feeling are these mental factors."
This must now be explained:
among the mental states and mental factors that arise simultaneously, how is it that they are called "mental factors" (*caitasika-dharma*)? Or, what is the meaning of the term *dharma*?
This is explained as follows:

"Quality (guṇa), qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), attribute (dharma), that which occurs in a measure (mātrāvṛtti), and likewise the dependent (āśrayī)—words such as these function in dependence upon a primary referent. (Abhidharmadīpa 119)
For words function with a limited application by means of specific qualities and attributes, depending upon a substance that serves as the primary qualificand.
What, then, is the primary [referent] here?
The mind is the primary [referent] of these.
If it is asked, "Why?
[the answer is: because of the grasping of the mere object and so forth.

For the mind is merely the apprehension of an object; when that object is apprehended by it, specific qualities such as perception, recollection, the recollection of characteristics, and investigation are grasped by means of mental factors such as ideation (*saṃjñā*), discernment (*prajñā*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera" here, [it refers to] the adherence to a self and its status as being like a king. Furthermore:
"Moreover, this is the seed of the activities of both purity and impurity. (Abhidh-d 120)
For it was said by the Blessed One: “Through the defilement of the mind, sentient beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, they are purified.
Therefore, the mind is primary, as it has been stated:
“Those who will subdue the mind— which wanders far, moves alone, is bodiless, and dwells in the cave— will be liberated from the bonds of Māra.
In this context, it “wanders far” because it performs the Teacher’s work for those to be trained throughout all world-systems.
It moves alone because of the absence of a second mind simultaneously;
it is bodiless because of the absence of physical form, and because its nature can only be inferred from its activity.
"Abiding in the cave" means by means of the power of the body;
"the manifestation of its activity" refers to its functions;
and "its properties" are the associated mental factors (*caitasika*).
The five types of mental factors (*caitta*) have been explained.
Others are also recited as being indeterminate (*aniyata*), such as applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), and so forth.
Regarding this, the following must be said:
In which mind are how many mental factors (caitta) present?
First, the mind of the desire realm (kāmāvacara) is of five types:
wholesome, unwholesome, and two kinds of neutral—namely, that which is uniquely associated with [unwholesome roots] and that which is associated with other afflictions (kleśa).
The indeterminate is of two kinds, known as the obscured-indeterminate and the unobscured-indeterminate.
In that regard, a mind belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) is necessarily accompanied by vitarka and vicāra; therefore, it arises together with twelve factors associated with the desire realm,
like a sun-god with his rays, being undefiled and neutral (akliṣṭāvyākṛta).
A mind of the desire realm that is unobscured-neutral necessarily arises together with the ten great ground dharmas and with vitarka and vicāra.
Likewise, the mind arises as obscured by eighteen mental factors.
In the desire realm, the mind associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
In that state, there are eighteen mental concomitants (*caitasika*).
The ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika), the six universal afflictive factors (kleśamahābhūmika), and applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra).
As before, views (dṛṣṭi) are not added. A wholesome mental state necessarily possesses twenty-two [factors]. (Abhidh-d 122)
The ten universal mental factors, the ten great wholesome universal mental factors, and applied thought and sustained thought.

An unwholesome mind arises together with twenty mental factors. In that case, there are twenty *caittas*: ten from the universal ground (*mahābhūmika*), six from the universal ground of afflictions (*kleśamahābhūmika*), two from the universal ground of the unwholesome (*akuśalamahābhūmika*), as well as applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
An "isolated" (*āveṇika*) mind is one in which ignorance alone is present, and no other affliction such as attachment (*rāga*) exists.
That which is associated with only delusion regarding views— just as there are twenty factors in the unwholesome state associated with views that is independent (āveṇika)—
is it not the case that view is an additional factor?

It is not greater; for a certain specific kind of wisdom (*prajñā*) alone is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), and that is recited among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*). But what, then, is this *vitarka* and what is *vicāra*?

Vitarka is characterized by coarseness of mind; it is also called "conceptualization" (saṃkalpa) as its secondary name, and it functions by discriminating the various modes of the signs of objects. Its activity is stirred up by the wind of perception (saṃjñā), and it is the cause for the arising of the coarse group of the five sensory consciousnesses. Vicāra, however, is characterized by subtlety of mind and is conducive to the activity of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
Thus, these two factors necessarily arise in every mind belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
This is an extreme rashness, that the coexistence of even two contradictory factors in a single moment of consciousness is asserted;
for it is not observed in the world that two contradictory things can abide together in one place—so says the author of the *Kośa*.

Regarding this, some say: "Just as clarified butter spat into water neither solidifies too much nor melts away too much, so too, through the conjunction of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), the mind becomes neither too subtle nor too coarse; thus, both have an operation therein.

If that were the case, then applied thought and sustained thought would become the causes (*nimitta*) of coarseness and subtlety, just as water is the cause of the solidification and melting of clarified butter, and not their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Others, however, say: "In the Sūtra, the formative forces of speech (*vāk-saṃskāra*) are stated to be applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*):
'Having applied thought and having sustained thought, one utters speech; not without having applied thought and sustained thought.
Among these, those that are coarse are applied thoughts."
Those which are subtle are the *vicāras*.
And if, within a single moment of mind, one factor is gross and another is subtle, what contradiction is there here?
There would be no contradiction if there were a difference in their genus (*jātibheda*).
However, within a single category, mildness and intensity cannot exist simultaneously;
yet, there is also a distinction between categories. If that is so, then that distinction must be explained.
But it is indeed difficult to explain.
Therefore, it is manifested by way of being weak or intense;
it does not become manifested in this manner because each of the classes [of beings] possesses its own degree of weakness or intensity.
Thus, this objection—which is like praising the qualities of the sidelong glances of a blind woman—is now undertaken;
for, failing to understand their definition, the procedure of this objection is falsely elaborated.
For, regarding those two [mental states] defined as stated above, it is merely asserted that they coexist in a single consciousness, not that they attain simultaneous predominance.
Just as in the case of knowledge and ignorance, or doubt and certainty, remain silent;
do not cause yourself to be mocked by the wise.
Furthermore, that view should be understood as being of three kinds, beginning with false view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
But one should speak more extensively regarding anger and the other [afflictions].
It becomes more intense due to the secondary afflictions (upakleśa) such as anger (krodha) and the rest;
that secondary affliction, such as anger, is "additional.

Furthermore, the mind associated with the primary afflictions (kleśa)—that is, conjoined with attachment (rāga), hostility (pratigha), pride (māna), and doubt (vicikitsā)—becomes even more intense because of those afflictions. Thus, there are twenty-one [mental factors].
Since torpor (middha) can occur everywhere, one should specify it wherever it may be present;
likewise, one should count regret (kaukṛtya) as an additional factor in certain cases.
Where there is torpor (*middha*), one should count that very factor as additional;
even where that alone is additional, it is so because of this rule regarding mental factors (*caitta*) stated for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Impurity, torpor, and remorse do not exist in the form realm;
furthermore, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) do not exist in the intermediate dhyāna, nor above it.
No unwholesome state—namely, torpor and remorse—is present in the first dhyāna and those above it.
Therefore, in that state, there are no [unwholesome mental factors] other than hostility, dissimulation, pride, and deceit; furthermore, shamelessness and lack of dread are also absent.
Whatever factors exist in the first dhyāna, those same ones exist in the intermediate dhyāna;
however, "applied thought" (*vitarka*) is not found there,
and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that the previously mentioned [factors] are also absent.
"And there is also no *vicāra* above [the intermediate dhyāna]";
that is, from the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) upwards, there is neither *vicāra* nor the previously mentioned [factors].
From the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that *māyā* and *śāṭhya* are also absent.
For as much as Brahmā’s deceit is recorded, it is due to his connection with the assembly;
for he was questioned by the monk Aśvajit in his own assembly: “Where do those four great elements cease without remainder?”

Not understanding that [they] "cease," he made this proclamation: "I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Lord, the Maker, the Fashioner, the Creator, the Originator, the Father of all beings. This matter is concluded.
This must be stated: why are the associated formations (saṃprayukta-saṃskāra) so called? This is now undertaken.
The associated formation is that which possesses fivefold equality;
the dissociated formation is to be understood as that which lacks such equality.

They are associated through five kinds of equality; these are known as equality of basis, object, aspect, time, and substance. "For just as the mind is one, so too each mental factor is one," and so forth, in detail.
Furthermore, he for whom these equalities do not exist is one who is dissociated.
The challenger asks: "In that case, would it follow that form (rūpa) is dissociated [from consciousness], as well as the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)?
This is now being answered.
Because there is no existence of distinct [entities], there is no such consequence for those things possessing form;
and because of the inclusion of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), it does not follow [that the same applies] to space and so forth.
