Indeed, because names are established through a specific application only among those things possessing form (rūpin), there is no such [unwanted] consequence for them.
Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the term "conditioned" (saṃskāra), it is established that the designation "dissociated" (viprayukta) does not apply to space and so forth.
What, then, are those dissociated formations? How many are they?
For we do not perceive their intrinsic nature.
Nor is there any practical purpose;
furthermore, these phenomena are not well-known in the world, nor in the words of the Buddha,
nor in treatises such as the Vedas.
Regarding this, it is further explained: "The thirteen dissociated formations are acquisition and the rest;
their characteristic mark will be stated as the speech of an authoritative person and their own activity. (Abhidharmadīpa 128)
As for the argument that [they are not accepted] because of the absence of intrinsic nature and activity,
both of these points will be addressed here;
as also for the claim that they are not recited in the words of the Buddha.
In that regard, the word of the authoritative one (āptavacana) concerning omniscience will be proclaimed.
As for the objection that [these matters] are not recited in the world, nor in the Vedas and other such texts—that is the challenge.

Indeed, those dharmas which have omniscience as their object do come within the range of the mental activity of those who have attained the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), such as the noble Maitreya, the elder Vasumitra, the teacher Aśvaghoṣa, and others.

And how does it become an object for the minds of those Bodhisattvas who possess clear intelligence, yet whose intellects are like infants— possessing little luster and having surpassed the mental activity of those who investigate the Abhidharma— within minds that are otherwise shrouded in darkness?
In that regard,
possession (prāpti) is conjunction (samanvitti), acquisition (labdhi), the state of possessing a dharma (dharmavattā), and its formal establishment (vyavasthiti).
"Acquisition" (*prāpti*), "possession" (*samanvāgama*), and "attainment" (*lābha*) are synonyms.

In every respect, one expresses entities solely through words; for just as this term "acquisition" is heard to be merely a verbal excrescence, so too these two terms "possession" and "attainment" are merely linguistic objects. Thus, the characteristic is not illuminated by means of synonymous names.
It exists;
therefore, let that non-deviant probans which establishes it be stated. To this we reply:

Lend your ear and fix your mind in one-pointed concentration. "The establishment of the possession of qualities" refers to the fact that, indeed, qualities (*dharmas*) are of three kinds: wholesome...

...and even in the case of form (*rūpa*), one possesses [the non-informative action] through a wholesome informative action (*vijñapti*) while it is currently occurring, as long as it continues to inform, and also through that which has passed;
this applies to those [actions] consisting of hearing and reflection, as well as to the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). (Abhidharmadīpa 130)
It also arises subsequently for those consisting of hearing and reflection;
it arises both simultaneously and subsequently for the two mindless attainments;
and for those who are previously undefiled, conditioned, and virtuous, it arises when they are "dusty."
It is held that [the attainment] occurs in three ways: together with the first acquisition, prior to it, or subsequent to it.
And for the untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) and for wholesome tainted aggregates (*kuśala-sāsrava*) that have not been previously practiced, there is no prior acquisition (*pūrvajā*).
Regarding these very ones just mentioned, it is said: "But above that, it is held to be threefold."
When it has been brought face-to-face by him, then it exists in two ways.
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of defiled and other wholesome [dharmas] is considered to be of three kinds;
that is, the acquisition of defiled aggregates (*skandha*) belongs to the three time periods,
as does that of the wholesome ones other than those [defiled ones].

From those [minds] that are untainted (anāsrava) and from those that are wholesome but tainted (kuśala-sāsrava) but not of the nature of mind (anucitta), the other wholesome-tainted [minds] arise only from those belonging to the three time periods.
The same applies to the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) [minds], as well as the minds of knowledge and emanation (jñāna-nirmāṇa-manas).
The term "belonging to the three time periods" continues [to apply].

Regarding the initial attainment of *nirvāṇa*: when there is the attainment of another [state] that is eternal at all times, it is restricted to the two time periods [past and present] upon its first attainment of *nirvāṇa*. However, for that which has not been attained in the future or the present, it is also [restricted to] the past.
"For another [dharma] that is eternal, it exists at all times.
Non-arising (*ajāti*) and present cessation through non-analytical consideration (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) always exist only in the future and the present.
But sometimes it is held to be threefold.
It has been stated that for one by whom [a dharma] has been acquired, it belongs to the three time periods. Possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession (*aprāpti*) have now been explained.
Homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) must be explained. What is this so-called homogeneity?
For in this teaching, there is not even a trace of the category of "generality" (*sāmānya*) and "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) as imagined by the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
What is this [homogeneity] that follows from the practice of that? This is now explained:
that which is the cause for sentient beings' inclination toward a single object is *sabhāgatā*.

Sabhāgatā is a real entity (*dravya*); it is the cause of similarity consisting in the shared inclination toward objects among sentient beings. Its technical designation in the treatise is *nikāyasabhāga*.
Furthermore, that [homogeneity] is both undifferentiated and differentiated.
It is undifferentiated as the homogeneity of sentient beings (*sattvasabhāgatā*) for all sentient beings;
it exists in each individual because of the equality of self-love, nourishment, and pleasure in all of them.

The specific [sabhāgatā], however, is the cause for the determination of differences among those very same sentient beings—such as those belonging to different elements (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), destinies (*gati*), modes of birth (*yoni*), castes (*jāti*), women, men, lay followers (*upāsaka*), monks (*bhikṣu*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—regarding their distinct inclinations toward a single object.
Indeed, if that [specific *sabhāgatā*] did not exist, the fault of a confusion in all worldly conventions regarding both the noble and the non-noble would follow;
but since it exists, this fault does not occur. Thus, there is a dharma called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*).
Regarding the phrase "the cause for delighting in a single object":
could there be a case where one would pass away and be reborn, yet neither relinquish nor acquire their own homogeneous class (*svasabhāgatā*)?
There are four alternatives:
the first alternative is one who, passing away from a certain state, is being reborn in that very same state;
the second is one entering into the fixed path of determination (*niyāma*).

For he abandons the homogeneity of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā) and acquires the homogeneity of a noble one (ārya-sabhāgatā), due to the transition to the third realm of existence (gati).
The fourth [alternative] is: setting aside these modes.

Now, what is the specific distinction between this state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and the homogeneity of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjanasabhāgatā*)? The homogeneity of ordinary persons is indeed of the nature already described; however, the state of being an ordinary person is the source of all misfortune, and thus the difference between them is very great.
Its distinctness is also established by authoritative scripture (*āptavacana*).
For it was said by the Blessed One: "If he comes here, he attains the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of human beings.
However, ordinary personhood (*pṛthagjanatva*) is neither thus attained nor abandoned.
The homogeneity (sabhāgatā) is established;
however, the author of the Kośa, by equating it with the category of "universal" (jāti) as imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas, clearly perceives a similarity in color between milk-rice and a crow.

Now, what is this so-called "state of non-perception" (āsaṃjñika)? It is explained as follows: "The state of non-perception is a karmic maturation (vipāka) which consists in the cutting off of the mind among those who possess perception. (Abhidh-d 134)

For those reborn among the gods who are non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), there arises a certain other dharma, dissociated from mind and born of maturation (*vipākaja*), which is called "non-perception" (*āsaṃjñika*). By means of this, the mind of those reborn there is suppressed for a period of time in the future,
so that it does not obtain the opportunity to arise.
Furthermore, that [state] has exclusively the nature of being born of maturation (*vipākaja*). Of what is it the maturation?
It is the maturation of the karma that completes the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
In which, then, does it occur? It occurs among the classes of gods.
Regarding this, he says: "Among the non-percipient beings."

The gods called *asaṃjñisattvāḥ* (non-percipient beings) are included within the class of the Bṛhatphala gods, like those in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntarika*). But do they never at any time possess perception?
They do possess it at the time of birth and at the time of death.
“Even after remaining for an extremely long time, those beings fall from that place due to the sudden arising of perception,” so says the scriptural reading.
Having fallen from there like those awakened from a long sleep, they are reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and nowhere else;
for those who have been so reborn necessarily possess karma to be experienced in a subsequent life within the sphere of desire (*kāmāvacara-aparaparyāyavedanīya-karma*).
Just as for the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, there is karma to be experienced upon rebirth among the gods.
What, then, is this attainment of non-perception?
It is explained as follows:
the pure attainment of non-perception occurs in the final dhyāna and brings about the cessation of the mind.
The state of non-perception (āsaṃjñika) is neutral (avyākṛta),
because it is a fruit of maturation (vipākaphala);
this [attainment], however, is wholesome (śubha).
Furthermore, this [attainment] is "in the final dhyāna," meaning it is comprised within the fourth dhyāna;
it is "that which obstructs the mind."
Just as that fruit brings about the cessation of the mind, so too does this [attainment] bring about the cessation of the mind.
Furthermore, by the mention of the "mind," the cessation of the mental factors (*caitta*) is established even though they are not explicitly mentioned, just as when the sun sets, its rays also set.
For what purpose, then, do practitioners (*yogin*) enter into this attainment?

Because they proceed with the desire for escape, they enter that attainment preceded by a mental orientation (*manaskāra*) based on the perception of liberation, out of a longing for release. Furthermore, this [attainment] is as follows:
For noble ones do not consider that [state] to be noble; rather, they regard it as a place of misfortune,
whereas some ordinary persons regard it as a place of liberation.
Furthermore, is this [attainment] obtained through rebirth or through detachment?
He says: no. What then?
It is obtained through application.
One produces that [state] with effort.

The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), which arises at the peak of existence (bhavāgra) for one desiring to abandon [the mind], is to be understood as the temporary suppression of the arising of mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma). Furthermore, this is brought into manifestation by yogins who, preceded by a mental attention characterized by the notion of dwelling, desire to experience a bliss resembling nirvāṇa.
And this attainment, born of the peak of existence,
is considered to be wholesome, noble, acquired through application, and of two types of fruition, or indefinite.
It is "to be experienced in two times," meaning it is to be experienced either upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) or in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*); furthermore,
this is also "of indefinite experience" (*aniyatavedanīya*).
For one who, having produced this [attainment], enters final nirvana, does not experience its ripening;
indeed, its ripening ripens as the four aggregates at the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
Furthermore, only an noble one (ārya) is able to produce this, not a non-noble one.
This is because of the fear of annihilation, the abandonment of the view of eternalism, and the generation of the power of the Noble Path.
Furthermore, for the Noble One, this attainment is acquired through application (*prayoga*) and not acquired through detachment (*vairāgya*).
Regarding this, the author of the *Kośa* asserts: "This attainment possesses mind."
(Jaini_94) “Indeed, it is the very mind of attainment (*samāpatti-citta*) that arises in opposition to other minds;
by means of this, there occurs for a period of time the mere non-occurrence of another mind.
Because it brings about a basis (*āśraya*) opposed to that [other mind], it is designated as ‘attainment’ (*samāpatti*).”

This [position] is not Buddhist. Why? Because it is incompatible with the fourfold mind, both according to scripture and through reasoning; for this state without mind is established by the fact that the nature of the mind has been extinguished. (Abhidharmadīpa 137)
In the peak of existence (bhavāgra), there are indeed four types of consciousness:
that born of maturation (vipākaja), the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), the wholesome acquired at birth (upapattilābhika), and the wholesome produced through application (prāyogika).
Among these four, which consciousness is said to be the cessation of other consciousnesses for one who has entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti)?
In that regard, first of all, as for that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) there, [he] ...
"attains realization of the truth through practice in this very life,
and not even at the time of death."

"And through the dissolution of the body, having transcended the gods who subsist on edible food, he is reborn in a certain divine, mind-made body. Having been reborn there, he repeatedly enters into and emerges from the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñāveditanirodha).
He understands as it truly is: 'This state exists.'"

In this regard, the Elder Udāyin said this to the Elder Śāriputra: "Venerable sir, do not speak thus. For he [Udāyin] thought: "The attainment of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the divine mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) have been taught by the Blessed One to belong to the level of the fourth dhyāna; how then could this be possible?

Thus was he answered by the Venerable Udāyin, who, being ignorant of falling away (*parihāṇi*) and confused regarding the Abhidharma, replied in that manner. [This was subsequently addressed] by the Blessed One.
The Supreme One spoke thus for the purpose of rebuking him: "Do you too, O deluded man, think that you can converse with the monk Śāriputra regarding the profound Abhidharma?
Thus, those belonging to other schools maintain that the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) belongs even to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
For them, this sūtra would be established even without [the possibility of] falling away.
However, this very point remains unestablished: that this [attainment] also exists on the level of the fourth dhyāna.
How so? Because of the statement: "There are nine successive attainments" (navānupūrvasamāpattayaḥ).
Because of this statement in the Sūtra,
the noble ones (santaḥ), having attained mastery over their desires, may even later bypass [the stages] and enter the leaping meditative attainment (vyutkrāntasamāpatti).
The two meditative attainments have been explained.
The subsistence of vitality, mind, and heat is the basis for the designation of the realms of existence (*gati*).
Both through scripture and through reasoning, it is accepted that this exists as a substantial entity (*dravya*).
"Life-span" (*āyus*) and "vitality" (*jīvita*) are not different in meaning.
For it is said in the Abhidharma: "What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
It is the life-span belonging to the three realms."
Furthermore, that [basis] is the "appropriation for the designation of a realm of existence" (gati-prajñapti-upādāna), because its intrinsic nature is born of maturation (vipākaja).
For it is said in the Sūtra: "Once maturation has occurred, one comes to be designated as a hell-being."
In this way, it continues until it reaches the reckoning of those who have attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, there is no other faculty born of maturation (*vipākaja*) that pervades the three realms which, persisting through the uninterrupted continuity of birth, could serve as the basis for the designation of a "destiny" (*gati*),
except for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Furthermore, how is it understood that this [unmanifest karma] exists? Both from scripture and from reasoning. First, as for the scripture: [it is as follows].
“When life, warmth, and consciousness— these abandon the body, then it lies cast away, insentient like a piece of wood.
For in the desire realm, the life-faculty necessarily coexists with the body-faculty and warmth.
That [element] necessarily co-exists with consciousness, yet it does not necessarily co-exist with the sense faculties such as the eye.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), however, it co-exists with all five faculties, beginning with the body;
nevertheless, it does not necessarily accompany the mind.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), however, everything coexists with consciousness,
except for the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) exists as a substantial entity (dravya), serving as the basis for the designation of the realms of existence (gati).

Otherwise, when the mind has ceased its wholesome states or is stainless, what could be conceived as the retribution-born basis for the designation of that destiny in a lower realm, by whose existence one would not have fallen away from it? Furthermore,

it is impossible to maintain that the seed of the consciousness of a lower realm— which serves as the basis for the designation of that destiny— belongs to those [states] free from outflows (*anāsrava*),
because the mind free from outflows functions toward the total eradication [of such seeds].

Nor can another consciousness belonging to that level be postulated, because a consciousness that has a non-conceptual object (*anākāra-ālambana*) is unestablished apart from the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
If it is argued that this is the mind-element (*manodhātu*), no; for that name is merely designated for the mental-consciousness element itself in a different state.
There is also a logical argument: because of its specific predominance, like the eye and other faculties.

The author of the *Kośa* states: "By the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one produces a projection of life-force born of karma; this is the sustaining of the formative forces of longevity (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra-adhiṣṭhāna-ja*). Thus, longevity is not a maturation (*vipāka*)."
In that case, what is the answer?
It is not necessary to state an answer there, because this [objection] does not apply to the sūtra.
It is not seen in the Vinaya and it contradicts the nature of reality (dharmatā).
Therefore, this should be disregarded like the words of a fool.
How, then, does it not descend into the Sūtra and not appear in the Vinaya?
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that one should ripen what is unripened through the cause of abandonment or through the cause of application."
"Or one may lead that which is already ripened by another method," and so forth in detail.
In the *Vinaya* as well, it is accepted that "karma of three kinds that is certain to be experienced cannot be turned back even by the world including the gods.
In the *Abhidharma* too, it is stated that "all immeasurable lifespans are projected [by karma]."
Its defects are restricted by factors such as time, place, and state;
thus, for the time being, [the objection] is not worthy of a reply because it deviates from scripture.
Nevertheless, a reasoned reply is now stated.
If the Blessed One, by the power of his meditative concentration (*samādhi*), were to produce at will a previously non-existent sentient being endowed with consciousness and sense-faculties,

or if he were to project his own life-force— which was not previously projected by prior karma— by the power of yoga, then the Buddha, the Blessed One, would become like Nārāyaṇa, because of the creation of a previously non-existent sentient being.
And because of his compassion, he would not enter final nirvana,

but would instead sever doubts regarding the fragmentation of the teaching; therefore, it should be understood that the Venerable One began this work as a gateway for entering the *Vaitulya* treatises.
Now, does death occur only through the exhaustion of the life-span, or otherwise as well?
It is stated in the *Prajñapti*: "Is there death through the exhaustion of the life-span but not through the exhaustion of merit and so forth?
This constitutes a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*)."
The first alternative is due to the exhaustion of karma that has maturation as its life-span; the second is due to [the exhaustion of] karma that has maturation as its resources;
the third is due to both.
The fourth [case] is by way of not avoiding the uneven [conditions].
It is stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna*: "Should it be said that life-force proceeds bound to a continuity (*santati*), or should it be said that, once arisen, it remains?"
He said: “It should be said that for beings of the desire realm who have entered either the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation, [the mind] proceeds bound to the continuum.
It should be said that for those who have entered [these attainments], it proceeds bound to the continuum.
And for beings of the form and formless realms who have entered them, it should be said that once arisen, it remains.”
What, then, is the meaning of this statement?
First, [the first type of non-informative action] is so called because it is subject to injury through injury to its basis (*āśraya*), since it is dependent upon that continuum (*santati*).
Second, [the second type] is so called because there is no injury to its basis at all, as in the case of its remaining once it has arisen.
The Kashmiris maintain that the first [attainment of a body] is with obstacles and the second is without obstacles;
therefore, untimely death exists.
It is said in the Sūtra: "There are four ways of obtaining a personal existence."

“There is an acquisition of a personal existence (*ātmabhāvapratilambha*) wherein one’s own volition (*ātmasaṃcetanā*) operates, but not the volition of another (*parasaṃcetanā*); thus there is a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*).

One’s own volition operates in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) among the gods who are deprived of their play (*krīḍāpramoṣaka*) and the gods who corrupt the mind (*manopradūṣaka*). For it is through excessive joy or the corruption of the mind that they fall from that state, and not otherwise.
And it should be stated that this applies to the Buddhas as well,
because they die of their own accord; for those who have entered the womb or an egg, only the volition of another can cause death.
Both [types of non-informative action] generally belong to others who dwell in the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
Neither belongs to all those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), to those belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyāvacara*),

and to certain ones among those in the desire realm— namely, hell-beings (*nāraka*), those who have entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those who have attained the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*), those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), royal sages (*rāja-ṛṣi*), messengers of the Victor (*jina-dūta*), those commissioned by the Victor, and so forth.
And for all Bodhisattvas in their final existence, as well as for the mothers carrying them in the womb and for Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*) carrying them in the womb—
the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has been explained.
The characteristics of the conditioned will now be explained.
What are they, and how many are there? This is being further elucidated:
Birth, duration, decay, and destruction constitute the fourfold mark of the conditioned.
Indeed, these four characteristics of the conditioned were taught by the Blessed One in the Abhidharma;
however, in the Sūtra, for the sake of the needs of those to be trained, these same four are stated as three by combining duration and change into one.
In the verse, however, two of these factors are shown by implication, being included within the meaning.
For stability (sthiti), desiring union with the dharma, remains while concealing that very dharma;
and proceeding in such a manner, it produces a particular exaltation of the mind in the world.

Therefore, it is observed that this subject matter is intended to inspire a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), as if Fortune (*Śrī*) were accompanied by the goddess of ill-fortune (*Kālakarṇī*)—namely, aging (*jarā*)—which the Blessed One has described under the name "alteration" (*anyathātva*).
For this reason, there are four [aspects]. Furthermore:
There are four [reasons] why [the self] does not exist as a persisting entity, because [characteristics such as] being a cause and so forth are not established.
For if there were no stability of a phenomenon (*dharma*),
it— while remaining within itself— would lack that specific excellence of power and efficacy known as its cause;
and for that which is seized by impermanence, there would be no power of production, and thus it would not perform any action.
Due to the absence of action, there would be an absence of fruit;
yet this undertaking is for the sake of the fruit.
Therefore, it is established that those who affirm the existence of the afterlife (āstikas), having rejected the position of the nihilists (nāstikas), accept the state [of moral responsibility].
The four [marks] are not established because of the absence of aging;
let there be duration, but aging is in no way tenable.
How so? For it has been said:
"If there is identity [between the old and the new], aging is not established; if there is difference, it is simply another entity.
Therefore, what is called 'aging' is not logically possible for a single entity."
In response to this, it is said: "The establishment of decay occurs through the loss of potency;
for when a dharma has manifested, it arises excited and projects its fruit."
If his power were not impaired by old age, he would project a second fruit as well;
yet he is unable to project it.

Therefore, it is understood that there exists an enemy called "old age" which, having worn him out and stripped him of his capacity, hands him over to the demoness of impermanence. Thus, it is rightly said: "The establishment of old age follows from the loss of power."
This which has been stated is not tenable, because it entails the fault of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
By speaking so briefly, you have effectively accepted the Sāṃkhya theory of transformation.
It is not [that you] have not accepted it, because—
It is not through transformation because of their difference;
for according to us, the phenomenon called "aging" is indeed one thing, and the subject (the dharmin) is another.

For the Sāṃkhya, however, transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the discarding of one attribute that is identical with the substrate (*dharmin*), while another attribute identical with that same substrate arises.
But how can there be a loss of power in a momentary phenomenon? It is as follows: because this [phenomenon], without abandoning its own nature—
The loss of capacity is established through both its singular agency and its destruction.
Indeed, if that which is endowed with such firmness projects one fruit, it would project a second fruit as well if it were possessed of that same [firmness];
nor could impermanence destroy this [cause] while it still possesses such power.
Therefore, it is understood that this entity, having undergone change, enters the mouth of the tigress of impermanence.

Thus, having projected one result, it is said that "it perishes. [The opponent claims: "The loss of capacity is established through both its single causal activity and its destruction. [We reply: This is not established.
Because destruction is without cause; for those things which possess a substantial nature and have causes are indeed observed to be impermanent. How so? Like a sprout.
There is no destruction of destruction;
therefore, it is causeless.
Furthermore, those things that exist subsequently have a prior cause, such as the contact of seeds and so forth with ashes.
Furthermore, there is no cause for destruction;
therefore, it does not occur subsequently.
In this regard, what was stated—that destruction occurs in dependence upon the alteration of the persistence of that which has arisen—is incorrect.
To this, the following objection is raised:

"Since [destruction] exists when there is birth, because it occurs upon the destruction of substance and activity, and because of scripture and logical reasoning, destruction also has a cause. (Abhidh-d 141)
The proposition is that destruction has a cause.
Why? Because it occurs when there is arising;
for it was said by the Blessed One: "When this exists, that comes to be."
...up to: "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces.
Furthermore, when there is something subject to arising, there is destruction;
therefore, it has a cause.
Furthermore, for one who holds that [the self] is causeless, it would exist even prior to birth, and thus birth itself would not occur; for either of two contradictory states would necessarily arise.
Or, because there is no contradiction between those two, the designation of them as such would be untenable, and the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would lack their defining characteristic.
If it is argued that destruction is merely the non-existence of a phenomenon, we say no;
because that [non-existence] is preceded by its existence.
Since that non-existence is preceded by existence, it too possesses a cause.
If it is argued that "there is nothing at all," we say no; for it is impossible for existence to be incompatible with existence.
Furthermore, if non-existence were incompatible with existence, it would follow that non-existence itself becomes an entity.
If there were no contradiction, it would follow that existence is eternal; if both [existence and non-existence] were absent, it would be a mere verbal expression.
And what kind of linguistic formulation is this: "When something exists, it comes to be, and its qualifier is not contradictory to that"?
Furthermore, this linguistic formulation—"and yet nothing at all"—is incoherent.
This mode of expression is also purposeless;
therefore, existence and non-existence are merely verbal objects.
If it is argued that there must be an existent object to be negated by virtue of the power of the negation itself, [we reply: no.
It does not exist;
for, like the horn of a hare, the word is a mere redundancy, and because the meaning of a double negation is untenable.
Furthermore, it is because only the activity [of the dharma] has ceased.
Indeed, when contrary conditions are present, not even mere action arises; it perishes.
Therefore, the word "destruction" is not devoid of meaning.
Why so? From both scripture and logical reasoning.

For it was said by the Blessed One: “For the cessation of unwholesome states that have arisen. Likewise it was said: “In this case, a certain person is a killer of living beings,” and so forth in detail.
Similarly: “There are three destructions called fire, water, and wind, by which [the worlds] up to the Śubhakṛtsna realm are destroyed in succession.”
Likewise: "Old age and death have birth as their condition. This also refers to rebirth (*upapatti*), because otherwise it would follow that birth itself is without a cause.
If indeed destruction were causeless even when its existence is not [previously] present,
then birth too would be causeless; however, this is not so, because birth is observed only when the collection of causal factors capable of producing it is present.
If it is argued that this [moment] has a cause, we say no;
for the same applies to its destruction, since one must admit the presence of another sufficient causal complex for that as well.
Thus, the characteristics have been explained.
The sets of names and so forth must be explained.
Indeed, they need not be explained,
for they do not exist apart from sound.
Because there is an absence of action in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
this [treatise] is commenced for the purpose of demonstrating that:
"The actions of conveying their own meanings arise dependent upon the sounds of speech."
The three, beginning with name (nāman), are traditionally taught as having "perception" (saṃjñā) and so forth as their alternative names.
Indeed, name and the other [factors] are dissociated [from consciousness] and are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*);
speech, however, is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), meaning that it is speech, utterance, and etymological explanation (*nirukti*).
Furthermore, those [names and so forth] arise dependent upon that [speech], and their application to objects occurs dependent upon etymological explanation.
They serve as representatives for an object that possesses knowledge.
Etymology (*nirukti*) is indeed a designation (*saṃjñā*),
because objects do not possess a single [common] designation.

Just as the groups of visual consciousness and the others function in dependence upon the five objects such as visible form, so too do these [mental factors] have their birth dependent upon vocal sound.
Therefore it has been said: "Speech operates upon the name."
"It illuminates the meaning of the name. Thus, the phonemes *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and so forth, arise together with speech and are established by it.
If it is argued that there is an impossibility of denoting [the whole] because speech-sounds follow their respective phonetic qualities even though they possess constituent parts, we say no;
for when a collection of distinct sounds constitutes the cognition, the capacity to denote that [object] is established.
Furthermore, its existence is determined by its activity.
And what is this [activity] called?
It is the act of conveying its own meaning.
Because the relationship between a name and its object is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), each name conveys its respective object; such is their established doctrine (*kṛtānta*).
Furthermore, these have other names such as "name" (nāma) and "conceptualization" (saṃjñā).
Among them, a synonym for "name" is "the act of conceptualizing," as in the case of [the word] "pot.
A synonym for "phrase" (pada) is "sentence" (vākya).
For example, as in "the jar is seen.
In some cases, it is said that [a word] is that by which specific actions, qualities, and times are understood.
The Abhidharmikas maintain: "A *pada* is a collection of as many meaningful words as are required to complete the intended meaning."

[The opponent claims: "A syllable (*akṣara*) is a synonym for a phoneme (*vyañjana*), such as this syllable *ka*. It is partless, formless, non-obstructive, free from the characteristics of matter (*rūpa*), capable of conveying meaning across the three times, and possesses unimpeded movement like the mind.
[Response: No, because that is unproven (*asiddha*).

Indeed, names and the rest are not established as something other than the sound of speech. It is the sound of speech itself—limited by the conventions established by those who assign designations to objects—which, having its parts grasped through memory as a composite whole, conveys the meaning to the listener. What, then, is the use of postulating names and the rest?
To this, the following objection is raised:
Others, such as names and so forth, [are not sound] because they reveal their objects without reaching them; for sound is an accumulation of atoms,
and it would have to reveal its object by reaching it.
It is like a lamp:
it is not able to reach objects located in places such as heaven that are either unborn or already destroyed.
Therefore, you must accept that a word does not convey an object.
Furthermore, [the object is not momentary] because sequential and simultaneous cognition would be impossible.
How so? Like a *balvaja* mat.
For here, many *balvaja* substances, each individually incapable, come together and, existing in the form of a rope, become endowed with the capacity for the action of pulling wood and the like.

Furthermore, words whose nature is that of a sentence— consisting of a collection of parts grasped by the intellect and arising in a temporal sequence— are not individually capable of conveying meaning;
nor do they convey it collectively, because they cannot coexist simultaneously, like blades of grass tied together.
Therefore, it is established that words do not convey any meaning because they cannot convey it either successively or simultaneously.
Furthermore, this is so because the relationship between the signified and the signifier, and so forth, is untenable.
How? Like a lamp.

For example, a lamp in the darkness, possessing the power to manifest and to be manifested by objects such as a jar, is taken up by those who desire to see the jar; yet no word whatsoever is connected to any object by any specific relation such that, having grasped it, we might cause [that object] to be manifested.
In this regard, first of all:
There is no relationship between the signifier and the signified as there is between a lamp [and its object], because that which has not had a convention established for it cannot be made known.
Nor is there a relationship called conjunction, because such a thing is impossible between the existent and the non-existent.
And because it is a quality (*guṇatva*), it does not exist through a relation called inherence (*samavāya*) in anything whatsoever;
for this very reason, some [maintain] that it is because it is a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*).
Therefore, since a relationship such as that between the signified and the signifier is untenable, we have correctly stated what we previously declared: that "the word does not signify the object."
If it is argued that conventional speech is the mark for the communication of meaning, we say no;

because speech, being produced dependent upon vitarka and vicāra, is itself something yet to be established [as a cause], and because it is logically impossible for it to communicate meaning either successively or simultaneously.
If it is argued that memory directed toward each individual phoneme communicates the meaning, we say no.
Because it possesses the same fault and because the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is a general rule (*utsarga*).
If it is argued that it is a "refinement" (*saṃskāra*), we say no;
for it is unestablished (*asiddha*) and has already been answered.
Furthermore, because the faults to be mentioned later would follow if one were to accept these as being merely conventional sounds occurring by chance.
Now, are these sets of names (nāmakāya) and so forth permanent or impermanent?
They should be understood as impermanent.
The word "but" (tu) has the sense of a qualification for the doctrine of impermanence;
it is the reason (*hetu*). If one asks, "What [is that reason]?"—
Thus it is said:
"Because it elucidates the meaning through dependence. (Abhidh-d 143)
How so? Like cognition (*jñāna*).
Just as cognition manifests an object in dependence upon causes such as the eye, in the same way, names and so forth also convey meaning in dependence upon causes such as sound.
Therefore, because they convey meaning dependently, they are impermanent.
If, then, it is names and so forth that convey the meaning, how is it that even the learned say, "the word conveys the meaning"?
To this, it is replied:
A word that makes its own form known, as well as the phonemes and so forth, certainly conveys meaning; it is by way of metaphorical designation that it is called "expressive" by the wise.
For speech proceeds directly toward the name; the meaning is that it expresses the name.

But the name, in turn, illuminates the object. Thus, speech—which follows each phoneme while expressing the name and manifesting its own form—proceeds as a continuous stream and is described as making the object known through the conceptualization of qualities (*guṇakalpanā*).
However, the object is neither the denotation of the word nor its illumination.
For this reason as well, sound does not convey meaning:
because, being composed of the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*), the unity of the sound is not tenable;
yet it is asserted that "e and ai are produced from the throat and palate."
Furthermore, it is not tenable for a single atomic term to function across two distinct locations;
however, this is tenable for a collection of atoms.
Even individual atoms do not convey meaning on their own.
Regarding the existence or non-existence of the spatial directions, because that [collection] does not exist,
it is determined that even a collection, since it is not perceived by those standing in the middle, does not convey [the meaning] through either of the two extremes; furthermore,
a collection does not exist as something distinct from its constituent members.
"How will it cause the meaning to be understood?

[To this, the answer is: "The collection of past phonemes, which depends upon the final phoneme, whose own nature is grasped by the mental cognition (*manobuddhi*), and which produces a cognition regarding the related object, causes the understanding to occur"—this is a logical designation.
On this point, the Mīmāṃsakas and Grammarians raise an objection.
This is not so, because it is unestablished.
Indeed, the fact that sound consists of atoms is not established;
therefore, this is no answer.
To these two, it is replied:
"Because of its resistance, sound is indeed obstructed by walls, enclosures, and so forth; therefore, sound is resistant. This is not so.
It is unestablished;
for since you are proving what is already established, it is not [a case of] non-establishment.
Indeed, that which you seek to prove—the state of being composed of atoms—is unestablished by way of its being resistant; therefore, this is incorrect.
In this regard, the following is established:
its establishment is through obstruction and so forth.
This is established even for those who merely hold the plow-handle: when one is inside the inner sanctum and the door is closed, the drums being beaten and the conchs being blown are not heard;
yet by the roar of the *hūṇa* flute, the city walls are brought down. Therefore, this accomplishment of the unaccomplished is manifested by the accomplished rogue, and not by the unaccomplished.
As for what is said—that "the word is the *sphoṭa*, while sound (*dhvani*) is a quality of the word"—it is replied:
no eternal word called *sphoṭa* is established as distinct from the resonance (*ghoṣa*).
Therefore, "sound" (*dhvani*), "word" (*śabda*), and "*sphoṭa*" are not different things.
Just as "hasta," "kara," and "pāṇi" are well-known in the world as synonyms for the hand, therefore: "Because they function sequentially, no object is denoted by the word. (Abhidharmadīpa 146)
This has been previously revealed;
do not let it be forgotten.

As for what is said by the Grammarians— that sound is apprehended by the intellect— and by the Vaiśeṣikas as well— that it is apprehended by the auditory organ, and that even though one sound differs from another, properties such as "soundness" (śabdatva) are grasped by the ear;
regarding these two views, this is stated:
A sound is not heard by means of hearing, nor is there any other mode of apprehension for what is heard;
he who would say otherwise would be a laughingstock to the wise.
Thus, in common worldly usage, *dhvani* is the word whose referent is well-understood;

therefore, the established position is that others, such as names (*nāman*) and so forth, have all things as their objects. These [names and so on] are restricted or unrestricted according to the specific object they illuminate.
In this regard, those things expressed by noble etymological interpretation that have the twelve sense-bases as their object possess a fixed connection with their designations;
and some things expressed by worldly etymological interpretation also have fixed designations.
Both of these convey the meaning for one who has established the linguistic convention.
However, those names and so forth which are assigned by fathers and others according to their own whim are called "indeterminate" or "arbitrary," such as *ḍittha*,
*ḍavittha*, and the like.
But the primary [names] come into being only upon the appearance of a Buddha and not otherwise.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "From the arising of the Tathāgatas, there is the arising of the collections of names, phrases, and syllables.
From this definitive declaration, it is understood that the Buddha is omniscient.
For those [scriptures] that are authorless (*apauruṣeya*) and illuminate the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), aggregates (*skandha*), and so forth, are primarily the domain of the Buddha alone;
and because of his realization of them, the Blessed One is designated as "Omniscient" (*sarvajña*). These, moreover, are as follows:
Those called "sentient" belong to the desire and form realms; they are outflowing and neutral.
For these are indeed called "sentient," and whoever manifests them is endowed with them.
That which is illuminated [is not included].
These [sounds] belong to the realms of desire and form because their production is dependent upon vocal sound;
they are exclusively out-flowing (*naiṣyandika*) and non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Just as these [factors] such as name-and-form are,
so too are maturation, homogeneity, and acquisitions, which are of two kinds.
The third quarter of the second chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.
The second chapter is completed.
The third chapter; the fourth quarter;
...; the second [verse] of the second [section].

The third [destruction] belongs to the third [dhyāna]; the fourth dhyāna is the summit of the destruction by wind. Here it is asked: why does destruction not occur in the fourth dhyāna? To this it is said:
Because there is an absence of calamities caused by sentient beings, there is no [destruction] in the fourth [dhyāna] according to the Sūtra;
since the celestial palaces (vimāna) are equal and indestructible, how could there be impermanence?
In the fourth dhyāna, indeed, external and internal defects do not exist; therefore, no destruction is produced.
For in the first dhyāna, applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), which are like fire, exist as defects;
in the second, joy (prīti), which is like water, exists as a defect that captivates the mind.
In the third dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation consist of wind;
therefore, in whichever meditative attainment there is a specific internal defect, there is destruction by a corresponding external factor.
In the fourth [dhyāna], however, no external calamity occurs; therefore, there is no destruction (*saṃvartanī*). If that is so, then the fourth dhyāna must be attained eternally.
Why? Because of "the equality of the celestial palaces" (*vimānasya samatvasya*).
"Because it does not perish through the exhaustion of karma."
Furthermore, how do these destructions occur, and in what sequence? This is explained:
first, seven [destructions] occur by fire, followed by one by water; when seven [destructions] by water have passed, again...
One [destruction] is by fire through seven [successive cycles], and thereafter one by wind.
There are seven destructions by means of fire,
and the eighth is by means of water;
thus there is a cycle of seven.
When that set of seven has passed, there is again a set of seven [eons] by means of fire;
when that too has passed, destruction occurs through a single wind-catastrophe.
That wind-catastrophe, however, always occurs following the end of seven sets of seven eons of fire.
Taken together, these amount to fifty-six destructions by fire,
seven destructions by water,
and one destruction by wind.

What, then, is the reason that after the seven cycles of fire, there is only one cycle of wind? This is explained: Immediately following the seven cycles of fire, there is one of wind; thus, by the very taking up of the lifespan, it serves as the fuel for the lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna deities. (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 3.102)
And by doing so, the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* is brought into conformity: "The lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna gods is sixty-four kalpas."
Now, for what reason does the destruction by earth not occur?
The reason for this is stated here:
because they share the same nature as defects such as wind, they do not bring about the destruction of sentient beings.
Because it corresponds [to the internal], the destruction of the earth is not considered an "internal" destruction.

Just as the cutting of the vital points (*marmaccheda*) of sentient beings occurs through the three—wind, bile, and phlegm—which have the characteristic of the earth-element, so too is the earth destroyed by fire, water, and wind. Furthermore, these are its destroyers because they are directed toward its destruction.
Moreover, it is because of the similarity [of the external elements] to the internal ones, as indicated by the term "internal" (*ādhyātmika*).

Just as there are three internal disturbances of the mind characterized by applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), inhalation (*ucchvāsa*), and exhalation (*praśvāsa*), so too there are external calamities characterized by the violent agitation of fire, water, and wind.
The fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti* is completed.
The third chapter is completed.
The Fourth Chapter, First Section.
Now, as for that which was stated: "The wind-mandala is filled by the two-fold [force] called the karma of sentient beings"—let this be explained.
What are those actions, and how many are they? Therefore, actions are introduced [as follows]:
"Action is held to be the cause of the causes for the rebirth of sentient beings, which bring about either misfortune or prosperity, and which produce the diversity of the world. (Abhidh-d 154)

Indeed, it is observed that among sentient beings there is the acquisition of inferior, middling, or superior births, as well as the success or failure of their physical bases, enjoyments, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the diversity of these two kinds of worlds, karma is the cause.
Therefore, I shall explain their true nature.
As for what was also asked—namely, "Which ones? And how many?"—that shall now be explained in detail.
In the Sūtra, after pointing out two types of action, it was said: "There are two actions: volitional action (*cetanā-karman*) and action following intention (*cetayitvā-karman*).
These, moreover, have been stated to be three. How so? They are: that which belongs to the body, that which consists of speech, and that which is mental, called volition (*cetanā*).
These actions are the cause of the world; it is not Īśvara or other such factors.

Indeed, these three types of actions—wholesome and unwholesome—are the causes of benefit and harm for both kinds of worlds, the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world; they are the cause of their arising, their prosperity, and their diversity, and not [caused by] a Lord (īśvara), time (kāla), the primal person (puruṣa), primordial matter (pradhāna), or other such factors.
In this regard, how the Lord (Īśvara) is not the cause has already been mentioned; now, however, it is being made even more clearly manifest:
"Because of the diversity of forms, because of production in succession, and because of the consequence that other things would likewise [be the cause]."

If, indeed, a single, eternal Lord were the cause of the world's origination, maintenance, and dissolution, then—since an effect must conform to its cause—these three contradictory states would have to occur simultaneously. Yet this is neither observed nor accepted; therefore, this [position] is untenable.
Furthermore, the world would be devoid of variety;
everything would arise simultaneously, and one would wander about naked with a skull-bowl in hand, acting in accordance with that [creator's] will.
But this is not the case.
Therefore, Īśvara is not the cause.
If it is argued that the existence of Īśvara is established because of his superior status as a specific lord over villages and so forth, we say no;
for in the case of village officials and the like, one observes dependence on others, impermanence, and the obstruction of their capacity to perform other functions.
Furthermore, this is because of the statement in the *Gomayapiṇḍopama-sūtra*,
and because we observe the censure of that [Mahādeva] in the *Bhāgavata* and other texts;
for indeed, the followers of the *Bhāgavata* and others are seen censuring Maheśvara.
And as for the followers of Maheśvara [who say] "Viṣṇu":
if it is argued that he produces [the world] through the power of asceticism while depending upon a cause, to that it is replied:
The practice of austerity does not depend on anything else, because of faults such as the loss of one's own position.

If [it is argued that] he creates the world—like a potter creating pots and so forth—depending upon auxiliary causes and possessing sovereignty obtained through the power of asceticism (*tapas*), then this is not so;
for if this were the case, the refutation of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) would be established.
That which was stated—that [the Lord] is eternal, unitary, independent, and the cause—is thereby undermined.

Furthermore, if one accepts the efficacy of the power of austerity, one necessarily accepts impermanence and dependence; and by accepting those, one accepts a lack of sovereignty. By this, the positions that accept time, the person (puruṣa), primordial matter (pradhāna), or other such causes, should be understood as refuted.
If indeed karma is the cause and not Īśvara and the like, how then does the world grasp that [latter] as its cause? To this we reply:
The power of karmas is awakened by means of ritual injunctions, time, the planets, and so forth.
Therefore, the designation of those [other factors] by that same term is employed through figurative usage (gauṇyā vṛttyā).
As it has been said:
“Fate, ordinance, necessity, intrinsic nature, time, the planets, the Lord, karma, destiny, merits, fortune, and the conjunction with the end— these are synonyms for what was done in the past.”
Furthermore:
"The conjunction of planets, the throbbing of the limbs, dreams, full jars, and so forth— these indicate to men the attainment of the fruition of their own karma."
For this reason as well, that designation is applied to them.
Furthermore, how are these three types of action established?
If they were established by way of their basis, there would be only one type, because all of them are based upon the body.
If it were by way of intrinsic nature, then vocal action alone would be established;
if it were by way of origination, [then all three would be so].
The action of the mind alone is attained, because it is originated by all [three types of action]. "By all three as well," say the Vaibhāṣikas.
Furthermore, these first two types of action each have two subdivisions.
How so? That is explained as follows:
the former [two] consist of informative and non-informative [action].
Bodily action indeed consists of bodily intimation and bodily non-intimation; vocal action likewise consists of vocal intimation and vocal non-intimation;
but the third type of action—
Volition is mental action.
For it was said by the Blessed One: “Action is volition and having willed.
Furthermore, that [action] is said to be threefold: “bodily action, vocal action, and mental action.
Now, what is the intrinsic nature of this bodily action? Is it, first of all, of the same nature as the body?
He states this [question]: Is vocal action of the nature of speech, or is it something other than the body, just as mental action is other than the mind?
In the Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti, the first quarter of the fourth chapter;
[now] the second quarter of the fourth chapter.
It is taught that [virtue] perishes:
"Just as food is consumed by fire and the cooking pot is ruined, so too is the virtue of one whose mind is wounded by malice, envy, and the like, due to their evil view. (Abhidharmadīpa 159)
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate truth, monkhood consists in being endowed with both conventional and true vision;
conventionally, it requires the attainment of only one, but in the absence of both, it does not exist in either way.
Indeed, the perfection of ethical discipline purified by the perfection of view is "monkhood" in the ultimate sense; one who lacks either of these two is a monk only conventionally;
but one who lacks both is neither a monk conventionally nor in the ultimate sense.
If, indeed, the eight classes [of practitioners] are not established without the vow (*saṃvara*), how then [is it that the Blessed One said]: "one who practices a single part,
one who practices a limited portion..."?
Is this same meaning also seen here in the passage, "one who practices to a great extent" and "one who practices in its entirety"?
Indeed, there is someone who is capable of abstaining from only a portion of what should not be done.
Since some are capable of renouncing all immoral conduct,
for this reason the Blessed One teaches that one may be a lay follower (*upāsaka*) even by renouncing only a portion of what should not be done.

For no one who is deficient in all the moral precepts becomes a lay follower merely by the desire to go for refuge, just as a six-ingredient medicinal compound does not function if even one or two of its ingredients are missing.
Now, as for what was said—"one goes for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha"—who are these [entities] such as the Buddha? This is explained as follows:
the primary designation "Buddha" applies to knowledge that is free from obscuration.
The conceptualization of qualities should also be understood with respect to their basis and their fruit.

Indeed, the Buddha is twofold: from the perspective of conventional truth and from the perspective of ultimate truth. Regarding the latter, as it is stated in the treatise: "When one goes for refuge to the Buddha, to what does one go for refuge?
One goes for refuge to those very dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) which constitute a Buddha."
"For they are the signs and marks that serve as the grounds for the application of the term 'Buddha'.
Even among those [three], unobstructed knowledge is primary; thus, "the Omniscient One" is what is commonly known in the world, and this is the Buddha in the ultimate sense.
Even conventionally, the term "Buddha" is applied to the form-body (*rūpakāya*), which is resplendent with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, as it is their substratum;
and the term "Buddha" is also applied to the fruits thereof, such as the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and great compassion.
Because it is eternal and pure, and because all misfortunes have ceased,
Dharma is likewise called Nirvana according to the primary conceptualization.

Nirvana is the ultimate dharma because it maintains its own characteristic as eternally unchanging, and because it is maintained absolutely by those who have attained it. However, the path belonging to the mental continuums of Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas is the dharma through the conceptualization of qualities.
Furthermore, the three Piṭakas are the dharma because they lead to the attainment of Nirvana.
The Noble Ones, the qualities of the disciples, and likewise the Saṅgha from the perspective of ultimate truth:
the path that exists within the mental continua of the nine types of non-learners (*aśaikṣa*) and the eighteen types of learners (*śaikṣa*) disciples is called the ultimate Saṅgha.
Conventionally, however, it is designated as the "Saṅgha of monks consisting of ordinary persons and virtuous ones."
Whoever goes for refuge to these [three] goes for refuge to the Triple Gem.
One who goes for refuge to these collections of the Buddha's qualities, which possess the characteristics as previously described, is one "who goes for refuge to the Three Jewels."
Furthermore, what is the intrinsic nature of the goings for refuge?
Their intrinsic nature consists of vocal intimation and the dharmas originating from it.
What, then, is the meaning of "refuge"?
The meaning of refuge is the meaning of protection,
because by relying upon it, one is completely liberated from all suffering.
For it was said by the Blessed One: “Driven by fear, many people go for refuge to mountains and forests, to groves and sacred trees.”
This refuge is not the best; this refuge is not the supreme.
Having come to this refuge, one is not liberated from all suffering.
But he who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
when he perceives the Four Noble Truths with wisdom—
Suffering, the origin of suffering, the transcendence of suffering,
and the noble eightfold path that leads to the security of Nirvana.
“For this indeed is the best refuge; this is the supreme refuge.
By coming to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
For this very reason, the goings for refuge serve as the gateway to the undertaking of all vows.
Because they take root in one who is endowed with right view.

Furthermore, what is the reason that among the training precepts (*śikṣāpada*), abstinence from sexual misconduct alone is established for a lay follower (*upāsaka*), and not from all unchaste conduct? And why is lying alone, among other natural misdeeds (*prakṛtisāvadya*), established as a training precept?

Why is it that, among all the faults involving the abandonment of counteractive qualities—such as harsh speech and so forth—it is specifically from the drinking of intoxicants that abstention is established as a training precept? To this it is said:
Sexual misconduct is censured by the virtuous because it results in the failure to refrain from [harming] others.
False speech is [the most blameworthy] because of its extreme wickedness; drinking intoxicants [is so] because it causes the loss of mindfulness.
For sexual misconduct is exceedingly censured in the world because it violates the spouses of others and leads to rebirth in the miserable states;
sexual abstinence is not so [censured].
Furthermore, for a householder, abstaining from sexual misconduct is easy,
whereas abstaining from unchastity is difficult.
Moreover, a noble one (ārya) obtains the restraint of non-action regarding sexual misconduct even when transitioning to another birth, but not so regarding unchastity.

Even regarding false speech, the Blessed One, because of its extreme wickedness, spoke with the utmost gravity concerning Rāhula: "Rāhula, for one who feels no shame and no remorse in false speech, I declare that there is nothing they would not do.
Furthermore, in the drinking of intoxicants, there occurs a loss of mindfulness.

Because the disturbance of all the precepts occurs [thereby], the Blessed One did not permit the drinking of intoxicants—even as much as a drop on the tip of a blade of kusha grass—despite its being a fault by prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
Now this must be stated:
regarding these three—the Prātimokṣa, Dhyāna, and Anāsrava restraints—is it the case that from whatever [basis] one is obtained, the remaining ones are also obtained from that same basis? We reply:
the restraint born of desire (kāmaja) is obtained from all [bases], both those that are present and those that are of two kinds.
The Prātimokṣa restraint is indeed acquired from all present primary, preparatory, and consecutive aggregates, bases, and elements, because it proceeds with sentient beings as its basis;
it is not acquired from those that are past or future, because they are reckoned as non-sentient.
This applies to both types [of action].
The two types of wisdom consisting of cultivation are obtained from actions pertaining to sentient beings and non-sentient things,
as well as from those that are naturally reprehensible or reprehensible by prohibition,
and specifically from the fundamental [actions] of the three times.

For these two are obtained only from the fundamental paths of action (*maula-karmapatha*), not from the preliminary (*prayoga*) or subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages, nor from offenses of mere designation (*prajñapti-sāvadya*);
and they are obtained from all times—that is, even from the past and future aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, there is a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) in this regard.

“There are those aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) from which the Prātimokṣa restraint is obtained, but not the meditative (dhyāna) or the outflow-free (anāsrava) restraints,” and so forth in detail.
The first alternative (koṭi) refers to [restraint] from present preparatory (sāmantaka) and subsequent (pṛṣṭha) stages, and from offenses of prohibition (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya).
The second alternative refers to [restraint] from past and future fundamental paths of action (maula-karmapatha).
The third [case] refers to the fundamental paths of action in the present;
the fourth refers to the preliminary and subsequent stages of the past and future.
Furthermore, are these two— restraint and non-restraint— obtained only with respect to all sentient beings,
from all constituent parts, and by all causes? Or is there some distinction?
In that regard, it is necessarily obtained as follows:
restraint from all classes of sentient beings is [obtained] by way of its constituent parts and causes;
[but] from all the constituent parts of restraint and from sentient beings, it is not [obtained] by way of causes.

Indeed, restraint is obtained from all sentient beings, and not from only some of them. However, regarding the members [of the precepts], there is a distinction: some obtain the bhikṣu restraint from all [members], while others obtain it from four.
The other [type of restraint] is different;
for the paths of action are the constituent parts of the two types of restraint (saṃvara).
Furthermore, by some way of speaking, they are [constituted] by all the causes.
By which one?
First, how [is it] by all, if non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are accepted as the causes?
And how [is it] by one, if weak, medium, and intense states of mind are accepted as the causes?
The restriction is stated by way of the final alternative:

there is one who abides in restraint toward all sentient beings, yet is not restrained in all its parts nor for all its causes, being one who undertakes the lay follower’s restraint, the one-day precept, or the novice monk’s restraint with a weak, middling, or intense mind.

There is one who, with respect to all sentient beings, is restrained in all limbs but not by all causes, when he undertakes the bhikṣu restraint with a weak, middling, or superior mind. There is one who, with respect to all sentient beings, is restrained in all limbs and by all causes, when he undertakes the three types of restraints with the three kinds of minds.

There is [a type of restraint] that exists toward all sentient beings and by means of all causes, but not by means of all limbs, which one undertakes with weak, medium, or intense states of mind regarding the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), the fasting day (*upavāsa*), or a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*).

However, there is no such [restraint] that does not exist toward all sentient beings; for one obtains the restraint by abiding in a virtuous intention (*kalyāṇāśaya*) that extends to all sentient beings, and not otherwise, because a sinful intention would not have ceased.
One who makes five restrictions obtains the Prātimokṣa restraint.

These are the restrictions of sentient being, limb, place, time, and occasion: "I refrain from this particular sentient being" is the restriction of sentient being; "from this particular limb" is the restriction of limb.
"In that place" is the restriction of location;
"for as long as a month, etc. is the restriction of time;
"except in battle" is the restriction of occasion.
If one were to accept it in such a manner, it would be merely good conduct (*sucarita*) and not restraint (*saṃvara*).
How is it that restraint is obtained with respect to things that are impossible [to avoid]?
Because one undertakes it with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) not to harm the life of any sentient being.
It has been explained how restraint is obtained.

Non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) also extends toward all sentient beings and all paths of action (*karmapatha*), but not through all causes simultaneously, because a weak or other [degrees of] mind cannot exist at once.
Who, then, are those who possess non-restraint?

Shepherds, poultry-keepers, pig-breeders, bird-catchers, fishermen, deer-hunters, thieves, executioners, prison wardens, elephant-trappers, dog-cookers, netters; kings, administrators of punishment, judges, those who have strayed from morality, and those who are unmerciful.
They are called *asaṃvarika* because they exist in non-restraint, or because non-restraint exists within them.

It has been stated from whom non-restraint (asaṃvara) is acquired; however, it was not explained how that acquisition occurs, so it is now begun: "The attainment of non-restraint is through action or through formal undertaking."
Non-informative [action] arises from other [causes] due to the distinction of the field, the constituent parts, and so forth.
Non-restraint is acquired through two causes:
either by action or by formal undertaking.
It is acquired by action through being born into such a family and performing such deeds.
"Even we, though not born into that family, shall live by this livelihood.
As for the acquisition of the remaining non-informative [karma] (*avijñapti*), it arises from the excellence of the field (*kṣetra*) and the excellence of the limb (*aṅga*).
Or, the field is of such a nature that non-informative karma arises merely by the act of planting in a grove and so forth.
Just as in the case of the bases of meritorious action consisting of material things,
one undertakes it with reverence,
thinking: "I shall not eat without having paid homage to the Buddha."
"I shall always perform [the practice] for a month or half a month," and so forth;
or, with such earnestness, one strives to perform a wholesome or unwholesome action from which its informative intimation (*vijñapti*) arises.
Thus has been explained how the acquisition of restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) occurs.
The relinquishment [of vows] must now be explained.
In that regard, first:
the relinquishment of the restraint pertaining to the desire realm occurs through the abandonment of the training and so forth.
Some say that [the path] is also for those who have committed a defeat; others say it is not so, because of its incompatibility.
The abandonment of the eightfold restraint pertaining to the desire realm occurs through five causes:

the renunciation of the training, the loss of the community membership (*nikāyasabhāga*), the appearance of both sexual organs, and the severance of the roots of wholesome merit; and for the eighth [type], by the passing of the night.
These, when combined, constitute five [causes].
Furthermore, what is the reason that these [vows] are abandoned?

It is because of the arising of an informative act (*vijñapti*) contrary to the undertaking, the abandonment of the basis (*āśraya*), the corruption of the basis, the cutting off of the cause (*nidāna*), and the projection [of the vow] being limited to that duration.
Others, however, say: "The abandonment of the vows of a monk or a novice occurs through any one of the four defeats (*patanīya*)."
"It is not so," because it is "due to non-connection. What, then, is this non-connection?
Non-connection means that the substance of the cloth does not perish from the destruction of the threads.
For the destruction of the whole does not necessarily follow from the destruction of its parts;
yet the Prātimokṣa restraint is of the nature of a whole.
Through the disturbance of its parts, it becomes perforated and defiled.

As it was said by the Blessed One: "He is immoral and possesses evil qualities. If it is argued that this is incorrect because it contradicts the Sūtras, they explain here: "In the Sūtra, the statement regarding destruction has another meaning, as in the case of envy, deceit, and so forth. (Abhidh-d 169)
In this regard, the Blessed One stated, "He ceases to be a monk," for the sake of maintaining the stability of the teaching and for the sake of censuring disciples of evil conduct.
As it is said: "One who is envious, stingy, deceitful, fraudulent, possessed of false views, and endowed with such faults—one who is of a rotten nature, a wicked monk—must be expelled.
Furthermore, it has been stated by those who know the reality of the purpose of the teaching and its disciples that one does not cease to be a monk merely because of the corruption of the mind.
The same should be understood here as well.
Therefore, a monk possesses only the characteristics previously described, and not as the author of the *Kośa* asserts:
"Due to the disappearance of the True Dharma, there are others [who are monks], but not because of the non-attainment of what was not previously attained."
Others, however, say that even upon the disappearance of the True Dharma, there is a relinquishing of the restraint;
but that is not so,
because at that time, what has not previously arisen does not arise.
But once arisen, it perishes by the very same causes already described.
Now, how is there the relinquishing of the meditative and the untainted restraints?
This is explained as follows:
"The wholesome [state] born of meditation is relinquished by changing levels and by falling away. (Abhidharmadīpa 170)
Indeed, all wholesome states attained through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are abandoned for two reasons:
either through rebirth by moving from one level to another— either upward or downward—
or through falling away (*parihāṇi*).
And because of the abandonment of the homogeneous class of the meditative attainment.
Likewise, the wholesome [state] attained in the formless realm is abandoned through the attainment of a fruit, the acquisition of a faculty, or through falling away;
just as the wholesome [state] attained in the form realm is abandoned by means of changing levels and falling away, so too is that attained in the formless realm.
However, the noble wholesome [state] is abandoned by three causes.
Through the attainment of a fruit, the previous path is abandoned;
through the refinement of the faculties (*akṣottāpana*), the path of dull faculties is abandoned; and through falling away (*parihāṇi*), the subsequent path is abandoned.
The fruit, or that which is distinguished by the fruit—
thus, in this way, restraint (saṃvara) is abandoned. Non-restraint (asaṃvara), however, is lost through the attainment of self-control, the relinquishing of life, and so forth.
The abandonment of non-restraint occurs through three causes:
through the attainment of restraint;
that is, if one enters into restraint or acquires meditative restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara) by obtaining concentration through the power of causes and conditions, non-restraint is thereby relinquished.
Because the opposing force is stronger;
because death causes the abandonment of the physical basis;
and because the emergence of both sexual organs causes the disintegration of the physical basis.
Even when one renounces weapons and water, there is no severance of non-restraint (asaṃvara) without a formal vow (saṃvara), because of the underlying intention not to act;
it is like the failure to cure a chronic disease merely by avoiding its causes.
Now, how is non-informative action (*avijñapti*) that is distinct from both restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) abandoned? This is explained:
"But the intermediate [non-informative action] is abandoned through the interruption of the impulse of the mind and so forth.
Indeed, because that impulse of faith or affliction by which the non-informative action was projected is interrupted, it too is interrupted.
It is like the motion of a potter’s wheel;
it is also interrupted by the abandonment of the formal undertaking,
and it is also interrupted by the cessation of the activity.
It is severed by the loss of objects such as shrines, monasteries, and fields;
it is also severed by the loss of life-span and the severance of the roots of merit.
That which is called "wholesome" pertaining to the desire realm is [severed] by these three: the cutting of the roots and so forth.
Furthermore, wholesome states of the desire realm that are immaterial in nature are abandoned for two reasons:
through the total severance of the roots of virtue,
and through rebirth in the form or formless realms.
The afflicted [states] belonging to the three realms are abandoned through the arising of their antidotes.
Indeed, all afflicted states that have a non-material nature are abandoned solely through the arising of their antidotes.
For whichever type of secondary affliction there is a specific path of abandonment, [that path effects its removal].
Therefore, he is abandoned along with his retinue; it cannot be otherwise.
Now, for which beings is there non-restraint (asaṃvara), and for which is there restraint (saṃvara)? This is explained:
"In all [realms] of desire, two; in the form [realm], two; one in the formless [realms], by way of acquisition."
Indeed, excluding all eunuchs, paṇḍakas, and so forth, as well as the inhabitants of Kuru,
restraint exists even among the gods;
thus, in these two destinies, both restraint and non-restraint are found.
"Not elsewhere."
Now we shall provide a detailed exposition of the actions (karma) mentioned in the Sūtra concerning their scope and so forth.
For it is said in the Sūtra: “There are three types of action: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Their characteristics are stated as follows:
Action that yields a desirable fruit is declared to be wholesome (*kuśala*);
