by the opposite [it is] unwholesome (*akuśala*), and other than these, it is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
That which indeed has a desirable maturation and leads to the attainment of nirvāṇa— either for a time or ultimately— by means of protecting one from suffering, that is wholesome (*kuśala*).
This is also an etymological derivation (*nirukti*):
because it brings about the forms of blameless gods and humans, like the forms brought about by a skilled painter;
this application of the word "wholesome" (*kuśala*) is based on a metaphorical comparison.
Just as a trained man who cuts kuśa grass with unblemished hands is designated as "skilled" (*kuśala*), so too one who performs another action without distortion is called "skilled.
By contrast, that which is the opposite is "unskillful" (*akuśala*).
Like camels, owls, and so forth;
"it is indeterminate because it is otherwise," since it does not produce both types of maturation.
Three other types of karma have also been taught:
meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable.
Regarding these, first:
The first [type of] merit belongs to the realm of desire; demerit is of an unwholesome nature.
That which pertains to the higher stages is "imperturbable" (āneñja), because it does not shake with respect to its maturation (vipāka).
For wholesome karma belonging to the desire realm is called "meritorious," while unwholesome karma is called "non-meritorious.
Karma belonging to the higher stages is called "imperturbable" (*āneñja*). Beyond that, in the two realms [of form and formlessness], wholesome karma is called "imperturbable."
Why, then, is this called "imperturbable" (*āneñjya*)?
Because it does not shake with respect to its maturation (*vipāka*).
For karma belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) [does shake] with respect to its maturation.
It fluctuates according to the principle of the *Lavaṇopama-sūtra*.
How so? Because there is no fixed rule;
for even karma belonging to one destiny may ripen in another destiny.
That which belongs to one class of gods may [also] belong to another class of gods;

for indeed, whatever karma conducive to size, strength, complexion, pleasure, enjoyments, and so forth would ripen among the gods, that very same karma sometimes ripens among humans, animals, or hungry ghosts due to the power of other conditions.
This is an exhortation regarding the *jāti* (class) of karma intended by the Blessed One, not an exhortation regarding the *dravya* (substantial entity).

Here he says: But surely the three dhyānas were described by the Blessed One as "subject to fluctuation" (*señjita*), in such passages as: "That which is here thought out (*vitarkita*) and deliberated upon (*vicārita*), this the Noble Ones call 'fluctuation' in this state," and so forth?
This was said with reference to their defects as meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). However, they are also described as "unshakable" (*āneñja*) in the *Āneñjasūtra*.
Beginning with the practice that leads to the state free from agitation.

Furthermore, three other types of karma are taught: "that to be experienced as pleasure, that to be experienced as pain, and that to be experienced as neither-pain-nor-pleasure. Among these, karma to be experienced as pleasure is wholesome karma from below the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.
It is to be experienced as equanimity elsewhere; however, that which is evil is to be experienced as suffering.
In that regard, wholesome karma up to the third dhyāna is said to be "to be experienced as pleasure.
Indeed, this much is the range of pleasant feeling.
From the fourth dhyāna onwards, that same [karma] is said to be "to be experienced as equanimity."
Unwholesome karma, however, is said to be "to be experienced as suffering. But is feeling itself the maturation? No, he says;
this is an explanation given in terms of what is predominant.
For happiness is intended as that which consists of the accumulation of four aggregates.
However, for the Dārṣṭāntikas, only pleasant feeling is maturation (*vipāka*), and only volition (*cetanā*) is karma.
For the Ābhidharmikas, however, the five aggregates are the cause of maturation, and the five aggregates themselves are the maturation.
But how, again, is karma that does not have feeling as its intrinsic nature said to be "to be experienced as pleasure"?
It is "to be experienced as pleasure" because it is beneficial to pleasant feeling;
or, it is so called because its maturation is to be experienced as pleasant.
But is it the case that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling does not exist below the fourth dhyāna?
Indeed, it is not that it does not exist. What then?
Even below, there is intermediate karma; for by means of dhyāna, even in the last [dhyāna], there is cessation.
Because it is accepted that there is simultaneous fruition of three [karmas], and because of the fruition of the intermediate dhyāna.
Indeed, karma to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant exists not only from the fourth dhyāna downwards, but also in the third, second, and first dhyānas.
Furthermore, one attains parinirvāṇa while abiding in equanimity after [the body] has attained parinirvāṇa.
Moreover, it is because the simultaneous maturation of the three types of results is desired.

For it has been said: "Could there be a ripening of three types of karma that occurs neither before nor after? It could: [the ripening] of karma to be experienced as pleasure would be form; [the ripening] of karma to be experienced as suffering would be the mental states and mental factors."
"Those associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are dissociated from the mind.
For this reason as well, there exists karma to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant even in the lower realms.
Furthermore, [it exists] because of the maturation of the intermediate dhyāna.
For in the intermediate dhyāna, no maturation other than equanimity matures as a feeling,
because of the absence of pleasure and pain therein.
Furthermore, action is fourfold, distinguished as that to be experienced in the present life and so forth.
This action, in brief, is of two kinds:
that which is determinate in its experience and that which is indeterminate in its experience.
In that regard, karma to be experienced with certainty (*niyatavedanīya*) is of three kinds:

karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*), and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*). These three types of karma constitute karma to be experienced with certainty; the fourth is karma to be experienced without certainty (*aniyatavedanīya*).
Among these, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) ripens in the very same birth in which it was performed;
karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) ripens in the second birth; and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) ripens from that point onward.
Therefore, among the four types of karma, by which one is birth projected?
Birth is projected by three [types of karma], excluding that which is called "pertaining to the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma*).
Indeed, the group-homogeneity (nikāyasabhāga) is not projected by karma to be experienced in the present life.
Now, in which realm or in which destiny is how many kinds of karma projected?
The projection of all four [kinds of karma] occurs everywhere except in hell;
for there is no ripening of wholesome [karma] there, due to the absence of desirable results.

Indeed, in all three realms and in all five destinies— with the exception of the hells— there is the projection of all four types of karma, both wholesome and unwholesome. For in the hells, wholesome karma to be experienced in the present life is not projected.

In that regard, because there is no desirable maturation (*vipāka*), another threefold [karma] is projected. Furthermore: "An ordinary person who is detached from it does not create karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*); a stable noble one (*ārya*) does not create [karma] for other [existences]; and even a wavering [noble one] does not [create karma] for the two roots of existence (*bhava-mūla*). (Abhidharmadīpa 180)

For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has become detached from a particular stage (*bhūmi*) becomes stable and possesses the quality of non-retrogression; he does not project karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedya*) in that stage, though he performs the other three types of karma.

An noble person (*āryapudgala*), however, being free from passion and not subject to retrogression, does not perform karma to be experienced upon rebirth or karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) in that stage.
For such a person is no longer capable of returning again to a lower level;

however, they may perform indeterminate karma that is to be experienced in the present life, specifically in the realm where they have been reborn—namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Furthermore, even a noble one (*ārya*) of the nature of falling away who has become free from passion for the desire realm, [is incapable of returning].
Or from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*);
it is impossible for those two to perform karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) or in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
What is the reason?
For he has fallen away from the fruit,
and there is no passing away for one who has fallen away from the fruit.
Now, does one in the intermediate state project karma, or does he not project it?
He says that it projects [rebirth].
In that regard, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) projects twenty-two types of karma:
the five stages of the womb (*garbhāvasthā*), namely the stages of the *kalala*, *arbuda*, *ghana*, *peśī*, and *praśākhā*.
There are five states of birth:
the states of infancy, childhood, youth, middle age, and old age.
These are projected as twenty through the distinction between those that are determinate and those that are indeterminate.
Because they belong to the same category (*nikāya*),
for this very reason, karma to be experienced in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not mentioned separately;
for it is projected by the very same [karma] that is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*).
Furthermore, what kind of karma is determinate and what is indeterminate?
That karma which is repeatedly practiced with a mind of intense passion or cruelty,
and that which is performed toward a "good field" (satkṣetra)— the fruit of these is determined.
If an action is performed with a fierce mind accompanied by intense afflictions,
or if it is performed while sprinkled with the water of thick faith,
or even if it is slight but practiced repeatedly;
Whatever wholesome or unwholesome action is performed in a field of merit, the fruit of that karma is determined accordingly.
Now, it is asked: what kind of action is that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*)?
It is said: "Due to the excellence of the field (*kṣetra*) and the intention (*āśaya*), the fruit ripens immediately;
and for one who has just emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and so forth, there is the operation of the fruit at once. (Abhidh-d 182)
In that regard, [the excellence of] the field is as in the *Daṇḍa-jātaka* and others;
[the excellence of] the intention is as in the *Bakala-jātaka*.
[This applies] to the liberation from sorrow and so forth.
But in what kind of field is that [merit] distinguished, such that its maturation ripens in the present life?
First, it is the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
"And for one who has just emerged from cessation [samāpatti] and so forth, there is the production of results at that very moment;

furthermore, among five types of persons—those who have emerged from the attainment of cessation, from non-contention, from loving-kindness, from the path of seeing, or from the fruit of arhatship—benefits and harms result in fruits to be experienced in the present life.
Indeed, one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation attains supreme peace."
Because one experiences dharmas similar to nirvāṇa,

even for one who has emerged from the concentration of non-affliction (*araṇā*), the mental continuum proceeds as it does when motivated by the resolute intention to benefit immeasurable sentient beings;
the same is true for one who has emerged from the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Because even one who has fallen into the stream of saṃsāra attains stainless knowledge,
and because even an Arhat has abandoned all afflictions, they exist in a stainless state.

Furthermore, when there is absolute detachment from the stage (bhūmi) to which a karma of fixed maturation— whether wholesome or unwholesome— belongs, that karma ripens in the present life; therefore,
because of the non-rearising [of rebirth] in that stage,
it is subsumed under "to-be-experienced-in-the-present-life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
Furthermore, what kind of action is this? It is that which is fixed as to its maturation; and this action should be understood as being fixed as to its maturation.
And one should know that this has a visible fruit;
indeed, its ripening matures within the present life (*dṛṣṭadharme*).
But what, then, is this?
This karma is the completing [cause].
It is not that which projects [the rebirth].
Since maturation (*vipāka*) is indeed primarily characterized by feeling (*vedanā*), this is investigated:
could there be a maturation of karma that is exclusively mental feeling and not bodily? Could there be one that is exclusively bodily and not mental? To this, he says:
The maturation of wholesome [karma] that is without investigation is exclusively mental feeling;
however, the bodily feeling resulting from karma to be experienced as suffering is desired [to be the maturation].
Wholesome karma that is indeed without investigation (avīcāra) exists from the intermediate dhyāna up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
The retribution (vipāka) of that wholesome karma without investigation is exclusively mental feeling.
Why is it not bodily?
Because that [unwholesome karma] necessarily possesses both vitarka and vicāra,
the ripening of unwholesome karma consisting of bodily suffering is exclusively bodily feeling. Why is it not mental?
For mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*).
If that is so, how is the feeling associated with the derangement of the minds of sentient beings—which occurs through the power of karma—not a maturation?
It is because in that case, the mind itself is not the maturation of karma.
What then? That which is the disturbance of the great elements is the ripening (*vipāka*);
therefore, the mind born from that is metaphorically designated by the term "ripening."
Furthermore, four kinds of karma have been taught: "There is black karma with black ripening; there is white karma with white ripening;
there is black-and-white karma with black-and-white ripening."

"There is action that is neither black nor white, which has no ripening [of fruit], and which leads to the destruction of action. Regarding this: "In the desire realm, impure action with ripening is black; action born of the form realm with ripening is white. Pure action, which effects the abandonment of those two, is of two kinds [black and white] in the desire realm. (Abhidharmadīpa 185)
Indeed, unwholesome karma is exclusively black because it is afflicted;
and it has a black ripening because its ripening is disagreeable.
However, that which belongs to the realm of form (rūpāpta) which is wholesome is exclusively white.
Because it is not interspersed with the unwholesome,
and because its ripening is white due to the desirability of its ripening.
Why is that which belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyāpta*) not mentioned?
For it is there that two kinds of maturation are found— namely, that pertaining to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and that pertaining to the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*)—
and it is precisely in that context that the threefold action of body, speech, and mind is described:
"The white action belonging to the desire realm is black-and-white because it is interspersed with the unwholesome."
It has both black and white ripening because its ripening is intermingled.

This is established from the perspective of the continuum (*santāna*), not by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); for there is no such karma or ripening that is simultaneously black and white, due to their mutual contradiction.
But if this were so, would not unwholesome karma also become black-and-white because it is interspersed with the wholesome?
Not necessarily; unwholesome karma is not invariably interspersed with the wholesome.
However, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because the unwholesome is powerful, it is the wholesome that is interspersed due to its weakness.
Untainted (*anāsrava*) karma leads to the exhaustion and abandonment of these three types of karma.

For it is neither black, because it is undefiled, nor white, because it lacks the whiteness of maturation (*vipāka*). Furthermore, this term "white" is used here with a specific underlying intention (*ābhiprāyika*).
However, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra* with reference to the qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*):
"Ānanda,
these dharmas are exclusively white and exclusively blameless."
And in the Śāstra it is said: "What are the white dharmas? They are the wholesome dharmas and the unobscured-neutral ones."
It is without ripening because it does not fall within the realms of existence and because it opposes the process of cyclic existence.
Furthermore, does all untainted (anāsrava) karma lead to the destruction of all three types of karma?
It is said: no. What then?
The four paths of seeing constitute the path of vision;
the paths of immediate succession in the desire realm constitute the path of cultivation. This [action] is what destroys black karma.
But that volition which exists in the ninth [path of liberation] is the destroyer of both black and white karma;
however, for the white [karma], it exists in the paths of immediate succession within each dhyāna.

In that regard, first, on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the twelvefold volition (*cetanā*) present in the four receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and in the eight uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) of detachment from the desire realm is that which effects the abandonment of black karma; this volition, to be understood as occurring in the uninterrupted path of detachment from the desire realm, is that which effects the destruction of both black and white karma.
However, in each meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), the fourfold volition present in the final uninterrupted path is that which destroys white karma.
What, then, is the reason that wholesome karma is abandoned only by the final path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and not by any other?
It is because its abandonment is not an abandonment of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for even when it has been abandoned, it can still manifest.
What, then, is it? It is through the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that have that [karma] as their object.
Therefore, as long as even a single type of affliction having that as its object remains, the abandonment of that [object] is not found;
and this is incorrect.
For that [defilement] has been abandoned, but it is not lost;
therefore, it manifests. This point is established.
It is said in the Sūtra: "There are three types of misconduct:
misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; likewise for good conduct."
What is their intrinsic nature?
In that regard, first:
all unwholesome action of body and so forth is considered misconduct (*duścarita*).
"Everything" means including the preliminary, the fundamental, and the subsequent stages.
Furthermore, the three beginning with covetousness constitute the three types of mental misconduct.
All unwholesome bodily action is misconduct of body;
likewise for misconduct of speech and mind.
Furthermore, although covetousness and so forth do not have the nature of action (*karma*), they do have the nature of mental misconduct.
“Covetousness and the others alone are of the nature of karma,” so say the Sthitibhāgīyas.
But that is not so, because of the fault of conflating karma with the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Sthitibhāgīyas are [a group of] Śākyas.
Those known by the second name, Lāṅgūlika,
maintain that covetousness and the other [non-virtues] have the nature of mental action (*manaskarma*).
For them, it follows that there is a confusion between karma and affliction (*kleśa*) as being one and the same.
The Kośakāra says: "What is the fault here?
If some affliction were also karma, then a crow would be a crane.

Furthermore, by conceptualizing a unity among afflictions and karmas—which are distinguished by their absolute differences in intrinsic nature, power, activity, and fruit—one would be accepting the views of the Sāṃkhyas and others."
By the word "also" (*api*), the three crookednesses (*vaṅka*), the three faults (*doṣa*), and the three stains (*kaṣāya*) mentioned in the Sūtra are further drawn in here.
Their characteristics, in due order, are as follows:
bodily action born of deceit is called "crookedness of body" (*kāyavaṅka*).
Because they belong to a crooked lineage,
speech and mental action born of deceit are called the crookedness of speech and mind.
Furthermore, those same three [actions] born of hatred are designated as the faults.
Because it follows from a corruption of the mind;
furthermore, bodily action born of attachment is called "bodily turbidity" because its nature is that of passion. In the same way, the turbidities of speech and mind are to be understood.
Furthermore, those three wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind should be understood as the three types of good conduct (*sucarita*).
These same three are called the three purities (*śauceya*).
In the mental continuum of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they are called the three silences (*mauneya*).

In this context, good conduct of body is the silence of body (*kāyamauneya*), and good conduct of speech is the silence of speech (*vāṅmauneya*); however, it is the mind itself that is designated as "the sage" (*muni*) due to the cessation of false intentions.
For through the cessation of that [mind], the conceptual chatter of body and speech comes to cease.
The etymological derivation (*nirukti*) is: "this belongs to the sage (*muni*), therefore it is 'silence' (*mauneya*). (Jaini_151)
Why, then, are the states of silence (mauneya) attributed only to the Arhat? Because he is a sage in the ultimate sense.
Indeed, he is called a sage because of the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (jalpa) consisting of the afflictions (kleśa).

Furthermore, this teaching on *mauneya* (sagehood) and *śauceya* (purity) was taught with reference to those who are devoted to false sagehood and purity; therefore, it is now set forth together with that [false] sagehood and purity.
That which is auspicious, beginning with non-covetousness and so forth, is called the three types of good conduct (*sucarita*).
This [threefold] conduct constitutes the root of two kinds of karma; the paths [of action] are ten, both auspicious and inauspicious.

Furthermore, these two categories known as good conduct (*sucarita*) and bad conduct (*duścarita*) consist of the ten wholesome and unwholesome paths of action (*karmapatha*), excluding their preliminary (*prayoga*) and subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages.
Among these, a portion of good bodily conduct consists of abstaining from intoxicants and so forth, giving, making offerings, and the like;
while that of good vocal conduct consists of pleasant speech and the like.
The wholesome volition of mental good conduct;
likewise, the bodily misconduct consists of the preliminary and subsequent stages of depriving others of life, wealth, or spouse;
and the verbal misconduct consists of harsh speech and so forth.
The unwholesome mental action that constitutes misconduct of mind is not included [among the primary paths of action] because it is not particularly gross;

however, that which is called the fundamental path of action consisting of abstaining from killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct is wholesome, because its grossness results in the most excellent fruit of great benefit.
However, that bodily movement which consists of seizing the life, wealth, or the wives of others is the fundamental [action], and it is an unwholesome path of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*).
In this same way, the other [paths of action] are to be understood according to their respective possibilities.
The second quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.
The third quarter of the fourth chapter.
This must now be explained:

Of these ten paths of action, how many have the nature of informative intimation (*vijñapti*), how many have the nature of non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*), and how many have the nature of both?
First, regarding the unwholesome ones:
The six [unmanifest actions] caused [to be performed] are also made into six by way of their two natures;
therein are killing, taking what is not given, false speech, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter.
These are not necessarily of the nature of manifest action (*vijñapti*).
For one who causes another to act, there is an absence of the fundamental informative intimation (*maulī-vijñapti*);
however, sexual misconduct is always twofold in nature, because it cannot be accomplished by means of another.
Those [actions] are also "sixfold" in that when one personally performs the six courses of action, such as taking life and so forth, they become twofold in nature,
because their intrinsic nature consists of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) form.
Furthermore, among the wholesome [factors], seven are to be known as twofold; those that are concentrated are to be known as onefold.
Indeed, the seven wholesome courses of action (karmapatha) that possess form are twofold,
because the morality of one in meditative absorption (samāhita-śīla) depends upon informative intimation (vijñapti).
However, those comprised within the dhyāna-restraint and the outflow-free (anāsrava) restraint have exclusively non-informative (avijñapti) as their intrinsic nature.
Because there is no manifest action for one who is in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
Regarding the non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) that exists in the preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*), it is the reverse in the subsequent stages (*pṛṣṭha*).
Indeed, when the preliminary stage begins its preparatory application (*prayoga*) with intense obsession (*paryavasthāna*), [it is accompanied by non-manifest action].
At that time, it is of two natures depending on whether it is through faith or intense passion;
when it is weak, it is merely informative action (*vijñapti*).
Conversely, in the subsequent [moments], there is necessarily non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
If, however, after having performed the course of action, one continues to exert effort therein, there would also be informative action (*vijñapti*).
But when one deprives [the victim] of life by means of a violent blow,
the informative action at that moment and the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) of that same moment constitute the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*).
For one is touched by the fault of taking life due to two causes:
through the preliminary effort and through the completion of the result.
Beyond that, the moments of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) constitute the aftermath (*pṛṣṭha*).
As long as one slaughters the animal, skins it, cleans it, sells it, cooks it, eats it, and praises it—
if even its moments of informative action (*vijñapti*) constitute the "consequent" (*pṛṣṭha*),
then the same should be applied to other cases as well, according to what is appropriate.
For covetousness and the other [unwholesome roots], there is neither preliminary application nor subsequent action; they constitute paths of action by their mere manifestation.
As the Blessed One said in the Sūtra: "Monks, taking life is threefold: born of greed, born of hatred, and born of delusion."
"up to and including wrong view.
Among these paths of action, some reach completion through greed,
while others do so through hatred.
For some it arises through delusion;
however, for all,
the application originates from the three roots.
Their preparatory action arises from the three unwholesome roots.

Among these, killing born of greed occurs, for example, by hunters, butchers, fishermen, fowlers, and the like, for the sake of their body parts. Killing born of hatred occurs, for instance, for the purpose of retaliating against an enemy.
That born of delusion belongs to those who perform sacrifices out of a sense of duty, to kings who kill out of trust in the authority of legal reciters,
and to the Persians and others who strike their mothers and fathers out of a sense of duty.
That born of greed is the taking of what is not given by one who steals it because he desires that object.
That born of hatred is for the sake of revenge;
that born of delusion is, for example, when kings act according to the authority of legal experts (*dharmapāṭhaka*) for the purpose of punishing those seen [to be at fault].
And as wicked Brāhmaṇas say: "All this was given by Prajāpati to the Brāhmaṇas; it is only through the weakness of the Brāhmaṇas that the *vṛṣalas* enjoy it."
"Therefore, when a Brahmin takes what belongs to another, he merely takes his own; he clothes himself in his own storehouse; it is his own that he gives.

Sexual misconduct born of greed consists of unchaste conduct toward the wives of others and so forth, due to passionate attachment to them. That born of hatred is for the purpose of retaliating against an enemy.
An example of that born of delusion is the sexual intercourse with one's mother and so forth among the Persians;
and in the Gosava sacrifice: "The Upahā drinks water, chews grass, and..."
"He approaches his mother, his sister, and women of the same clan.
False speech and the other [non-virtues] arise from greed and hatred as previously explained.
False speech arising from delusion is as it has been said:
“O King, a lie does not cause harm when joined with jest, nor among women, nor at the time of marriage;
nor when life is at stake, nor when all one's wealth is being seized.”

"They say that five kinds of falsehoods are not sinful. However, slander and the others are born of delusion (*moha*), being incited by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); so too is the prattle of false treatises such as the Vedas.
Covetousness and the others are born from the three roots [of greed, hatred, and delusion]. (Abhidharmadīpa 191)
Covetousness and the others, however, because they arise immediately after greed, are born from the three roots.
Thus have the unwholesome paths of action been explained.
As for the wholesome [paths of action], both their preliminary applications and their subsequent stages are born from the three wholesome roots.
However, the preliminary application and the subsequent conclusion of wholesome [actions] arise from the three roots,
because they are originated by a wholesome mind and because those [roots] exist therein.
By what, moreover, is the completion of these paths of action brought about?
This is explained as follows:
the completion of killing, harsh speech, and malice occurs through hatred.
Indeed, the completion of killing, harsh speech, and malice occurs through hatred,
because of the manifestation of a mind intent on abandonment and harshness.
Theft, sexual intercourse with another's wife, and covetousness reach their completion through greed;
likewise, taking what is not given, adultery, and covetousness are completed by greed.
However, false view is completed through delusion.
Indeed, the completion of wrong view occurs through delusion;
one brings it to its conclusion when addressed by those who are excessively deluded.
It is held by others that for the remaining [wrong views], it is completed by three [causes].
What others are there?
False speech, slander, and frivolous chatter;
the completion of these occurs through all three: by greed, hatred, or delusion.
Now, what is the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for these four sections? It is said:
"The basis for all four of these should be known in their respective order:
sentient beings, enjoyments, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and name (*nāman*). (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 194)
In that regard, killing and so forth have sentient beings as their basis;
sexual misconduct with another's wife and so forth have objects of enjoyment as their basis;
and false view has name-and-form as its basis.
False speech and the other [unwholesome actions] have the collection of names as their basis.
Furthermore, how does the path of action (karmapatha) come to be for one who personally commits the taking of life, and how so for the others up to wrong view?
The characteristics of the paths of action must be explained;
that is now undertaken.
Taking life is the intentional killing of another without error.
Indeed, if one, having reflected with the thought "I shall kill" or "I am killing this one," deprives another of life with an undeluded mind,
in that way taking life occurs.
Vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed wind (*vāyu*); it functions depending upon the body and the mind.
To cause that to fall away is "taking life" (*prāṇātipāta*).
No, because [that interpretation] is untenable.
Indeed, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are admitted to be associated with destruction and to perish at every moment.

Since such phenomena lack the activity of a power of stability, and since there is no distinction between future phenomena—whether of similar or dissimilar kinds—insofar as they are all equally devoid of self (*anātmaka*), what could happen to what by means of which destroyer?
Regarding this, the Sautrāntikas offer a rebuttal: "No."
"It is established like the extinguishing of a lamp, the ringing of a bell, or the cessation of sound;
no, for the case is the same.

However, the resolution here is as follows: when the killer brings about the impairment of the causal capacity [of the victim], there occurs the taking of life because he creates an obstacle to the establishment of the power and activity of future formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, to whom does that life belong which is deprived by it, or what are those vital breaths? [The answer is: It belongs to that which is conventionally established.
The Nagnāṭas maintain that for a person— detailed as "having such a name and such a lineage"—
demerit arises from the killing of a living being even without prior intention, just as burning results from touching fire.
For them, this same consequence would apply even to looking at or touching another's wife.

Regarding the plucking of the hair of those who are satisfied, angry, naked wanderers, Vāhlīkas, or Nirgranthas, the ritualists (yājñika) maintain that even merit arises from the intentional killing of living beings.
How so? It is like the consumption of poison.

It is as follows: for example, the consumption of a certain poison may lead to benefit when preceded by a mantra, whereas it leads to harm when not preceded by a mantra; [the opponent claims] it is just like that. [The author replies: No, because one does not observe the capacity to kill an animal through the mere use of a mantra, in the absence of repeated swallowing or the application of a weapon.

Furthermore, because a sacrifice consisting merely of an offering of a flour-made goat lacks the capacity to produce the religious merit (*yajñadharma*) arising from the slaughter of an animal and so forth;
and moreover, because poison is observed to possess the dual capacity for both killing and restoring life—
wherein, preceded by mantras, it restores some to life while it does not restore others who are afflicted by misfortune or impending death.
Even without being preceded by mantras, some things revive while others do not,
because the effects of consumed poison are relative.
Furthermore, although the mantras of the Śabaras and others have the power to neutralize the capacity of poison to kill, no such power is observed in them for destroying sin.
Furthermore, because the defining characteristics of dharma and adharma consist in non-abandonment [of their respective natures] through harm and non-harm;
if it is argued that dharma is manifested by actions such as the *juhoti* sacrifice, we say no.
Because its nature is unestablished and because its manifestation is untenable.
If it is argued that the apūrva is merely an action, we say no.
Because the eternality of action is untenable and its etymological definition is untenable.
Taking the wealth of another that has not been relinquished is called "taking what is not given" (adattādāna).
The term "without error" carries over [from the previous rule].
If one appropriates another's property with the thought that it is a gift or through theft, [it constitutes stealing].

Sexual misconduct consists of approaching another's wife; it is characterized by various conceptual distinctions. Indeed, approaching those who should not be approached is also sexual misconduct, and it comprises many types of conceptual variations.

He approaches one who should not be approached—whether it be his mother, his daughter, or one protected by another—or even his own wife, he approaches her in a non-genital part or in an improper place; or he approaches her while she is observing a religious vow.
It is said that this is done "without error."
False speech is the statement of something otherwise than it is by one who knows the facts, out of a malicious intent.
Indeed, false speech occurs in dependence upon the cognitions of both the speaker and the listener.
If the speaker is knowledgeable regarding the matters at hand, yet conceals them and speaks otherwise out of a malicious intent,
and the listener likewise understands it in that way, [it constitutes false speech].
At that time, his false speech becomes a path to the lower realms.
Indeed, those eight ignoble modes of discourse mentioned in the *Māhakīmātṛ-sūtra* and elsewhere,

as well as the eight noble ones— “claiming to have seen what was not seen is an ignoble mode of discourse; [claiming to have heard, sensed, or known what was not heard, sensed, or known is an ignoble mode of discourse]...”
To claim to have heard, inferred, or cognized what has not been seen, heard, inferred, or cognized is ignoble worldly discourse;
likewise, to claim not to have seen, heard, inferred, or cognized what has been seen, heard, inferred, or cognized is ignoble worldly discourse.
In the opposite case, however, there are exactly eight noble conventions (*āryavyavahāra*).
Furthermore, their definition is explained as follows:
"That which is apprehended by vision, hearing, and so forth, by the senses, and by the mind..."
It is said that these are seen, heard, sensed, and known, respectively.
That which is indeed perceived by the eye and experienced by both visual consciousness and mental consciousness is called "seen.
That which is experienced by the ear and by both auditory consciousness and mental consciousness is called "heard.
That which is experienced by the three—nose, tongue, and body—and by their respective consciousnesses along with mental consciousness is called "sensed" (or "cognized").
Because they grasp objects that are to be attained, and because their object is substantial food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra),
the word "mata" there is a synonym for "desired."

Furthermore, that which is experienced by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is "cognized" (*vijñāta*), because the process of determination is completed through its conceptual ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*).
This point is settled; let us now return to the subject at hand.
If one were to bring about a transformation by means of the body, would there be false speech? It could be so.
This is explained as follows: it could be that one does not exert oneself with the body and yet is touched by the fault of taking life.

There may be a case where one exerts oneself through speech, yet does not exert oneself through speech, and is nevertheless touched by the fault of false speech; there may be a case where one exerts oneself through the body, yet does not exert oneself through the body or through speech.
And one would be touched by both types of fault;
for there is the example of the seers' mental malice and the case of the *proṣadha* [vow].
But how, in the absence of a manifest action (*vijñapti*), can the unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) belonging to the desire realm be established as a path of action (*karmapatha*) in that case?
For when there is movement of the mind, movement of the body—consisting of the primary elements and their derivatives—necessarily follows; therefore, effort must be applied here.
False speech has been explained.
Slanderous speech is a divisive utterance; specifically, that which is spoken by one with a defiled mind for the purpose of alienating others, without error, is called slander.
Harsh speech, on the other hand, is that which is unpleasant.
Harsh speech is that utterance of one with an afflicted mind who is not mistaken.
Others say that afflicted frivolous talk is like singing, storytelling, and so forth.
Indeed, all defiled speech constitutes frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
Regarding that quality (*guṇa*) by virtue of whose presence a word is applied to a substance, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote it. And what is that quality?
It is precisely frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
One who possesses this is a frivolous talker (*saṃbhinnapralāpī*);
the state of being such is frivolous talkativeness (*saṃbhinnapralāpitvam*).
Others, however, say:

whatever other defiled speech there is besides these three kinds—false speech and so forth—such as flattery, singing, dancing, and the treatises of non-Buddhist schools, all that is frivolous chatter (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
Covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is the longing for the property of others; ill-will (*vyāpāda*) has sentient beings as its object;
and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is the view that there is no cause [for suffering]. *Abhidharmadīpa* 199.
Covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is, first of all, the longing for what belongs to an enemy:

"O, would that what belongs to others were mine! This desire for objects, known as improper greed (*viṣamalobha*), is called covetousness. Furthermore, ill-will (*vyāpāda*) is indeed hostility (*pratigha*) with the intention of abandoning sentient beings.

Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is that view, opinion, and so forth, which destroys either the cause, the fruit, or the action, or a real entity (*sadvastu*). Furthermore, when this wrong view has reached its maximum intensity in nine grades, it completely cuts off the nine grades of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*),
just as in the case of the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
As for what is stated in the treatise: "Which are the superior unwholesome roots by which one cuts off the wholesome roots?
And which are those that one first eliminates when attaining detachment from the desire realm?
This is not a fault.
Because it is brought about by the roots of unwholesomeness,
that karma is metaphorically attributed to those very false views;
just as fire alone is the burner of a village, while the thieves are merely its instigators, so it is in this case.

Only those [roots] belonging to the desire realm that are acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*) are severed, because those acquired through application (*prāyogika*) have already been lost previously.
For thus it was said by the Blessed One: "This person is endowed with both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas," and so forth.
In that regard, this person is endowed with wholesome dharmas of two kinds without distinction—those acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and those acquired by birth (*upapattilābhika*).
These wholesome dharmas of this person will disappear: the applied ones through gradual cessation, and...
Because that [state] was previously abandoned;
furthermore, he possesses a root of merit that is accompanied by mindfulness, uninterrupted, and acquired at birth,
which at another time— (Jaini_167)
"It will be completely and utterly eradicated;
through its eradication, one shall come to be reckoned as 'one whose roots of virtue are severed.
Therefore, the followers of the Sugata maintain that wrong view is the root of all unwholesome states."
“The subtle seed of wholesome dharmas resides within that unwholesome mind, from which a wholesome mind arises again when the collection of conditions is present,” so says the author of the *Kośa*.
The author of the *Dīpa* maintains that this is not so, because it contradicts both reason and scripture.

First, regarding the contradiction with reason: we observe that a dissimilar fruit does not arise from a dissimilar cause—just as rice cannot come from a barley seed—and likewise, [wholesome states] do not arise from wrong view through proper mental attention, a favorable voice, or the like.
If it is argued that [the eye and form are causes] just as consciousness arises from the eye and form, we say no;
because when the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) exists, the eye and form are merely instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*),
like the churning stick in the production of curd.
Furthermore, because of the occurrence of one or the other among contradictory things;
for it is never observed that contradictory things such as pleasure and pain, or light and darkness, can coexist in a single location,
nor is there any mutual relationship between seed and fruit [in such cases].
Furthermore, because you admit that the seed is the mind itself:
for you, it is precisely the unwholesome mind that is accepted as the seed.
Since that [unwholesome mind] performs an action contrary to a wholesome moment of mind, it is impossible for even a trace of its seed to persist in another, distinct mind.
And because the answer has already been stated;
for the answer has been explained here in detail,
so let it be remembered.
There is also a contradiction with scripture, for it is said: "Everything will be cut off by everything. ... [otherwise] the seed, while being destroyed, would be understood as remaining.
Thus have the paths of action been explained along with their characteristics.
What, then, is the meaning of "path of action" (karmapatha) as characterized by its defining marks?
They are called paths of action because they are both actions and the paths for that which is called action—namely, volition (*cetanā*).
Among these, seven are paths of action in the sense that they are both actions and the paths for action.
The three [unwholesome roots], covetousness and the rest, are paths of action, not the action itself;
for volition is that which is associated with them.
The meaning is that, through association and under their influence, one proceeds and performs formative activity (*abhisaṃskaroti*).
But that is indeed action (*karman*) itself, not a path of action (*karmapatha*);
for it does not proceed under the influence of the three.
This is what is said:
Volition (*cetanā*) is not itself the path of action; rather, it is by means of these [paths] that sentient beings are set in motion.
Furthermore, with how many paths of action does volition arise and proceed simultaneously? To address this, it is begun as follows:
Simultaneously with as many as eight unwholesome volitions.
First, it occurs with one [mental factor]:

when covetousness and so forth manifest in the absence of any other [defilement], or when one with an unafflicted mind brings them to completion through their application regarding any of the material [objects].
It occurs with two [mental factors].
In the case of killing a living being with a malicious mind,
or in the case of taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, or frivolous speech when one is possessed by covetousness,
[the path of action] occurs together with three [mental factors].
When one with a malicious mind simultaneously kills and steals another's living being;
or when one possessed by covetousness brings two material things to completion through that same application—these occur together with exactly three [paths of action].
They coexist with four.
For one who intends to cause a schism, whether in pleasant speech or harsh speech—
therein, indeed, there is one mental [course of action] and three vocal ones;
or for one who has entered into covetousness and so forth, when another person carries out the application and reaches the completion of the other three.
In this manner, it should be applied to five, six, or seven [factors].
It occurs together with eight [factors]:
when, having performed the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) in six [of the bases], one commits sexual misconduct oneself by sending another [to do so] upon the completion of the act.
Thus, first of all, it is unwholesome.

Regarding the statement that [the mind] "indeed proceeds together with wholesome paths of action up to ten," this is a general rule (*utsṛṣṭi*). This is its exception (*apavāda*): "not with one, eight, or five."
Indeed, it does not occur with one, five, or eight [factors] together;
rather, it occurs with two.

For one abiding in the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), there is the non-sensory consciousness (*avijñāna*) associated with the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) as comprised within the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), as well as the wisdom (*prajñā*) and vision (*dṛṣṭi*) associated with that.
It exists together with three [mental factors] in a mental consciousness associated with right view,
wherein there is no restraint (saṃvara).
There are four [paths] when a lay follower (*upāsaka*) with an unwholesome or neutral mind undertakes the novice monk’s restraint (*śrāmaṇera-saṃvara*).
There are six when that same undertaking occurs during the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
There are seven when that very undertaking occurs within a wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
And when one with an unwholesome or neutral mind undertakes the bhikṣu restraint;
or when one with the nine wholesome [mental states] undertakes it during the five sensory consciousnesses;
or when it is associated with the knowledge of destruction and non-arising within the mental consciousness, specifically when that [consciousness] is comprised within meditative absorption.
In ten ways, it occurs otherwise than that: in a wholesome mental consciousness, specifically when undertaking the *bhikṣu* vow;
and in all volition associated with the meditative (*dhyāna*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) vows, except for the two knowledges of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Furthermore, it may coexist even with a single [factor] apart from the vows, when one whose mind is otherwise undertakes the abstention from a single limb [of the path].
It may also occur with five or eight [paths of action]:
when one simultaneously undertakes two or five limbs of a wholesome mental consciousness.
Furthermore, in which realm of existence (gati) do how many wholesome and unwholesome paths of action exist, either through manifest activity or by way of possession?
Idle chatter, malice, and harshness ripen in hell in two ways.
These three—frivolous speech, harsh speech, and ill-will—exist in hell both by way of manifestation and by way of possession.
Covetousness and wrong view are considered to be exactly like that.
Indeed, some say that covetousness and wrong view also exist in two ways.
Others, however, say: covetousness and wrong view exist only by way of possession (*samanvāgama*),
because of the absence of objects that could provoke passion and because the results of karma are directly perceived.
And this [argument] is without foundation.
Regarding that, first, the claim that it is "due to the excessive intensity of craving and ignorance" was previously refuted as being partial.
The triad beginning with covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is likewise [absent], and in Uttarakuru there are two kinds of idle chatter (*pralāpana*). (Abhidh-d 202)
In Kuru, likewise, there are only these three: covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view.

However, others say that they exist only through possession (*samānvāgama*) and not through manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāva*), because there is no sense of "mine" or possessiveness, because the mental continuum is gentle, because there is an absence of objects for resentment, and because there is no intention toward evil.
The ten unwholesome [paths of action] exist elsewhere, excluding the hells and Uttarakuru; within the desire realm, these ten unwholesome ones are found in two ways.
In all places, however, the three wholesome [paths of action] are present.
"The three virtuous ones" refers to non-covetousness, non-malice, and right view; these three exist everywhere—in all three realms and in all five destinies—in two ways.
Furthermore, for those in the formless realm, noble ones, and non-percipient beings, the seven material [faculties] are acquired through possession.

In the formless realms (*ārūpya*), indeed, only the noble ones (*ārya*) and those in the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*) possess the past and future untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*). For, having produced and then ceased the untainted morality (*anāsrava-śīla*) based on the support of up to the sixth stage (*bhūmi*)—namely, the restraint of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-saṃvara*)—one is reborn in the formless realms; by that [restraint], one possesses it in the past. One also possesses it in the future based on the support of all six stages.
But it does not exist through actual manifestation, because the formless realms consist of only four aggregates and because non-percipient beings are without mind;
for the manifestation of that restraint is dependent upon a real, existing mind.
Excluding the Kurus and the hells, they exist everywhere else in two ways;
that is, excluding the Kurus and the hells,
these seven wholesome paths of action exist elsewhere by way of actual manifestation.
However, among animals and hungry ghosts, they are exclusively free from restraint;
in the form realm, they are exclusively comprised within restraint; elsewhere, they are both ways.
Indeed, these paths of action are of two kinds.
All ten [paths of action] yield the fruits of maturation (vipāka), outflow (niṣyanda), and predominance (adhipati).
In that regard, when all unwholesome actions have been practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed, one is reborn in the hells; this is their fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*).
If one returns to this state and enters the common lot of human beings, one becomes short-lived due to the taking of life.
Through taking what is not given, one suffers the loss of wealth;
through sexual misconduct, one has a rival wife;
through false speech, one is frequently subjected to slander.
Through malicious speech one has unstable friends; through harsh speech one hears unpleasant sounds;
through frivolous chatter one's words are not taken to heart.
Through covetousness, there is intense passion; through malice, intense hatred;
and through wrong view, intense delusion.
Thus, this is their outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*):
through the excessive practice of taking life, external things become deficient in vitality;
through taking what is not given, they yield meager fruits, have scant harvests, and are subject to frequent lightning strikes.
Through sexual misconduct they are strewn with dust;
through false speech they are foul-smelling;
through slander they are uneven, with highs and lows.
Through harsh speech, they are unpleasant to the touch and full of thorns; through frivolous chatter, their fruits ripen irregularly; and through covetousness, their fruits ripen prematurely.
Through ill-will, the fruits of their actions are bitter;
through wrong view, the fruits are inferior to the seed or even non-existent.
This is their fruit of predominance.
Furthermore, this [result] consists of suffering brought about by misery, a short lifespan due to being killed,
and a lack of vigor due to the destruction of vitality; these are its threefold fruit.
Because he caused another to experience painful sensation, he is reborn in the hells;
because he cut off another's desired life, he is short-lived;
and because he destroyed another's vitality, external things become weak in their potency.
The same should be applied to others as well.
For the wholesome paths of action, these three fruits should likewise be characterized by the opposite [of the unwholesome ones].
By practicing the abstention from taking life, one is reborn among the gods.
If he returns here to the common lot of human beings, he becomes long-lived;
by his very sovereignty, external things become exceedingly magnificent.
All this should be understood as the opposite [of the previous case].
Regarding the five fruits previously mentioned here, which action among them is endowed with how many fruits?
Action on the path of immediate succession possesses all five fruits.
Noble action that is stainless possesses four; likewise, other wholesome or unwholesome actions [possess four].
On the path of abandonment that is still with outflows (*sāsrava*), karma becomes fruitful by way of five fruits.
Those similar or superior dharmas of the same kind that arise subsequently are its *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruit).
Its *vipāka-phala* (ripening fruit) is the ripening determined to belong to its own level.
The fruit of dissociation is the abandonment of the afflictions.
The fruit of human effort consists of those phenomena produced by the power of that [abandonment];
it is not so for those that arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, the path of liberation that has arisen immediately thereafter,
that which is cultivated in the future, and that abandonment— by means of these, the arising of its attainment occurs.
It should be understood that the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) consists of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) other than its own nature, excluding those that have arisen previously.
Furthermore, it is logical that abandonment (*prahāṇa*) is also the sovereign fruit of that path;
others hold that this is because one realizes it through the sovereignty of that [path].
As for that action which belongs to the path of stainless abandonment, it possesses four fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
"The same applies to other [actions], whether wholesome or unwholesome";
that is, any other impure (*sāsrava*) action, whether wholesome or unwholesome, [is likewise].
Furthermore, any wholesome contaminated action other than the path of abandonment, as well as any unwholesome action, also possesses exactly four fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation.
The other [uncontaminated] should be known as pure; likewise, it is neutral in three ways.

Furthermore, that which is uncontaminated (anāsrava) and distinct from the path of abandonment, as well as that which is neutral (avyākṛta), is [neutral] in three ways, excluding the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) and the fruit of disconnection (visaṃyogaphala).
The results of a wholesome [action] are four, two, and three, respectively, for those that are wholesome and so forth.
For wholesome karma, wholesome dharmas constitute four fruits, excluding the ripening fruit (vipākaphala);
unwholesome dharmas constitute two, namely the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) and the sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala);
and neutral dharmas constitute three, excluding the outflow fruit (niṣyandaphala) and the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyogaphala).
Of the unwholesome, there are two, three, and four [results] respectively.
For unwholesome karma, wholesome dharmas are its two results—the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*).
Unwholesome [dharmas] are its three results, excluding the ripened result (*vipāka-phala*) and the result of disconnection (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
The four neutral [dharmas] are [the fruits], excluding the fruit of disjunction (*visaṃyogaphala*).
For even a neutral dharma can be the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of unwholesome dharmas;
for example, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) belonging to the desire realm.
[These are] the universal [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of origin.
As for the neutral [state], those [results] are two, three, and three respectively, starting with the wholesome.
For neutral (avyākṛta) karma, wholesome factors (kuśalā dharmāḥ) are two fruits: the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) and the sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala).
Unwholesome factors (akuśalāḥ) are three fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyogaphala).
For neutral factors, those same three [fruits] apply.
All four [kinds of karma] pertain to the past;
two pertain to the intermediate [present] existence; three pertain to one's own future birth; and two pertain to future births other than one's own.
In this context, "all" refers to those belonging to the three time periods.
For past karma, past, future, and present dharmas constitute four fruits, excluding the fruit of disconnection (visaṃyoga).
For present karma as well, future dharmas constitute these same four fruits.
However, present dharmas are two fruits of present karma: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
For unborn [karma], unborn dharmas are three fruits, excluding the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of disjunction (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
Four, two, or three [fruits] belong to other levels;
the dharmas of one's own level are, as far as possible, four fruits of karma, excluding the fruit of disjunction (*visaṃyogaphala*).
If those dharmas of another level are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are three [fruits].
Excluding the fruits of maturation (vipākaphala) and disjunction (visaṃyogaphala),
for those not included within the realms (anādhātupatita), a flow-on fruit (niṣyandaphala) belonging to another stage is not precluded;
however, if they are with outflows (sāsrava), there are two.
Regarding the fruit of human effort and the sovereign fruit:
for a learner (śaikṣa), there are three [fruits] beginning with that of a learner; for the karma of one beyond learning (aśaikṣa), those same three apply.
For the karma of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the dharmas of one in training constitute three fruits,
excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*).
The same applies to the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner possess exactly three fruits, excluding the fruit of outflow and the fruit of maturation.
For the karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), the [results] are respectively one, three, and two; for the last [karma], however, they are two,
two, and five.
For the karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), the dharmas of one in training (śaikṣa) constitute one fruit, namely the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala);
the dharmas beyond training constitute three fruits, excluding the fruition fruit (vipākaphala) and the fruit of disconnection (visaṃyogaphala);
and the dharmas that are neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training constitute two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) and the dominant fruit.

Furthermore, for those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣānāśaikṣa), learner (śaikṣa) dharmas have two fruits: the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) and the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala).
It is the same for non-learner (aśaikṣa) dharmas.
For those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, there are five fruits.
But regarding karma to be abandoned by vision: // Abhidh-d_211 //
Three, four, and one are taught as the [results] of those things to be abandoned by vision and so forth.
Indeed, for karma that is to be abandoned by vision, there are three results—
excluding the result of maturation (vipākaphala) and the result of dissociation (visaṃyogaphala).
Those to be abandoned by cultivation have four fruits, excluding the fruit of disjunction;
those not to be abandoned have one fruit, the sovereign fruit.
But those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation are considered to be of two, four, and three kinds respectively.
Respectively, one, two, and four [fruits] belong to karma that is not to be abandoned;
however, for karma that is to be abandoned by cultivation, the factors to be abandoned by vision are indeed two:
the fruit of human effort and the sovereign fruit.
Those [dharmas] to be abandoned by cultivation have four fruits, excluding the fruit of disjunction;
those not to be abandoned have three, excluding the fruits of maturation and outflow.
However, for karma that is not to be abandoned, the factors to be abandoned by seeing constitute one fruit, the sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala);
those to be abandoned by cultivation constitute two fruits: the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) and the sovereign fruit.
Those not to be abandoned consist of four fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation.
Now, does a single karma project a single birth, or do many? That is shown as follows: "A birth is projected by one [karma], and it is fulfilled by many. (Abhidh-d 213)
Indeed, by a single karma, one entire birth is projected;
however, it is fulfilled by many [karmas].
For example, a painter projects the entirety of a form with a single brush-stroke.
"In the same way, he fills [the world] with many [beings].
Now, as for that which was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, this world has its own karma as its property"—what is this so-called "having one's own karma as one's property"?
Now this is undertaken:

Whatever wholesome or unwholesome action of one's own body, speech, or mind has passed away while yielding its fruit, that is considered "the state of being the owner of one's actions" (karmasvakatā). Abhidh-d_214 //

Indeed, that wholesome or unwholesome action of body, speech, and mind which was performed by oneself in the past and is now yielding its fruit—this is to be understood as "the ownership of one's own actions" (karmasvakatā).
But how, when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are fragile, disintegrating moment by moment, and have no mutual agreement [on identity],
and when there exists no permanent agent or enjoyer, can it be said that one is the owner of one's own actions (*karmasvakatā*)?
To this, the following response is given:
Conventionally, because the fruit of those actions is seen within the continuum of the aggregates, agency and enjoyership are taught; however, these are denied for that which is eternal.
Indeed, action is undertaken for the sake of a specific exaltation of one's own self, with the thought:

"May I obtain a birth endowed with distinguished knowledge, wisdom, happiness, beauty, radiance, charm, and excellence. However, if the self were eternal and inactive, there would be no distinction between its prior and subsequent states; thus, its agency would be utterly inconsistent with the principles of logic.

However, when there is the arising of a distinct subsequent aggregate within the continuum of the aggregates, it is like the production of a distinct fruit through the assistance of seeds, water, sprinkling, and so forth;
this has already been explained previously.
This must now be stated:
there is a fourfold set [of propositions] regarding whether one possesses ownership of one's own karma (*karmasvakatā*) while that karma does not exist for him.
Indeed, there is a fourfold set [of propositions] regarding whether one possesses ownership of one's own karma and yet is not established in the ripening (*vipāka*) of that karma.
The first [fruit] belongs to one who abides in that fruit, because of the abandonment of that karma.
If one is established in the fruit of that action, then that action becomes exhausted.
The second [type of person] is one who abides in the fruit of that [path], because of their connection with that action;
the third is one endowed with both; but the fourth is one who possesses neither.
There may be ownership of karma, yet one will not experience its fruit.
This is the second tetralemma.
Regarding that, the first alternative is as follows:
The first [fruit] should be known as belonging to one established in that fruit, while the last [fruit] belongs to the final fruit.

The second [type of action] is that whose ripening is certain; the third is that because its ripening is not fixed; the third is that which possesses both [certainty and fixity]; but the fourth is that which lacks both.
The third tetralemma:
there may be one who is endowed with karma but does not experience its fruit;
indeed, there may be one who is possessed of karma yet does not experience the fruit of that karma.
There are four alternatives;
the first [alternative] refers to that which has ceased through the ripening of what was given, such as the future and so forth.
The second [type] is by means of action whose maturation is certain but which is deficient;
the third is for one who is free from both; and the fourth is for one who is devoid of both.
Now, regarding that which is stated in the treatise as action performed with yoga and action performed without yoga—what is their defining characteristic?
That is explained:
action performed without yoga is defiled by the primary and secondary afflictions (kleśa-upakleśa).
And some wise ones say that it is devoid of the marks of training and so forth.

Indeed, whatever defiled action of body, speech, or mind is corrupted by the primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa-upakleśa*), all that is improperly performed (*ayogavihita*), because it is originated by improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
Others, however, say: "That which is devoid of training (*śikṣā-vyapeta*), such as [the rules] on how one should walk, how one should stand, and so forth."
However, that vocal action which is deficient in gender and number, incoherent, and meaningless is "performed without yoga" (ayogavihita),
because it deviates from the prescribed rule. By contrast, that which is the opposite should be understood as "performed with yoga" (yogavihita).
The third quarter of the fourth chapter in the Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti.
The Fourth Chapter, Fourth Section: Now,

having personally awakened to this most profound and difficult-to-comprehend principle of the ownership of one's own actions (*karmasvakatā*), which dispels the darkness of false views such as those concerning primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the person (*puruṣa*), and a creator god (*īśvara*), who [would teach it] for the benefit of the world?
If you ask, "Does he demonstrate [this]? we reply:
that person is indeed a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, does he become a bodhisattva from the moment of generating the thought of enlightenment (cittotpāda) onwards?
Now, is it by means of the projection of karma characterized by marks (*lākṣaṇika-karma*), or rather by that of one in their final existence (*caramabhavika*)?
To address this, the following is introduced:
From what point until when is a bodhisattva irreversible?
It is from the moment they don the armor of awakening, having resolved upon the welfare of the world.
From the moment he approached the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, as his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), and followed the path of the right hand shown by him,

his intellect became established in thorough mental attention (yoniśo-manasikāra). He beheld the entire world— without protection, without refuge, and without resort— caught in the great whirlpool of the five destinies,
within the salt-water of the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
On a shore presided over by the rākṣasa of karma,
with its waters haunted by the crocodiles of evil friends,
and its waves of craving tossed by the winds of conceptualization regarding sense objects such as form;

Beholding [the world] submerged in the great ocean of saṃsāra, its boat of intellect tossed about by the helmsman of delusion, his heart filled with compassion, he extends the arm of his vigor to rescue it and generates this irreversible thought:
"This world, whose eye of wisdom is struck down by the darkness of ignorance, must be ferried across by me by means of the bridge of ethical discipline, illuminated by the radiance of right view."
This world is corrupted by the poison from the fangs of the serpent of aversion; I must pacify it with the antidote of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

This world has its mind overcome by the playful movements of the demoness of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); I must cause it to attain the bliss of the cessation of craving through the power of tranquility (*śamatha*).

This world is possessed by the demonic seizure of grasping (*parāmarśa*); I must lead it into the fearless state of the deathless (*amṛta*) by means of the auspicious rite of the bliss of liberation (*vimokṣa*).

This world has its intellect mounted upon the mountain peak of pride; I must shatter those mountains of pride with the thunderbolt of knowledge that all phenomena are governed by one's own karma, and establish them in the state of peace where arrogance, intoxication, and resentment have been stilled.

This world has hearts pierced by the thorns of doubt and indecision; I must extract the thorn of uncertainty with the probe of the analytical investigation of dependent origination and cause it to drink the nectar of immortality.
This world is caught within the fangs of the sea-monsters of old age, sickness, and death; I must lead it to the bliss of nirvana, which is free from all misfortune.
"This world is impoverished of the wealth of virtues such as faith; therefore, I must establish it upon the great station of sovereign virtue, inlaid with the jewels of the factors of enlightenment.
It is because of this irreversible generation of the thought of awakening that one is called a "Bodhisattva"; such is the teacher's instruction.
As for what is stated in the treatise— "From what point does a bodhisattva [begin]? From the point when he performs karma that results in the maturation of the marks"—
this is not a fault.
Because he—
when performing characteristic actions, not destined for the states of woe,
born of a great family, with complete faculties, and delighting in gathering his own assembly— [Abhidharmadīpa 224]

When this person becomes fixed in these stations— namely, being male, remembering past lives, being eloquent, and being endowed with wisdom, vigor, and action— then he attains manifestation among gods and humans. (Abhidharmadīpa 225)
Therefore, from this point—the *Jñānaprasthāna*—onward, the Bodhisattva is described with this intention:
"For he, over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya*), accumulates the ocean of qualities of the Dharma-body; however, he accumulates that supporting body over a hundred eons. (Abhidh-d 226)
Endowed with the thirty-two marks and radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics,
even the minds of enemies are instantly pacified upon seeing him.

Indeed, this is the natural law (*dharmatā*): that for the Blessed Ones, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, the Supreme Persons, who for three incalculable eons (*kalpāsaṃkhyeya*) have practiced the mastery of the wealth of virtues such as faith, ethical discipline, learning, renunciation, and wisdom without abandoning them, there is the complete perfection of the practice of the Dharma-body;
whereas for Pratyekabuddhas who are like the rhinoceros horn, it is accomplished in a hundred eons.

Through sixty eons, the perfection of the Dharma-body and its practice is achieved by those foremost among the wise; through forty eons, by those most excellent among the possessors of supernatural powers; and through twenty eons, by those preeminent among the retainers of what they have heard.

Furthermore, there is the birth-body of the Blessed Ones, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, which serves as the basis for enlightenment, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and resplendent with the eighty secondary characteristics;

upon seeing it, even the minds of those on the side of Māra and of the heterodox teachers— whose intellects are defiled by aversion arising from their own conceptual constructions— are filled with serene faith.
What, then, are those thirty-two marks of a great man (dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa),
or what are the eighty secondary characteristics (aśītyanuvyañjana)?
This is now demonstrated:
In this regard, first, these are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man:
the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have well-planted feet because they tread upon the surface of the earth evenly. (1)
Because his hands and feet are marked with wheels that have a thousand spokes, hubs, and rims, and are complete in every aspect, he has hands and feet marked with wheels. // 2 //
Because his hands and feet have long fingers, he has long digits. // 3 //
Because they are long and broad, their heels and feet are elongated. // 4 //
Because their hands and feet are as soft and delicate as young, tender cotton down, they have soft and youthful palms and soles. // 5 //
Their feet are webbed like those of a noble king of swans, because they are covered by a fine network of veins as variegated as polished red gold. // 6 //
Because their ankles are well-formed and elevated, they have high-arched feet. // 7 //
They have calves like those of the eneya deer because their calves are rounded and well-proportioned, tapering gradually from top to bottom. // 8 //
Because his arms are long, he does not need to bend his body to touch the surface of his knees with his palms. // 9 //
Because he possesses the marks of a supremely handsome and well-concealed person, his private organ is withdrawn into a sheath, like that of a noble elephant or horse. // 10 //
Because their height is equal to the span of their bodies, they are well-proportioned like a banyan tree. // 11 //
Because his body hairs grow upward in successive order, he has body hairs that point upward. // 12 //
Because their body hairs are well-distributed, unique, blue-black, and grow individually, each hair is blue-black and curls to the right. // 13 //
They are golden-colored because they shine with a radiance extending for one fathom, resembling the luster of refined gold. // 14 //
Because their skin is as smooth as well-refined silver and gold, and because it is free from the afflictions of dust and dirt, they have subtle skin. // 15 //
Because their hands, feet, shoulders, and necks are well-developed, they possess bodies with seven prominent elevations. // 16 //
With shoulders well-rounded and broad, their chests are smooth like a surface of golden stone, and the space between their shoulders is filled out. // 17 //
Because his upper body is broad and well-knit like that of a lion, he has the upper half of his body like a lion’s (siṃhapūrvārdhakāya). // 18 //
Because they are ten *tāla*s in height, being well-proportioned and without curvature, their limbs are large and straight. // 19 //
