Because the region of the collarbones is concealed by flesh accumulated all around, they have well-rounded shoulders. // 20 //
Because there are twenty teeth evenly aligned both above and below, he has forty teeth. // 21 //
Because they are of equal size, being neither protruding nor recessed, his teeth are even. // 22 //
Because they are situated without intervals, his teeth are closely set. // 23 //
Their teeth are white, like jasmine, snow, or a conch shell, because they possess the whiteness of these. // 24 //
They have lion-like jaws because their large jaws are smooth, rounded, well-developed, and beautiful to behold. // 25 //

Because they possess a knowledge corresponding to the discernment of the essence of flavors, which is not overwhelmed by wind, bile, or phlegm, they have attained the supreme excellence of taste. // 26 //
Because their tongues are broad and supple, covering the entire circle of the face, they possess long and thin tongues. // 27 //
Because their voices possess the five qualities of being deep, lovely, heart-stirring, clear, and pleasant to hear, they have voices like that of Brahmā. // 28 //
They speak as charmingly as the kalaviṅka bird, with a resonance like the sound of a drum. // 29 //
Because their color is like that of a blue lotus interspersed with white and black regions and unblemished red veins, they have deep blue eyes. // 30 //
Because the eyelashes of those situated above and below are perfectly curved, unconfused, and long, they are called "cow-lashed" (gopakṣman). // 31 //

Because their heads are adorned with the *uṣṇīṣa* due to having a head-jewel (*vajraja*) consisting of bones that are well-rounded, symmetrical, regular, and beautifully developed; and because their faces are marked by the *ūrṇā* due to eyebrows that are curved, illuminated by a white *ūrṇā* hair which is as pure as a conch shell and curls to the right—these are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man belonging to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
The eighty secondary marks are also described: for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have nails that are not broad, but are soft, copper-colored, high, and glossy. (1)
Their fingers are rounded, continuous, regular, and well-proportioned.
Their network of veins is rendered thin and hidden by their lack of fat. // 3 //
Their ankles are not protruding, symmetrical, and sharp. // 4 //
Their feet are even, not crooked, red, and glossy. // 5 //
Their graceful gaits were like those of the lion, the elephant, the bull, and the king of swans, turning toward the right.
Their two shanks are hairless, well-knit, and equal in measurement. // 7 //
Their knees are well-rounded, symmetrical, firm, and hidden. // 8 //
His beautiful thighs are plump, firm, even, and gradually tapering, resembling the trunk of a plantain tree. // 9 //
His chest is broad, elevated, free of hair, and shaped like a half-moon. // 10 //
Their waist-regions are beautiful, with smooth, well-knit, square navels and long, lovely hip-cavities. // 11 //
Their navels are deep, without fissures, red in color, and spiral to the right. // 12 //
Their bellies are smooth, hairy, firm, and gradually tapering toward the navel. // 13 //
Their sixth abdominal region is neither sunken nor protruding, but is well-rounded. // 14 //
Their flanks are well-proportioned, muscular, neither too long nor too short, and smooth. // 15 //
Their backs are beautiful, with joints that are invisible and well-knit, marked by fine, long lines, and endowed with a diamond-like shape that is neither uneven nor thick, but slender. // 16 //
Their hearts have broad, well-developed, and firm joints. // 17 //
His chest is even, elevated, and broad. // 18 //
Their breasts were of even redness, encircled by fine lines resembling the whorls of conch shells that were neither too thick nor too prominent. // 19 //
Because they were born in a place far removed from their hearts, the space between their breasts was wide. // 20 //
Because their flesh is well-developed and not overly broad, their armpits are elevated. // 21 //
Their eyes are large, firm, well-knit, deeply set, and even. // 22 //
Their buttocks are coarse, broad, sunken in flesh, uneven, and disproportionate in size. // 23 //
Their arms are like the trunks of elephants—hidden at the joints, fleshy, firm, smooth, and symmetrical. // 24 //
Their forearms are firm like those of a lion, with smooth, fine hair spiraling upward. // 25 //
Their hands are even, copper-colored, and long. // 26 //
The lines on his palms are deep, unbroken, unconfused, curved, long, smooth, thin, and copper-colored. // 27 //
The joints of their fingers are reddish and crowded together, made fine by being pressed against one another. // 28 //
The fingers have pupils whose measurement exceeds that of the ring-finger joints. // 29 //
Their body hairs are neither too many nor too few, soft, glossy, well-set at the roots, and uniform in length. // 30 //
They possess a luster that is glossy, uncontracted, unhurt, and substantial. // 31 //
Just as colors appear indistinct when touched by cold or heat, so too are the castes [indistinct]. // 32 //
The flesh is firm, dense, neither too thick nor too thin. // 33 //
Their blood has the fragrance of clear, smooth, and sweet sandalwood, as crimson as the hibiscus flower. // 34 //
They possess thick, firm, and well-formed veins and bones, covered with flesh. // 35 //
The joints of their bones are hidden and remain fixed like the knots of a serpent. // 36 //
They possess well-knit bodies because their bodies are as indestructible as a diamond. //37//
Their major and minor limbs were beautiful and well-proportioned. // 38 //
Their bodies were gradually developed, well-polished, delicate, radiant, and translucent. // 39 //
Free from gadflies, moles, and black spots. // 40 //
One whose bracelets have fallen off due to the weakness caused by old age. // 41 //
They have eliminated bodily distractions through the practice of the lion’s posture. // 42 //
Their shadows are pure, gentle, and untainted by the impurities of sweat. // 43 //
They possess a splendor equal to that of blazing jewels, great medicinal herbs, the moon, and the sun. // 44 //
Endowed with the supreme weightiness of the best of mountains. // 45 //
They possess a touch as pleasant as the seasonal breeze and the Kālindī river. // 46 //
The fragrance from their pores is like that of sweet, soft, and fragrant flowers and sandalwood. // 47 //
Their breath at all times possesses a fragrance equal to that of a freshly blossomed blue lotus. // 48 //
Their voices are marvelous, soft, long-drawn, smooth, compact, free from noise, and devoid of labored breathing. // 49 //

Furthermore, due to the affliction of fasting and eating unwholesome food, their voices do not suffer any change in tone, even while they continue teaching the Dharma without ceasing through transformations.
Their blood-stained mouths are neither too contracted nor too wide open. // 51 //
Those of pure conduct. // 52 //
Situated in their proper places, they are heated, distinct, and fully complete in their characteristics. // 53 //
Because they are pleasing on all sides, they are such that one never tires of beholding them. // 54 //
Their conch-like necks were neither too short nor too long, well-rounded, full, and adorned with three folds. // 55 //
Their chins are of equal proportion, firm, straight, short, and broad. // 56 //
Their lips are as red as the bimba fruit, long, even, smooth, and beautiful. // 57 //
The flesh of their teeth is as smooth as the *bandhūka* flower. // 58 //
Their teeth are clean, lustrous, even-set, and not diminished. // 59 //
His fangs are arranged in sequence, smooth, sharp, even, and white. // 60 //
Their momentary smiles were revealed by the rays of light from their right teeth, which possessed a purposeful intent. // 61 //
Their tongues are free from impurities, soft, copper-colored, and glossy. // 62 //
His palate is the color of an elephant’s palate, with a network of flesh that is eternally warm and smooth. // 63 //
Their noses are prominent, long, well-proportioned, and high. // 64 //
Their beards were black, curled, soft, firm at the roots, and glossy, though thin. // 65 //
Their cheeks are neither protruding nor sharp, but are fleshy, smooth, and well-rounded. // 66 //
Their beautiful cheeks are firm and well-developed, like a mirror. // 67 //
Their beautiful ears are plump, long, symmetrical, and free from blemish.
The temples, which are shaped like full moons, are deep and well-knit at the junctions of the forehead, ears, and cheeks. // 69 //
Their eyes are wide, long, smooth, sweet, clear, and even. // 70 //
Their eyelashes are curved upward as if smiling. // 71 //
Their glances are gentle, radiant, steady, and possess well-knit joints.
Because their power is immeasurable, they are free from the opening and closing of eyes. // 73 //
Her eyebrows are long, dark, smooth, gradually tapering, glossy, and fine. // 74 //
Their broad foreheads are shaped like half-moons and are as smooth as plates of gold. // 75 //
Their faces are like the orb of the full moon. // 76 //
Their skull-bones are as solidly compact as a single mass of vajra. // 77 //
Their heads have the perfectly full shape of an umbrella. // 78 //

Their hair is arranged in the form of auspicious svastikas and nandyāvartas, which are smooth, well-gathered, free from the defect of graying, not disheveled, glossy like bees, soft, firmly rooted, and fragrant. // 79 //
Whose heads are not beheld by the worlds of the gods, asuras, humans, and others. // 80 //
Now, how should that primordial bodhicitta of the bodhisattvas be regarded in terms of its firmness?
This cannot be illustrated by means of any worldly object.
Why? Because:
Mount Meru is destroyed by the wind at the end of an eon, the ocean by fire, and the thunderbolt by the thunderbolt; yet that mind remains unchanging.
To what is it included?
Which one is it?
Of how many kinds is it?
What is its precursor, at what time does it arise, or who produces it?
This is now explained:
That which belongs to the realm of desire, born from the sixth [consciousness], is threefold: compassion, faith, and the succession of others.
When a Buddha appears, a man or a woman attains that first mind.
That very first bodhicitta is indeed included within the desire realm;
it means it is born from the sixth [consciousness], namely, born from the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
It is of three types: that acquired at birth, that consisting of hearing, and that consisting of reflection.
It is associated with a mental attention that is preceded by compassion and abounds in faith;
it arises only when there is the appearance of a Buddha and not in the absence of the Buddha's teaching;
and it is produced by either a man or a woman, and by no one else.

For the sake of increasing the sprout of the great tree of Buddhahood— which pervades all realms and states of existence— of this jewel of the mind that serves as the locus for the seed of enlightenment,

the Bodhisattva gradually practices the qualities such as the perfections (pāramitās), whose nature will be described later, which consist of the four foundations beginning with wisdom and serve as the causes and conditions analogous to the application of earth, water, and so forth. But how, then, does the fulfillment of the perfections of giving and the rest occur in sequence?
In that regard, first:
"The fulfillment of generosity belongs to one who gives everything, to everyone, at all times.
Indeed, while abiding in the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya*), the bodhisattva does not give everything to everyone, nor at all times.
In the second [stage], one gives everything to everyone at all times, but not everything;
in the third, one bestows everything upon everyone at all times.
By this much, the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) becomes fulfilled.
Not abandoning self-restraint even at the point of death is called the excellence of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, when one does not violate even a single precept, such as the prohibition against taking life, even at the cost of sacrificing one's own life, to that extent the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) should be known as fulfilled.
In this regard, the examples of the daughter of the king of the cranes and others, as well as the story of the monk, should be cited.
Regarding the perfection of vigor:

by praising the Blessed One Tiṣya, the Truly Perfectly Awakened One, with a single verse while standing on one foot for seven days, Śākyamuni fulfilled the perfection of vigor and turned back nine eons [of rebirth].
However, for the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), its fulfillment occurs in the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) subsequent to the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi).
Indeed, "the fulfillment of all [perfections] is established in the knowledge of destruction. (Abhidharmadīpa 231)
Such is the scripture (*āgama*).
Regarding this, however, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that "the perfections of patience and meditation are not distinct entities from morality and wisdom, because they are their attendants.
But the Vinaya-holding Vaibhāṣikas recite four perfections in the Vinaya.
Furthermore, regarding this, some whose intellects have been excluded from the Buddha’s word say: “The Blessed One did not teach the path of the bodhisattva within the Three Baskets.
They should be addressed as follows:
“Sirs, you are indeed mistaken in this regard, because...”
The three bases of meritorious action and so forth are the teachings on the means for attaining that;
likewise, there is the fourfold empowerment and the instruction of the seven true dharmas.
The seven yogas, the three aggregates, and the three trainings and so forth have been taught;
likewise, the four perfections have also been proclaimed in the Vinaya.

And the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment were explicitly taught by the Self-Existent One as the causes for all forms of awakening, categorized as threefold according to their degrees of weakness and so forth.
Therefore, there is no path to enlightenment other than the three baskets (piṭaka) beginning with the Sūtras;
whoever here should speak of something else would be speaking the words of Māra.

For it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, that which does not enter into the Sūtras, is not seen in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)—this is not the teaching of the Teacher. This is the instruction regarding the black [teaching].
The "white instruction" is the opposite of this.

Indeed, that which was spoken by the Blessed One, the Buddha, and compiled by the redactors of the councils—such as the Elder Mahākāśyapa and the Elder Ānanda—into summary verses (*uddāna-gāthā*) within the four Āgamas, that alone is to be accepted. This point is concluded.
This must now be explained:
through which kinds of eons is Buddhahood attained by means of three incalculable [periods]?
This triad of incalculables is considered to consist of great eons.

If there is no number for *kalpas*, how then is it determined that there are three? It is certainly not that number does not exist; rather, there is another place called "the incalculable" (*asaṃkhya*), which stands above this [number].
Indeed, this name "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) refers to a specific distinction of numerical position;
it is not intended to mean that no number exists at all.
Now, during his conduct as a bodhisattva across these three incalculable eons, how many Buddhas did the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Perfectly Awakened One, attend upon?
Regarding this, they explain as follows:
in the first incalculable eon, there were seventy-five thousand;
in the second, seventy-six thousand.
In the third [incalculable eon], there were seventy-seven [Buddhas].
Furthermore, at the conclusion of which incalculable eon did which Buddha appear?
Regarding this as well, they describe it as follows:
The first incalculable aeon was completed under the Perfectly Enlightened One Ratnaśikhin;
the second under the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara;
and the third was completed under the Blessed One Vipaśyin.
Under which Perfectly Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) was the thought of enlightenment first generated for the state of Buddhahood? Under Śākyamuni.

Śākyamuni by name existed at the beginning of the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya*), when the Blessed One, having been born as Bhārgava, performed service by attending to him with pleasant water and personal ministrations, and thus first generated the thought of enlightenment, thinking: "May I also become like this."
"May I become such a type"—
this very thought was further strengthened once more by King Prabhāsetu.
At what time, then, do the Blessed Buddhas—the suns of the Buddhas—appear?
That is now undertaken: the arising of the Jinas occurs during the period of decline, as long as the lifespan is one hundred years.
In the case of two [types of] Pratyekabuddhas, it is at their maximum; in the case of Cakravartins, [it is likewise].
Indeed, the arising of Buddhas occurs during the period of decline (*apakarṣa*) of the eon; that of Pratyekabuddhas occurs during both the periods of increase (*utkarṣa*) and decline;
and that of Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*) occurs only during the period of increase.
Furthermore, this is the fixed rule for universal monarchs (*cakravartin*):
their arising is not held to occur when the lifespan is below eighty thousand years;
that is, the arising of universal monarchs occurs when the lifespan is eighty thousand years or more, but not below that.
These [kings] possess wheels made of gold, silver, copper, and iron, by the power of their merit.
There are indeed four kinds of wheel-turning monarchs: those with golden wheels, those with silver wheels, and those with copper wheels.
And they possess wheels of copper due to the excellence of their own merit;
and these [kings] are, respectively, lords of four, three, two, and one continent.
Now, as for what was said: "Therefore, there is no path to enlightenment other than the three baskets (piṭaka) beginning with the Sūtras";
if that is so, and there is no difference in the path for Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas, then there should likewise be no difference in their fruits.
This is not a fault, because:

"Even though the means of accomplishment are equal, there is a distinction between them due to the difference in the faculties and so forth, just as there is a difference in the results of giving between two mothers who seek worldly existence and liberation respectively. (Abhidharmadīpa 239)

Indeed, whatever quality has been taught by the Blessed One after awakening to perfect enlightenment, which serves as the cause for attaining the two types of liberation, all of that conforms to the Three Baskets (*piṭakatraya*).
Furthermore, those two types of liberation are attained by three kinds of persons.
By the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, by the Pratyekabuddha, and by the Noble Śrāvaka;
furthermore, although they have all entered the same path to awakening, there is a distinction among them due to differences in their faculties, vows, and obscurations.
It is just as when two mothers give the same object in the same field [of charity], yet because of a difference in their intention, the result is not the same. (Jaini 205)

Just as that fruit occurs, so too for the three types of persons who aspire to the supreme goal, although they have entered upon the same path, there arises a distinction in their results due to differences such as the sharpness and repeated practice of their application in the constant, dense, and uninterrupted cultivation of the faculty of aspiration.
Furthermore,
due to the intensity of the cultivation of compassion, as well as [the intensity] of one's own self-awareness and mind,
a distinction is likewise established for the teacher who possesses the awareness of others.
In this regard, the cultivation of compassion by the Blessed Buddha proceeds with predominance; for the Pratyekabuddha, self-awareness and reflection proceed with predominance;
and for the Śrāvaka, awareness of others and the voice of another [proceed with predominance].

Furthermore, even in the absence of another's voice, because in one's final birth the realization of causes, conditions, and results is attained through the power of thorough mental attention (*suyoniśomanaskāra*), one first realizes the path to the supreme good (*niśreyasa*)—which had been entirely lost—by means of the power of causes and conditions, and subsequently receives instruction from others; and so forth.
Now, when the liberation is equal for the three who have attained realization, what is the distinction? It is said:
"The greatness of the Teacher arises in three ways from the cause, the reality, and the fruit;
even though the liberation is equal, it is because the three attain different types of awakening. (Abhidharmadīpa 241)

In this regard, the greatness of the Blessed Buddha is first established by way of its cause: because over three incalculable eons, through the light of the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, he has dispelled the cataracts of ignorance in the minds of those to be trained.

It is also established by way of its intrinsic nature, because its essential character consists of the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the foundations of mindfulness, great compassion, and so forth.
It is also established by way of its fruit.
Because his teaching is established as unimpeded throughout the worlds including the gods, and because he has conquered the four Māras.
Now, as for this birth-body of the Supreme Person, which is distinguished above all beings— is it subject to an indefinite duration, or is it subject to a definite duration? To that, it is replied:
The Buddha-body is projected when the Buddha is present face-to-face,
and not at any other time,
because of its being most distinguished by knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmayajñāna*).
Furthermore, in that regard:
each individual mark of the Sage is produced from one hundred merits plus one.
In that regard, fifty volitions constitute the preliminary application and fifty constitute the subsequent conclusion;
by means of one [volition], it projects their defining characteristic.
Furthermore, what are those fifty volitions? It is said:
Just as there are paths of action, so too are the three types of merit and so forth intended;
there are five for each path of action.
The purification of the fundamental paths of action consists of the absence of affliction by discursive thought during the preliminary stages, the maintenance of mindfulness,
and the dedication toward nirvāṇa.
All of these have that as their object and constitute the fifty preparatory applications.
On the back [of the body] there are also exactly this many.
However, others say that Buddhas have two types of bodily bases:
those based on the birth-body (*janma-śarīra*) and...

They have the thirty-two marks of a great person as their object, and they have the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are based upon the Dharma-body, as their object; they are comprised within the preliminary stages and the subsequent stages. Others, however, say: the volition of abstaining from taking life—divided into weak, medium, strong, stronger, and strongest—is to be applied to gods and humans.
Some maintain that there are two kinds of oceans, four continents, sixteen hells, animals, hungry ghosts, the twenty gods of the six desire realms, and the gods of the form and formless realms;
the Blessed One feels compassion for all of these.

They describe it thus: setting aside the Bodhisattva who is close [to enlightenment], the measure of a single merit is the fruit consisting of the enjoyment, sovereignty, and lordship of all sentient beings.
Now, as for what was stated— 'the perfection of giving' (dānapāramitā)—
in that regard, what is the compound [analysis], what is the grammatical derivation of the word "giving," or what is the intrinsic nature of giving?
This is explained as follows:
the resolute intellect regarding the perfection of giving is the perfection of giving; the same should be stated for the remaining perfections as well.
Furthermore, as for what is asked— ‘What is the means (sādhana) of this word “giving,” or what is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of giving?’— to that it is replied:
For generosity is that by which one gives, with regard to the welfare of oneself, others, and so forth.
The reality of that [reality] consists of the actions of body and so forth, which in some cases is the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
Furthermore, this word "giving" (*dāna*) is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*);
it is called "giving" because one gives by means of it, just like the word "measure" (*māna*).
In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the hand and so forth] being considered "giving" (dāna).
If, on the other hand, "giving" is understood as an action-noun (*karmasādhana*)— meaning that which is given is "giving"—
then there would be the undesirable consequence of gold and the like being considered "giving."
Let it be so; what is the fault?
There is an absence of ripened fruit (vipākaphala), because gold and such things are indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Let it then be derived solely as an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*). [Objection:
But was it not stated that this would lead to an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to the hands and so forth?
[Reply: This is not a fault.
This [treatise] is commenced for the purpose of excluding rivalry, fame, concealment, service, and so forth, because it is embraced by the three types of wholesome action.
"In view of one's own and others' welfare, etc. means in view of benefiting oneself and others, and so on.
For the sake of benefiting oneself, for the sake of benefiting others, and for the sake of benefiting both;
by the word "etcetera," it is also included out of a desire for worship.
Furthermore, its intrinsic nature is the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) of the body and so forth.
In some cases, however, it refers to the actions of body, speech, and mind;
here, mental action should be understood as including its associated mental factors and its retinue.
Furthermore, this is what constitutes giving:
Because of its preeminence, the Sage has declared that it indeed yields the fruit of great enjoyment.
Although it is the cause for both heaven and liberation, this gift is applied primarily toward great enjoyment;
furthermore, regarding this very gift:
some give gifts for the sake of accomplishing their own welfare, the welfare of others, or both.
Some are for the sake of following the conduct of the virtuous, while others are for neither purpose.
Indeed, for two reasons— one who desires to bring about his own welfare and one who has set out to accomplish the welfare of both— bestows such a gift endowed with these qualities:
for the sake of accumulating roots of merit for himself, and for the sake of nourishing the sense faculties and the great elements of another.

In that regard, giving for one's own benefit alone is as when an ordinary person gives to a shrine after the Blessed One has attained final nirvāṇa; giving solely for the sake of others is as when an Arhat gives to the Saṅgha;
and giving for the sake of both is when one who is not free from passion gives to the Saṅgha. This [giving] does not result in the experience of desired dharmas.

That which one who is worthy gives to a shrine for the sake of neither [self nor others] does not become [karma] to be experienced in the present life; rather, it is solely for the purpose of demonstrating the abiding on the path praised by holy beings.
Furthermore, how is this gift distinguished by way of its fruit? It is said:
"The excellence of its fruit is taught to arise from the excellence of the donor, the object, and so forth.
In that regard, what is the distinction of the donor, what is the distinction of the object, and what is the distinction of the field?
Therefore, by means of qualities such as faith, the donor gives with [attitudes] such as reverence.

When a donor gives while possessing conviction in the certainty of the connection between cause and fruit, being virtuous, of good character, and well-versed in the words of the Buddha; when he is free from stinginess and open-handed; when he gives with the benefit of Nirvana in mind, respectfully, with his own hand, at the proper time, and without harming others—he indeed...
From that [giving], one obtains a fruit endowed with qualities such as being honored;
therefore, by giving with honor, one becomes a recipient of honor.
By giving with one's own hand, one gains a preference for magnificent enjoyments and resources.
Through giving at the proper time, one obtains enjoyments at the proper time;
through not harming others, one obtains possessions that cannot be confiscated and are not shared with others due to lack of enemies, calamities, and so forth.
To this extent, the giver is distinguished.
What is the object?
The object is that which is endowed with qualities such as color and so forth, and which bestows fruits such as beauty and the like.
If a thing is endowed with color, fragrance, taste, and touch, it is then distinguished.
From that, there arise, respectively, physical beauty, renown, popularity, delicacy, and the quality of having limbs pleasant to the touch;
thus the thing becomes distinguished.
The field is distinguished by the factors known as qualities (*guṇa*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and benefit (*upakāra*).
A field becomes superior according to its qualities;
starting from animals up to humans, qualities increase in a gradual sequence until they reach the Buddha.
As it has been said: “Having given a gift to one who has gone to the animal realm, a hundredfold maturation is to be expected;
having given to a human being who is of immoral conduct, a thousandfold [maturation].
Thus, the field is distinguished by the particularity of suffering.

As it is said regarding the bases of meritorious action consisting of material things: "Giving to the sick, giving to those who attend to the sick, giving during cold spells, during heat waves, and so forth," and so on in detail.
Because of the distinction in the nature of their assistance;
as in the case of parents and other benefactors who rescue one from the dangers of wild forests, difficult terrains, wildernesses, or calamities caused by spirits.
As it has been said: "From a distinction in volition arises a distinction in the fruit."
Now, how does the distinction of volition arise? We reply:
"The mildness and so forth of the action [arise] from the mildness and so forth of the underlying intention (āśaya) and other factors. (Abhidharmadīpa 248)
Indeed, among the causes [of karma], action is distinguished by the specific qualities such as mildness;

the distinction of karma arises from the mildness and so forth of the intention (*āśaya*), volition (*cetanā*), application (*prayoga*), basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), field (*kṣetra*), and subsequent result (*pṛṣṭha*).
Among these, "intention" (*āśaya*) refers to the underlying purpose, such as when one projects a course of action through volition, thinking, "I shall do this and that," or "I will do it."
The application is the bodily and vocal action that serves as its basis;
the basis is the course of action (karmapatha);
and the field is the recipient to whom the object is offered.
What is called "repetition" (pṛṣṭha) is that which, having been performed once, is performed again either once or repeatedly.
As it has been said: "A gift to the noble ones yields immeasurable fruit. Now, is the fruit for all non-noble ones measurable? No, he says:
"Even to a child who bestows the Dharma, to a father, to a mother, or to a sick person..."
The gift to a Bodhisattva is immeasurable, as is that for the sake of another existence.
Giving even to these five types of ordinary persons becomes immeasurable.
Now, to whom and by giving to whom does a gift yield the highest fruit? That is explained: [the gift] of a bodhisattva, as well as that which is the eighth [gift] of another.
The wise have declared that which is most excellent for an Arhat to bestow upon another Arhat.

Indeed, when a bodhisattva gives a gift with the resolute intention for the welfare of all sentient beings, that is foremost because it has the fruit of the supreme goal; for the Blessed One has taught eight kinds of giving in the Sūtra: "giving upon approaching," "giving out of fear," "he gave to me," [and so forth].
"He will give me a gift;
gifts have been given by my ancestors;
he gives for the sake of heaven."
"For the sake of fame...

up to: for the attainment of the supreme goal, he gives; this is the foremost gift. And when one who is free from passion for the three realms, an Arhat, gives a gift to another Arhat—this gift is the foremost. Thus it is said.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "I declare that for intentional karma that has been performed and accumulated, there is no fruit that is not experienced.
Now, what is this that is "performed" or "accumulated"? It is said:
that which, having been deliberated upon, has been projected, and has been strengthened by completion and so forth.
And that accumulated karma is considered to be devoid of an antidote.

In this regard, one should consider that what is "projected" (ākṣipta) is not done unintentionally or by chance; rather, it is that which, having been performed, is subsequently fulfilled by completing volitions and is reinforced by subsequent actions,
and for which there is no counteragent such as remorse.
That karma is said to be accumulated.
How can there be the arising of merit regarding mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth when there is no recipient? We reply:
"Because of one's own quality of renunciation, mental factors arise toward objects of veneration (*caitya*), such as in the act of worship;
even without a recipient, there is a fruit, just like dwelling in loving-kindness (*maitrī*). (Abhidharmadīpa 252)

For example, great sages who dwell in loving-kindness do not actually bestow happiness upon the world, yet they nevertheless receive immeasurable merit; likewise, in the case of shrines and the like, they maintain that the production of merit arises solely from the clarity of one's own mind through the power of resolute conviction in those qualities.
It is said in the Sūtra: "There are two kinds of giving:
the gift of Dharma and the gift of material things.
Among these, the gift of material things has already been explained.
The gift of Dharma is described as follows:
The nature of the gift of Dharma has speech as its object, consisting of reality, names, and so forth;
because its nature is indeterminate (avyākṛta), it is not like the gift of food and other such things. (Abhidh-d 253)
Just as material giving (*āmiṣadāna*) has the nature of the three types of action because it is wholesome, whereas food and drink do not,
for they have the nature of gold and so forth because they are neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Similarly, because it consists of skillfulness in speech, the gift of Dharma has speech as its intrinsic nature;
it does not have the name-group (nāmakāya) and so forth as its intrinsic nature.
The basis of meritorious action consisting of giving has been explained;
now that consisting of ethical discipline is undertaken.
Ethical discipline has been explained as virtuous form (*rūpa*) according to its various classifications.
Wholesome form alone constitutes the basis of meritorious action consisting of morality (*śīlamaya-puṇyakriyāvastu*);
furthermore, that consists of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) form.
Non-informative form is also divided into three types, being comprised within the Prātimokṣa, meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
That too has been explained in detail.
Furthermore, this basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline (*śīlamaya-puṇyakriyāvastu*) has both great wealth as its fruit and liberation as its fruit.
This is due to the distinction of the dedication of the vow;
however, because that [dedication] is predominant, it is stated in the treatise that [the practice] leads to rebirth in heaven.
Furthermore, this ethical discipline (śīla) is both pure and impure.
In that regard, it is pure when it is not defiled by faults such as immorality (dauḥśīlya) or the roots of unwholesomeness.
And that which is the factor for the pacification of its opposite is here called "the word" (śabda).
Indeed, that ethical discipline which is not defiled by the eight types of misconduct such as taking life,
nor impaired by the afflictions and secondary afflictions— such as wrong view— that give rise to them,
and which is embraced by the applications of mindfulness and so forth, which are the antidotes to those afflictions and secondary afflictions;
And that which is dedicated toward nirvāṇa does not become a seed for saṃsāra;
others say this is due to five reasons:
it is purified by the fundamental paths of action, [and so forth].
It is purified by the preparatory stages,
unassailed by discursive thoughts,
and sustained by mindfulness.
And that which is directed toward *nirvāṇa* is considered pure ethical discipline (*śīla*);
its opposite should be understood as impure.
Thus has been explained the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline.
That which consists of cultivation (bhāvanāmaya) is explained as follows: merit that is concentrated (samāhita) here is called "cultivation" because it is the cultivation of the mind.
That merit which has the nature of meditative concentration (samādhi) and is concentrated is termed "cultivation."
Why?
Because of the cultivation of the mind (*cittabhāvanā*).

Just as sesame oil perfumed with flowers such as the *campaka* becomes permeated by them, so too the mind is said to be cultivated and perfumed by those mental factors (*dharma*) associated with that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and those that arise simultaneously with it.
Because it consists of that [object],
and because it is not thus unconcentrated;

rather, the mind associated with qualities such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) should be understood as a basis for meritorious action consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-puṇyakriyāvastu*), being indeed concentrated (*samāhita*).
Furthermore, how is this "basis of meritorious action" (puṇyakriyāvastu) to be understood? Is it that merit, action, and the basis are each [separately] the "basis of meritorious action"—
this being a *dvandva* compound characterized by a collective aggregate— or is it that the basis of merit and action is the "basis of meritorious action"?
Now, as for the term *puṇyakriyāvastu*—is it "the basis of meritorious action"?
Let it be so, provided there is no fault.
And how is there no fault?
In that regard, first of all:
because its intrinsic nature consists of bodily and vocal actions, it is "merit" (puṇya) due to being threefold and wholesome;
because its essence is action, it is "activity" (kriyā).
Because it is the basis for the volition that originates it, it is a "thing" (*vastu*).
That volition which originates it is both merit and action; the factors co-arising with it are merit alone.
That which consists of morality (*śīlamaya*), however, is exclusively bodily and vocal action, and thus it is threefold.

That which consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) is loving-kindness (*maitrī*); it is both merit (*puṇya*) and the basis for meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*). The volition (*cetanā*) associated with that [loving-kindness], through the influence of loving-kindness, constitutes the formative activities (*abhisaṃskāra*); the volition co-arising with loving-kindness and morality (*śīla*) constitute both merit and meritorious action.
Others [assert that] those co-existent factors are merit alone.

Furthermore, although all this merit consisting in cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) is a basis for meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*), it is taught by the All-Seeing One that, because it is predominant among all causes, it leads to liberation (*apavarga*). Abhidh-d_256.

Since cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is indeed the most proximate cause for attaining the supreme goal, the Blessed One stated that it is precisely the root of virtue consisting of cultivation that is prescribed for the sake of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).
Having explained the threefold purity by way of the divisions of the bases of meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*),
the distinction of the pure is now further explained by another threefold division:
In this teaching, the roots of merit are briefly held to be of three kinds: those conducive to merit, those conducive to nirvāṇa, and likewise those conducive to penetration.

That which leads to merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*) is that by which one takes up the seed for rebirth among gods and humans, and projects a fruit for the attainment of high status, noble lineage, great wealth, the form of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), Śakra, Puṣpaketu, Brahmā, and so forth.

That which leads to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) is that by which, through abiding in an unshakable intention for liberation, one necessarily becomes one whose nature is to attain final nirvāṇa. That which leads to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) consists of the four stages beginning with "heat" (*ūṣmagata*).
Now, regarding that which is called in the world "writing, sealing, calculation, and enumeration"—what is their intrinsic nature? It is said:

Writing, sealing, and calculation have as their characteristic the actions of body and speech; enumeration, moreover, should be understood as having the nature of mental action. (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 258)

In that regard, first, concerning script and seals: that which is produced by yoga as an origination of bodily action is "script. Script consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); however, the action by which syllables (*akṣara*) are brought forth is called "script.
That which is engraved upon ivory, horn, gold, and so forth is a "seal" (*mudrā*).
However, that action by which one digs is called "action.
Poetry, too, when set in motion by yoga, is the arising of vocal action consisting of the five aggregates.
Calculation, as well, is mental action set in motion by yoga.
That which is conceptualized by the mind regarding phenomena, together with its attendants, has the nature of the four aggregates.
The fourth chapter is completed in the Abhidharmadīpa, in the commentary known as the Vibhāṣāprabhā.
The Fifth Chapter. First Pāda. Ritual actions have been explained.

Now, as for this world, it accumulates karmas that cause it to revolve and whirl within the wheel of the five destinies; abandoning what should be done, it engages in actions that ought not to be done, and forsaking the right path, it takes recourse to the wrong way.
Having abandoned the Supreme Brahman, which is supremely tranquil, one takes birth in *saṃsāra*, which is a nest for manifold sufferings and calamities; as to what the cause of this is, it is said:

"I shall explain those afflictions (*kleśa*)—attachment and the rest—which bind one to existence and by whose power the world is inclined toward what should not be done and becomes a partaker of suffering. (Abhidharmadīpa 259)
Furthermore, those afflictions,
by means of their specific distinctions arising from the activity produced by their own powers,
are addressed by names such as "latent tendencies" (anuśaya) and so forth, having assumed general designations.

In this regard, first, they are called *kleśas* because they afflict [the mind] due to their own activity arising from general designations; they are called *anuśayas* because they lie latent (*anuśerate*);
and they are called *āsravas* because, starting from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) down to the Avīci hell, they flow out of and cause the mental continuum to flow out.

They are called *āsravas* because they flow [toward rebirth]; they are called *saṃyojanas* because they bind one here; they are called *granthas* because they tie together; and they are called *yogas* because they yoke [one to suffering].
They are called floods (*ogha*) because they carry away; they are called grasping (*upādāna*) because they take hold. "Affliction" (*kleśa*) is their general name.
In this regard, what are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and how many are there?
This is now elucidated:
attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong views.
These six underlying tendencies are said to be the obstructors of the gateway to the higher good.
Indeed, these six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are stated in the treatise to be the causes for the progression of *saṃsāra* and the obstructors of the path to the highest good (*śreyas*).
Their etymological definition is as follows: they are called "underlying tendencies" because they follow along with the continuum (*saṃtāna*), like rust on iron or stains on clothing;
or else, they are called "underlying tendencies" because they bind [the mind] closely (*anubadhnanti*).
Like land-dwelling and water-dwelling creatures;
these are to be understood by way of their mode of life,
like the consumption of asafoetida and similar substances.
And from the perspective of the fruit [of their actions], it is like the falling away from births as a pigeon, a snake, and a pig;
and from the perspective of the person, it is like Nanda, Aṅgulimāla, Sunakṣatra, and others.
Now, how are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) such as attachment (*rāga*) to be understood?
Are attachment and the others themselves the latent dispositions, or are they the latent dispositions of attachment and the others? And what follows from this?
If it is argued that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are nothing other than passion (*rāga*) and so forth, there is a contradiction with the Sūtra:

“In this case, a certain person does not frequently dwell with a mind obsessed by the obsession of sensual passion; he understands, as it truly is, the subsequent escape from the arisen obsession of sensual passion.
For him, that obsession of sensual passion—having been thoroughly and correctly subdued—is abandoned along with its latent disposition (*sānuśaya*). (Jaini_221)

If it is argued that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are [identical to] passion (*rāga*) and so forth, there would be the consequence of [admitting] dissociated latent dispositions (*viprayuktānuśaya*), which contradicts the Abhidharma: "The latent disposition of sensual passion (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) is associated with three faculties (*indriya*).
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that only a karmadhāraya compound is intended here, and not a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound.
But was it not already stated that this contradicts the Sūtra?

"With latent tendency" (*sānuśaya*) means "with a continuous connection" (*sānubandha*). Alternatively, the word "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) in the Sūtra is used figuratively for "possession" (*prāpti*), just as fire is said to be "suffering."
In the Abhidharma, however, the term *anuśaya* refers strictly to the defilement (*kleśa*) itself;
therefore, the *anuśayas* are exclusively associated (*saṃprayukta*).
"But it is correct in the manner of the Dārṣṭāntikas," says the author of the Kośa.
And how [is it] for the Dārṣṭāntikas?
“The latent tendency of sensual desire is the *kāmarāgānuśaya*. Furthermore, the latent tendency is neither associated (*saṃprayukta*) nor dissociated (*viprayukta*).”
Because it is not a separate substance:
for a dormant affliction is called a latent tendency (*anuśaya*),
whereas one that has awakened is called an outburst (*paryavasthāna*).
And what is its dormancy? It is the persistence of the state of a seed when it has not become manifest. What is its awakening?
Manifestation.
What is this so-called "seed-state"?
It is the power within the personal existence (ātmabhāva) to produce afflictions, which has been generated by previous afflictions.
And just as sprouts and so forth possess the capacity to produce rice-fruits, which arises from rice-fruits;

[if that is so], then why is it stated in the *Ṣaṭṣaṭka-sūtra* itself that "affliction" (*kleśa*) is "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*), as in: "In him, there exists a latent tendency of passion toward pleasant feeling"?
There is no fault because of the statement "it exists.
It is not an underlying tendency (anuśaya) at that very moment;
when then? When it is dormant (prasupta).
"Or rather, this is a metaphorical application of the term 'fruit' to the cause.
This [statement] reveals the Sautrāntikas' internal laziness regarding listening to the principles of the Buddha’s word.
How so?
Because the answer has already been stated;
the answer to this has been given here in the investigation of karma and also in the *Tattvasaptati*,
so let that be remembered.
Do not forget this!
Furthermore,

it is pointed out that in the position of the Sautrāntikas— which conceives of a seed-like mental capacity (*citta-śakti*) as a latent impression (*bhāvanā*)— there are faults such as its being neither identical to nor different from the [resulting] cessation that follows.

If it is argued that the establishment of the Middle Way occurs through the non-existence of "otherness" and "non-otherness," and through the acceptance of the destruction of the mind while the state of seed-impressions (*bīja-vāsanā*) persists—[we reply: no.
For if the intrinsic nature, power, and activity of the mind are absent, those two extremes cannot be established; thus, the Middle Way is untenable, like a staff made of sky-flowers.
Furthermore, these...
Due to the twofold division of attachment, seven are considered; due to the divisions of views, ten are traditionally taught.
Furthermore, they should be known as ninety-eight through the distinctions of realms, aspects, and so forth.
In this regard, the distinction between attachment to the body and attachment to existence will be explained later.
The distinction among views is fivefold, according to the divisions of the view of a self-identity and so forth.
Furthermore, we shall explain the distinction among attachments in two ways.

Furthermore, all these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), according to their occurrence and through the distinctions of realm (*dhātu*), aspect (*ākāra*), and type (*prakāra*), become ninety-eight. Regarding this, some scholars demonstrate that,
by way of the distinction of realms, there are thirty-six belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) which are to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Thirty-two are to be abandoned by vision;
thirty-one belonging to the realm of form are to be abandoned by both [vision and cultivation],
twenty-eight of which are to be abandoned by vision, excluding the five [afflictions] associated with resistance.
The same applies to those belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
In that regard, how do those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) become thirty-six?
It is through the distinction of the fixed categories of factors to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The views also number thirty-six due to the distinctions of realm, aspect, and type.
Resistance is fivefold because of its restriction to the realms.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate their classification in accordance with the verses.

In that regard, among these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*), and how many up to those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*)?
First, concerning the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*):

for each truth beginning with suffering, there are respectively ten, seven, seven, and eight to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the other truths; thus, there are thirty-two [tendencies] in the realm of desire to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and so forth.
Because they hold divergent views regarding those [matters];
in this same way, one should state the case for the form and formless realms by means of inference.
Attachment is divided into two types: that called *kāmarāga* (sensual attachment) and that called *bhavarāga* (attachment to existence).
This division occurs because the former generally functions outwardly, while the latter functions inwardly and so forth.
In due order,
the classification of attachment has been explained;
now the classification of views is being set forth.
The view of a self-identity, the two types of grasping at extremes, false view,
and the adherence to views and to rites and rituals— these are the five views.
Furthermore, when these are further divided according to the distinctions of elements (*dhātu*), types, and aspects, they become ninety-eight:
thirty-six belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and thirty-one belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
There are thirty-one [afflictions] belonging to the formless realm,
due to the fixed determination of the types to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation.
Furthermore, among these [factors], how many in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are to be abandoned by seeing (darśanaheya), and how many up to those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya)?
This is now clarified: here, ten are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkhadṛggheya).
All ten [afflictions] here in the desire realm are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*), because they are all erroneously directed toward suffering.
Seven are to be abandoned by the vision of the cause (*hetudarśanaheya*).

From these ten, one excludes the triad consisting of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the misapprehension of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
These same eight [factors] are abandoned by the vision of the seven [stages] of liberation; they are destroyed by the vision of the Path.

Having abandoned the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), these [other afflictions] are also to be abandoned solely by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*), because they are erroneously directed toward the aggregates that have become the fruit (*phalabhūta-skandha*),
because they take as their object what is to be abandoned by vision, and because they grasp at [the aggregates] as being permanent.
Furthermore, the four [defilements] beginning with attachment are to be known as being exhausted by the two paths.

Those [defilements] are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), because they are the objective supports (*ālambana*) for those four—attachment and the others; therefore, through their abandonment, those [four] are also abandoned, just as when a pillar falls, the supporting beam falls along with it.

However, those four specific-characteristic defilements (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*)—namely attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance—are to be understood as abandonable by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Furthermore,
since these arise by the power of each respective conceptualization (*kalpa*), view and doubt [operate] when there is a destruction of vision;
indeed, even though the object does not exist, these two proceed by grasping the aggregates (*skandhas*) in the form of distorted perceptions and uncertainty.

Therefore, these [defilements] are to be abandoned by vision; just as doubt regarding the existence of a core substance disappears merely by opening up the mind, so it is with regard to form, and likewise with regard to the formless, except for the latent tendency of resistance.
Just as they have been explained in the desire realm, so too should they be understood in the form and formless realms,
with the exception of the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*).

For in that state, because the mental continuum is moistened by calm abiding (*śamatha*) and because there is an absence of the signs of aversion (*pratigha*), the latent tendency of aversion does not exist.
Therein, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) each consist of one type, as they are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering alone.
False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) each consist of four types.
Because they are to be abandoned by the vision of the Four Truths,
the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is of two types, being abandoned by the vision of suffering and the path;
attachment and the other [afflictions] are of five types.
Because they are to be abandoned through the vision and cultivation of the Four Noble Truths, these amount to thirty-six in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

There are thirty-one in the form realm (rūpadhātu) and thirty-one in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu); thus, in total, there are ninety-eight [defilements] to be abandoned through vision and cultivation.
Of these, furthermore, eighty-eight are to be abandoned by vision,
and ten are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Now, regarding these eighty-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*): are they abandoned by the path of vision alone?
No, he says. What then?
Those which are to be abandoned by receptivity (*kṣānti*) at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) are considered to be abandoned by vision alone.
For those [defilements] are to be abandoned exclusively by the receptivity to subsequent knowledge;
however, those to be abandoned by knowledge are destroyed in that [state] through cultivation alone.

In the same way, in the other stages as well, those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are to be abandoned by knowledge are eliminated for both noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) solely through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). However, the remaining ones are abandoned in both ways.

Indeed, in the remaining stages, according to what is appropriate and as far as possible, those latent dispositions bound by the receptivities (*kṣānti*) to the dharma and its subsequent cognition (*anvaya*) are to be abandoned by vision (*darśanaheya*) for noble ones.
And it should be understood that these are also to be abandoned by cultivation for ordinary persons (pṛthagjana).

Now, regarding these five views which are divided into thirty-six types according to the distinctions of realms (*dhātu*), aspects (*ākāra*), and modes (*prakāra*), what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of each? To address this, it is said:
"The view that 'I' and 'mine' exists is known as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)."
The two graspings of annihilation and permanence are considered to be included within the view of grasping at extremes.

Due to the power of causal conditions and from hearing false teachings, ordinary persons harbor a grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), thinking "I" and "mine"; this is called the view of a self-existent body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding its etymology: it is a view that settles upon or perishes with the body, and because its mode of apprehension is inverted, it is termed *satkāya-dṛṣṭi*.
This very view is of two kinds, distinguished by the aspects of "self" and "belonging to self."
Furthermore, there are five views of self that take the five aggregates as their object,
and fifteen views of "mine. Taken together, these twenty modes are explained as the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Due to the perversion regarding that which is grasped by those two—the unreal entity called "self"—there arises either the grasping at permanence through association with bad persons, or the view of grasping at extremes through the grasping at permanence.
The denial of cause and effect is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
By the mention of "cause and effect," the inclusion of "substance" and "activity" should be understood.
Through this, the complete inclusion of wrong view as taught in the treatise should be understood.
Adherence to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) should be known as the grasping of an inferior thing as superior.

Indeed, that which consists of [clinging to] causes and paths that are not [the true ones] is called "observances and rituals" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Furthermore, every contaminated (*sāsrava*) thing is "inferior" (*hīna*) because it is inferior even to the state of an Arhat.
Here, one should understand that the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has been elided.
The adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the grasping of views and so forth.

One regards the four views and inferior things as supreme, thinking, "How is this view supreme?"—that is, one regards this view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), which consists of the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*) belonging to an inferior person, as supreme, thinking, "I shall honor myself; thus Vāsudeva will be honored here."
"There is no gift; [the world] will proceed according to its own pleasure," and so forth.
Clinging to causes and paths where there are none as being the true cause and path is the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

For example, to view that the five aggregates of grasping—which are caused by primordial matter (*prakṛti*), God (*īśvara*), the Person (*puruṣa*), and so on—are not caused by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), but rather to see a non-cause as a cause.
And [they teach] the wrong path, such as entering fire or water, and [the attainment of] heaven or liberation through the knowledge of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.

Here, "virtue" (*śīla*) refers to the performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice; among its constituent acts, the three beginning with the *pratijuhoti* are internal (*antaraṅga*), while those beginning with the immolation of animals (*paśvālambhana*) are external (*bahiraṅga*).
The lifelong practice of both of these is *śīla*.
As it has been said: "This sacrificial session (*satra*) which one performs as the *agnihotra* lasts until old age and death.
*Vrata* refers to the service of the fire pertaining to Agni, and the performance of the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* hymn and others pertaining to Śukra, because water has Śukra as its presiding deity.

They say that one is purified and liberated by these [practices], such as the Vārhaspatya, the Aupaniṣada, the Godānīya, the Jaṭāvatāraṇa, or the Govrata and other such vows. Those very ones who follow the dharma of the three Vedas— Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and so forth— are not the cause, because they consist of the appropriated aggregates (upādāna-skandha).
Furthermore, it has been explained in detail that [these acts] are neither eternal nor supreme;

and such things as the immolation of animals or entering fire and water are not causes for heaven or liberation, because giving, ethical discipline, and meditative cultivation are the true causes thereof.
Therefore, this is a perverted view known as the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

If, then, adherence to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) proceeds by way of causes such as a primal person (puruṣa) or a Lord (īśvara), does it follow that it is to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudayadarśanaprahātavya)?
This is not so.
Because he has taken up the wrong path through the delusion of suffering, he must indeed be expelled by that [correct] view.
One is deluded by the intellect regarding the aggregates of grasping, which are of the nature of suffering, and regarding Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others, who are not the cause [of liberation].
Therefore, it is precisely where one is deluded that [the delusion] is abandoned through the vision of non-perversion; and likewise on the wrong path.
Because one who is deluded by the notion that it is the true path is abandoned through the correct vision of one's own path,
it is established that the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is to be abandoned by both [vision and cultivation].
Since the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed by the observation of mere phenomena (*dharmamātra*), [it is abandoned by vision].
In the clear realization of suffering, that [defilement] as well is abandoned by that very vision; therefore, it too [is abandoned by the vision of suffering].
When, indeed, the cognition that phenomena are merely phenomena has arisen for him— [perceiving them] as impermanent, suffering,
and empty—
And when it is realized that "all phenomena are without self," at that very moment there occurs the cutting off of the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
as well as the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) which is set in motion by it; thus, even that [view] which has been acquired is completely eradicated.

In that regard, since the vision of phenomena—characterized by any one of the aspects such as impermanence and so forth—arises solely from the clear realization of suffering, it is established that these two views are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering alone.
Now, as for these four inversions—such as "the permanent in the impermanent" and so forth—what is their intrinsic nature?
This is now undertaken: two [inversions] arise from the adherence to views, and one from the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
But the other type of perversion is conceived as being half of the [perversion of] grasping at extremes.
In that regard, first of all,
from the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the two inversions of pleasure and purity are conceptualized;
from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the inversion of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) arises.
"The half of the view of grasping at extremes (*antargrāhadṛṣṭi*) is designated as the inversion of permanence" (Jaini 235).
But does this not follow that it would be [a portion] of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)? No, because it is a different type of view.
The view of annihilation is a different view from the view of eternalism.

However, one who propounds a self (*ātmavādī*), conceiving the person itself as an independent agent, master, and self, accepts "this is mine"; therefore, this is simply the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Moreover, if "mine" were a distinct view, then "by me," "for me," and so forth, would also have to be distinct views.
Therefore, these should be regarded as mere synonyms for the conceit of "I" (ahaṃkāra).
But are not all afflictions (kleśas) perversions (viparyāsa), since they function erroneously? Why, then, is it said that there are only four?

This is not a fault, because: "The statement regarding 'perversion' (viparyāsa) applies only to these [three], due to the power of [wrong] views, because of the activity of determination, superimposition, and the opposite [of reality], with respect to both mind (citta) and perception (saṃjñā). (Abhidharmadīpa 274)
Because of judging things perversely, because of superimposition, and because of absolute error;
for none of the other afflictions possesses all these [characteristics] together.
Although wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) do judge things [perversely],...
And [the view of selfhood] is exclusively erroneous,

whereas the adherence to precepts and vows is not exclusively erroneous, because it can coexist with the attainment of detachment from sensual desires and so forth, since it does not involve the destruction of a substantial entity.
Other afflictions are not investigative;
thus, there are only four.
But is it not said in the Sūtra: "To perceive the impermanent as permanent is a perversion of perception"?
"The perversion of mind (*cittaviparyāsa*) is indeed the perversion of view (*dṛṣṭiviparyāsa*), and so on up to [the perversion regarding] the self (*ātman*); thus there are twelve.
This is not a fault, for perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) are not determinative (*nitīraka*).
Therefore, the designation "perversion" (viparyāsa) applies only to the four views by their very nature;
as for the statement that "mind and perception [are perverted] through the power of view," that is merely a figurative expression.
For perception (saṃjñā), having fallen into the conventional usage of worldly affairs, grasps the signs of an object (ālambananimitta) erroneously through the power of vision;

and the mind (citta) follows its lead. Therefore, it is these two alone that are grasped. Even in the world, one is said to have "perverted perception" and a "perverted mind," but not "perverted feeling" (vedanā) or "perverted volition" (cetana).
Now, is there some distinction regarding the latent tendency of pride (mānānuśaya) similar to that of the latent tendencies of views (dṛṣṭyanuśaya)?
He says: "There is.
How so? It is shown as follows:

There are seven types of conceit; from three [types] arise nine types of conceit, which are further divided into three kinds based on the three ways of exalting oneself and so forth—namely, the existence of self-exaltation and the like, and the non-existence thereof.
Now, this classification of the detailed and concise explanation of this verse is presented.

In that regard, pride (*māna*) is the inflation of the mind by means of any object whatsoever on the part of one who is deluded regarding the efficacy of being the owner of one's own karma (*karmasvakatā*). This pride, as it is currently being examined, is sevenfold.
excessive pride, pride beyond pride,
and the pride of "I am";
conceit, inferiority complex, and false pride.
The detailed exposition of these is as found in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
But surely, in the *Jñānaprasthāna*, nine types of conceit (*mānavidhā*) are taught, namely: "I am superior" is a type of conceit;
"I am equal" is a type of conceit based precisely on that [same] view.
The manner of conceit is as follows: "I am inferior to one who is my equal";
"There is one superior to me, there is one equal to me, there is one inferior to me";
"There is no one superior to me, there is no one equal to me, there is no one inferior to me."

In that regard, the type of overweening pride (*atimāna*) based on the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the thought, "I am superior. The type of pride (*māna*) based on that same view is the thought, "I am equal.
The type of inferiority-pride (*ūnamāna*) based on that same view is the thought, "I am inferior."

"There is one superior to me" is the type of inferior pride (*ūnamāna*); "there is one equal to me" is the type of pride (*māna*); "there is one who is my equal" is the type of pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*).
"There is no one superior to me" is the form of pride;
"there is no one equal to me" is the form of over-pride;
"there is no one inferior to me" is the form of lesser pride.
Thus, these nine types of conceit are established as being derived from three kinds of conceit: conceit (*māna*), excessive conceit (*adhimāna*), and inferior conceit (*ūnamāna*).

All seven of these conceits are to be abandoned through both vision (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), according to the *Sthavira-kṣemaka-sūtra*: "In regard to these five aggregates of clinging, the conceit 'I am' remains unabandoned."
Furthermore, does everything that is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya) and not yet abandoned manifest for a noble one (ārya)? No, he says;
for even some things that have been abandoned do manifest.
Such as the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā), torpor (middha), the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya), and the eight [faculties] beginning with the eye.
Indeed, even though certain [defilements] have not been abandoned, they do not manifest;
for example, the outbursts of killing and so forth, remorse, and the various types of impurity.
Furthermore, the desire for non-existence does not arise in a noble one (ārya) due to the absence of its cause.

Indeed, by means of whichever afflictive obsession one would intentionally commit the taking of life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, or false speech— even if such killing and so forth have not been abandoned, they do not manifest because they are to be abandoned by cultivation;
furthermore, unwholesome remorse does not manifest, nor do the nine types of pride manifest.
Even though craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavyā*), it does not manifest;
nor, as indicated by the word "and" (*ca*), does a certain portion of craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) manifest, such as:
"O, may I become Airāvaṇa, the king of nāgas! O, may I become the lord of the asuras, such as Vemacitra!"
"O, may I indeed obtain birth among the Northern Kurus," and so forth.
But what is the reason that these [afflictions], even though they have not been abandoned, do not manifest in a Noble One?
It is because emptiness has been well-cultivated and because he understands the connection between karma and its fruit.
And because it is nourished by [wrong] views.
In that regard, the various forms of pride and the conceit "I am" are nourished by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The outbursts of affliction such as killing are nourished by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) is nourished by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
The sphere of craving for existence is nourished by the view of eternalism;

thus, because the afflictions that nourish it are absent, the [wrong] views and so forth do not venture to ascend into the continuum of the noble one (ārya). Furthermore, even unwholesome remorse (kaukṛtya) has not been abandoned by the noble one who is not yet free from passion, yet it does not arise for him because it is produced by [the application of] medical treatment.
Now, for what reason are the universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) established as distinct groups of afflictions?
This is undertaken [to explain]:
"The establishment of the universals is based precisely upon suffering and its origin."

Indeed, the proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin are universal, because they constitute the basis for all those types of views that are to be abandoned by that [vision]. (Abhidh-d 277)

Indeed, because the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing those two—namely, those designated as suffering and its origin—which will be described hereafter, have established themselves in both [realms].
But are all [factors] to be abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering? Are not the universal [factors] to be abandoned?
He says: No. What then?
Doubt, the five views, ignorance—whether mixed with them or independent—are [to be abandoned through the vision of suffering].
Seven are universal; from suffering, there are four [objects] derived from these.

The seven views, the two types of doubt, and the ignorance associated with them— as well as independent ignorance, which is of two kinds— constitute eleven proclivities (*anuśaya*). These should be known as universal within their own realm and level (*svadhātubhūmi-sarvatraga*) in each respective realm, because they take the entirety of their own realm and level as their object.
And these, when totaled together, constitute thirty-three universal [factors].
Furthermore, these universal [factors] are eleven in substance; however, they are considered to be seven by name,
because the three types of ignorance and the two types of doubt share the same names.
Now, why are attachment, aversion, and pride not universal? This is explained:
Attachment, aversion, and pride, however, function with reference to specific objects.
Indeed, these afflictions characterized by their own specific marks arise by taking each individual affliction as their object without exception; therefore, they are not omnipresent.
However, because doubt and the other [afflictions] exist in different modes, they do not simultaneously pervade all their own levels;
because they take other realms as their objects, only those previously mentioned are "pervasive" (sarvaga).
Furthermore, among these, nine belong to the higher realms; of those, excluding the first two views— namely,
the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)— the other nine are universal (*sarvatraga*) with respect to a different realm.
But are only the latent dispositions (anuśaya) universal?
No, he says. What then?
Their co-existent dharmas, excluding their acquisitions (prāpti), are also universal. *Abhidharmadīpa* 281.

Those factors such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth that coexist with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya), as well as [the characteristics] such as birth (jāti) and so forth, are also universal because they share the same fruit as them.

Furthermore, among those ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many have contaminated objects (*sāsravālambana*) and how many have uncontaminated objects (*anāsravālambana*)? To address this:
ignorance (*avidyā*) is associated with both doubt (*kāṅkṣā*) and false view (*mithyādṛk*), as well as when it occurs alone.
These six are abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path for those with pure vision.
The false view, doubt, and the ignorance associated with them—along with independent ignorance—that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path:
these six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) in each realm have the untainted (anāsrava) as their object;
the remaining ones have the tainted (sāsrava) as their object.
Now, among these [factors] which have pure objects, how many take cessation as their object, and how many take the counteragent of a stage as their object? This is explained:
Nirvāṇa is the object of those abiding on the path only of its own stage; [the path] belongs to nine stages.
That which has a visible object is distinct [from the invisible], because of its state of being a cause, due to its causal nature.
The cessation of one's own level alone is the object of false views and so forth that take cessation as their object;

for those belonging to the desire realm, it is the cessation of the desire realm, and likewise up to those belonging to the level of the peak of existence, it is the cessation of the peak of existence itself.
However, for those [afflictions] belonging to the desire realm that take the Path as their object, all afflictions belonging to their own level have the Path as their object. Furthermore,

even for those false views and so forth belonging to the eight levels of the form and formless realms, the Path belonging to the nine levels and associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), which serves as the antidote to the form and formless realms, is their object.
But what is the reason that cessation is apprehended as an object by means of wrong view, and not by the path? It is said:
"Because it is the cause, and because of its state as a cause."
For the path is characterized by mutual causality, whereas cessation is not; such is the distinction.
Now, why are attachment, aversion, pride, and the adherence to views and ascetic rules not admitted to have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object? To this it is replied:
Attachment does not [have the untainted as its object] because it lacks a cause for power; nor does aversion, because there is no offense.
Because they are exceedingly tranquil, the [other] views do not exist as entities.
In that regard, first of all, if attachment were to have the untainted as its object, it would— because it would proceed from a longing for nirvāṇa, like the desire for wholesome dharmas—
not be something to be abandoned by yogins.
Hatred, too, arises toward an object that causes harm.
