Liberation, however, is beneficial because it is the cessation of all suffering.
Pride, on the other hand, is characterized by elevation due to a lack of tranquility;
therefore, stainless dharmas are those which destroy it.
Furthermore, if the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*) were to have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, they would attain the status of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, it is only the previously mentioned latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have the stainless as their sphere of activity.

Now, among these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many adhere by way of their object (*ālambana*) and how many by way of association (*saṃprayoga*)? An omnipresent (*sarvaga*) underlying tendency adheres to its entire [sphere]; one that is not omnipresent adheres to its own level (*bhūmi*) by way of its object, and to its own category (*nikāya*). (Abhidh-d 285)
Indeed, the omnipresent factors are of two kinds:
those that are omnipresent within their own element and stage, and those that are omnipresent across different elements and stages.
Even those that are not all-pervading are of two kinds:
those with contaminated objects and those with uncontaminated objects.

Among those, those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) which are universal (*sarvatraga*) within their own realm and level (*svadhātubhūmi*) adhere (*anuśerate*) by way of their object (*ālambanataḥ*) to the entirety of that fivefold [category] of their own realm and level. However, those which are not universal but have contaminated objects (*sāsravālambana*) adhere by way of their object to their own category (*nikāya*) within their own level—

namely, those to be abandoned by seeing suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) adhere only to the category to be abandoned by seeing suffering, up to those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*) adhering only to the category to be abandoned by cultivation.
And because they do not take it as their own, because it is an adversary, and because it belongs to a higher stage, the path is not the object-domain [of those proclivities].
The phrase "they adhere by way of being an object" is understood to carry over.
What is the reason?
Because objects belonging to other stages and those that are untainted (*anāsrava*) are neither appropriated nor are they concordant with [the view of self].
For it is only when an object has been appropriated by the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) that a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) is able to persist within it.

However, because there is no occurrence of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) or craving (*tṛṣṇā*) with respect to an untainted object (*anāsrava-vastu*) or an object belonging to a higher stage (*ūrdhvabhūmika*), they do not lie latent (*anuśerate*) therein. But with respect to their own associated [factors], when those are not abandoned, they lie latent by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).
The phrase "they adhere" is understood as the governing topic.

Whatever latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is associated with a particular factor (*dharma*), that disposition adheres to that associated factor by way of association (*saṃprayoga*), as long as it remains unabandoned;
this is what the word "but" (*tu*) specifies.

Consequently, this is also established: those [defilements] that have the untainted as their object, and those that have objects belonging to different realms and stages, increase through association alone;
whereas those that have the tainted as their object increase both through the object and through association within their own stage.
Why, then, are these called "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*)? This is explained as follows:
it was previously mentioned incidentally but not set forth as a formal sūtra;
that is now being presented as it occurs in the sūtras.
Because these [defilements] adhere [to the person] through the analogies of a nurse, clothing, and dirt, and through the manner of birds and aquatic creatures,
they are therefore known as *anuśayas* (latent tendencies).
Furthermore:

"Because these [defilements] lie latent within even the momentary atoms (paramāṇu) through their own modes such as desire and so forth, they are therefore considered 'latent tendencies' (anuśaya). (Abhidharmadīpa 288)
In this regard, attachment (*rāga*) occurs by way of a desirable aspect, like eating pieces of sugar-cane with milk;
whereas aversion (*dveṣa*) occurs by way of an undesirable aspect, like eating sour gruel with *kodrava* grain, and so forth.
They are called "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*) because they adhere even to some subtle things, such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) and moments (*kṣaṇa*).

According to the principle of etymology (*nirukta*), they are called "proclivities" (*anuśaya*) because they first abandon their state of acquisition (*prāpti*) and subsequently adhere through active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
The rest has already been explained previously.
The first quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.
The second section of the fifth chapter:
Now, among these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and how many are neutral (*avyākṛta*)?
That is now begun:

The first two views are considered obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) in the desire realm; however, in the two [higher] realms, all defilements (*mala*) are likewise obscured-unspecified. *Abhidharmadīpa* 289.
First, regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):

the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), along with the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with them, are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

The view of a self-identity is not unwholesome (*akuśala*) because it is not in contradiction with giving, morality, and cultivation, and because it is contrary to the total eradication of the roots of wholesomeness (*kuśalamūla-samuccheda*).
It is not wholesome because its aspect is inverted.
If it is argued that it is unwholesome like craving (*tṛṣṇā*), we say no;
for when craving reaches its peak, one is seen to engage in every kind of improper action.

The view of grasping at extremes (*antargrāhadṛṣṭi*) is also not unwholesome, because it functions toward the cessation of rebirth; it is contrary to *nirvāṇa* yet conducive to spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). As the Blessed One said: "This view, namely 'nothing whatsoever is acceptable to me'—this view leads to non-attachment, not to attachment.

Likewise it was said: "Among the views formulated by outsiders, this is the foremost: 'May I neither be, nor may there be anything belonging to me; may I not come to be, nor may there be anything belonging to me.'"
In the realms of form and formlessness, all [defilements] are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) stains;
because they are suppressed by meditative concentration and attainment, they are unable to manifest again.
But wholesome dharmas, because their fruit is non-afflictive, are capable of producing maturation (vipāka).

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*)— excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with them— are unwholesome (*akuśala*),
because they produce results that entail affliction.
Furthermore, among these, how many are unwholesome roots and how many are not? This is explained:
"From among these, greed, hatred, and delusion—these three alone are the unwholesome roots, by virtue of their connection with five reasons. (Abhidharmadīpa 290)

Those phenomena which are unwholesome, which are roots of the unwholesome, which are to be abandoned by vision and cultivation, which are of five types, and which pertain to the six groups of consciousness—these alone are intended to be the roots of the unwholesome.
Furthermore, just as unwholesome latent dispositions have roots, do the indeterminate ones likewise have them?
The indeterminate dyad also has three roots equal to those:
ignorance, [wrong] view, and craving; not doubt, pride, or views.
“There are indeed three roots of the indeterminate:
indeterminate ignorance, craving, and wisdom,” say the Kaśmīris;
for the meaning of “root” is the meaning of “cause.”
Furthermore, unobscured-neutral wisdom (*anivṛtāvyākṛtā prajñā*) functions as a cause; therefore, this too is an indeterminate root (*avyākṛtamūla*).
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is not an indeterminate root, nor is pride (*māna*).
Because of their mobility, their upward orientation, and their lack of pervasiveness, respectively:
for doubt (*vicikitsā*) is indeed mobile; the meaning of "root" (*mūla*) is the sense of being established (*pratiṣṭhā*);
and pride (*māna*), characterized by loftiness, is upward-oriented.
Furthermore, roots function by moving downward,
yet these two afflictions do not belong to the six groups of consciousness;
therefore, because they are not all-pervasive, they are not established among the roots.
The outsiders maintain that craving, views, pride, and ignorance are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
because of the statement in the *Dhyāyi-sūtra*.
For there are three types of meditators, distinguished by those who practice meditation dominated by craving, views, and pride.
And since all those [factors] arise through the power of ignorance, they are only four; however, this is not your view. Why?
Because you have failed to understand the meaning of the Sūtra, and because your argument regarding the meditator (*dhyāyin*) is devoid of reason. (Abhidharmadīpa 292)
Indeed, this instruction regarding the three types of meditators is not intended as a definitive teaching on the roots of the indeterminate.
What, then, is its purpose?
It is intended for the turning away from the meditative resolve of those practitioners who have fallen into error; thus, what was stated previously is correct.

Now, regarding those fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛtavastu*) mentioned in the Sūtra: are they called "indeterminate points" because they cannot be classified as either wholesome or unwholesome? No, it is said; rather, it is because they are to be set aside (*sthāpanīya*).
The best of speakers explained the four ways of answering questions for the sake of training his disciples in debate, as well as the fourfold set of positions.
Indeed, having undertaken the three bases of discourse, having understood the four modes of answering, and having comprehended the four positions,
one should engage in debate by establishing one's own position through the five members of a syllogism within an assembly; it should not be done otherwise, according to this definitive rule.
What, then, are those four types of prophecy (vyākaraṇa),
and what are those four positions (sthiti)? This is now elucidated:
There are four types of [definitive] answers: that which is categorical, that which is analytical, that which is by way of questioning, and that which is to be set aside;
as, for example, [the questions concerning] death, birth, excellence, life, and the difference between substances. *Abhidharmadīpa* 294.

In that regard, a categorical explanation (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*) is as follows: "Is it the case that whoever is born, all of them die? One should answer, "Yes. Or: "Is it the case that whoever dies, all of them are born? [One should answer, "Yes."]
An answer should be given by way of analysis: "One whose outflows are exhausted is not born; all others are born.
[If asked,] "Is a human being superior or inferior? an answer should be given by asking a counter-question: "With reference to whom do you ask?"
Is it the gods or animals and so forth? If one begins with the gods, it should be said that he is inferior; if, however, one begins with animals, it should be declared that he is superior.
Is the person other than the aggregates or not other?
This question is to be set aside, because it is impossible to provide a definitive answer regarding the identity or difference of that which exists and that which does not exist.
It is like the description of the fragrance or foul odor of a flower in the sky.
Four abidings are taught:
one is designated as "speaking on the basis," another is called "conceptualization," another is named "the path," and the last is designated as "speaking from knowledge."
For some proponent abides in what is possible and impossible— that is, in what is and is not established— while another does not so abide;
the former is one with whom one may converse, but the latter is one with whom one should not converse.
One abides in conceptual construction;

he who abides in the illustrative example within the conceptualized, which establishes the meaning of the illustrated point, is one with whom it can be discussed; and he who does not so abide is one with whom it cannot be discussed.
Thus, one who abides in such knowledge-assertion on the path is called "one who speaks the truth";
however, one who does not so abide is called "one of evil intellect.
This must now be explained.
Now, by which underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) is one bound to which object (*vastu*)?
In this regard, objects are of five kinds, beginning with the field-object (*kṣetravastu*).
Here, it should be understood that the object of bondage (*saṃyogavastu*) is the subject under discussion.
That [bondage] is twofold: by way of the restriction of basis and object, and by way of the restriction of mode.

Among these, first, by way of the restriction of basis and object, one is bound to visible forms as objects by means of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the group of visual consciousness.
In those [factors] associated with it, they exist through association;
and these belong to the spheres of mind and mental objects (*manodharmāyatana*).
Likewise, up to the consciousnesses of the body, they exist through the object (*ālambana*) according to their respective domains.
In regard to those associated with it, [it exists] by way of association;
in regard to the twelve bases belonging to the mental consciousness aggregate, [it exists] by way of being the object;
and in regard to those associated with it, [it exists] by way of association.
Such is the determination of the basis and the object.
However, according to the restriction of their modes, one is bound by way of the object to the universal [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering within the five classes;
and by way of association, to those [factors] associated with them.
But by the non-universal [mental factors], there is [contamination] through the object within their own category,
and through association within those that are associated;
thus, in all cases, it should be stated according to what is possible.
Now, according to the determination of the past, future, and present, which person (pudgala) is bound to which object by which latent disposition (anuśaya)?
This is set forth:
"One who exists in the present with pride, aversion, and attachment, whose activities have not yet ceased..."
Where [a defilement] has arisen and has not been abandoned, one is bound to that object.
For these—pride, hostility, and attachment—are afflictions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇakleśa*) because they have real entities as their objects.
However, views, doubt, and so forth are afflictions of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇakleśa*).

Therefore, it should be understood that one is associated with these [afflictions] such as pride, whether past or present, in relation to that object in which they have arisen and have not yet been abandoned.
For these do not arise in everyone everywhere, because they are afflictions characterized by their own specific nature (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The continuum of the aggregates (skandhasantati) is conjoined with these unarisen mental [factors], with all others belonging to its own time-period, and likewise with all those that have not yet arisen, as well as with the remaining [factors].
The phrase "as they have been abandoned" carries over [from the previous context].
Indeed, for whichever past category of affliction has been abandoned, its future category is likewise [abandoned].
Therefore, those [afflictions] such as pride and attachment that are future and not yet abandoned—by means of these, one is bound to all objects belonging to the three times.
Because mental [afflictions] can arise with those [objects] as their focal points, and because mental states have the three time periods as their objects;

therefore, one is bound by other future [afflictions], such as attachment and so forth, to a future object alone; by past [afflictions], to a past object alone; and by present [afflictions], to a present object alone.
For those belonging to the five groups of sensory consciousness are distinct from the mental ones.

Consequently, it is established that one is bound by past and present mental [factors] that have not been abandoned, even with respect to an object belonging to a different time period; and it is not only by these future mental factors that one is bound everywhere—what then? One is also bound by those belonging to the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*).

However, by way of those future factors belonging to the five groups of sensory consciousness which are of a nature not to arise (*anutpattidharmaka*), one is bound everywhere with respect to objects belonging to all three time periods.
Because its object is past, future, or present,

one is bound to all objects belonging to the three time periods by means of the universal afflictions— namely, those called views, doubt, and ignorance— even though these belong to the three time periods;
this is because they are universal afflictions, and the phrase "as long as they have not been abandoned" continues to apply here.
But how is it known that passion and the other [afflictions] arise with respect to past and other objects, and that one becomes bound to them by means of those [afflictions]?
It is known from the Sūtra itself;
for the Blessed One said: "There are three types of phenomena that serve as bases for desire and passion."
There are past phenomena that are the basis for desire and lust, as well as those of the future and present.
Depending upon past phenomena that are the basis for desire and lust, desire arises.
When desire has arisen, one should be said to be associated with those factors, not dissociated from them.
Likewise: "In whatever form—past, future, or present—there arises either attachment or aversion..."
And so forth.
But who, then, is joined here [in this bondage], when all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty?
Is it by means of a self (ātman) that is eternal, stable, permanent, and subject to no change, or by means of what belongs to a self (ātmīya)?

As it has been said: "Karma exists and its maturation (vipāka) exists, but no agent (kāraka) is found who, having cast off these aggregates (skandhas), reconnects with other aggregates—except for the conventional designation of phenomena (dharmasaṃketa)," and so forth in detail.
To this, the rebuttal is: "The continuum of the aggregates is conjoined.

For within the continuum of the aggregates, due to the conceit of a single identity in the continuity of the characteristics of the aggregates, there is the designation of a "sentient being" through conventional usage; thus, there is no fault.
Furthermore, from these three,
only two are established here as real, while the third exists only figuratively.
The two consisting of the "union of things" exist in the ultimate sense, whereas the third object, called "sentient being," exists only conventionally.
But why, then, does this pair exist from the perspective of ultimate reality? To this it is said:
"Because they are the causes of both existence and non-existence, and because they are embraced by those who stand in the middle. (Abhidharmadīpa 298)

The fruit of actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is determined by the necessity of their qualities and defects. Furthermore: "And because they are accepted by those who are impartial"; those who are impartial are said to be those whose afflictions have been removed.
By them, the wholesome has been grasped as wholesome and the unwholesome as unwholesome; virtues have been grasped as virtues and faults as faults;
and their results have been grasped as desirable as desirable and undesirable as undesirable.
Thus it is established that the first two are the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*), while the third exists only figuratively.
This is indeed logical.
As for what has been stated—that which arises dependently from the causes and conditions of things exists in the ultimate sense because it is to be personally realized within oneself—this is correct.
And since passion and the other [defilements] have those as their objects, they exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*).
As for that which was said—that one is bound by the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the three time periods to past and future entities—that is merely a rash and boastful assertion.
Who, then, desires this [existence of] the past, the future, and so forth as substantial? The Abhidharmikas say: [they do].
Indeed, there are four types of disputants in this teaching.
Which are the four? That is explained as follows:
"All exists," "there is a partial existence," "all does not exist," and another,
"the proponent of the indeterminate existence"— these are remembered as the four proponents.
In that regard, for the Sarvāstivāda, there are the three time periods (*adhvan*), which they call the "three constants" (*dhruva-traya*).
However, for the Vibhajyavādins and the Dārṣṭāntikas, it is only the portion designated as the present time period.
For the Vaitulikas, who are proponents of the emptiness of non-connection (*ayoga-śūnyatā-vādin*), [it is otherwise].
"Everything does not exist.
Even for one who asserts the indeterminate entity of a person (*pudgala*), the person exists substantially;
in this regard, however—
Among these, the first disputant is the one who possesses correctness;
however, the others, who pride themselves on logic, are excluded from both reasoning and scripture.
Indeed, this first proponent known as the Sarvāstivāda is a true proponent (sadvādī) because he speaks in accordance with reason and scripture;
other proponents— the Dārṣṭāntikas, Vaitulikās, and Paudgalikas— do not speak in accordance with reason and scripture.
Those who take pride in their own reasoning,
because they are false speakers, should be categorized among the ranks of the Lokāyatikas, the Nihilists, and the Nagnāṭas.
And for this reason, I shall demonstrate that everything is omnipresent.
Who, then, among these Sarvāstivādins deserves to be considered correct?
This very point is now being elucidated.
Indeed, this proponent—
Because he maintains the existence of the three time periods and the three constants by way of their functional activity,
the first fourfold school is therefore called Sarvāstivāda.
Indeed, this Sarvāstivāda has undergone a fourfold division.
How so? That is now undertaken:
two are known as the Bhāvānyathika and the Lakṣaṇānyathika, and another is the Avasthānyathika.
Another is the "one who asserts otherwise-ness" (anyathānyathika);
the third is the proponent of reasoning (yuktivādin).

In this regard, the Venerable Dharmatrāta is the proponent of the alteration of state (*bhāvānyathika*). For he says: "When a dharma proceeds through the time-periods (*adhvan*), only its state—such as being future and so forth—becomes otherwise; there is no alteration of its substance (*dravya*)."
Just as when gold is fashioned into another form such as a bracelet, there is no destruction of the gold even though the previous form is destroyed;
or just as when milk transforms into curd, there is a relinquishing of its taste, potency, and post-digestive effect, but not of its color— so too,
because he adheres to the position of Vārṣagaṇya, he should be regarded as belonging to that very school.

Because this [Venerable Ghoṣaka], a proponent of the alteration of characteristics (*lakṣaṇānyathika*), maintains that there is transformation characterized by the various states of a substance that remains constant—whether defined by its genus, its specific characteristic, or its collective form. Here, the Venerable Ghoṣaka observes that a past dharma is endowed with its past characteristic and is not devoid of its future and present characteristics;
likewise for the future and present [dharmas].
Just as a man may be attached to one woman while not being detached from others,
so too for this [Vaibhāṣika] there is a confusion of the time periods (*adhvasaṃkara*), because he accepts that a single dharma possesses the characteristics of all three times.
This [view] of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) must also be led into the snare;
the Venerable Vasumitra is one who maintains that change occurs through a difference in state (*avasthānyathika*).

He indeed said: "When a dharma proceeds through the time-periods (adhvan), having reached various successive states, it is designated as being 'otherwise and otherwise' because of the transformation consisting of the distinction between different states, yet without abandoning its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva). It is just as a single counting-stick placed in the 'units' position is called 'one'."
That same [unit] is a hundred in the hundredth place and a thousand in the thousandth place.
The Venerable Buddhadeva is one who holds a different view;
he says:
When a dharma proceeds through the time periods (adhvan), it is described as being different and yet different by observing what precedes and follows it;
however, there is no alteration in its essential nature (bhāva) nor any alteration in its substance (dravya).
For example, a single woman is called a "mother" in relation to one who preceded her and a "daughter" in relation to one who followed her.
In the same way, a dharma is called "past" in relation to the future and the present;
likewise, each of the others is so designated in relation to the other two.
For this single past time-period as well, there arises the fault of the consequence that it would become three time-periods by depending on its preceding and succeeding moments.
Among these four Sarvāstivādins, the third is the Elder Vasumitra, who rejected the twenty-five principles and demolished the doctrine of the accumulation of atoms;
therefore, he alone should be determined to be an authoritative and trustworthy person (*āpta*) because he follows both reason and scripture.
Even the Venerable Buddhadeva is not accepted [as an authority], as he aligns himself with the faction of the non-Buddhist heretics (*tīrthika*).

The Venerable Ghoṣaka, too, because he maintains that there is no confusion of the time periods (*adhva*), asserts that each individual time period possesses the characteristics of all three time periods;
therefore, the third position alone is free from fault,
since he seeks to establish the distinction between the time periods by means of their functional activity (*kāritra*).
While performing that [action], one is in the present path; once it is completed, one is in the past; while it is not yet completed, one is in the future.

Regarding those phenomena belonging to the three time periods— past, future, and present— which were indeed taught by the Blessed One as established by their own nature (*svabhāva*), this Master maintains that they possess a distinction of states (*avasthābheda*) through the medium of activity (*kriyā*), without abandoning their essential form (*svarūpa*), their capacity being awakened by the presence of a causal complex (*hetusāmagrī*).
For a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskāra*) possessing activity is called "present."
That very [substance], when its activity has ceased, is the past; when it has not yet undertaken activity, it is the future.

This being the case, the three times share a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇya*) and are delimited by an operation based on a single locus (*ekādhiṣṭhāna-vyāpāra-paricchedyatva*), which is thus logically established.

Otherwise, in the absence of a single substance as the cause for the genus, there would be a lack of common substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), and consequently, a lack of connection with the three times would result.
Here the opponent says: No, because the designation of past and future objects is established through conceptual construction (*prajñapti*).

[The respondent replies: No, because if ultimate substance (*paramārtha-dravya*) does not exist, a designation by way of conceptual construction is untenable, as it would lack a basis (*anadhiṣṭhāna*).
If it is argued that the designation [of existence] depends upon the present, we say no;
for existence is untenable in the absence of the nature, stability, capacity, and activity of the present,
and because there can be no relation of dependence between the existent and the non-existent.

The characteristic of existence (*sattvalakṣaṇa*) of past and other categories of entities is now illuminated: "That mark which is perceived by the intellect is called 'designation' (*saṃjñā*); it is fourfold:
in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), both, and also by way of dependence. (Abhidharmadīpa 304)

Indeed, that objective entity whose characteristic is discerned through a definition of phenomena (*dharmopalakṣaṇā*) that is non-erroneous in form, and which possesses an essential nature established by its own-being (*svabhāvasiddhasvarūpa*), is called a "real substance" (*saddravya*). Furthermore, when that reality is analyzed, it is of four kinds.
That which is eternal in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), comprised of its own-being, and never abandons its own self-nature—[is the first kind].
That which possesses a relationship with a subject that is non-human and whose object is designated by a distinguished cognition is called ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).

On the other hand, that which is indicated as having the nature of a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*) for the sake of conventional usage, based upon many ultimately real things, is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*).
Such as, for example, a jar, a cloth, a forest, a person (*pudgala*), and so forth.
Some things function in both ways,
such as earth and so forth; some [function] with respect to sentient beings, such as father and son, teacher and disciple, agent and action, and so on.
Now, as for what was stated—that past and future phenomena exist substantially—this is a mere assertion, since no scripture or reasoning has been provided.

Therefore, this point must be established through both scripture and reasoning; thus, the following proposition is put forward: "The past and the unarisen exist, because they are spoken of by the Buddha, just like the present."
And because it is not within the range of mental cognition, its existence is like that of the present.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, past form exists; if past form did not exist, these beings would not be attached to past form.
But because past form exists, therefore these beings are attached to past form.
The same should be stated for future and present [form].
If it is argued that this is a particle (nipāta) resembling an inflected word, we say no;

for that [undesired] consequence would follow even in the case of a present [tense]. Furthermore, because the subsequent member, which denotes an action, requires grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the preceding member, which must likewise denote an action.
Furthermore, it was said by the Blessed One: "Form, whether past or future, is impermanent; what need is there to mention the present?
Seeing thus, the learned noble disciple is indifferent toward past form and does not delight in future form."
"One practices for the sake of revulsion toward, detachment from, and the cessation of present form.
If past form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not be free from longing for past form;
but because past form does exist, the learned noble disciple is free from longing for past form," and so forth.
Thus it has been said: "Śāriputra, that action which is past, exhausted, ceased, vanished, and transformed—does that exist?

"If that action, Śāriputra, did not exist, then on account of that cause and that condition, a person here would not, upon the breakup of the body after death, be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, or a downfall in the hells," and so forth in detail.
If it is argued that there is no fault because this statement was made with reference to the cultivation of the mental impression (*cittabhāvanā*) deposited by that [action], we say: no.
Because it has already been answered;
for this argument has already been refuted. Why do you repeat yourself like a sesame-press?

Furthermore, because it is logically untenable for the mind and the mental states being cultivated through meditation to possess their own intrinsic nature, power, and activity— just like oil that has been saturated with fragrance—
and because of the faults regarding identity and difference that will be discussed later;
if you argue that [the self] does not exist because of the *Paramārthaśūnyatā-sūtra*, we say no.
Because its meaning has not been fully understood, and because it is precisely from that [text] that the existence of the future and so forth is established.
In this regard, it might be argued: "In the *Paramārthaśūnyatā-sūtra*, the Blessed One..."
The non-existence of the future and so forth has been clearly demonstrated.
For it is stated therein: "The eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation," and so on in detail.
Furthermore, if the past and the future were to exist as real entities, it would follow that one must accept the faults of coming and going;
but this is not so. Why? Because of a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra.
For this very reason, the existence of the future and so forth is established. First, the meaning of the sutra is as follows:
it was stated that "the eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere."
"When ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation"—this is for the purpose of explaining the prohibitions regarding the doctrines stated in the Veda and for the purpose of refuting the Sāṃkhya view;
for it is said in the Veda: "Of that which undergoes dissolution into the five elements, the eye, having come from the sun, returns again to that very place;
the ear [returns] to space."
The nose is earth;
the tongue is water;
the body is air.
"Mind is water" means it is *soma*.
To refute that, the Blessed One said: "When the eye arises, it does not come from anywhere," and so forth in detail.
Indeed, the Sāṃkhyas also declare: "The eye comes from the *pradhāna* and dissolves back into that very same place."
And in order to refute that [objection], the Blessed One said: "The eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere.

For indeed, phenomena designated as future, past, atoms, and non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) do not abide in a specific location or spatial dimension; thus, their coming and going are logically untenable.
What, then, is the meaning of the statement?
—“It comes into being after not having been;
and having come into being, it passes away.

For the eye is of two kinds: that which exists as a substantial reality (*dravyasat*) in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*), and that which, though existing, is unawakened. Both [of these] are such.
The other [consciousness] is one that has already awakened and has undertaken activity;
having previously depended upon its causes, it takes up activity and awakens— this is the meaning.
And the second [type] possesses active function;
for it is said that it perishes by relinquishing its activity. Alternatively, this is stated for the purpose of refuting the Sāṃkhya doctrine.

Indeed, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that there is one eternal cause which, without abandoning its own nature, repeatedly assumes various specific forms of transformation and evolves into various specific effects.
To refute this, the Blessed One said: "The eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation.
Having not previously existed, the eye takes on the form of activity for a mere moment in the present time, and having abandoned it, it again passes beyond sight.
Furthermore, for this very reason, the existence of the future is established.
That which was stated in this very Sūtra—“the eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere”—is demonstrated here:
this eye, assuming its activity through the influence of the conditions consisting in the proximity of the collection of internal and external causes, does not come from anywhere.
If it is asked, "How then can that existence [of the agent] be established?"—[the answer is:

because the suffix *śānac* is prescribed when the agent is possessed of primary existence (*mukhyasattā*), as in the case of "one who is being obstructed" (*nirudhyamāna*). Therefore, this Sūtra is relied upon by the Sautrāntikas for the sake of undermining their own position, like the raising of a poorly conjured Vetāla.

Thus, the existence of the three time periods is established by scripture (*āgama*). It is also established by reasoning (*yukti*): "And because it is the object of cognition, its existence is like that of the present.
For indeed, it is by means of a cognition possessing the form of that [object] that the specific and general characteristics (*svasāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of a given object are determined.
That which is illuminated by the collection of names (nāmakāya) and the collection of dharmas (dharmakāya) spoken by the Buddha exists in the ultimate sense.
How so? Like the present eye, visible forms, and so forth.
Indeed, the learned understand that the relationship between knowledge and the object of knowledge, and between the designation and the designated, is unconditioned (akṛtaka).
If it is argued that there is indeed cognition even with respect to a non-existent object, it is replied to this:
There is no cognition with a non-existent object, neither according to scripture nor through logical reasoning.

First, regarding scripture: the Blessed One has said, "Dependent upon the eye and visible forms, visual consciousness arises; likewise, dependent upon the mind and mental phenomena (*dharmas*), mental consciousness arises. All that exists is just this much. In this context, mental consciousness has as its objects the conditioned phenomena belonging to the three time periods as well as unconditioned phenomena.
The five groups of consciousness have the five present objects as their objective supports.
It has never been stated anywhere that they have a non-existent object, nor does it exist such that there would be an absence of cognition regarding that object.
Thus it is said: “That which does not exist in the world, I shall see,” and so forth in detail. (Jaini_270)
Likewise: "The coming together of the three is contact;
feeling is co-arisen," and so forth.
By this, the relationship between the designation and the designated is refuted.
This being so, the middle way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) is demonstrated in this sūtra as follows:

conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty in one respect—namely, with respect to that which is falsely imagined, such as a person (*puruṣa*), the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), or unreal imagination (*abhūta-parikalpa*);
yet they are not empty in another respect.
That is to say, by means of both specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
As stated in the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*: "Having known the arising of the world, that which does not exist in the world does not come to be;
having known the cessation of the world, that which exists in the world does not [permanently] exist. Having abandoned these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by way of the middle way.

Furthermore, this pair known as existence and non-existence cannot logically reside in a single substratum because they are contradictory; nor can it be without a substratum, nor can it be based on something empty like a flower in the sky.
This is also established by reasoning, for the relationship between knowledge and the object of knowledge, and between the designation and the designated, is uncreated.

If it is argued that the cognition and the verbal expression "there is no rabbit's horn" have a non-existent object, we reply: "In that case, there is a negation of the relation between the horse and the horn with respect to something else. (Abhidh-d 306)
If this negation of things such as a rabbit's horn does not exist, then what is there to be negated?
Is it that there is no cognition having a non-existent object, or no verbal expression having a non-existent referent?
To this, it is replied:
"Furthermore, there is the negation of a relationship in dependence upon something else.
Here, the threefold relationship—such as that of cause and effect—which was previously observed in cases like the horns of a cow, is denied in the case of things like the horns of a rabbit.

If a horn were present even on the head of a rabbit, it would have been perceived just like those [horns] in the same manner, given that a relationship with the space-element (ākāśadhātu) upon the mere head of a rabbit is observed.
And yet, [the absence] is not perceived.

Therefore, the word "hare's horn" is merely a verbal excrescence dependent on another relation; it is illuminated by the negative particle (*nañ*) as being dependent on a cognition of a connection with some other related entity.
However, no denotation or denoted object whatsoever is accepted as having the nature of a negation. Thus it is established that every cognition has an existent object.
By this, the [alleged] unarisen and destroyed cow-horn is refuted.
One should understand that the cow-horn will arise or has been destroyed only upon seeing the mere head of the cow enveloped by the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*).
If it is argued that there exists a cognition with a non-existent object because the cognition that negates the thirteen bases (*āyatana*) has existence as its object, we say no.
For this has been determined by the Blessed One himself as being merely a matter of words.
Indeed, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Hastatālopama-sūtra*: "All this is just this much: namely, the eye and forms, up to the mind and mental objects (*dharmas*).
Whoever, having rejected this pair, [speaks of] another pair that is either knowable or expressible—"
"Or he might fabricate [an answer], such that for him there would be nothing more than mere words;
or, when questioned, he would not understand, or he would fall into confusion in his reply—just as it is because that [matter] is not within his domain. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, just as there is the expression "the horn of a hare" along with its corresponding referent, the statement "it does not exist" is also a mere verbal entity devoid of any connection to a referent designated by the word "horn.
By this, the sixth aggregate (skandha) is refuted.
Moreover, it is because of the negation of a cognition that is contrary to the objects of the five aggregates.
It is like the refutation of the cognition of a fire-brand circle and like the refutation of the cognition of a double moon.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Whoever perceives [a self], they all perceive only these [aggregates]."
"Those who perceive the five aggregates of clinging perceive them [as such]"—this indicates that this delusion regarding a permanent self-substance exists with respect to the aggregates.
Furthermore, it is because it is logically untenable for the negative particle (*nañ*) to have either an existent or a non-existent object of negation;
for it is not capable of negating an object that is already existent.

For if one were able to negate an existing object, then kings would not maintain elephants and horses, and they would say, "Bandits do not exist. If this were said, there would be an absence of bandits;
yet this is not the case.
Now, if one were to negate that which is non-existent,
then by negating a non-entity, it would follow that the entity itself exists.
Therefore, neither the cow’s horn nor the rabbit’s horn is what is negated by the negative particle *nañ*.
What then?
By means of the cognition dependent on the relationship between a hare and the element of space, cognitions of the non-relationship of substances such as cow-horns are illuminated.
Thus, it is established that cognition always has an existent object.
The same applies elsewhere as well:
when an object such as form has perished, a cognition arises;
that cognition has the aspect of non-existence for knowledge, just as it does for the Teacher or for another's mind.
Furthermore, even with respect to an object such as form that has passed away, cognition indeed arises only when that object exists;
for a cognition does not arise having a non-existent thing as its objective support.
It has been established that cognition possesses an existent objective support.
And it has been stated that our substance does not perish;
we shall further establish above that this very substance, such as form (rūpa) and so forth, which was previously experienced, is what is grasped by that memory.
How then does that memory of a deceased Devadatta or the memory of a jar arise?
Regarding the past and future bases for the designations "Devadatta" and "pot," we reply:
indeed, that ignorance arises with the appearance of what is non-existent, just like the cognition of a person in relation to a tree stump and so forth.
But for the Teacher who is free from ignorance, there arises only a cognition of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which has the aspect of reality (*tattvākāra*).
Just as, for example, in one who knows the minds of others, a cognition arises having the aspect of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇākāra*),
yet he also knows them otherwise by virtue of the influence of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of that [cognition's] capacity.
In the same way, by virtue of that capacity, one apprehends the future and past designations—characterized as "Devadatta" or "jar"—with respect to form and the other [sensory objects].
For this reason as well, the past and the future exist:
because they serve as factors for the arising of joy, the arising of fear, agitation, and the arising of memory.
For indeed, by bringing to mind a friend or an enemy from the past or the future, joy, fear, and so forth come into being.
And those [mental states] cannot be signless.
How so? Like the present. For example, when a friend or an enemy is present, joy, fear, and so forth arise; they do not arise when they are absent. It is just like that.
Furthermore,
because the manifestation of power occurs when all its constituent parts are present, it is like the form of a jar illuminated by a lamp.
Indeed, for a future entity that already exists and is grasped by the totality of past and present auxiliary causes, only its power becomes manifest.
How so? "Like the form of a jar together with a lamp.
That is to say, just as the power of a jar's own manifestation, though existing in the dark, occurs when the totality of causes such as a lamp is present, so it is in this case.
For this reason as well, the future exists.
Because it is to be accomplished by an agent (*janīhākartṛ*), like the five modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*).
That is to say: "it exists," "it transforms," "it grows," "it wanes," and "it perishes"—these five modifications of being occur when there is an agent possessed of primary existence (*mukhyasattā*).
In the same way, this sixth modification of being, "it is born" (*jāyate*), ought also to occur when there is an agent possessed of primary existence.

Furthermore, being in the process of arising (*jāyamānatā*) is not existence (*sattā*), because if they were not in a relation of coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*), there would follow the faults of the loss of non-difference and the confusion of categories.
If one accepts their lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), then due to the absence of a relationship between them, it is impossible to designate them as belonging to a single locus.
Moreover, in the absence of actions such as "being in the process of arising," existence itself is untenable.
How so? Like the horn of a hare.
If it is argued that this is "figurative existence" (*upacārasattā*), we say no; for figurative existence occurs only when primary existence (*mukhyasattā*) exists.
And because of the faults that will be stated hereafter;

for this reason as well, [the self] exists—because an existent thing is observed to be a constituent part of an action, just like an object that is to be modified or an object that is to be reached. (Abhidh-d 309)
For example, when there is an object to be modified (*vikārya-karman*), an instrument is observed, as in "he makes a mat from grass.
And when there is an object to be reached (*prāpya-karman*), as in "Devadatta goes to the village" and "he sees the sun," the actions of going and seeing occur with respect to an object.

In the same way, even with respect to an object to be produced (*nirvartya-karman*), provided that the primary substance exists, the action of making a jar performed by the agent Devadatta is logically established.
The Sāṃkhya observes: that which already exists is born,
just as curd exists within milk,
because of the identity between cause and effect.
In response to that, it is stated: A second birth is not possible for an entity that has already been born.
For if, indeed, transformations such as curd existed in milk, or sprouts and so forth in a seed, or the embryo (kalala) and so forth in the semen and blood; [then a second birth would be plausible].
Once these have been produced, their birth again—like that of milk and so forth—is not tenable;
and how it is not tenable has already been demonstrated previously.

The Vaiśeṣika maintains: the substance of a jar, which does not exist within the potsherds, and the substance of a cloth, which does not exist within the threads, are produced from the conjunction of the potsherds and the threads.
And by means of a figurative conceptualization, the existence that is the agent of production is designated with reference to an object in a remote state;
regarding this as well, the substance consisting of the whole together with its parts has already been refuted previously.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated—that the agent of production is designated by means of metaphorical existence—we reply: because of the absence of qualities, there is no secondary existence where primary existence does not exist. *Abhidharmadīpa* 310.

For it is not tenable to metaphorically attribute the existence of an effect to its causes—whether in the case of primary existence, the absence of qualities, the absence of parts, or the non-existence prior to production.
Why?
Because when there is a similarity (*sādharmya*), there is a figurative expression (*vyāhāra*) based on its occurrence [in that object], just like the term "sweet speech.

For example, in the case of "Devadatta has sweet speech," since the quality of sweetness exists in the substance of molasses or honey—which possesses the quality of sweetness—and this desirability constitutes a similarity with speech, the word "sweetness" is applied to the speech.
The word "moon" is applied after seeing a resemblance to the moon's luster in the face of a maiden;
and the word "cow" is applied to a Vāhīka person because of the common property of dullness, as in such expressions as, "This Vāhīka is a cow," and so forth.

Furthermore, there is not even a trace of the scent of any quality or part in the threads or in their conjunction prior to the production [of the effect], since the effect is devoid of self-nature (nirātman).
Nor can it be maintained that any effect whatsoever is produced even slightly,
because of the admission that the completion [of the cause] and the existence [of the effect] are simultaneous.
If it is argued that a mere entity, previously unnameable and separated [from its qualities], arises, we say no;
for this has already been answered.
For my part, however, there exists an illustrative example characterized by the brilliance of ten million moons.
The birth of one who possesses a primary gender-sign is desired, just like that of a child and so forth.
For this term "birth" (janman) refers to the act of emerging [from the womb] and so forth, not to the manifestation of that which was previously non-existent.
How so? "Like a child. Just as a child, who is already possessed of primary existence, is said to be "born" upon emerging from the mother's womb.
"It is the same here as well.
The proponent of the illustrative example (dārṣṭāntika) indeed says: "The metaphorical designation of a 'selfless producer' (nirātmakajanikartṛ) is applied to the causal potencies.
To him we reply:
The sky might be filled with sky-flowers, and a frog might possess matted hair,
if intrinsic nature were to arise after having previously not existed through the power of mental cultivation.

For there is no arising of anything non-existent, such as a rabbit’s horn, because that would entail the absurd consequence of the arising of all non-existent things since there is no distinction between them in their lack of self-nature (*nairātmya*).

Furthermore, it is impossible for those things caused by it to possess an established power of self-existence during the times of their being born, having been born, or perishing. Moreover, because causes are of the same nature as their effects, they must be non-existent prior to production.
Because it is non-existent, it would incur the fault of being logically untenable.
Furthermore, why does a non-entity not become an entity?
Because it lacks connection with stability, power, and activity.
If it is asked, "What is this lack of connection?
it is then revealed:
[It concerns] dharmas that have abandoned the power of stability and arise accompanied by destruction.
Speak, my dear friend: how does a thing attain the status of a real entity through dependent origination?
In this world, indeed, for all things that possess an origin, destruction is causeless and is eternally present.
And when that [destruction] exists, the powers of birth, stability, and activity do not exist, because they are contradictory. When those [powers] are absent, the cause itself has likewise perished.
Therefore, tell me: in the absence of this [self], depending upon what does a non-existent, selfless thing attain the status of being a "thing"?
How can cause and effect be established for you?

For it is only when things exist that there is the conventional designation of name and named, knowledge and the object of knowledge, action and its instrument, cause and fruit, and so forth, through their mutual dependence.
Now, if there is no such thing as non-existence that is the opposite of existence, how then can it be said that "that existence has perished"?
Therefore, this is merely a matter of words on your part.
For me, however, it is logical that the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary exists only when both are present;
because in the world, mutual assistance is observed only between two things that exist.
In the same way, there can be no injury to a horse's horn or a snake's foot.

Furthermore, the metaphorical designation of a causal relationship between benefit and injury occurs only when both exist; this is well known even to infants, and it does not apply to two non-existent things, nor to one existent and one non-existent thing.
The Vaitulika calculates thus: "Whatever is dependently originated does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Indeed, that which is without intrinsic nature and without self (*anātman*), being born in dependence upon causes, has no intrinsic nature at all."
For that [effect] does not exist individually in its causes, nor in parts, nor anywhere else;

nor does it exist in the collection of causes, because its form is absent there. And since it does not exist anywhere, by what intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) could it arise? Thus, intrinsic nature does not exist.
And how can that which has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) be said to exist?
Therefore, because all phenomena (dharmas) lack intrinsic nature—like a firebrand’s circle—they are selfless (nirātman).
In response to this, it is declared:
That which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature exists otherwise than that.
This is a theological discourse (*brahmodya*): that which is dependently originated exists by way of its conventional nature, like a forest or a collection;
whereas that which exists ultimately arises as a mere state, capacity, form, and activity dependent [on causes].
In that case, what assistance do its causes provide to that which already exists? To this it is replied:
they certainly do not provide any assistance regarding the existence of its substantial intrinsic nature (*dravyasvabhāva*).

Furthermore, the designation of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not dependent [on anything else]. What then? Causes merely produce a state for an entity that already exists, just as ministers [confer] the kingship upon a prince who already possesses his own self-nature. (Abhidh-d 316)

Just as when a noble prince exists, his ministers, together with their assembled forces, perform the duties of kingship merely by supporting and favoring him, so too it should be understood that although a future entity already exists, causes and conditions, having come together, exercise sovereignty and dominance over what is called the "present," which consists of nothing more than its characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
Others, however, describe it thus:
"When there is a collection of factors, efficacy arises, just as in the case of accumulated atoms for the purpose of perceiving a self. (Abhidh-d 317)

Just as a collection of atoms is perceived by the eye while individual atoms are not perceived, so too should it be understood that when the causal totality is present, the capacity for action arises in phenomena.

The Venerable Kumāralāta observes that when light enters through a window, there are gaps on both sides; however, while the light itself is visible, the gaps situated along the sides of that light must be inferred. By this, the existence of two temporal periods for phenomena is explained.
Having attained the excellence of knowledge, the sages perceive them; for that intellect indeed consists of the three births.
But for one who thinks that past karma ceases to exist and that the future does not yet exist, it is declared: "For him, a non-existent past karma produces a future fruit that is also non-existent;
clearly, a son of a barren woman is born from the womb of a celestial nymph. (Abhidh-d 318)
For you, existence in the present time is not tenable,
because of the absence of cause and effect in the past and future, like the birth of a son from a barren woman's womb.
Here the Dārṣṭāntikas raise an objection: "We do not say that the past does not exist in every respect.
What then? It does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyātman*), but it exists as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptyātman*). To this, the following reply is given:
Because it lacks the characteristics of a real entity and because its status as a substantial reality is unestablished,
that which is future or past does not possess the nature of a conceptual reality.
For everything that exists as a conceptual designation (prajñaptisat) possesses an appropriation (sopādāna).

And it is not possible for an appropriation to be present [simultaneously with its object], because the future and the past do not exist. Therefore, since there can be no conceptual designation for that which lacks an appropriation, this [position] is untenable.
If, then, the future substance of the eye and so forth exists, why does it not see, why is it not seen, and why does it not cognize?
It is because its activity (*kāritra*) is not manifest.
Regarding this, the author of the Kośa asks: "What is the obstacle? If the eye exists, why does it not see?"
We say:
a deficiency of factors is indeed observed; for even when the eye exists, there is no perception of form if the lamp or other factors are deficient.
He replies: "If everything exists at all times, how can there be a deficiency of factors?
We say:
"That existence of everything is not eternal."
Indeed, the members [of dependent origination] belonging to the three time periods are intended here.
In that regard, for some [members], there is an absence; due to that deficiency, it does not perform its function. He refutes this:
In that case, how is it so?
Is the activity [distinct] from that characteristic or from that substance,
and is it something other than them or rather not other?
To this we reply:

Listen, seated as you are among the virtuous disciples; for the profundity of the teachings of the Omniscient One cannot be understood by mere reasoning alone, even by the world together with its gods.
For this reason, O gentle one, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is indeed difficult to understand.
Nevertheless, let it be heard.

The projection of a fruit by that which has acquired its capacity through its occurrence in the present time-path and through the grasping of the factors of the causal complex is designated as "activity" (kāritra).

Indeed, when a future dharma enters the present time-path through the acquisition of internal and external causal complexes, that projection of a fruit by the dharma which has thereby acquired its capacity is called "activity" (*kāritra*).
And this functioning in the present time is designated as "activity.
In this regard, for one who asserts that activity is not distinct [from the dharma], it follows that the dharma must abandon its substantial nature (*dravyasvabhāva*).
In the treatise, however, it is said:

"The nature of form is neither its present state nor its pastness or unarisenness; therefore, the essence of form is not held to undergo alteration through the transition between the time-periods (adhvan). *Abhidharmadīpa* 322.
If there is no alteration in the substantial self, then what is it that arises in dependence upon causes? We reply:
A certain state (*avasthā*) of an existing entity arises;
likewise its capacity (*śakti*), likewise its time (*velā*), likewise its existence (*sattā*), and likewise its activity (*kriyā*). (Abhidharmadīpa 323)
In this context, power (*śakti*) is that which depends on the accumulation of capacities in various states and on action; it is the efficacy produced by dependence on action.
Action is that which has its fruit yet to come.
Time, known as the "present," is the duration of the operation of substances.
Form is a specific aggregation of atoms;
existence is a conceptual reality (prajñaptisatya) termed "awakening.
Thus, all of this has a nature that is dependent upon and attached to the presence of a collection of internal and external causes.
Regarding this, a Vaitulika who has strayed from the Sarvāstivāda school says: "We too shall postulate three natures.
To him it should be replied:
"The world is pervaded by conceptual constructions that delight the minds of fools."
But that conceptual construction which is grasped by the minds of the wise is difficult to find.
Indeed, these three natures (svabhāva) imagined by you have already been refuted. In this same manner, other false conceptualizations (asat-parikalpa) should also be dispelled.
Thus, this is another point of branding for the "cocoon-maker" (Kośakāraka), characterized by delusion regarding the temporal periods (adhvan).
This incidental section is concluded; let us now proceed with the treatise itself.
This has been explained: with respect to which object, by which afflictions, and in which state one is bound.
Now this must be stated:
is one bound to that object whose [affliction] has not been abandoned?

Is that object which one is bound to still unabandoned? Whatever object is unabandoned, one is bound to that object. However, there may be an object to which one is bound, yet that object is not unabandoned, as is the case, for instance, on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Bound by other universal [defilements], when the exhaustion through the vision of suffering has been abandoned— that is,

when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen— the entity to be abandoned by the vision of suffering becomes abandoned. Even though that has been abandoned, what is to be abandoned by the vision of origin remains unabandoned.
One is bound by those universal [afflictions] that have it as their object;
likewise on the path of cultivation—
even when a previous category has been abandoned— one remains bound by the remaining [afflictions] that take it as their object.
It should be understood that even when whichever among the nine types has been previously abandoned, one remains bound by the remaining afflictions that take that [abandoned type] as their object.

Now, with respect to which object do how many latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere? In this regard, first the determination of the objects must be shown: which phenomenon (dharma) is the object of which consciousness?
From that very [source], it is clearly understood how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhere to such-and-such an object.
Thus, this thicket of the Abhidharma is expanded:
sixteen categories of phenomena (*dharma*) are to be known, each consisting of the nature of the three realms of existence.
And likewise, the consciousnesses are fivefold and stainless.

To begin with, phenomena (*dharmas*) in the desire, form, and formless realms are each of five types: those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and so forth, and those not to be abandoned, as well as the stainless ones; thus, there are sixteen.
Consciousnesses (*vijñānas*) are to be understood in the same way.
In that regard, first, the Abhidharmika, when questioned by others,
should characterize the elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), truths (satya), and their various modes (prakāra),
being impelled by the knowledge of the comprehension of phenomena (dharma-saṃgraha-vijñāna-jñāna) and the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).

If questioned regarding the consciousness that encompasses the Dharma, one should identify it by subsuming it under the elements, bases, and aggregates. If questioned regarding the cognitions, one should identify it by subsuming it under the truths.
If questioned regarding the latent dispositions, one should explain it by subsuming it under their various modes.
Thus, being undeluded, he gives the explanation.
In that regard, sixteen factors are proposed concerning the consciousnesses:
which factors are the objects of which consciousness?
This is now revealed:

Those [defilements] belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its cause, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation, have their objects within the range of one's own three [categories], one [category] of the form realm, and the stainless [unconditioned]; they are the objects of the mind.

Indeed, the factors belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*), the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) each become the objective domain (*gocara*) of five consciousnesses.
Which five?
They are the objects of their own three [consciousnesses], and of the consciousness belonging to the desire realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
[It is the object] of that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and is associated with the universal [defilements] (*sarvatraga-saṃprayukta*);
of that which is wholesome and to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*);
and of one [type] belonging to the form realm (*rūpāpta*), namely, that which is wholesome and to be abandoned by cultivation, as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*).
In the same way, those [defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of the origin and through cultivation should also be stated.
These same three dharmas [are the objects] of those [dharmas] belonging to one's own level and the three lower levels, while those that are pure have as their objects the dharmas born of form.
For a dharma of the realm of form (rūpāvacara) that is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering is the object of eight consciousnesses.
Of its own three [categories], of the one above the three lower [categories], and of the stainless (amala);
of the three belonging to its own realm as previously stated;

and of those belonging to the lower realm, namely the two belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin and which have the dissimilar realm as their object.

And [the objects] of the wholesome [state] to be abandoned by cultivation are the wholesome state of the higher [realm] belonging to the formless realm that is to be abandoned by cultivation, and the untainted (anāsrava) [state].
In the same way, those to be abandoned by the vision of origin and by cultivation are to be stated.
Those pertaining to the formless realm have as their objects the three categories pertaining to the three realms and the stainless (nirmala).
Those same three factors belonging to the formless realm are the objects of ten consciousnesses: specifically,
of the three [consciousnesses] from each of the three realms.
And [this applies] to these very same [dharmas] as well as to the untainted (anāsrava).
Thus, first of all, the dharmas belonging to the three realms that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, and those to be abandoned by cultivation, have been explained.

All [defilements] are to be understood as having their own category as their predominant object, and they are abandoned through the vision of equality and the destruction of views; all those belonging to the three realms that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path are to be known as having as their sphere of activity the mind predominant toward their own category.

For a dharma of the desire realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation is the objective support for the five consciousnesses, just like those [dharmas] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and so forth.
And for that which belongs to its own category (*svanaikāyika*) and is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaprahātavya*), there are six [objects].
In the same way, that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*) should also be understood.

Regarding those belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) which are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, as before, each is the object of eight consciousnesses; with the addition of that which belongs to its own category, they become the objects of nine.

In the same way, the two [formless-sphere] consciousnesses belonging to the formless realm have eleven objects as their cognitive domain—namely, the ten previously mentioned plus one additional object from their own category.
Thus, the fifteen dharmas have been explained.
Those free from afflictions (niṣkleśa) have as their range the [dharmas] obtained in the three realms, the last three [pure] categories, and the immaculate (nirmala).

Among the five categories belonging to the three realms, those which are the final three in each— namely, those designated as to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and by cultivation—
and the untainted [dharmas]: thus, untainted dharmas become the objects of ten consciousnesses.
Furthermore, this same summary of the meaning is illuminated by the following verse:
That which belongs to the desire realm has five objects; that which belongs to the form realm has eight as its domain;
that which belongs to the formless realm pertains to ten [realms], while the stainless [unconditioned] pertains to ten alone.

Consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision and cultivation of the origin of suffering—belonging to the three realms as well as being untainted (*anāsrava*)—has as its object five, eight, ten, and ten types of consciousness respectively.

Thus, having established these sixteen minds belonging to the three realms (of five kinds) and the untainted mind with respect to these sixteen factors, one should apply the function of the latent dispositions.
In that regard, first, the factors to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm consist of ten latent dispositions.

The mental states and mental factors associated with that [ignorance], together with their primary and secondary characteristics (salakṣaṇānulakṣaṇa), as well as non-attainment (aprāpti) and the attainments of attainment (prāptiprāpti)—
these phenomena are the objects of the five consciousnesses and of all consciousness that is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya).
[The object] of that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin, associated with the universal [defilements];
of that which is wholesome and non-afflicted, to be abandoned by cultivation;
and of both types of wholesome-with-outflows and the neutral.

[The objects] of the non-afflicted [mind] of the form realm are the wholesome-with-outflows and the non-afflicted-neutral [minds], specifically those associated with the stages of heat (uṣmagata) and so forth, as well as the liberations (vimokṣa), the immeasurables (apramāṇa), and so on. Furthermore,

the objects of the neutral [mind] are the mind-born [minds] arising from maturation (vipākaja) associated with pleasure, joy, and equanimity, as well as the untainted (anāsrava) [minds] associated with the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkhadharmajñāna), the knowledge of the dharma of origination (samudayadharmajñāna), and their respective patiences (kṣānti).
Regarding consciousness:
therein, within untainted consciousness, no latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere; however, within tainted consciousness, first of all—
Regarding the objects of desire, the dharmas of the higher realms, and consciousness, the three [categories] belonging to their own level,
those of the form realm to be abandoned by cultivation, and the universal [defilements] adhere as latent dispositions.

In a consciousness belonging to the desire realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm— those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation— lie dormant. However, in an undefiled consciousness of the form realm, only the universal (*sarvatraga*) dispositions of the form realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation, which have the phenomena of the desire realm as their object, lie dormant.

Four [types of] abandonment belong to one's own sphere; furthermore, three belonging to the form realm, along with those of the formless realm, are abandoned through cultivation together with the universal [defilements].
The meaning is that when the object and the subject-object relationship have indeed shifted, consciousness [arises];
the previous ones belonging to the desire realm and the form realm are as previously described.
By what means do they become predominant?
First, regarding the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the fourth category consists of those factors to be abandoned by the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya).
How so?

That consciousness which is associated with the receptivity (kṣānti) toward the knowledge of suffering and its origin has as its object the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
That object, indeed, belongs to the consciousness associated with false view, doubt, and ignorance that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path.

Within that consciousness, those [defilements] having the untainted as their object lie dormant through association (*saṃprayoga*), while those having the tainted as their object lie dormant through the object itself (*ālambana*).
Thus, there are four groups belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
However, when consciousness belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) is associated with universal [mental factors], it takes as its object those that are not universal.
Thus, there are three groups belonging to the form realm.

However, the object of that non-afflicted consciousness belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna— which has the desire realm as its object, is associated with the heat-stage (*ūṣmagata*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the beautiful [perceptions] (*śubha*), and is conjoined with the mental application of equanimity (*upekṣopavicāra*)— is that very [desire realm]. Furthermore, it is taken as an object by the wholesome [consciousness] of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Therefore, in that [realm], the universal [defilements] and those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya) adhere as latent tendencies (anuśerate).
What has been stated regarding [the defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering applies likewise to the second [truth], and similarly to the fifth [truth].
In this same way, it should be understood regarding the two consciousnesses to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), as previously described.
However, this is the distinction:
all [factors] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) are [abandoned] with respect to suffering.
And [the contaminants] universal in the origin:
in the case of the origin, all those to be abandoned by the vision of the origin,
as well as the universal ones to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, [are abandoned].
Everything else is the same;
those [defilements] which have the contaminated as their object also increase in relation to their own [realm] and in the third [realm].
The third consciousness is that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation;
there too, these three are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and have contaminated objects as their focal point.
But when there is a transformation, those belonging to the desire realm that take conditioned objects as their support—
namely, the four categories within the desire realm that have cessation as an object to be abandoned by seeing and which have contaminated objects as their support— are transformed.
For those [latent dispositions] which have the untainted as their object adhere to consciousness when that consciousness has nirvāṇa as its object, not when it has consciousness itself as its object;
the rest is to be explained as before.

The meaning is that the four [categories of] defilements belonging to the previous [three] groups, as well as those to be abandoned through the cultivation of the path leading to the origin of suffering, persist;
this is also the case for the fourth group, just as for the third.

Furthermore, in the fourth consciousness, which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path, there are three [proclivities] belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path, as well as those belonging to the form realm that have contaminated objects—namely, the universal ones and those to be abandoned by cultivation.
