But when [the consciousness] has been transformed, four [defilements] belonging to the desire realm [remain], as before; however, excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-heya*). When consciousness has indeed been transformed, there are three belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*): those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-heya*), by the vision of origin (*samudayadarśana-heya*), and by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The formless [factors] are universal and are to be abandoned by cultivation.
This concludes the consciousness belonging to the desire realm.
In the first [dhyāna] of the form realm, there are three from below; indeed, there are also three in its own [level].
The formless [defilements] are omnipresent, along with those abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Indeed, within the first consciousness of the realm of form, there are three belonging to the realm of desire that have the suffering and origin [truths] and the dissimilar realm as their objects, by way of association.
However, the non-omnipresent [defilements], by way of their objects, are those to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the three belonging to their own [realm].
These very same [defilements] belonging to the formless realm are universal and are to be abandoned by cultivation.
When there is a transformation [of the basis], three [defilements] of the lower realms are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin, and by cultivation.
And four [factors] are [included] from their own element.
And those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of the path exist in consciousness associated with the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering and its origin.

The four categories belonging to the formless realm also increase [as latent dispositions] with respect to the truths of suffering and its origin, because they take as their objects the minds associated with the false view of the path and so forth. Just as in the second [truth], it is exactly the same in the fifth as well. *Abhidharmadīpa* 338.
In the second [category] as well, there are three belonging to the desire realm and the form realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin,
as well as those belonging to the formless realm that are omnipresent and to be abandoned through cultivation.
Those [defilements] which have the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) as their object, as well as those belonging to their own level, also adhere (*anuśerate*) even to the third [level],
just as has been explained. However, when there is a transformation [of the basis], those pertaining to the form realm (*rūpāpta*) have conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-artha*) as their objects.
Those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, excluding those that have the unconditioned as their object.
The rest, however, should be understood as before; in the fourth [dhyāna] it is also like the third.
There are three belonging to the desire realm, known as those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin and by cultivation;
and there are four belonging to the formless realm.
Excluding that which is called cessation;
"also in the fourth," meaning in what is to be abandoned by the vision of the path, it is "like the third."
This should be understood:

just as in the third [dhyāna], those belonging to its own category that have outflowing objects (*sāsravālambana*) increase, so too in the fourth [dhyāna], those belonging to its own category that have outflowing objects increase.
When [the mind] has undergone transformation as in the third [dhyāna],
there are four belonging to the form realm (rūpāvacara)— known as those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origin, the path, and cultivation—
and three belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara).
There are four [defilements] belonging to the formless realm, excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation;
and three [are excluded] from the path. The section on the form realm is completed.
One should understand [the first dhyāna] as being without form (ārūpya) and so forth.
Among their own [categories], there are three; those pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those pertaining to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are each threefold.

The three pertaining to the desire realm are those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*), the vision of origin (*samudaya*), and by cultivation (*bhāvanā*); these are the very same [three].
Those pertaining to the form realm are likewise these same three.
In the second and likewise in the fifth [dhyāna], when there is a transformation like that of those who have attained the form realm.
Even when [the realm] has been overturned, there are three [categories], excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path;
in the form and formless realms, there are four, excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Just as in the first, second, and fifth [stages],
so too in the third [stage], these very same [factors] have as their objects both internal and contaminated things.
Indeed, in the third stage as well, these very ones have as their objects "internal and contaminated things."
Having undergone transformation, they have attained their own realm and take conditioned phenomena as their object.
Indeed, when [the mind] has undergone revolution, all those belonging to the formless realm, with the exception of those whose objects are the unconditioned, [attain it].
The explanation regarding "otherness" (*anyatva*) and so forth in the fourth [case] should be stated as in the third;
those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) should be explained as before:
"in the fourth also, as in the third."
However, here those with outflows as their objects become predominant;
but once consciousness has been transformed, the wise one should explain it as being like the first case.
When consciousness has indeed undergone transformation (*parāvṛtta*), there are three belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*),
excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path;
and four belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
Excluding those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*),

when consciousness has as its object dharmas not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*) and is associated with the uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-darśana-heya*),
three [categories of] latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) belonging to the three realms adhere therein.
The object-of-object [consciousness], however, takes as its objects the categories [of phenomena] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origin, and the path, as well as by cultivation;
it is also taken as an object by that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation when it has a contaminated object.
Among these, there are four categories whose objects are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Excluding that which has cessation as its object,
for those [proclivities] do not adhere to consciousness when it has nirvana as its object, but they do adhere to it when it has consciousness as its object.
The sixteen types of consciousness have been completed,
and within them, the analysis of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) has been established. Now, the [analysis of] the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) and the others must be discussed.
This is taught:
The category to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, along with all-pervading [defilements], lies latent in two ways; those belonging to the formless realm lie latent in the eye-faculty.

Indeed, in the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) and the universal (*sarvatraga*) ones belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) adhere.

The same should be stated, in detail, for everything from the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), the form-element (*rūpadhātu*), and the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), up to the body-consciousness-element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*) and the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Now, regarding the consciousness that has the eye-faculty as its object, the categories [of dharmas] to be explained are as follows: In the range of the eye-faculty, there are three groups each of those belonging to the desire realm and the form realm, which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, the vision of the origin, and by cultivation. (Abhidharmadīpa 345)

The formless [defilements] are to be abandoned by cultivation, as are the universal [defilements], and they underlie [the mind]. Indeed, when consciousness has the eye-faculty as its object, there are those belonging to the desire realm and the form realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin and by cultivation,
as well as those belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
The universal [defilements] also underlie [their respective realms];
however, when there is a transformation [of the basis], four [remain], excluding those associated with the view of identity and the view of extremes.
However, regarding the consciousness that takes as its object the object of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), four categories of proclivities (*anuśaya*) adhere to it,
excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaheya*).
For that consciousness which has the eye-faculty as its object is associated with [all mental factors] in every case.
That too is the object of the universal [mental factors].
Thus, in the case of threefold transformation, it is so;

however, in the case of twofold transformation, the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is indeed the object of the mind associated with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, that object belongs to the desire realm and is to be abandoned by the vision of the path;
it consists of the consciousnesses associated with false view, doubt, and ignorance.
Within those consciousnesses, there are objects free from outflows by way of association.
However, those which have outflow-tainted objects (sāsravālambana) increase by way of their objects;
thus, the fourth category—those to be abandoned by the vision of the path—is augmented.
This being so, there are four categories belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara).
There are four belonging to the formless realm;
all together, there are four belonging to the three realms.
Indeed, the eye faculty is the object of the wholesome sphere of infinite space.
In that regard, the universal [defilements] belonging to the formless realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya) underlie [the mind].
Furthermore, within a mind associated with the universal [defilements], the non-universal [defilements] increase; thus, there are three.
Moreover, for a consciousness associated with the receptivities (kṣānti) to the knowledge that takes suffering and its origin as its object, the eye faculty is the objective support.
That is the object of the consciousness associated with false view and so forth, which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path to the formless realm.
Among those [afflictions], they have the uncontaminated as their object through association (*saṃprayoga*), while they have the contaminated as their object through the object itself (*ālambana*).
In this way, there are likewise four classes belonging to the formless realm.
Regarding the faculty of suffering, however, that which belongs to the desire realm [is associated] with its own [mental factors] together with the universal ones;
but as for the consciousness that has that as its object, the categories [of defilements] adhere to it.
The three [types of] form belonging to the desire realm are abandoned through universal application and cultivation;
however, when there is a transition to another [realm], four [types] belonging to the desire realm persist as latent dispositions (anuśerate).
From the final existence in the realm of form (rūpabhava), all universal proclivities (sarvagā) to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya) persist;
furthermore, four [proclivities] persist due to the non-reversal of the two [obstructions].
In the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), in the mind that takes it as its object, and also in the sphere of its activity,
the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the desire realm and so forth, as well as those that are omnipresent (*sarvaga*), adhere according to their respective conditions.
In that regard, first of all,
the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is of seven kinds:
that belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*).
The realm of form consists of five types, as does the untainted;
thus, in brief, these constitute the objective support for twelve kinds of consciousness.
[The object] consists of four types of the desire realm— excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation—
five types of the form realm, two types of the formless realm (those to be abandoned by the vision of the path and by cultivation), and the untainted [dharma].
This is the twelvefold consciousness that has the faculty of pleasure as its object.
Among these, as appropriate, there are the four classes belonging to the desire realm, those belonging to the form realm having conditioned phenomena as their objects,
and two classes belonging to the formless realm.
Regarding the statement that "the universal proclivities (anuśaya) adhere":

furthermore, that consciousness which has the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) as its object—that mind which takes such a consciousness as its object—is a mind whose object is the object of the faculty of pleasure.
In that [mind], how many proclivities adhere?
Now, that twelvefold mind which has the faculty of pleasure as its object— of what consciousness is it the object?

It is the object of that same twelvefold [mind], and furthermore, of the two types belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin [of suffering].
This is the fourteen-fold consciousness that has the faculty of pleasure as its object.

In this regard, having added the two types belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin, there are four groups belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) and the formless realm, as well as those belonging to the form realm (rūpāvacara) which have conditioned phenomena as their objects; for it is stated [in the source] "according to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*) that these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhere.
And because of the word "also" (api), it should be understood [that this applies as well].
However, all [factors] comprised within the three realms are included in the mind-faculty;
in the consciousness that takes them as its object, they have all conditioned phenomena as their domain.

Indeed, regarding the mental faculty (*manaindriya*), those [defilements] belonging to all three realms—even those that have *nirvāṇa* as their object—also [increase] by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).
Furthermore, consciousness that has the mental faculty as its object has conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as its object;
therefore, those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have conditioned phenomena as their object increase therein.
Only those [defilements] that have conditioned phenomena as their object persist in the transformation;
there is no distinction whatsoever here regarding the twofold transformation.
Or, according to the previous principle, one should understand that here too, when there is a transformation, it is the function of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that must be recognized;
it should be seen that even when there is a twofold transformation, there is no difference whatsoever in this regard.
Now, it is taught which minds arise immediately after which of the sixteen minds:
"From a mind of the desire realm that is to be abandoned by seeing suffering and so forth, six minds may arise immediately after it; from one of the higher realms, five or five. (Abhidh-d 353)

For one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), immediately after a mind that is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*) and so forth, there arise five minds of its own level and a sixth, which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*), from the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna.
When such a person passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there arise for him five minds belonging to that [new] realm.
Thus, for one being reborn in the formless realms, there are five formless [attainments].
One should specify the minds of one born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) as being either one,
five, six, seven, or even ten.
In this context, "one" refers to the mind produced through cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) belonging to the upper preparatory stage (*upari-sāmantaka*) of one who is free from passion.

"Six" refers to the mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), which is to be abandoned by cultivation and is the fruit of the first dhyāna for one who is free from passion.
"Five" refers to those belonging to its own level (*svabhauma*).
"Or seven": the wholesome, contaminated [state] to be abandoned by cultivation from the vicinity of the higher realms.
"Or ten": for one who has fallen from the form realm and is being reborn in the desire or form realms.
One should observe these minds of one born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu):
five belong to its own realm, and ten others at the time of death.
For one being reborn among those who possess form and sensual desires, there are ten [faculties] present there:
five belonging to oneself and five from elsewhere. This point has been explained.
Now it must be explained:
how is it that this "mind accompanied by latent tendencies" (sānuśaya) was mentioned?
To this, it is said:
Because it acts as an associate and because it lies latent within, the mind is considered "with proclivities" (sānuśaya).
It is designated in two ways—as defiled and non-defiled—or in one way [as being with proclivities].

Indeed, the mind is said to be "with latent tendencies" (sānuśaya) by way of two modes: by way of being an associate and by way of being a latent tendency. Among these, an afflicted mind is "with latent tendencies" for two reasons: because its afflictions have not been abandoned.

Furthermore, the non-afflicted [state] is of one kind: it is simply the cultivation of assistance. In that regard, an afflicted mind is "with latent tendencies" (*sānuśaya*) because of the unabandoned latent tendencies associated with it, and also because of the unabandoned [latent tendencies] that have it as their object.
How, in this case, does a latent tendency that is associated with a certain mind indeed lie latent within that mind when it is unabandoned?
For as long as that mental continuum is gripped and presided over by the specific acquisition of those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
and as long as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) has established its footing within that mental continuum for the arising of future outflow-results (*niṣyanda-phala*),
so long is that latent disposition said to "lie latent" (*anuśete*) in that mind.

Furthermore, when the fangs of the venomous snake of that affliction have been broken by the destruction of its acquisition (*prāpti*), even though the affliction still exists within that mind, it does not adhere (*anuśayati*) through association because it does not produce harm;
and it is said to be "eternal" because, while having that [object] as its focal point, it does not exercise its activity.
When that object has been defiled by the aspect of revulsion toward the path, it is said that the latent tendency no longer adheres even by way of its object.
However, a defilement can never be extracted from the mind like a stalk from a reed, nor can it be separated from the mind or destroyed, nor can it be turned away from its own object.
For it has been said: "Is there ever a case where a phenomenon that is the object of another phenomenon is not the object of that phenomenon?"
He said: "Never.
Therefore, that mind is "with latent tendencies" (*sānuśaya*) by way of being an associate, because it does not abandon its state as an associate;
however, it is not "with latent tendencies" by way of being a latent tendency itself, because no harm arises therein.
Furthermore, which mind is possessed of latent tendencies (*sānuśaya*)?
That which belongs to the three realms, each being of five types;
moreover, each is further divided into two kinds.

[The defilements] are distinguished as universal and non-universal, with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*), and as having afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*) objects.
Among these, that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) is [the mind] associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
And it is "with latent tendencies" (*sānuśaya*) because it increases along with that view of a self-identity and its associated ignorance (*avidyā*) acting as its companions.

With the remaining [defilements] belonging to its own category and with those universal defilements to be abandoned by the vision of the origin, it is associated by way of being a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) alone;
with the remaining ones, it is not in either way.
In the same manner, a mind associated with all [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and to be abandoned by the vision of the origin should be inferred accordingly.
That which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation is associated with false view;
likewise, it is also [associated] in both ways with the ignorance associated with that [false view].
As for the remaining [defilements], they exist as latent dispositions (anuśaya) by way of being associated with their own category of contaminated objects and by way of being universal.
Those belonging to its own category that have the untainted as their object, and those other than them, do not possess both [characteristics].
In the same way, this should be stated for those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and those to be abandoned by the vision of the path, according to what is applicable.
That which is associated with attachment and is to be abandoned by cultivation [is also to be understood in this way].
By that [defilement] itself and by the ignorance associated with it, [the object is abandoned] in both ways;
by the remaining proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) and by the universal (sarvatraga) ones, [it is abandoned] through cultivation;
by others, neither way.
In the same way, other [factors] associated with what is to be abandoned by cultivation should also be stated according to their respective application.

However, that which is non-defiled is "with underlying tendencies" (sānuśaya) solely by virtue of the presence of the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) belonging to its own category and those that are omnipresent.
What, then, is the sequence of the manifestation of these latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)? It is said as follows:
Delusion (*moha*) is the foremost of all afflictions;
therefore, it is the precursor of the afflictions.

From delusion arises the view of a self-identity; from that, the view of grasping at extremes; from that, doubt and false views; from those, attachment to precepts and vows; and from that, attachment to views.
Attachment and pride extend toward one's own [view], while hatred extends toward others;
this sequence of theirs should be understood as such because of the predominance of their respective activities.

In this case, first, for the fool who is deluded regarding suffering— which consists of the five aggregates of clinging— and who does not understand the five aggregates of clinging as being the fruit [of action], the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises through the grasping of a sentient being, a life-force, a person, and a self. From that, there arises for him the view of grasping at extremes, characterized by the grasping at the extremes of eternalism and nihilism.
It occurs to him as follows: "If this person is eternal and unchanging, what is the use of dharma, since he is neither benefited by happiness nor afflicted by suffering?
On the other hand, if he is impermanent and subject to annihilation, even then, what is the use of dharma? As he reflects in this way, doubt arises.
Through the increase of doubt, one brings about false view;

because of the insistence on what is not a cause as being a cause, and because of grasping the inferior as supreme, one draws in the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
From that, attachment to one's own view, pride, and hatred toward others are extended.

Indeed, for one who is pierced by the influence of the demon of false view (*mithyādarśana-bhūtagraha*), who proceeds toward what is not the highest good with the notion that it is the highest good, and who is firmly attached to the idea that what is foremost is actually the foremost, passion arises for his own side and aversion toward the opposing side is set in motion. Therefore, it is said: "It should be known that because of the abundance of such activity, this is their sequence."
We, however, observe that the lack of restriction regarding their activity is considered to arise from association with good and bad friends;

for it is generally the opinion of the teachers that the manifestation and operation of these qualities, such as faith and so forth, as well as of the afflictions, proceed from contact with virtuous friends and evil friends respectively.
Furthermore, this [affliction] arises— certain afflictions arise from all three causes being complete.
Some [defilements] arise through three powers—the power of the cause (*hetu*), the power of application (*prayoga*), and the power of the object (*viṣaya*); some arise through two.

Among these, the power of the cause refers to the arising [of defilements] from the cultivation of causes such as the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and omnipresent (*sarvatraga*) causes; it functions through the relinquishing of present possession (*prāpti*), as illustrated by the examples of Meghikā and others.

The power of application (*prayogabala*) consists in the presence of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) and so forth. The power of conditions (*pratyayabala*) consists in the occurrence of the appearance of objects that have not been fully understood; the illustration for this is the *Arhatparihāṇisūtra*.
The second quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.

The third quarter of the fifth chapter: Now, these three outflows (āsravas) have been declared by the Blessed One— "the outflow of sensual desire (kāmāsrava), the outflow of existence (bhavāsrava), and the outflow of ignorance (avidyāsrava)."
What is the intrinsic nature of these?
This is now undertaken: All defilements (*kleśa*) associated with ignorance (*avyavidyā*) in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) are considered the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*).
Excluding sloth and restlessness, the outflow of existence (bhavāsrava) is so called because it is uniform throughout the higher realms.
For all these are equal because they are obscured and indeterminate, and because they function inwardly.
However, that which is called ignorance is [the root] because it is the foundation; it pertains to all realms.
Indeed, ignorance is the root of saṃsāra.

For it was said by the Blessed One: “Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces (saṃskāra). Likewise: “Whatever miserable destinies there may be in this world or the next, they all have their root in ignorance.”
In that regard, first, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*) consists of forty-one entities:
attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), and pride (*māna*) each being of five types, thus making fifteen;
and there are four types of doubt (*vicikitsā*).
There are twelve views and ten envelopments;
these forty-one entities are designated as the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
The outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) consists of fifty-four entities:
twenty are attachment and pride,
and eight are doubts.
Excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), there are twenty-four views (*dṛṣṭi*) and two envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) called lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*),
because they are dependent on other factors.
The outflow of ignorance consists of fifteen substances;
these, taken together, constitute one hundred and eight substances as the intrinsic nature of the outflows.
Likewise, the floods and yokes are the same, excluding those associated with [wrong] views; however, they are treated separately due to their distinct intensity.
Indeed, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*) is precisely the flood of sensual desire (*kāmaugha*) and the yoke of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*),
excluding views (*dṛṣṭi*).
However, because views are sharp, they are established separately among the floods and the yokes.
For views are primarily characterized by the functions of seizing and clinging; thus,
all afflictions other than views seize and cause one to cling.
In the same way, views are also singular.
This being so, the flood of desire (*kāmaugha*) consists of twenty-nine entities:
fifteen are [comprised of] attachment, hostility, and pride; [the remaining fourteen are] the four floods of views, ignorance, and the rest.
There are four types of doubt.
There are ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
The flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) consists of twenty-eight entities.
Attachment and pride consist of twenty [substances];
doubt consists of eight;
and the flood of views consists of thirty-six substances.
The flood of ignorance consists of fifteen substances;
the yokes are to be understood in exactly the same way.
That ignorance constitutes two types of clinging as previously described, while two consist of views;
all four together constitute one [type of clinging] because they rely upon the wrong path and so forth.
The remaining [fetters] belong to the three realms, but the last two proceed by way of their own existence (*sātmabhāva*).
Among them, the *kāmayoga* (fetter of desire) together with ignorance constitutes *kāmopādāna* (clinging to sensual pleasure), which consists of thirty-four entities:
twenty are attachment, hostility, pride, and ignorance; [the remaining fourteen are the other afflictions].
There are four types of doubt and ten forms of obsession. The yoke of existence itself, together with ignorance, constitutes the clinging to the doctrine of self.
There are thirty-eight substances:
greed, pride, and ignorance constitute thirty;
doubt constitutes eight.

Having extracted the clinging to rules and observances from the yoke of views, there are thirty entities for the clinging to views and six entities for the clinging to rules and observances. Why, then, has this been extracted from among the views?
"Because it relies upon wrong paths and the like.
For this [view] stands in opposition to the true path and is deceptive regarding both sides;
for even householders have been deceived by it, perceiving fasting and such practices to be the path to heaven.
Even those who have gone forth [into homelessness] [cling] because they seek to return to purity by avoiding desired objects.
"The remaining ones belong to the three realms";
views are the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*).
The adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) belonging to the three realms constitutes the clinging of adherence (*parāmarśopādāna*).
The outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), however, belongs to one realm;
the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), however, belongs to two realms.
Therefore, that "last" pair consists exclusively of *sārvadhātuka* [affixes],
because they arise from the manifestation of the self-nature [of the action].
"Indeed, this [defilement] proceeds by taking the personal existence (ātmabhāva) as its object.
These very latent dispositions (anuśaya), moreover,
are shown in five ways through such terms as "fetters" (saṃyojana) and so forth.

They are explained by dividing them into five types according to the distinctions of fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
There are nine fetters in this [system], including envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*).
Because they share the nature of being objects of intolerance, views (*dṛṣṭi*) constitute two separate fetters. *Abhidharmadīpa* 364.

The remaining five latent tendencies (anuśaya) are indeed taught in the Sūtra as nine fetters (saṃyojana): the fetters of attachment (anunaya), aversion (pratigha), pride (māna), ignorance (avidyā), adherence to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), envy (īrṣyā), and avarice (mātsarya).
Among these, the fetter of attachment is craving (rāga) belonging to the three realms.
In this manner, the others should be explained as appropriate.
The fetter of views consists of three views; the fetter of grasping consists of two views.
But what is the reason that, among the fetters, three views are stated separately as the "fetter of views"?

Furthermore, why are two views (*dṛṣṭi*) designated separately as the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*)? This is explained: "Because of the commonality of grasping at [real] entities, the views constitute two fetters";
for indeed, the eighteen [instances of] substance are comprised within the three views.
The two views of grasping (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*) are indeed included within the eighteen [fettering tendencies];
furthermore, there is a commonality of name between the two.
Therefore, these two are stated to constitute a single fetter (*saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, in another place, the Blessed One has stated that the fetters (saṃyojana) are fivefold, and again fivefold,
as those belonging to the lower portion (avarabhāgīya) and those belonging to the higher portion (ūrdhvabhāgīya).
The first and last views are craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmacchanda*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), each occurring twice;
among these, there are five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), namely:
the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmacchanda*), and ill-will (*vyāpāda*).

For these are called "fettering to the lower part" (avarabhāgīya) because they pertain to the desire realm (kāmadhātu). Indeed, the desire realm is "lower," and these [fetters] are conducive to it. Because by two [of them] there is no transcending of the desire realm, while by three there is a bringing back again.
Through sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*), one does not transcend the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Even if one has transcended it by means of the three beginning with the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one returns again, due to their similarity to gatekeepers and attendants.
Others, however, say: by means of these three, one does not transcend the inferiority of sentient beings, namely, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
By two [fetters], there is the inferiority of the realm, namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Now, when for a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*)—upon the complete abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*)—six afflictions (*kleśa*) have been abandoned, for what reason does he set aside the three views and mention only these three: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)? To this it is said:
Because it is stated that two and one are to be abandoned by vision (*dṛg-heya*), and because they are grasped by way of being abandoned by vision,
these three are thus illustrated, even though they all share the quality of being abandonable by vision.
Indeed, when the instigator is grasped, that which is instigated is also grasped, just as when a lamp and its light are grasped together.
In this context, by means of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) which is instigated by it is grasped;
and by means of the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is instigated.
Through doubt, wrong view is set in motion;
therefore, by the mention of the cause, the mention of the effect should be understood.
Alternatively, the afflictions are of three kinds: those of a single type, [those of multiple types, and those of all types].
They are of two kinds and four kinds;
therein, those of one kind are included by means of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
By means of the adherence to rules and rituals, they are grasped in two ways;
by means of doubt, they are grasped in four ways.
We say: Because they are the source of all misfortune, because they act as adversaries to the Path,
and because they lack true investigation, the three fetters (saṃyojana) are taught.
Indeed, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the root of all stains of misfortune, of the afflictions (*kleśa*), and of the three realms of existence.
Therefore, when it is uprooted, the entire tree of misfortune is destroyed.
Furthermore, the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which clings to a false path, stands as an adversary to the truly real Path.
By means of that abandoned right path, there is entry into the city of liberation.
Furthermore, doubt constitutes an obstruction to the practice of the path beginning with right view;
when that doubt is abandoned, the path—preceded by right view and right resolve—proceeds without hindrance.
Thus, even though there are eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned, only three are mentioned.
The Vaibhāṣikas, however, observe that these three are presented as obstacles to liberation.

Just as there are indeed three obstacles to traveling on a path—namely, the lack of desire to go, the taking of a wrong path, and the failure to set out on the journey due to doubt regarding the multiplicity of paths—so too are these three obstacles to liberation.
Thus, there are three obstacles to proceeding toward liberation:
through the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one who has become terrified of liberation develops a lack of desire to go;
through the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), because of grasping at other paths, there is a deviation from the path.

Since doubt (*vicikitsā*) consists in not practicing the path when there is uncertainty regarding it, the Blessed One—by indicating that the abandonment of these obstacles to proceeding toward liberation belongs to the stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*)—specified only three afflictions (*kleśa*).
Just as he spoke of the fivefold lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), so too did he explain the five higher-tier fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) in the Sūtra:
"The two [fetters] born of the form and formless realms are attachment (*rāga*); pride (*māna*), delusion (*moha*), and restlessness (*uddhava*) are the three."
There are indeed five higher fetters,
namely: attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, [doubt, pride, and ignorance].
Excitement, pride, and ignorance:
as long as these are not abandoned, sentient beings do not transcend the two higher realms.
The section on the fetters (saṃyojana) is completed. Now the bonds (bandhana) are explained.
There are three bonds.
Attachment is a bond; aversion and delusion are bonds.
By these, sentient beings of the three realms are bound, as appropriate, in the prison of saṃsāra.
Why, then, are these called "bonds"? To this it is said:
Because they underlie the three types of sensation and because of their firmness, there are three bonds.
Indeed, the three bonds are explained by virtue of the three types of sensation (*vedanā*):
therein, attachment (*rāga*) underlies pleasant sensation,
and aversion (*dveṣa*) underlies painful sensation.
Delusion pertains to that which is neither painful nor pleasant.
These three root afflictions exist on the levels of the six consciousnesses and are of five types.
Therefore, because of their firmness, they are designated by the term "bonds."
Furthermore, in another sutra, the Blessed One declared: "The knots are said to be four, because they bind the two sides:
those called covetousness, as well as hatred, and likewise the two types of grasping. (Abhidh-d 370)
In this regard, a householder, bound to sense objects by covetousness, becomes further fettered by hatred when he initiates a dispute against those who obstruct them.

A renunciant, bound by the dogmatic adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), is bound by the dogmatic adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)—namely, the clinging to the conviction that "only this is the truth" upon hearing criticisms of those very rules and observances.
Thus, there are four [types of bondage].
The primary afflictions have been explained; however, the secondary afflictions (upakleśas) are to be understood as those such as "impetuousness" (saṃrambha) and so forth, as previously described.
Alternatively, all afflicted mental factors (caitasika) designated as the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) are secondary afflictions.
Those which are indeed afflictions (*kleśa*) are also secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) because they defile the mind.

However, in this context, those included among the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), the afflictions (*kleśa*), and the stains (*mala*), as well as those enumerated in the *Kṣudravastuka*, should be understood [as the primary ones].
Furthermore, whatever other mental factors (*caitasika*) are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), these too are designated as "secondary afflictions."
What, then, are those stains of affliction (*kleśamala*), or what are the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*)? In this regard:
there are first the six other stains of affliction known as secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
These are called:
guile (śāṭhya), enmity (upanāha), spite (pradāśa), deceit (māyā), intoxication (mada), and cruelty (viheṭhanā).
In this context, *śāṭhya* (dissimulation) is crookedness of mind, the lack of rectitude, and the state of being bent.
*Upanāha* (enmity) is the outflow of resentment (*pratigha*), which maintains a continuity of hostility and consists in watching for one's faults.
*Pradāśa* (vindictiveness) is the stubborn adherence to what is unrighteous even when one is being conciliated.
Deceit (*māyā*) is that which produces a false appearance for the purpose of deceiving others.

Intoxication (*mada*) is pride of mind; it arises from attachment to the excellence of one's own form, family, power, wealth, youth, health, and retinue, and it is the basis for negligence, giving rise to various disturbances of the sense faculties.
Ill-will toward sentient beings, harmfulness, and cruelty are synonyms.
Thus, the six stains of the afflictions have been explained.
The ten envelopments (paryavasthāna) are stated as follows:
Laziness, envy, lack of shame, lack of dread, torpor, drowsiness, restlessness, anger, avarice, and remorse—these are the tenfold envelopments. (Abhidh-d 373)
For these are not *anuśayas* because they lack persistent continuity;
indeed, these possess no firm persistence, whereas *anuśayas* have firm persistence.
Therefore, these are called *paryavasthānas* (envelopments) because they merely envelop the mind for a limited period of time.
*Mrakṣa* is the concealment of one's own faults; it is called *mrakṣa* because it smears the mind.
*Īrṣyā* is the inability to endure the prosperity of others.

*Ahri* is the lack of shame when observing one's own self while performing an improper act; *anapatrāpya* is the lack of shame when observing others. *Styāna* is the unserviceability of the body, a term synonymous with *tandrī* (drowsiness).

Drowsiness (*middha*) is the unserviceability of body and mind; it is the contraction of the mind known as sleep, and it is exclusively a defiled entanglement (*paryavasthāna*). Restlessness (*auddhatya*) is the lack of tranquility of the mind.
Anger (*krodha*) is a state of ferocity arising from the cause of another's harm, characterized by an unwillingness to let go.
Avarice (*mātsarya*) is an attachment to one's own objects;
its etymological derivation is "may this not slip away from me."
The state of having done what is evil is remorse;
thus, these are the ten envelopments (paryavasthāna).
Now, among these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), stains (*mala*), and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), which is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of which root affliction (*mūlakleśa*), such as attachment?
This is what is now undertaken.
From these, there arise the outflows of attachment, such as shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and so forth.
These are indeed the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that are the outflows of passion (*rāga-niṣyanda*); namely:

shamelessness, restlessness, intoxication (*mada*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), hypocrisy (*kuhana*), flattery (*lapanā*), hinting (*naimittikatā*), belittling others (*naiṣpeśikatā*), the desire to obtain gain through gain, evil desires (*pāpecchatā*), great desires (*mahecchatā*), covetousness (*icchāsvitā*), discursive thoughts regarding sensual pleasures, kin, and one’s native land, association with evil friends, and so forth.
Among these, lack of shame (*ahrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), and pride (*mada*) have their characteristics already explained.
*Kuhanā* (hypocrisy) is a specific mental factor that fabricates deportment for the sake of seeing unreal qualities, arising from greed for gain, honor, and fame.
*Lapanā* (flattery) is the act of speaking pleasant words regarding one's virtues for the sake of gain and so forth.
*Naimittikatā* (hinting) is a specific mental factor that acts by displaying signs of needing material requisites.

*Naiṣpeṣikatā* (extortion) is a mental factor that acts by crushing others with words regarding their faults while they possess virtues. *Lābhena lābhasya niścikīrṣatā* (seeking gain through gain) is the desire to acquire further profit by proclaiming one's already obtained gains.
The desire for others to esteem one's non-existent qualities is the wish for evil;
the longing for gain, honor, and followers is great desire;
and the desire for others to esteem one's actual qualities out of greed is the wish for gain.
Thought associated with sensual desire is the thought of sensuality (*kāmavitarka*).

The thought of one who is overwhelmed by affection for kinsmen— concerning the means of maintaining a household and sustaining a livelihood, such as bringing and giving away daughters in marriage, agriculture, trade, and service to kings, as well as the means for allaying fears from kings, thieves, and so forth— is the thought of kinship (*jñātivitarka*).
For one who is dissatisfied with sufficient means of livelihood, there is intimacy with worldly friends;

for one whose mind is carried away by desire and attachment, there is "reflection on the countryside"—the mental preoccupation with the beauty of those regions, their abundance of food, security, and plenty of milk products, sugarcane derivatives, wheat, rice, and so forth; and for those who have fallen away from morality, right view, and proper conduct, there is association with them out of a sense of pleasure, which constitutes intimacy with evil friends.
Concealment, lack of shame, torpor, drowsiness, and so forth, arise from delusion.
In that context, there are concealment (*mrakṣa*), lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*), sloth (*styāna*), and torpor (*middha*);
by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), sinking (*laya*), lack of mental attention (*amanasikāra*), and lack of respect (*anādara*) are also included.
Harsh speech, sloth, lack of faith, and so forth [are the obstacles].
Among these, what is called "depression" (*laya*) is a contraction of the mind arising from self-contempt regarding the abandonment of faults and the acquisition of virtues;
it is a lack of mental attention due to an attitude of indifference toward the application of wholesome qualities.
Lack of respect and disregard for virtues and those possessing virtues;
malice toward those who teach the Dharma and the use of counter-spells;
and a specific mental factor characterized by yawning, the closing of the eyelids, and sleepiness, which is called *styāna* or lethargy.
The mind's lack of equanimity regarding food is the failure to penetrate the moderation in eating that is conducive to the side of wholesome qualities.
Regret arises from doubt; anger and the like originate from hatred.
Indeed, regret has the characteristics already described and is produced by doubt;
anger and the others are the outflows of hatred.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), envy (*īrṣyā*), intolerance (*akṣānti*), resentment (*upanāha*), spite (*pradāśa*), agitation (*saṃrambha*), and others are included.
Among these, envy has the characteristic previously described. Intolerance (*akṣānti*) is the inability to endure what ought to be endured.
Upanāha is the failure to desist from attending to one's vulnerabilities. Pradāśa is the stubborn insistence even on pride that ought to be abandoned.
Saṃrambha is the agitation of a distracted mind arising from the trembling of the hands, feet, lips, cheeks, and body of one who wishes to crush others.
Being prone to constant harassment by means of mere signs;
being stubborn and making a habit of frequent quarreling due to grumbling;
and the engagement of one whose mind is averse to pleasure while recollecting desirable objects—this is called discontent (*arati*).
Lack of kindness in the mind is crookedness.
A discursive thought applied toward malice is a discursive thought of malice (*vyāpādavitarka*).
A discursive thought associated with harmfulness is a discursive thought of harmfulness (*vihiṃsāvitarka*).
Negligence, arrogance, cruelty, deceit, guile, and hypocrisy.
Furthermore, physical rigidity and so forth should be understood as arising from a mixture [of these factors].

Among them, *pramāda* (heedlessness) is the state of being inclined toward faults and not being oriented toward virtues. *Stambha* (arrogance) is the lack of humility toward those worthy of veneration.

The mental factor that causes one to follow after evil out of compliance with others is *mārdvakṣyam* (?). Deceit (*māyā*) is the mental factor that produces a false appearance in order to deceive others.
Guile (*śāṭhya*) is crookedness of mind.
Yawning (*vijṛmbhikā*) is a mental factor that causes the body to bend and unbend, arising from the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The perception of diversity (*nānātvasaṃjñā*) consists of various perceptions of objects produced by the afflictions.
Physical rigidity (*kāyadauṣṭhulya*) is the bodily disorder resulting from illness caused by excessive exertion or irregularity in eating.
Not training in the virtues of spiritual friends is following what is discordant;
it is the arousal of afflictions and the reflection upon the prosperity of others, which is a reflection associated with the success of others.
These and others should be understood as arising from a mixture [of afflictions]. Envy is the outflow of the adherence to views; deceit is the outflow of views. *Abhidharmadīpa* 376.
The previously described characteristic of *pradāśa* (maliciousness) is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of *parāmarśa* (misapprehension);
*śāṭhya* (dissimulation) is that which arises from *dṛṣṭi* (wrong view).
Now, which affliction is associated with which feeling?
With reference to this, it is begun:
"The association of attachment is with mental joy and with pleasure."
Attachment is indeed associated with pleasure and mental joy;
hatred is said to be associated with mental grief and physical pain.
The term "conjunction" (saṃyoga) carries over [from the previous context].
Indeed, aversion (pratigha) is associated with suffering (duḥkha) and mental distress (daurmanasya).
Delusion (moha) is associated with all [five] faculties,
as well as with the two mental feelings (caitasī vitti), and with false view (asaddṛṣṭi).
For false view is associated with both mental distress and mental pleasure,
respectively, for those who perform evil deeds and those who perform meritorious deeds;
and doubt is associated with mental distress.
For one who is in doubt and desires certainty is bound by mental distress;
for the others, it is by mental ease.
The remaining latent dispositions— the four views and pride—
are associated with mental pleasure (*saumanasya*), because they function in a joyful mode.
However, through equanimity (*upekṣā*), all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) without exception are associated with it;
indeed, at the time when the continuity of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is severed, equanimity necessarily becomes manifest.
This is the rule for those belonging to the desire realm.
Indeed, this rule is to be understood as applying to the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the desire sphere (kāmāvacara).
However, for those born in other realms, [the abandonment] occurs according to their own [factors] at each respective level.

In whichever stage there are as many faculties as exist, therein also those belonging to the four groups of consciousness are associated with those belonging to the four groups of consciousness, and those belonging to the mental level are associated only with those belonging to the mental level, according to possibility.
The association of the primary afflictions with the faculties has been explained. Now the association of the secondary afflictions is stated:
envy is associated with mental distress, as are regret and anger.
And likewise from biting, from binding, and from injury.
Indeed, envy, regret, anger, spite, enmity, and harmfulness are associated with mental distress.
Avarice is associated with either mental distress or mental joy;
for when one is requested by another but does not give, one feels ashamed and becomes mentally distressed.
Others, however, explain that it is associated with mental joy because, being a derivative of greed, it functions in the form of exhilaration.
By two [factors], deceit (māyā) as well as guile (śāṭhya), concealment (mrakṣa), and likewise torpor (middha).
Deceit, guile, and torpor are associated with both mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and mental ease (*saumanasya*);
for sometimes one who is in high spirits deceives another,
and sometimes one who is in low spirits does so.
In this manner, it continues up to the point of "even while sleeping."
Intoxication (mada), however, is associated with the aggregate of mental pleasure (sumanas) and with happiness (sukha).
In the third dhyāna it is associated with happiness; below that, with mental joy (saumanasya); and above that, with equanimity (upekṣā).
Because the word "tu" (however) functions as a qualifier, this distinction is obtained.
Lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, and restlessness [are associated] with five [faculties].
Shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are associated with all five faculties;

for these four envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) belong both to the category of the great unwholesome ground (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*) and the category of the great afflictive ground (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*).
This must now be explained: among these, which is to be abandoned by what? First, regarding those ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*):
Lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, torpor, and likewise restlessness.
...in the Abhidharmadīpa, in the commentary known as the Vibhāṣāprabhā, the third quarter of the fifth chapter.
.........the fifth chapter is completed.
The Sixth Chapter, First Section: ...
[is] coarse.
Therefore, that [the mindfulness of phenomena] comes first.
After that is the application of mindfulness of feeling, which is coarser than the other two, like the aggregate of feeling.
After that is the application of mindfulness of mind, which is easy to characterize because its intrinsic nature is the distinct cognition of form and so forth.
The factors (*dharmas*), however, consist of the associated [factors] such as perception and volition,
the dissociated [factors] such as acquisition (*prāpti*),
and the conditioned phenomena; because they are extremely subtle, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is placed at the end.
For this very reason, the generation stage is also exactly like that;
for generally, sentient beings are averse to liberation because they delight in the enjoyment of forms and so forth, and they take pleasure in sensation because their minds are unsubdued.
That lack of self-control arises from passion and the like,
while self-control arises from faith and the like;
furthermore, there are four [applications of mindfulness] because they serve as the antidotes to the four perversions.
The examination of the body is indeed the antidote to the perversion of perceiving the impure as pure;
the examination of sensation is the antidote to the perversion of perceiving suffering as happiness;
and the examination of the mind is the antidote to the perversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent.
Because the mind changes rapidly,
the investigation of phenomena (*dharmaparīkṣā*) serves as the antidote to the perversion of perceiving a self in what is not-self.
Through the manifold nature of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), the perversion of perceiving a single self is overturned.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is understood that they serve as antidotes to the four types of nutriment and the five aggregates, as appropriate.

At that time, that practitioner of yoga (yogācāra) understands them through the final [application of mindfulness], which takes everything as its object, by means of [contemplating them as] impermanent and so forth;
for the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) has a mixed object, because it takes three, four, or five aggregates as its object.
However, that which has the five aggregates as its object is designated as the "general object.
By means of that, one contemplates all four foundations of mindfulness collectively through four aspects: as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self.
Thereafter, the yogin further analyzes the body by breaking it down into a collection of atoms and a succession of moments, observing it atom by atom and moment by moment.
Or, the yogi perceives within the signs the forms of the impure parts of the seed and so forth—such as the *kalala* and other stages—both separately and mixed together.

Beyond that, when there is the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that all phenomena are of the same nature through their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), such as impermanence and so on, as appropriate, there occurs the suppression and abandonment of the notions of "I" and "mine.
Through that abandonment, even defects such as passion and the like are suppressed by the two types of knowledge consisting of hearing and reflection.
Furthermore, by which application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) here does the absolute destruction of the afflictions (kleśa) occur? We reply:
the absolute destruction of the afflictions occurs through the final [application of mindfulness] or through that which has a mixed object (saṃbhinnālambana).

Indeed, by means of the application of mindfulness with a combined object (*saṃsarga-smṛtyupasthāna*), which has a non-differentiated object (*asaṃbhinnālambana*), the complete abandonment of the afflictions (*atyantakleśaprahāṇa*) is accomplished;
the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative.

Because these three are intended to have objects that are not mixed, they are considered twofold according to the distinction between being with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Then again, for one who views the aggregates as impermanent and so forth, there arises the direct perception of their arising and passing away.
It subsequently arises with respect to the aggregates, like the illusion of a whirling firebrand;
and this is the culmination of the roots of virtue consisting in the applications of mindfulness.
For one who indeed practices the aspect of impermanence, there arises at every moment the vision of the arising and passing away of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
"Like the whirling of a wheel, etc."—
thus he contemplates the dependent origination of the aggregates.
As he perceives their arising and ceasing at every moment, it occurs to him: "In what way do these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) proceed as a continuum and yet are not cut off?

He then perceives dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), [seeing] the conditioned phenomena belonging to the three times as established by the fixed necessity of the relationship between cause and fruit;
and from that, once again, dependent origination.
Having caused him to fall upon the truths, someone then examines him;
having fully realized their impermanence and suffering, [he proceeds] further from there.

Having applied each individual limb to the [four] truths and contemplated them as impermanent and suffering, and having seen that they are without an agent, devoid of activity, and arise dependent upon conditions,
one cultivates the aspect of reality: "there is no self" in all of them.

In that regard, one perceives [phenomena] as empty because they lack an independent agent, since they perform their functions through auxiliary conditions without being under their own control; and one perceives them as selfless because their arising is dependent on others. "Having seen that all things are selfless, one cultivates the aspect of reality."
For one who practices that [meditation] and perceives both the absence of a presiding controller and dependence,
there exists here no person whatsoever— neither Parameṣṭhin nor Īśvara— who is independent and singular.
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are merely the unfolding of dependent origination, possessing natures established by their own specific and general characteristics;
thus, for one who investigates in this way,
a firm understanding of selflessness (nairātmya) regarding all dharmas arises.
As it has been said:
“When one perceives with wisdom that all phenomena are without self, then one becomes weary of suffering; this is the path to purification.”
Now, why is the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyākāra*) not taught here? To this it is said:
Because [dharmas] are not empty by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the Seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*) has been proclaimed;
and because that [seal] has already been stated, the aspect of emptiness is not taught. (Abhidh-d 390)

Indeed, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are not empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because the characteristics of solidity and so forth, as well as the activities of supporting and so forth, belonging to earth, water, fire, air, and the rest, are directly perceived. Furthermore, this is due to the capacity of defects such as passion (*rāga*) and virtues such as faith (*śraddhā*) to cause the mind’s continuum to become impure or pure, respectively. And their capacity is evident, just as one observes the taste, potency, post-digestive transformation, and specific power of substances such as *harītakī*, *citraka*, and *dantī*; therefore, all phenomena possess the power of intrinsic nature, as established by the Seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*).
The "aspect of emptiness" has not been mentioned [previously];
therefore, it is not mentioned here either. Alternatively, by the non-mention of that, its mention is implied.
And by the statement of the aspect of selflessness, emptiness is also stated.
Thus, with a mind firmly established in selflessness, one correctly examines the lineages, gateways, aggregates, and so forth— beginning with the elements—
by means of their respective specific and general characteristics.
Once the elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and aggregates (skandha) have been distinguished by their specific and general characteristics,
skill regarding each aggregate— starting from its intrinsic nature and so forth— is subsequently produced in truth through the seven points, step by step.

"One understands form as it really is: the arising of form, the cessation of form, the path leading to the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form—and so on, up to consciousness.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "A monk who is skilled in these seven points and who examines the three kinds of meaning will quickly bring about the destruction of the outflows."
The first quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.
In the second quarter of the sixth chapter:

Now, for that yogin, regarding the roots of merit such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the knowable object previously seen is [to be cultivated] by way of the establishment of the aspects of the truths, according to the principle of the manifestation of aspects consisting of hearing and reflection that were not previously practiced.
As he gradually rubs the fire-drill of the origin of the truth of suffering with faith and vigor as his assistants, seeking the fire of the knowledge of reality, [the heat arises].
From that, there arises knowledge conforming to the aspects, which leads to the determination of tranquility; it consists of cultivation, is called "Heat," and is accompanied by its followers.

Indeed, that stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), being developed to its highest degree, possesses sixteen aspects— four for each Truth— consisting of the general application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna); it serves as the precursor for the fire of the Noble Path, just as smoke is the precursor for fire.
And when that is attained, tranquility (*śama*) becomes imminent; therefore, it is called "the cultivation consisting of the determination for tranquility" (*śamaniyāmaka-bhāvanāmaya*).

Because the mind is made firm through the power of concentration (*samādhi*) based on the restraint of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-saṃvara*), one cultivates the mind like a *campaka* flower in sesame oil.

And that which is "concomitant" has the five aggregates as its intrinsic nature; and from the satisfaction of the cognition of selflessness, a clarity arises with respect to each aggregate: "This is merely the aggregates, the objective basis for the view of a real body; herein there is no self or anything belonging to a self."
Then, in the same way, the summits (mūrdhānaḥ) overcome false views;
because they possess greater capacity than the heats (ūṣmagata), they further increase faith in the Jewels.
Beyond that, there are likewise sixteen aspects of the Summits (*mūrdhan*);
furthermore, their specific distinction is this:
they possess the quality of having impaired the power of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Because of that protection, they do not sever their roots of virtue;
they possess a distinction superior to the "heat" stage, and their faith in the Three Jewels increases.
Indeed, within those [stages], clarity regarding the three Jewels, such as the Buddha and so forth, increases in its three aspects to an intense degree.
Not by way of the aggregates, because even at the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata), there is already satisfaction with that cognition; [the same applies] to the "summits" (mūrdhan) and so forth—
in both cases, the latter [alternative] is the one accepted.

In both the initial application and the subsequent increase [of mindfulness], the present foundation of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated, and that very same one is cultivated as future.
The view of the aggregates and so forth is not cultivated by one who perceives nirvāṇa.
Indeed, the notion of the aggregates is not cultivated by one who perceives the cessation of the aggregates.
However, one should point out that the aspects (ākāra) are of the same kind everywhere in this context.
Just as they are in the present, so too are those in the future cultivated.
One of those [past] should be seen as present during the stage of increase;
however, one of the four [present] is present during the stage of increase.
In this case, all four [foundations of mindfulness] are certainly cultivated in their future state;
indeed, when liberation is present at the end, they are all fully present in their future state.
But upon cessation, the present application of mindfulness to phenomena is cultivated, while the four future ones are cultivated.
Indeed, all aspects (ākāra) are cultivated through the acquisition of the lineage (gotra).
For when the lineages have been acquired, all sixteen aspects are cultivated here with respect to the truth of cessation (nirodhasatya).
However, upon the acquisition of the lineage, it should be understood that there is cultivation of the homogeneous aspects (sabhāgākāra).
The lineages (*gotra*) are the objects (*ālambana*) for the first two truths;
therefore, there is no cultivation of discordant aspects (*visabhāga-ākāra*) here.
In the case of the universal permeation at the stage of the Summits (mūrdhan), through the fueling of the non-permeation of cessation,
the four [knowledges] called "Dharma" are indeed present and future.
When arranging the form of the head, and during the fueling by non-obstruction and non-diffusion,
the application of mindfulness to phenomena is present, and the four future ones are cultivated.
In that [stage], all aspects are cultivated due to the attainment of the lineage;
they arise from any one of all [the truths] for the sake of increasing the three truths.
In that [state], the four future [moments] are cultivated with certainty; all aspects (ākāra) are to be known. Listen regarding the application of the receptivities (kṣānti). Abhidh-d_403.
In all cases, the four final [knowledges] have arisen; indeed, the future ones are also cultivated there in their entirety as future aspects.
In the supreme dharmas of the present, there is the application of mindfulness called "dharma";
however, all four are cultivated in those [future states] because of their certainty.
Indeed, there are four aspects because they resemble the path of seeing;
this should be understood in the same way as [the aspects] in the path of heat regarding the path of vision.
One should indicate that at the final stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), the present [knowledge] is directed toward the future;
likewise, there are four future [knowledges], which constitute the cultivation of the sixteen aspects.
Furthermore, even above that, for the Noble One, upon the arising of all previously unattained qualities,
having set aside that which consists of hearing and reflection, and having eliminated the most subtle of the subtle [obscurations], [the path of cultivation proceeds].
Thus, in this way, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness by the noble one is to be understood.
On the path of exertion for a beginner, through the conquest of the four stages,
one truly attains four future [knowledges] from among those [eight].
In the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), all [knowledges] are future;
in the final dhyāna, in the eight paths beginning with the preparatory stage (*prayoga-mārga*), they are as previously stated.
One should know that there are three [moments] in the ninth [dhyāna], due to entering the fundamental stage;
however, in the preliminary application (sāmantaka), there may be four, or else the last one.
In the case of the supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) of the divine eye and ear, as well as in the liberations (vimokṣa) and so forth,
one present [moment] is first [attained], while four are indeed future.
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds, there are three [kinds of objects], while for the four [knowledges] beginning with the recollection of past lives, all four are future;
for the last [knowledge], however, all are future.
Regarding the formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*), one may speak of any one of the three;
however, when they have actually arisen before one's eyes, one should specify only those three.
However, regarding the final [attainment] of the formless and the totalities (kṛtsna), one should cite it as being present;
indeed, when speaking of the three that have not yet arisen, one must state them as such with certainty.
Indeed, for the Noble One, during the application toward detachment and even during its abandonment,
all [the dharmas] that have not yet arisen— whether they be of the same or different types— attain the four future acquisitions.
In the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), all future [qualities] except for the last are liberated;
however, in the case of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and so forth, one should point out that all qualities belong exclusively to the non-noble (*anārya*).
And likewise regarding the knowledge of former abodes at the end, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid),
as well as the obstruction to the undertaking of other meditative absorptions, it is exactly the same.
Likewise, when subtle perception arises in the formless liberations and so forth,
four future [dharmas] that have not yet become any of the others indeed arise.
But regarding the most subtle [object], one should say that there is one past [application of mindfulness] and three future ones;
thus has this cultivation of the applications of mindfulness been explained in brief.
With reference to the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), this aid to penetration consists of fourfold cultivation;

because it serves as the gateway for entering the Sangha of monks who are the supreme field of merit in the ultimate sense, it consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) and not of hearing (*śrutamaya*) or reflection (*cintāmaya*).
How much less, then, could there be that which is acquired at birth?
It was with this in mind that the Blessed One said: "Alas, these two deluded men have fallen away from this Dharma and Vinaya, wherein even 'heat' does not exist for such deluded men.
And all of this...
It belongs to six stages, has sixteen aspects, and consists of the five aggregates, excluding acquisitions.
"Sixfold-grounded" refers to one who possesses the path of seeing;
"sixteen aspects."
Like the path of seeing,
it consists of the five aggregates together with their attendants, excluding acquisitions (*prāpti*);
for acquisitions themselves do not have the nature of the "levels of heat" (*ūṣmagata*) and so forth.
For if they possessed that intrinsic nature, there would be the manifestation of the noble [levels] such as "Heat" (uṣmagata) for them;
yet this is not accepted.

Because there is no purpose for one who is already endowed with the vision of the truths, or for one who has already seen the truths, to bring the application of the vision of the truths into manifestation.
He asks: "What, then, are those sixteen aspects through the cultivation of which one becomes a stream-enterer? This is explained:
one examines suffering by means of four aspects—the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

In that regard, with the exception of the bodhisattva, one whose conduct is dominated by craving generally [meditates] on the aspect of impermanence; one who has an excess of laziness on the aspect of suffering;
and one whose conduct is dominated by the view of "mine" on the aspect of emptiness.

One whose conduct is dominated by the view of self [contemplates] through the aspect of non-self; one whose conduct is dominated by the view of no-cause [contemplates] origination through cause, origin, production, and condition.

From the perspective of origination, one whose conduct is characterized by the view of a single cause; from the perspective of arising, one whose conduct is characterized by the view of an eternal cause; from the perspective of conditions, one whose conduct is characterized by the view that things are produced without prior intelligence; and from the perspectives of cessation, peace, excellence, and renunciation, [one contemplates] cessation.

Through these four, there is cessation. One whose conduct is dominated by the view that "there is no liberation" [contemplates] from the perspective of cessation; one whose conduct is dominated by the view that [the self] possesses a body and so forth [contemplates] from the perspective of peace;
and one whose conduct is dominated by sensual pleasure [contemplates] from the perspective of excellence.
One who practices the bliss of meditative absorption and so forth [regards it] as an escape;
one who has entered upon the path of the correct method regards the path as leading to liberation.
By means of these four paths, [one attains deliverance].

One who conducts themselves according to the view that "there is no path to liberation" is [deficient] in terms of the path; one who conducts themselves according to the view that [liberation comes] through "arduous austerities" is [deficient] in terms of the principle;
and one who conducts themselves according to the mundane path of detachment is [deficient] in terms of practice.
One who repeatedly falls away from the mundane path [regarding] the state of definitive deliverance—
thus, at such an initial stage, even a single person is examined by all during a time of deviation.

Because [the afflictions] appear as diseases, boils, thorns, blows, and so forth, yet there is no absolute abandonment by means of them, they are said to be precisely the sixteen aspects of the noble ones;
I shall demonstrate this further on, following the verses.

Furthermore, after the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), there indeed follows penetration (*nirvedha*), which is called the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). Because it is a certain piercing [through] [the obscurations], it is therefore called "penetration. (Abhidh-d 422)
This has been previously explained.
Delight in the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering is the stainless vision of the dharma;
immediately thereafter, the firm resolve toward that very same [suffering] is the subsequent knowledge of the dharma.
Indeed, immediately after the mundane supreme dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), there arises the vision that perceives only the dharmas, which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and supramundane (*lokottara*).

As it is said in the Sūtra: "Immediately after the mundane supreme dharmas, one enters the state of certainty (*niyāma*) simultaneously; upon entering which, one transcends the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)."
Immediately following that, there is the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*), which is of a determinative nature.

The distinction is this: through *kṣānti* one cuts off the acquisition of bondage (*saṃyogaprāpti*), whereas through knowledge (*jñāna*) one brings about the acquisition of dissociation (*visaṃyogaprāpti*).
