In this same way, for each of the [remaining] three truths, there likewise arises a twofold subsequent cognition (*anvayadhī*).

Immediately following the two moments of the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), there arises the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge itself regarding the suffering of the form and formless realms.
This should be understood in the same manner for each of the three truths. Furthermore, in this regard:
In that context, the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (darśanamārga) should be known as being without end.

Excluding the final moment, the path of seeing consists of fifteen intrinsic natures; however, that which was set aside is indeed the final moment, for it is the fruit of the path of cultivation by virtue of the accomplishment of its purpose.
Indeed, for the yoga teacher, there are five [levels], beginning with the *abhi*... and ending with the *srotas*.
Furthermore, regarding this fifth [type of person], he indeed practices the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) in a mixed manner; thus, as the fifth, he goes to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Rebirth in the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) is indeed the fruit of the practice of mixing the meditative absorptions.
One is a candidate for the four formless attainments; another is one who attains nirvana upon seeing [the truths].
The fivefold division of the non-returner who goes upward has been stated;
however, the one who goes to the formless realm is indicated as being fourfold, excluding the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state from those previously mentioned.
Thus, these constitute six [types].
The seventh is one who attains nirvana in the present life, who enters final nirvana in this very birth.
Furthermore, by dividing each of these three into three types, there are nine who go to the realm of form (*rūpagā*).
Indeed, these non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who go to the realm of form consist of three types:

those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and [those who attain parinirvāṇa] after being born (*ūrdhvastrotas*).
And the one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
For the latter three non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are all those who attain parinirvāṇa upon being reborn (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*),
because they attain parinirvāṇa without having [further] been reborn [in the form realm].
Each of these is further divided into three types, making nine non-returners (*anāgāmin*) in total.

How so? First, regarding those who attain *parinirvāṇa* in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*): there is a distinction based on whether they attain *parinirvāṇa* immediately upon arising, after having gone a short distance, or when they have drawn near to rebirth. Regarding those who attain *parinirvāṇa* upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*): there is a distinction based on whether they attain it with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*) or without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Regarding those who "stream upward" (*ūrdhvastrotas*): there is a distinction based on whether they are "leapers" (*pluta*), etc.
Furthermore, its specific distinctions should be understood through the classification of karma, afflictions (kleśa), and faculties (indriya).

Furthermore, among these three or nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*), their distinctions should be understood according to the appropriate application of differences in karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and faculties (*indriya*).

First, regarding the three, there is a distinction by way of karma, because they have accumulated karma to be experienced respectively upon rebirth (*abhinirvṛtti-vedanīya*), upon birth (*upapatti-vedanīya*), or in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*).
From the perspective of the afflictions, it is due to the manifestation of weak, medium, or intense afflictions;
from the perspective of the faculties, it is due to the distinction between sharp, medium, or dull faculties.

If, then, there are nine types of non-returners due to the differences in their afflictions and faculties, how is it that seven destinations of the true persons (*satpuruṣagati*) are taught in the Sūtra?
To this, it is explained:
The sixfold good destination is considered to be together with the one who flows upwards (*ūrdhva-srotas*), making seven types in total.
Here, two types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are established as sixfold by dividing each of them three times over.
However, the third, the one who flows upwards, is mentioned without subdivision in order to avoid confusion.
Thus, the destination of the true persons (satpuruṣagati) has been taught in seven ways.

Why, then, is the destination of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) not taught as the destination of true persons in the *Satpuruṣasūtra*, even though they possess the [required] characteristics? To this it is said:
"Because their conduct does not lead to definitive emergence (nairyāṇika), only these [others] are declared to have the 'good destination' (sadgati). (Abhidh-d 428)
Because for a non-returner (anāgāmin), existence occurs only when there is [a basis], and not when it is absent;
whereas for the other two [types of persons], existence occurs whether it is wholesome or unwholesome.
And because a non-returner does not return again to that place from which he has departed.
But those two perform coming and going; therefore, that movement is taught as belonging to him alone, and not to the other two.
But is it not the case that even a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who has undergone a change of birth is established as being within the destiny of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*)?
No, he says; because:
"For a noble one (*ārya*) who has turned back from existence does not go to another realm here."
For in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), it is possible for a noble one (ārya) who has undergone a change of birth to go to another realm;
however, a noble one who has undergone a change of birth in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) does not go to another realm, because they attain final nirvana (parinirvāṇa) in that very same birth.
And as for this noble one who has undergone a change of birth in the realm of desire who was mentioned:
And this [person] possesses upward movement; he is not incapable, nor does he suffer loss of progress.

Regarding one who has been reborn in a higher realm and is a noble one (ārya) bound for the higher realms: for both of these, there is neither the transformation of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) nor falling away (parihāṇi).

Because the Noble Path has become more firmly established in the continuum through dwelling in another birth, and because of the attainment of a specific basis (āśraya-viśeṣa), for such a noble one, there is no transformation of the faculties or falling away upon entering the form or formless realms in another birth.
Now, as for what was said regarding "the intermingling of meditative absorptions" (*dhyāna-vyavakiraṇa*), which absorption is the first to be intermingled?
It is the last one that is intermingled first, because perfection is achieved through the mixing of two moments.

For in the fourth absorption, there is a concentration (*samādhi*) characterized by an abundance of the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*) and which is fully serviceable (*sarvakarmaṇya*); it is because of its manifestation [that this occurs].
When there is an increase in the basis (*āśraya*), there is an increase in immortality (*amṛta*), by which one is able to intermingle the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
How, then, are the meditative absorptions intermingled?
First of all, one enters the fourth meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) in an uninterrupted flow that is free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, having emerged from that, he enters again into that very same contaminated state associated with a continuous flow.
Then, having risen from that once more, he likewise shortens those flows until he remains for two moments in the uncontaminated state; this is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*).
Accomplishment (*siddhi*), however, results from the intermingling of the two moments.

But when one is able to manifest a single worldly state immediately after a single untainted moment, and an untainted state effortlessly immediately after a single worldly moment— in this way, through the mixing of the tainted with the untainted, the intermingling of the dhyānas is accomplished.
For what purpose, then, is the intermingling of dhyānas? It is said:
for the sake of emergence, for the sake of bliss, and indeed for the sake of apprehending the afflictions.
The meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are intermingled for three reasons:
for the sake of rebirth, for the sake of dwelling in happiness, and out of fear regarding the abandonment of afflictions (kleśa).
Among these, one who has attained [right] view does so through both a longing for rebirth and a fondness for meditative attainment.
One who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), however, does so due to the two aforementioned causes and also due to fear of the afflictions (kleśa).
Furthermore, even an Arhat who is liberated at all times (asamayavimukta) does so for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra),
while one who is liberated occasionally (samayavimukta) does so out of fear of the afflictions.
And as for this "intermingling" that has been described,
from its fivefold nature, the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsabhūmi) are traditionally taught.
For that intermingling of the fourth dhyāna is of five types, distinguished as weak, medium, strong, stronger, and strongest.
Therefore, because the causes are fivefold, the fruit is also fivefold.
Furthermore, these Pure Abodes have never before been seen by any ordinary beings whatsoever.

From the Peak of Existence down to the Brahma-world and the World of Indra, and from the Avīci hell upwards, this has never been seen before by any foolish ordinary beings, except for those in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
This concludes the second quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Abhidharmapradīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.
The third section of the sixth chapter:
He who attains the attainment of cessation is a "body-witness."
Indeed, that non-returner who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*),
because he directly realizes with his body a state that resembles nirvāṇa.
That state, indeed, arises by means of the body as its support.
One is also called an "attainer of cessation" because of the acquisition of its attainment.
From the abandonment of eight parts of the peak of existence up to the candidate for arhatship.

Starting from the detachment from the first dhyāna and beginning with the abandonment of one type [of affliction], up until the abandonment of the eight types of afflictions of the peak of existence (bhavāgra), one should be regarded as a candidate for arhatship.

And he who abides in the final path of uninterrupted transition (ānantaryamārga) called "diamond-like" (vajropama), for the sake of abandoning even the ninth category of the peak of existence (bhavāgra), should be understood as one who has entered the final fruit (the fruit of Arhatship).
For the sake of that fruit, is the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) necessarily co-referential with it, or not? [The answer is: It may or may not be.

Does that which arises by the power of that diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi)—known as the final path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) arising from that power—have the same object of focus as it, or not?
[It does not], because the knowledge of destruction (kṣaya-jñāna) has the four truths as its object.
Upon attaining that [state], he becomes an Aśaikṣa, an Arhat honored by the three worlds,
dissociated from all afflictions, and one who has reached the further shore of the three trainings.

Indeed, because he has abandoned the three outflows without remainder and has reached the further shore of the three trainings, he is worthy of veneration even by the world including the Brahmās; thus he is called an Arhat.
Furthermore, among these three paths, which one is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and which one is without outflows (*nirāsrava*)? It is said:
The path called cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is of two kinds, distinguished by being defiled or undefiled;
however, that called seeing (*darśanamārga*) should be known as entirely without outflows.

It should be understood that even that which is called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa) belongs to those who have gradually attained greater freedom from passion, those who are partially free from passion, and those who are not yet free from passion; it is eternally stainless.
Furthermore, which [stage] does it transcend?
That is explained:
"The stainless one transcends the peak of existence... (Abhidh-d 437).

In that regard, first, for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), there are the four dhyānas, the three formless attainments (ārūpya), the preparatory stage (anāgamya), and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
For one in training (śaikṣa), however, there are six, excluding the three formless attainments.
What, then, is the reason for this?

Because, having abandoned that which is with distinction, one attains a superior fruit. Indeed, here he who, abiding on a path distinguished by its fruit, transitions his faculties, abandons the path of dull faculties together with its fruit and its distinction, and attains only the fruit comprised within the path of sharp faculties.

Furthermore, when one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) transforms his faculties by relying on the formless realm (*ārūpyabhūmi*), he is necessarily situated on the path of distinction for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala-viśeṣamārga*); yet, there is no fruit of non-returning that is comprised within the formless realm.

This is the reason why the Blessed One said: "He who, having abandoned the afflictions here, possesses the five qualities of being 'not easily shaken' (the *āhāryadharma*), is a perfected trainee (*paripūrṇaśaikṣa*)."
To what extent is one a perfected trainee?
A trainee is perfected by three [qualities], beginning with restraint; an Arhat is perfected by two.
Indeed, the perfection of a learner (*śaikṣa*) occurs through three causes:
meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), faculties (*indriya*), and fruits (*phala*).

For example, this applies to one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and is a witness to the realm of desire (*kāmasākṣin*); however, there would be no perfection due to the deficiency of even one of these, let alone the deficiency of all of them.
For example, it is as follows for a learner (*śaikṣa*) who is not yet free from passion for the realm of desire but is resolved through faith: first, there is such a case for the learner.
For one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), it is by means of both faculties and meditative attainments;
that is to say, for one liberated in both ways (*ubhayabhāgavimukta*) and for one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*).
The third quarter of the sixth chapter in the Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti.
The fourth quarter of the sixth chapter:

The path has been described as being of many kinds, distinguished by the mundane and supramundane paths of seeing and cultivation, and the paths of those beyond training and those still in training. That [path], however—
Furthermore, the path should be understood, in brief, as being fourfold:

that which is called the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), characterized by the commencement [of realization] and its excellence, respectively.
In this context, the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) means the commencement of the fruit of the roots of merit.
Immediately following that is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), by which one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is that which occurs upon being liberated from the obstructions to be abandoned by that [path of uninterrupted transition].

The path of distinction arises in the continuum as an accompaniment to the acquisition of dissociation; it is characterized by the progression toward excellence for the sake of attaining other roots of merit beyond that point.
Furthermore, the Path has been described by the Blessed One with the word "practice" (pratipad) because it leads to the city of liberation: "There are four practices:
there is the practice that is pleasant with slow direct knowledge; there is the practice that is pleasant with quick direct knowledge."
“There is that which is painful with slow direct knowledge;
there is that which is painful with quick direct knowledge.
Furthermore, their classification according to the faculties and the stages is now demonstrated as follows:
For one of sharp faculties, the practice in the fundamental dhyānas is easy and brings swift super-knowledge; however, for one of dull intellect, it is slow elsewhere due to the opposite conditions.
Indeed, the path within the four fundamental dhyānas is the "pleasant practice.
For one of sharp faculties, it is a "swift superknowledge" because it proceeds without effort there;
it is pleasant like liberation because it proceeds without effort due to the balance between calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vidarśanā).

In that very [first] stage, it is the slow superknowledge (*dhandhābhijñā*) for one of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*). However, in the other five stages—comprising the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntarika*), and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*)—it is not so, because it is not embraced by the factors [of the path] and because there is a deficiency in calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vidarśanā*) in the preparatory stage, the intermediate dhyāna, and the three formless attainments. (Jaini_356)
Furthermore, the untainted path is the practice for one of sharp faculties,
which is difficult but brings swift direct knowledge;
for one of dull faculties, it is difficult and brings slow direct knowledge.
But how can the noble path be suffering? It is not of the nature of suffering, nor is it associated with suffering.
This is not a fault.
Because the intention is that it is intended [as such] due to being conveyed through effort.
Furthermore, this path is also designated by the term "factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣya*): "The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path.
But what is this enlightenment (*bodhi*)?
Enlightenment (bodhi) is considered to be the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) as well as the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādadhī);
its factors consist of eleven [knowledges], while by name they are thirty-seven.
Furthermore, this awakening, which consists of the knowledge of destruction and non-arising, is divided into three types according to the distinction of persons;
there are three awakenings:
the awakening of a Buddha, the awakening of a Pratyekabuddha, and the awakening of a Śrāvaka.
For that [Mahāyāna] consists of the supreme factors of nirvāṇa; it is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) for all three types of awakening because of its preeminence.
The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*), distinguished by the categories of weak, middling, and intense, constitute the Mahāyāna.
It is said that the vehicles of the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas are distinguished by the categories of weak, middling, and intense.
Furthermore, the factors conducive to that threefold awakening are the applications of mindfulness and so forth; they are thirty-seven by name, but eleven in substance.
These consist of the five faculties beginning with faith, the five powers, and the six consisting of joy, serenity, equanimity, right intention, right speech, and right action.
Therefore, this is said:
"That [state] consists of equanimity, joy, and volition, along with the five faculties beginning with faith;
it arises from two forms together with pliancy, though there is a distinction of names based on their specific aspects. (Abhidh-d 442)
In this context, the powers are the very faculties; wisdom itself is the application of mindfulness;
that which is called right exertion is vigor; and the bases of psychic power are the stabilization of the mind.
But how is it that a single energy is taught in four ways? That is explained as follows:
the abandonment of faults, the non-arising [of faults], the arising of virtues, and their increase.
For that which he performs all at once is indeed the fourfold abandonment.
Indeed, that energy which is for the abandonment of arisen defects such as passion and so forth, and for the non-arising of those not yet arisen;
and that energy which is for the arising of unarisen qualities such as the foundations of mindfulness and the bases of psychic power, and for the maintenance of those already arisen.
There are four right efforts due to the distinction in the accomplishment of their respective purposes.
The bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are the concentrations drawn forth by the mind through desire, exertion, investigation, and volition; they are the sources for the perfection of qualities.
The concentration that is accomplished by making zeal the dominant factor is "concentration through zeal.
Because the accomplishment of qualities such as concentration has its root in the zeal for the roots of virtue,
it is therefore called "concentration through zeal."
All the perfections of the qualities arise from that.
Thus, concentration (samādhi) is accomplished by making vigor, mind, and investigation the dominant factors; this is the fourfold concentration consisting of desire, vigor, mind, and investigation.

Accompanied by each of the formative forces of abandonment—namely, desire, vigor, mindfulness, wisdom, faith, pliancy, volition, and equanimity—and embraced by desire, vigor, mind, and investigation, it brings about the perfection of all qualities.
This is by virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).
For if there is no desire for wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*), how could there be the undertaking of their attainment?
And even if vigor (*vīrya*) has been undertaken, if the mind does not become truly upright (*praguṇa*), the accomplishment of the task will not occur.
Just as when one has churned the fire-drill, even after the interruption of the process has ceased, it returns once more to a state of coolness; so it is here.
For the sake of sustaining effort, the mind is intended as the dominant factor.

Even when the mind is thus inclined, if one does not perceive and avoid subtle secondary afflictions of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), or those that are contrary to concentration, [the effort will not be sustained].

However, if one does not discern the qualities— which consist of general characteristics, capacities, functions, and the factors of the supreme goal— and does not accumulate them through wisdom, then for such a person who has initiated effort in an improper manner, even this triad does not lead to the accomplishment of the purpose.

In this way, the capacity of the eight formative forces of abandonment— namely, zeal, effort, faith, mindfulness, awareness, pliancy, volition, and equanimity— to sustain meditative concentration should be understood according to their respective applications.
The five faculties, beginning with faith, are called the "faculties" because they exercise mastery over the three types of enlightenment;
that same set is described by the term "powers" because they are unassailable.
Indeed, the five faculties— consisting of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom— are established among the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika).
This is because these five, beginning with faith, possess a preeminent sovereignty in the attainment of the three types of enlightenment and are found across all stages (bhūmi).
Furthermore, the classification of those beginning with the Arhat occurs based on the distinctions of superior, medium, weak, and extremely weak among these [faculties].

These very [faculties] are called "faculties" (indriya) in the context of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣya), and not the [faculties] beginning with the eye and ending with the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya).
Because these very [faculties] possess the marks of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
Here, there are two kinds of Indras:

the lords of the mind (*cittaiśvara*) and the lords of wealth (*dhanaīśvara*); therefore, based on the principle that "the faculty (*indriya*) is that which has Indra as its mark," they are called faculties.

Just as there are insignia such as turbans and the like for lords of the earth by which they are recognized as "this one is a lord of the earth," and just as lords of the earth are identified by their ornaments and enjoyments, so too for the lords of the mind who are enriched with the noble wealth, faith and the other [faculties] serve as their stainless insignia— [faculties] in which opposing factors have been suppressed and abandoned.

In that regard, first, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of faith (*śraddhā*) is this: as one contemplates the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, the mind attains clarity because they are endowed with truly existent qualities and are free from defects; and regarding their qualities, a state of longing characterized by clarity itself arises. Alternatively, through the correct analytical investigation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and so forth, there comes to be conviction regarding karma, its fruits, and the like.
And thus, the clarity of the mind that arises from such conviction is the dharma called faith (*śraddhā*), which is associated with the mind;
just as within a collection of qualities such as a mirror and so forth, there are other distinct qualities such as the clarity of the mirror.
In this way, although the collection of phenomena such as mind (*citta*) and so forth is formless (*arūpin*), there are other phenomena such as faith (*śraddhā*) and the rest;
yet, because it serves as the basis for them, because of its preeminence, and because it persists throughout the continuum, it is designated by the term "mind.

That which is called vigor (*vīrya*) has the characteristic of mental exertion; or, having considered that one is capable of achieving a goal, one exerts oneself in various ways toward that purpose—thus it is vigor.

The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) is the non-erroneous verbalization and recognition regarding the body and so forth once they have been discerned by wisdom; it is that non-forgetfulness by which, when an object has been determined, no confusion occurs in the mind.
The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) is characterized by one-pointedness of mind.
The mental states that grasp objects and their subjects are called "one-pointed" when the mind has that single object as its focus.
For when the mind is unstable, flickering among various objects, the ascertainment of reality does not occur.
Indeed, it is just as a man mounted on a galloping horse that is fleeing cannot perceive those coming toward him, even if they are people he has seen before.

For humans and others, it is impossible to discern the specific characteristics [of objects] when the mind—which wanders toward many objects and changes rapidly—is thus distracted; consequently, there is no discernment of the true nature (*tattva*) of objects such as the body.
However, when the mind is held for a long time upon a single object by means of concentration (*samādhi*), like a skilled charioteer, then one discerns the true nature of phenomena (*dharma*).
Therefore, just as paint adheres to a wall, *samādhi* is the support of the mind upon its object.
*Pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā* is that which discerns specific and general characteristics;

it perceives the reality of the body and so forth as if standing directly before one, as if attained, as if adhered to, and as if seen from behind. This is because of such discernment (*upalakṣaṇāt*).

The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). Although a discernment of objects according to their specific domain exists in all states of consciousness, it does not function in accordance with reality; therefore, it is not considered a faculty.

These very faculties—faith and the others—are called "powers" (*bala*) because they serve as the primary limbs for a yogin who has entered the battle against the afflictions (*kleśa*) in order to conquer the army of the afflictions, just as elephants and other mounts are for a king. Thus they are called powers.
The seven factors of enlightenment were taught by the Teacher for the purpose of awakening;
they are called "enlightenment" in the ultimate sense because they provide assistance up to the very end.
Although they are equal in being factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika*), these seven factors specifically constitute the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Indeed, their preeminence lies in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), precisely because one stands upon the realization of the truths already seen.

Among the qualities and defects regarding the nature and so forth of phenomena as characterized by discernment, the limb of enlightenment consisting of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is taught first for the purpose of removing the defect of forgetfulness.

Joy is pliancy (*prasrabdhi*). For one whose mind and body are scorched by the fever of passion and other afflictions, just as one who has plunged into a pool of cool water when heated by the summer sun, that quality which brings refreshment to body and mind through the manifestation of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is pliancy.

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is that state of mental evenness which, as the antidote to partiality toward attachment and aversion, observes the objects of knowledge as they truly are; it is the absence of volitional effort toward either side and is characterized by an inclination toward *nirvāṇa*. This is called the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
Furthermore, among these, the three beginning with joy (*prīti*) remain to be explained, while the other four have already been explained previously.
Moreover, among those seven factors, wisdom (*buddhi*)—characterized by the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*)—is both enlightenment (*bodhi*) and a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
For awakening is indeed knowledge, and knowledge is wisdom; the remaining factors are merely limbs.
Furthermore, those [factors]—
joy, pliancy, and equanimity— are considered limbs [of enlightenment] for that reason already stated:
one whose entire collection of faculties is nourished by joy, pliancy, and equanimity that are free from worldly desire attains awakening with ease and without agitation.
Furthermore, because the reasons for defining their characteristics have been stated, they possess the nature of factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
This is because the fourfold group beginning with intention (*saṃkalpa*) conforms to the path toward what is to be known. (Abhidh-d 448)
The term "being a limb" (aṅgatā) continues [to apply].
Right intention, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are limbs because they conform to the Path, just as right view, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are.
Furthermore, this is the summary of the true nature of the Noble Path:
it has wisdom as its light, the stage of subtle conceptualization, morality as its retinue, and mindfulness and vigor as its friends;
it enjoys the bliss of all meditative absorptions, and this path resides in the two abodes of liberation. *Abhidharmadīpa* 449.
The predominance of the sevenfold group [of factors] occurs in the stages beginning with "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) and so forth; here,
however,
it should be understood according to their respective order in relation to the paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and vision (*darśanamārga*).

In that regard, the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are characterized by the stage of the beginner, because they consist in the observation of the intrinsic nature of the body and so forth.
The right exertions (samyakprahāṇa) occur during the stages of "heat" (ūṣmagata);
for there, by perceiving the disadvantages of saṃsāra and the advantages of nirvāṇa, one relies upon powerful vigor and thereby crosses over to the further shore of saṃsāra.

At the stage of the Summits (*mūrdhan*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are manifested; because one attains the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) therein, when the mind is restrained, there is no falling back, and thus one never becomes poor in the wealth of virtuous qualities.
The faculties (*indriya*) [are predominant] at the stages of Patience (*kṣānti*), because through their sovereignty, there is the absolute cessation of rebirth in the miserable states.
The powers (*bala*) [are predominant] at the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*agradharma*), because they cannot be crushed by the afflictions.

The factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) hold primacy on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) because, through the cultivation of the path likened to the handle of an axe, there is the abandonment of all afflictions without remainder;
or alternatively, because when the stains are abandoned in their ninefold manner, one draws near to awakening (bodhi).

On the path of seeing (darśanamārga), the factors of the path (mārgāṅga) exist because they arise for the purpose of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing, thereby swiftly transcending the three realms.
However, the deviation from the sequential order is for the sake of conforming to the manner of teaching.
Now, why is the mind (*citta*), which serves as the substratum (*dharmin*) for mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), not established among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*)?

And why are phenomena such as perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), attention (*manaskāra*), zeal (*chanda*), and resolve (*adhimokṣa*) also not established among the factors conducive to enlightenment?
This is now explained:

The mind is not like a king because it follows after both virtues and faults; rather, the mind indeed occupies the position of a king. By purifying that mind through the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣyadharma*), the bliss of liberation is attained.
Just as the mind follows after virtues, so too does it follow after faults.
As it has been said: "Sentient beings are defiled by the defilement of the mind; they are purified by the cause of the purification of the mind.
For them, passion and the other [afflictions] are the causes of defilement.
Faith and the other [wholesome factors] bring about purification; therefore, the mind is not established [as being identical to them].
Because they conform to conventional usage, a designation (saṃjñā) is indeed not intended for these [factors].
For designations generally follow conventional usage, whereas the factors conducive to enlightenment exclusively belong to the side of the ultimate truth.
Because it is inclined toward the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and because it is designated as the "path" (*mārga*), volition (*cetanā*) is not [included].
Indeed, volition is not mentioned because it brings about desirable and undesirable maturation, and because it is denoted by the word "path.
Attention (*manaskāra*) is not included because it is not primary, since it functions through both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Mental attention (*manaskāra*) is also secondary because it is merely a constituent part of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and because it functions through both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because it is predominant in the initiation of action, zeal (*chanda*) is not [merely] vigor; for it nourishes vigor. Indeed, zeal, which consists in the desire to act, is manifested as the initiation of action, and it further strengthens vigor.
That vigor continues from the completion of the task of attaining awakening until [the end];
it is not resolve because of superimposition, nor is it contact because it is difficult to discern.
For the most part, resolve indeed operates within the mental applications of resolute conviction (*adhimukta-manaskāra*).
Contact (*sparśa*), moreover, has a mode of activity that is difficult to discern because it arises merely from the coming together of the three [factors].
Therefore, it was not mentioned.
The noble lineages consist of moral dread and shame; because they function as a lack of confidence,
the four noble lineages and moral dread and shame are not factors conducive to enlightenment, just like a newly ordained monk who lacks confidence.
It is not non-heedlessness because it is subordinate to another; nor is it non-harming because it does not involve injury.
Indeed, heedfulness is the storekeeper of vigor;
and non-violence is not mentioned [separately] because it is merely the antidote to harming.
Because they function by taking sentient beings as their basis, loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth, do not have phenomena as their basis;
indeed, the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣya) have phenomena as their basis, whereas loving-kindness and the others are exclusively based on sentient beings.
Furthermore, because they are only a partial portion of the limbs of the path and the faculties, the states of verified confidence (avetyaprasāda) are also not included.

Indeed, the verified confidences (*avetyaprasāda*) are not mentioned among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*) because they have as their intrinsic nature only a portion of the path-factors and consist only of a portion of the faculties. Furthermore, non-hatred is not included among the roots of the wholesome, because it has sentient beings as its objective domain;
for non-hatred proceeds by taking sentient beings as its basis.
Therefore, it is not a factor of enlightenment;
because of its indifference, it is not nirvana; and because of its remoteness, it is not the voice of another.
Nirvana is indeed devoid of activity, whereas the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ) possess activity.
Furthermore, the voice of another, being an external factor for awakening, is remote from the state of being a constituent part of awakening;
therefore, only thirty-seven factors are truly conducive to awakening.
Furthermore, how many of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣya) are with outflows (sāsrava), and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)?
This is demonstrated as follows:
The limbs of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are free from passion (arajaska), because they exist in the state closest to enlightenment.
The others, both with outflows and without outflows, are to be understood accordingly.
The factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), because they are the most proximate to enlightenment.
All other [factors], however, are both tainted and untainted; for all wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) lead to the noble path and are directed toward the intention for *nirvāṇa*.
They are called "factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣya*) because they exist as limbs that are either near to or distant from the three types of enlightenment.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "I have realized the ancient path," according to this statement.
However, in the treatise, those factors such as right view and so forth which are taught following the factors of enlightenment are [declared to be] untainted (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, on which stage do how many factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣya) exist?

In the first dhyāna, all [thirty-seven] are present in its fundamental state; in the preparatory stage (anāgamya), they are present with the exception of joy (prīti). In the second dhyāna, they are present with the further exception of applied thought (vitarka); and in the two [subsequent dhyānas], they are present with the exception of these two [joy and applied thought].

They should be understood as being derived from the factors of morality (*śīlāṅga*), from those two [the first two dhyānas], and from all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) within the three formless realms; however, in the desire realm, they are devoid of the factors of enlightenment.
In that regard, first of all, all thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment are present in the fundamental dhyānas; however,
in the preparatory stage (anāgamya), they are devoid of joy,
because joy is absent there.
This stage is common to both those who are free from passion and those who are not; therefore, joy (*prīti*) is absent.
In the second dhyāna, however, all [factors] are present except for applied thought (*saṃkalpa*).
In the third and fourth dhyānas, thirty-five factors are present, excluding both applied thought and joy.
By the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) there are also thirty-five [factors], excluding joy (*prīti*) and intention (*saṃkalpa*).
In the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), there are [twenty-two] by means of the three—right speech, right action, and right livelihood—and by means of joy and intention.
At the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as well, there are twenty-five, excluding the three limbs of morality (*śīlāṅga*), joy, intention, and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
In the desire realm (kāmadhātu) as well, there are thirty [factors] excluding the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga).

Furthermore, for those who maintain that only the path-factors (mārgāṅga) are untainted (anāsrava), for them the remaining factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣya) exist even when those [path-factors] are excluded. This point is settled.
However, this must be stated:
regarding the section on the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika*), those four which were first mentioned therein by the learned—
In the entry into the state of certainty (*nyāma*), the attainment of detachment (*vairāgya*), the acquisition of the fruits (*phala*), and the increase of the faculties (*indriya*).
The first entry into the state of certainty,
the first attainment of detachment,
and the first attainment of the fruit.

Regarding the increase of other faculties and their first occurrence among those four types of first occurrences: for each of these, there is the respective [attainment] of the eight dustless path-factors (*mārgāṅga*). Among them, the gain and non-gain within the time-periods (adhvan) should be understood as having nine bases. *Abhidharmadīpa* 461.

Since the attainment of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) is inevitable for one engaged in the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*), it must be stated: upon seeing which truth is there the acquisition of which verified clarity?
This is now explained:
Upon the realization of three truths, there is the acquisition of verified clarity regarding ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the Dharma.
Upon the vision of the truth of the path, there is also [vision] regarding the spheres of the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
While realizing the truth of suffering, one acquires the virtues dear to the noble ones and gains verified confidence (avetyaprasāda) in the Dharma.
In which Dharma?
In that very truth of suffering.
All this is merely phenomena (*dharma-mātra*), meaning it is merely the twelve sense-bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).
Herein, there exists no single underlying substratum (*dharmin*)—whether called a genus (*jāti*) or a substance (*dravya*)—that persists through all its various manifestations.
Nor do there exist here any person (*puruṣa*), life-principle (*jīva*), or individual (*pudgala*), nor any limits of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); these are selfless (*nirātman*), like the horns of a hare.
Thus, for one who realizes the origin [of suffering], there is the attainment of two things;
it should be understood that the same applies for one who realizes its cessation.
However, upon the vision of the truth of the path, clarity of faith is attained toward the Buddha, the Blessed One, and toward his Saṅgha.
The Blessed One is the knower of the path and the teacher of the path, who proclaims the truly existent path.

Furthermore, there is serene confidence—characterized by the nature of twofold faith—toward those disciples, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who have entered that path and are bulls among men; and toward those lion-like Bodhisattvas whose mental dispositions are illuminated by the lamp of the seven true dharmas and others, who dwell in the cave of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
This is now explained in detail.

The faith directed toward the path and so forth, which has the [Four] Truths as its object, arising from the Buddhist Saṅgha and through the power of present reliance, is this "verified clarity regarding the Dharma."
Furthermore, that dharma consists of nirvāṇa and the path belonging to the continuum of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, who is this Buddha, and what is faith in him? It is explained as follows: "One who is himself awakened through the destruction of the darkness of the sleep of delusion and the opening of the eye of wisdom—that is the Buddha. Faith in his qualities is considered 'serene confidence' (prasāda) toward the Victor. (Abhidharmadīpa 464)
For the meaning of the word "Buddha" is twofold: primary and secondary.
Among these, the first consists of the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that constitute a Buddha.

As for the secondary sense, it has already been demonstrated that the term "Buddha" is appropriately applied to the physical body which serves as the support for those dharmas, as well as to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) which are the fruits thereof.

Faith that takes as its object the qualities of those persons (pudgala) enriched with the virtues of the learners (śaikṣa) and the non-learners (aśaikṣa)— that faith which has those qualities as its focal point is clarity (prasāda) within the domain of the conditioned (saṃskṛta).
For it is said in the Sūtra: "Venerable sir, how many in the world are worthy of offerings?
Householder, there are two: those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Among them, there are eighteen [types of] those in training and nine [types of] those in training."
Thus is the detailed account.
The stainlessness of the precepts is likewise their clarity (*prasāda*).
Furthermore, how many of these exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*) and how many exist nominally (*nāmataḥ*)? Substantially, there are only two; nominally, however, there are four. *Abhidharmadīpa* 466.

Faith is divided into three types according to the distinction of its objects, namely the Three Jewels; and the virtues dear to the Noble Ones are treated as one. Furthermore, regarding that [last category], there is the expression "serene clarity" (*vaimalyaprasāda*), for that which is stainless is said to be serene.
This must now be explained:

Why is it that although a learner (*śaikṣa*) is endowed with right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and right liberation (*samyagvimukti*), he is described as a "learner who has attained the goal" (*prātipada*) when endowed with eight factors, whereas an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*) is said to be so endowed with ten? To this it is replied:
Because the learner (*śaikṣa*) still possesses remaining bonds, liberation (*vimukti*) is not considered a constituent factor (*aṅga*).
Although it exists for the learner, it is not called a factor because it has not been manifested;
for even when that [liberation] is present, the learner remains bound by the fetters of the afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus liberation is not logically applicable.
What, then, is this liberation, and how many kinds are there?
This is explained:
because its nature consists of the resolute conviction toward liberation, it is twofold, by way of being eternal or non-eternal.
It is twofold both by way of difference in essential nature and by way of difference in mode;
that is, by way of difference in intrinsic being, it has the nature of liberation and resolute conviction.
Furthermore, there is a difference in mode due to the distinction between the perishable and the imperishable.

It is conventional because it is distinguished by the absence of passion, the absence of aversion, and the absence of ignorance; or alternatively, because it is distinguished by being pleasant, unshakable, and non-differentiated.
Now, what is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)? It is said as follows: that very awakening (*bodhi*) previously mentioned is called right knowledge.
It has been stated that awakening consists of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
These alone should be understood as right knowledge.
Furthermore, which mind is liberated?
Is it that which has arisen and ceased, or that which has not yet arisen and ceased, or that which has merely arisen?
The future mind of one beyond training is liberated from the obstruction of the afflictions.

Someone indeed says: "The future mind, when it is being produced, is liberated through liberation from the time-periods; however, all that is future is liberated from the obscuration of afflictions through liberation of the continuum.
That, moreover, is precisely the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because of the removal of the obstacles consisting in the acquisition (*prāpti*) of primary and secondary afflictions."

Furthermore, whatever karma associated with the realms of form and formlessness that results in rebirth—even if it acts as an obstacle to the attainment of arhatship—is all abandoned by the diamond-like concentration; thus, through the removal of these hindrances, the entire future mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is liberated.
But in the ultimate sense, it is only the phenomena (*dharma*) that train; for it is said:
"In the world, because of the activity of a phenomenon, even the substratum (*dharmin*) is considered to be active.
When the phenomenon known as heat performs the activity of burning fuel and so forth, the substratum, fire itself, is also said to be active.
Just as when wood is burned by fire, one metaphorically says "I have been burned by Devadatta" with respect to the activity of the fire's burning,

so too, when the factors of existence (dharmas) are engaged in the training that abandons the afflictions (kleśas), one says "the monk is an adept" (aśaikṣa) in consideration of their connection [to that state].
However, the Path, having assumed its functional activity, eliminates the obscuration thereof.

By the word "tu" (but), the meaning is "precisely while ceasing," for it is only in the case of that which is present that the capacity [for action] is established due to its connection with activity.
Now, as for this unconditioned liberation and the three elements, such as the element of abandonment and so forth:
Are they therefore different from that, or rather non-different? We reply:

That very eternal liberation is what is described in the Sūtra as the three elements (dhātu) beginning with dispassion (virāga); for the threefold division is made in consideration of [different perspectives]. *Abhidharmadīpa* 470.
Indeed, their threefold nature is stated in consideration of specific designations. How so?
Detachment is the liberation from passion; that which is called abandonment is the destruction of other [defilements];
and the element of cessation is the cessation of other things characterized by grasping. (Abhidh-d 471)
Indeed, the abandonment of attachment is called the element of dispassion (*virāga-dhātu*).
The abandonment of other afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) is the element of abandonment (*prahāṇa-dhātu*).
The cessation of all other entities associated with grasping (*sopādāna-vastu*) is designated as the element of cessation (*nirodha-dhātu*).
Is it the case that by whatever object one becomes weary, one also becomes detached from that same object?
This is a question with four alternatives. How so?
The yogi becomes weary through an intellect that takes the cause of suffering as its object.
But one who was attached becomes dispassionate; from that [arise] four groups of ten million.
One becomes weary through the patiences and the cognitions regarding suffering and its origin, and not by others.

As for becoming detached, one who is attached becomes detached by means of all the patiences and cognitions regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—those by which one abandons the afflictions.
Thus, there are four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).

In this regard, one who has already become free from passion for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and enters the path of certainty (*niyāma*) does not become dispassionate through the two receptivities (*kṣānti*) toward the dharma of suffering and its origin, nor through the two cognitions (*jñāna*) of those dharmas. This is because [these states] have already been abandoned previously; they do not abandon [the passions] through the two receptivities because these are not their antidotes, and they do not [abandon them] through the two cognitions. Even on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one does not become dispassionate through the cognitions of suffering and its origin included within the path—specifically those of the preparatory (*prayoga*) and liberated (*vimukti*) stages—because one is already liberated. However, one becomes weary (*nirvidyate*) because the objects of focus are things that have already been seen with revulsion.

The second alternative: one who is not yet free from passion for sensual pleasures becomes dispassionate when entering the fixed course (*niyāma*) through the receptivities (*kṣānti*) to the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge of cessation and the path; yet, while proceeding toward detachment from the three realms on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) by means of the knowledges (*jñāna*) of cessation and the path, he does not become weary. Both [dispassion and weariness] occur because his objective supports are things that inspire joy.

One who is already free from passion for sensual desires, when entering the path of certainty (*niyāma*), attains detachment from the three realms through the receptivities to the knowledge of the dharma and subsequent knowledge of suffering and its origin, as well as during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) through the knowledges of suffering and its origin.

One who is not both [free from desire and entering the path of certainty]—that is, one who enters the path of certainty while already free from passion for sensual desires—attains it through the two receptivities to the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation and the path, through the two knowledges of those dharmas, and through the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation and the path during the path of cultivation by means of the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and their counterparts.
These three realms are themselves designated by the three terms: the notion of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃjñā*), the notion of dispassion (*virāgasaṃjñā*), and the notion of cessation (*nirodhasaṃjñā*).
In detail, however, there are the ten perceptions, beginning with the perception of impermanence; from these [arise] the [meditations on] the foul and so forth.
Three are the application of the path, one is the path itself, and the last three are the fruit.

The perception of foulness, the perception of death, and the perception of non-delight in the entire world constitute the application of the path; and the path itself is described by these four perceptions: impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The fruit is declared by means of the notions of abandonment, detachment, and cessation.
Furthermore, among these, how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
It should be known that the triad beginning with the perception of impurity is indeed with outflows.
The others are both with stains (*samala*) and stainless (*nirmala*); one should understand that the nine stages are stainless.
The three perceptions—the perception of impurity, the perception of death, and the perception of non-delight in all worlds—are associated with outflows (sāsrava).
However, the remaining ones are both with and without outflows;
it should be understood that those belonging to the nine stages which are without outflows are untainted (anāsrava).
One should observe the final [perfection] within the eleven stages, beginning with the dhyānas;
one should know that the fourth, fifth, and sixth [perfections] exist within the seven stages.
In the *Abhidharmadīpa*, the commentary known as the *Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti*, this is the fourth quarter of the sixth chapter.
And the sixth chapter is completed.
The Seventh Chapter, First Section.
Here it is said: This path consisting of three aggregates was taught by the Blessed One.
Among these, the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) has been explained in detail in the chapter on action (*karma*);
the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhiskandha*) will be explained in the eighth chapter;
now, the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*) must be explained.
Thus, having begun this [treatise], it is said: "This world, deluded regarding reality, is bewildered concerning the reality that is to be known.
I shall explain those forms of knowledge in detail, starting from their essential nature. (Abhidh-d 476)
What, then, are these [knowledges], and how many are they? This is explained:

Having set aside [the categories of] genus and substance, their division is declared to be tenfold by way of their opposites and so forth, under the names of dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and the rest. *Abhidharmadīpa* 477.

Indeed, if one were to rely on the genus (*jāti*), there would be the fallacy of [the term] applying to only one instance; whereas if one were to rely on the substance (*dravya*), there would be an infinity [of instances], and that is impossible to express.

Therefore, setting aside both of these, we shall explain in detail everything regarding the perspective by which they become ten, as well as their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
In that regard, first:
there are two [knowledges] with respect to the specific objects of the Dharma and its subsequent [knowledge]; four [knowledges] with respect to suffering and so forth;
two [knowledges] through conventional and other-mind [knowledges]; and two [knowledges] through cessation and non-arising.
Indeed, the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge are distinguished by the dharma and subsequent [knowledges] themselves.
However, the four [knowledges] beginning with that of suffering are distinguished by the four noble truths which are their own respective objects.
Furthermore, conventional knowledge and knowledge of others' minds are distinguished by conventional [knowledge] and knowledge of others' minds, respectively.
The two types of knowledge— the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising— are distinguished by destruction and by non-arising again.
Alternatively, they are distinguished by their remedies, their applications, their intrinsic natures, their aspects, and their spheres of activity.
Its establishment should be understood either by way of its function or by way of its accumulation.
In this context, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is the antidote to the discordant factors belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is the antidote to the discordant factors belonging to the form and formless realms.
Knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) arises from application, because one applies oneself with the thought, "I shall know the mind."
By way of intrinsic nature, conventional knowledge exists even among ants and the like, because it is present there as well.
By way of the aspects of the truths and their objects, there are four knowledges.
By way of function, there is the knowledge of destruction, because its task has been fully accomplished.
The knowledge of non-arising arises from the accumulation of causes, because it is accumulated by all untainted knowledges acting as its homogeneous causes.

In order to eliminate delusion regarding the elements (dhātu), the truths (satya), the objects (artha), and the mind (citta), as well as regarding birth, destruction, and non-arising, their classification is indeed tenfold.
In that regard, delusion concerning the elements (*dhātu*) is removed by two [knowledges]: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Delusion concerning the truths (*satya*) is removed by four [knowledges], beginning with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
Delusion concerning the meaning (*artha*) is removed by conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Confusion regarding the mind [is overcome] by the knowledge of others' minds;
confusion regarding birth by the knowledge of destruction; and confusion regarding rebirth by the knowledge of non-arising. Thus, the Blessed One has taught that there are exactly ten knowledges.
Neither too many nor too few.
Furthermore, in this context,
the comprehension of thorough knowledge and so forth regarding suffering and the rest is the fruit of the cognition of their destruction.

The aspect of the path (*pratipadākāra*) is established by the opposition to the claim that "suffering has been fully understood and its origin abandoned" [but not yet realized and cultivated], or by the opposition to the claim of those who do not undertake practice that "purity comes through saṃsāra itself.

The aspect of leading to deliverance (*nairyāṇikākāra*) is established by the opposition to the perception of the mundane path of detachment as being Mara, because of the deception of attaining a non-definitive detachment, and by the opposition to the lack of high regard for anything at all.
Now, what is this phenomenon called "aspect" (ākāra),
and what is performed by it?
Both of these are now explained:
The wise have the form of constant activity, whereas those with forms are dependent on supports.
Wisdom is indeed said to be the aspect (*ākāra*).
In that case, wisdom itself would not possess an aspect, because two instances of wisdom cannot exist simultaneously.
Consequently, it follows that not all mental factors (*caitasika*) would possess aspects.
Indeed, we do not say that it possesses an aspect (*sākāra*) or consists of a single aspect (*ekākāra*) because of its association with wisdom (*prajñā*).

What then? It means that it possesses an aspect because it makes [the object] its own function—that is, because it grasps the objective support (*ālambana*). But what is that which is made to possess an aspect?
That which has an aspect (*sākāra*) is that which performs an act (*ākārya*).
Whatever exists, whether substantially (*dravyataḥ*) or as a designation (*prajñaptitaḥ*), is that which is acted upon.
However, mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) possess aspects; the meaning is that they grasp objects.

Furthermore, what is knowledge (jñāna), and how many applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are there? Knowledge of another's mind consists of three; that which has the designation "dharma" and the wisdom of cessation consist of four applications of mindfulness. Knowledge other than these is held to be distinct from them.
Knowledge of others' minds consists indeed of three [foundations of mindfulness], namely those called feeling, mind, and phenomena.
Knowledge of cessation is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
Other knowledges, excluding knowledge of others' minds and knowledge of cessation, are the four foundations of mindfulness.
Now, for which cognition are how many cognitions the object? Nine cognitions are the domain of the cognition of the path and the cognition of dharmas.
For each of the path-dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges (*mārga-dharmānvaya-jñāna*), nine knowledges are the object.
Specifically, for the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), this excludes conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);
for the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), it excludes subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
For subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the object is dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).

For the two cognitions of suffering and its cause—the cognitions of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) and origin (*samudayajñāna*)—the objects are conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and contaminated knowledge of others' minds (*sāsravaparacittajñāna*). Each of these has two as its object.
For the four— namely, conventional knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of exhaustion, and knowledge of non-arising— all ten knowledges are their objects;
there is nothing else.
Indeed, the knowledge of cessation does not have knowledge as its objective support.
Furthermore, having established ten factors, it must be stated which cognition has how many factors as its object.
How so? That is explained:
five factors—those pertaining to the three realms, those consisting of the path, and those that are eternal—[are the objects].
Having divided it into two for the sake of etymological derivation, one should demonstrate the objective domain of knowledge.
Having divided the phenomena of the three realms each into two— associated and dissociated—

and having likewise divided those not associated [with the realms] into two by means of the same distinction between associated and dissociated, and having also divided the unconditioned into two by means of the distinction between wholesome and neutral, there are thus ten.
In that regard, all ten categories of phenomena are the object of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

For dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), the objects are five: those associated with the desire realm, the untainted (*anāsrava*) associated and dissociated [factors], the unwholesome, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

For subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), there are seven [objects]: those associated with the form and formless realms, the untainted (*anāsrava*), the associated and dissociated wholesome, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
For the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are three: those associated with the desire and form realms, and the untainted—exclusively the associated.
For the knowledges of suffering and its origin, there are six: those associated with the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as the associated and dissociated.
For the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), there is one [object], which is exclusively the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and wholesome (*kuśala*).
For the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), there are two: the untainted (*anāsrava*) associated [factors] and the untainted dissociated [factors].
For the knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), nine factors are the object, excluding the neutral (*avyākṛta*) unconditioned.
This must now be explained: who is endowed with how many knowledges?
First of all, every ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is endowed with only conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
However, this is the fixed rule:
in the first cognition of the path of seeing, one is endowed with three cognitions;
in the second moment, one is endowed with three—conventional cognition, the cognition of suffering, and the cognition of phenomena.
Having become detached from each of the four [dhyānas] in turn, one whose mind is directed elsewhere [attains the fruit] through wisdom.
From this point onward, one knowledge increases in each of four moments of mind.
That is to say: in the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāne*), subsequent knowledge increases;
in the dharma-knowledge regarding origin (*samudayadharmajñāne*), the knowledge of origin increases.
In the dharma-knowledge of cessation, the dharma-knowledge of cessation increases;
in the dharma-knowledge of the path, the dharma-knowledge of the path increases.
However, in the subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as in the receptivities (*kṣānti*), there is no increase of previously unknown knowledge.
However, it should be stated that for one who is free from passion (vītarāga) regarding all [objects], the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) increases.
The first quarter of the seventh chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.
The second quarter of the seventh chapter;
this must now be discussed.
On which stage, in which state, or for which person are how many knowledges cultivated?
That is now begun: In the three dhyānas, in the detachment from the desire realm, and on the final path of liberation.
And in the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the fundamental dhyānas, there is the cultivation of knowable objects yet to come.
In the case of an ordinary person (*bāla*), when producing the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the dhyānas, and so forth,
as well as during the paths of preparation (*prayoga*) and liberation (*vimukti*), there is [the knowledge of others' minds] through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) regarding other mental states.

Indeed, for a beginner, at the final path of liberation during detachment from the first three dhyānas, as well as in the preparatory path of the fundamental dhyānas and in the generation of the roots of virtue such as the applications of mindfulness, it should be understood that there is cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) with respect to the future.

However, for the Noble One on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) of their own kind are cultivated. Indeed, if either a patience or a knowledge of that same kind has become manifest, then precisely that which is of its own kind is cultivated as future.
It is not of a different class nor does it have a different object, because its function is distinct;
and it is conventional regarding the subsequent knowledge concerning what is termed suffering and its cause.

Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is indeed cultivated during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the three moments of mind known as the subsequent knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation; it is not cultivated during the dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*),
because the goal has not yet been achieved, for the mastery of the objects and aspects (*ālambanākāra*) is not yet fully completed.
Why, then, does conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) undergo cultivation (*bhāvanā*) therein? This is explained:
because they share the same antidote (*pratipakṣa*), due to their being cultivated as the path (*mārgāyitatva*) toward those [objects].
Just as the three subsequent patiences (*anvayakṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) are the antidotes for the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by them, [so too is conventional knowledge].
Likewise, those conventional cognitions (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) are also antidotes;
for they too have functioned as the path during the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Therefore, that [conventional cognition] is called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*), because it is obtained at the conclusion of the three truths.
For this very reason, it is called "conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization" (*ābhisamayāntika-saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Indeed, during the cultivation of the knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), these would constitute the intermediate stages of clear realization.
And although this [knowledge] is of a nature that does not arise (*anutpatti-dharmaka*), it is nevertheless considered as a true reality (*saddharma*).
Why, then, is that [state] necessarily of a nature not to arise?
Because its arising is obstructed by reliance upon those who follow through faith or through the Dharma;
and when the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) has become manifest, it does not arise.
Therefore, one cultivates precisely the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharma*).
Furthermore, this [cultivation] pertains to the seven stages, belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), and shares the same stages as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The cultivation of the path of seeing has been explained.
They are to be explained in the context of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
However, regarding the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) termed "the path," either six or seven [knowledges] are cultivated.
Specifically, when the mind of the present subsequent knowledge exists within the path of cultivation for one who is not yet free from passion (*avītarāga*), six are cultivated.
Excluding conventional knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising,
seven future knowledges are cultivated by one who is free from passion, having added the knowledge of others' minds. Furthermore,
in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), that which follows is cultivated, and no other cognition of the mind.

Even for one who still possesses passion (*sarāga*), from that sixteenth moment onwards on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), until one becomes free from passion (*vītarāga*) regarding the desire realm, seven knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated in all the paths of preparation (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), liberation (*vimukti*), and excellence (*viśeṣa*). This is with the exception of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
In the paths of abandonment and liberation, prior to the final liberation,
conventional knowledge is not cultivated because it does not serve as an antidote to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).

In the case of detachment from the four dhyānas and the first three formless attainments, in the five supernormal powers, in the penetration of the unshakable [state], and in the dhyāna cultivated through intermingling,
for a trainee (śaikṣa) in all the paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga), there are exactly seven knowledges (jñāna).
...in the Abhidharmadīpa, in the commentary known as the Vibhāṣāprabhā, the second quarter of the seventh chapter is completed.
The third section of the seventh chapter is to be understood through detailed explanations concerning location, substance, cause, and maturation.
In that regard, concerning the past, future, and present, there occurs a variety of projection and being projected, as well as the undertaking of specific actions (*pratikarmasamādāna*).
For some [actions] are performed impulsively under the influence of conditions, while others are performed with a conscious mind.
Furthermore, having undertaken something, one acts with the thought, "I must live by means of this action.
Likewise, one acts either having undertaken it or not having undertaken it, thinking, "This is dharma" or "This is adharma.
And its profundity is to be understood through the analysis of its bases and so forth.

In that context, "abode" (*sthāna*) is so called because it provides the opportunity for those things whose arising depends upon the future; "cause" (*hetu*) is also so called because it is that by which [the thing] is produced, as it has been said: "The basis (*vastu*) is called the abode and the locus."
The basis (*vastu*) together with its locus (*sthāna*) is as follows:
for example, the intrinsic nature of the act of killing a living being;
that living being itself; the purpose for which it is killed; and the collection of conditions (*pratyayasāmagrī*) by means of which all this occurs—this constitutes the "basis."
Why? Because the locus, the cause, and the maturation are mentioned separately.
Indeed, that which is its locus, that which is made its locus, that karma which is its cause, and that which has that as its cause—[all these are distinct].
"This is the ripening of this karma, and that is of another"—
this [knowledge] consists of eight knowledges in its nature, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
That which extends without obstruction regarding the intrinsic nature and other aspects of the meditative absorptions and so forth,
and is designated as the knowledge of the meditative absorptions and so forth— that is the power consisting of the nine knowledges.

The power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti) is indeed that power which is unimpeded with respect to the classification and purification of affliction (saṃkleśa) and purification (vyavadāna) within the category of cessation— that is, regarding the classification and purification of affliction and purification of the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments. In this context, the fourfold set beginning with affliction consists of the stages conducive to decline, distinction, stability, and penetration, distinguished by being "with relish" (sāsvāda), "pure" (śuddha), "untainted" (anāsrava), and so forth.
This power of knowledge regarding meditative absorption, liberation, concentration, and attainment should be understood as consisting of nine types of knowledge.

That which operates in discerning the faculties of sentient beings—whether they are superior, inferior, or middling—is the power of knowledge regarding the faculties; it consists of nine types of cognition.

The power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties (*indriyaparāparajñānabala*) is the unimpeded knowledge regarding the threefold capacity of all sentient beings to attain their welfare; this power consists of nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
That which operates toward the threefold inclinations of sentient beings— beginning with the inferior and so forth—
and which is designated as the cognition of various dispositions, is the power consisting of nine types.

Indeed, that unimpeded knowledge regarding the inferior, middling, and superior inclinations of all sentient beings is the power of knowledge of various inclinations; it consists of exactly nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation.
That which is called the consideration of various elements (nānādhātu) and proceeds for the sake of sentient beings,
consisting of nine types of knowledge— such is the power of wisdom regarding various elements.

Furthermore, those elements (*dhātu*) which are the latencies (*vāsanā*) from the practice of virtues, faults, sciences, arts, and activities in previous births—these indeed should be understood specifically as the elements here.
Because they abide in the sense of being a lineage (*gotra*), they should be known as the dispositions (*āśaya*); and it is said that one "conducts oneself" by virtue of them.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "Beings harmonize according to their elements."
