That wisdom which knows the distinctions among destinies, dharmas, and noble ones according to their various conditions—
that is the tenth power, the knowledge of the path leading everywhere.

Indeed, that unimpeded knowledge regarding the factors that bring about the rebirth of sentient beings and those that cause their cessation is the power of the knowledge of the path leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*).
It should be viewed as being like a specific medicinal herb for the worthy.

For sentient beings of various dispositions (*nānā-dhātu*) and manifold elements who are capable of liberation, it is like a specific medicinal herb that serves as both a general and a specific antidote for the abandonment of all afflictions.

And he knows everywhere the cause of rebirth; by means of this, within a single continuum of the elements (*dhātu*), he correctly recognizes everything—whether one is capable or incapable of entering [the path] according to the power of whichever state of mind one has attained. Thus, omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is also explained. This very [knowledge], through the abandonment of the path along with its results, consists of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).
But some [hold that it consists] of nine knowledges, because they take only the path as the object.
That which is called conventional knowledge perceiving one's own past lives is considered the power of recollecting former births, together with its fruit.

This indicates his mastery in discerning the various connections among the diverse pleasures and pains of sentient beings within the successions of past births— both his own and those of others— just as one determines the meaning of signs through mental attention while meditating on dream-omens.
Indeed, it is just as when one has repeatedly seen dreams indicating future events and, by observing that those events generally correspond to them once they have come to pass, a certainty arises.
Just as signs of the Dharma arise within the mental attentions of those in meditative absorption, and through them the discernment of phenomena becomes perfectly clear,
even so is the seal of the Blessed One known with respect to all phenomena;
how much more so, then, regarding the seals connected to the maturation of karma?
Thus, this power consists precisely of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

The knowledge regarding the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings that functions across other time periods is called the power of the cognition of death and rebirth; it is described as being like the previous [powers].
Based on the knowledge that relies upon the divine eye, one becomes independent of others regarding the knowledge that enters into the variety of karmic fruits and conducts;
it is the same for objects in the present as well.
That knowledge relying upon the divine eye is manifested in the future limit (aparānta) together with the knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
This, therefore, consists precisely of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The cognition of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) consists of six cognitions, or alternatively, ten.
Therefore, what task for those to be trained remains now for the Blessed One?
The destruction of the outflows.

Whatever knowledge pertains to anyone at any time, and by whatever methods of descent and teaching it is accomplished without effort—that the Blessed One knows in all its aspects through this wisdom, and no one else.
Therefore, this power belongs to him alone and not to another.
Furthermore, this [power] has the nature of the six knowledges, or consists of ten aspects.
If it is knowledge regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), there are six [knowledges],
excluding the knowledge of others' minds, suffering, origin, and the path.
Now, when there is knowledge and vision regarding destruction along with its means,
there are ten knowledges.
Thus, the intrinsic nature of the ten powers has been explained.
The restriction regarding the aspects (ākāra) must be stated; that is now being expressed:
"In this [system], the first [knowledge] has sixteen aspects, while the subsequent ones have others as well. (Abhidharmadīpa 500)
The seventh has sixteen aspects and two undivided forms;
the second, however, has eight aspects and consists of nine knowledges.
The power of a Tathāgata is said to be known in twelve forms.
The power of knowing what is possible and impossible proceeds by way of sixteen aspects.

Furthermore, if one intends to speak of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) as being accompanied by its means, that power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows is also sixteenfold, along with those other [aspects] distinct from it.
Now, that [power] consists merely of destruction;
the seventh power, the knowledge of the path leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*), which consists of the aspects of the six knowledges, likewise possesses sixteen aspects.

However, the two—the power of the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) and the power of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapatti-jñānabala*)—are powers whose aspects are not differentiated.
The second, however, is the power of knowledge regarding the ripening of karma, which has eight aspects.
As for the power of knowledge regarding meditative concentrations and attainments, its nature consists of nine knowledges; it proceeds by means of those same twelve aspects.
Whatever else has not been mentioned should be inferred accordingly.
Furthermore, what is its object?
Its object is everything; here, the first [type] has all things as its object, while the last relies upon tranquility.
The power of knowing what is possible and impossible has all things as its object;
the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows has either nirvana or the four noble truths as its object.
The [first] two have existence as their cause and object; the seventh has the truths as its domain.
The power of knowledge regarding the ripening of karma has existence as its sphere.
The power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere has the four truths as its object.
For that which is designated as the eighth, the meaning of the verbal root, is indeed [the object] past and so forth.
The power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives has as its objective domain the realms of the past and so forth.
Indeed, the ninth [power] has conditioned phenomena as its object for the sake of form;

the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth has the sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana) as its domain, while whatever remains among the others should be understood as having conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) as their range.
Furthermore, in this regard:
This term "power" (bala) is dependent on two factors; however, power itself consists in being unimpeded.
And it is characterized by the expectation of overcoming others and by being entirely unimpeded;
indeed, that which possesses unobstructed power is called "strength.
The tenfold mental strength of the Blessed One has been explained.
The bodily [power] is also described as follows:
"In every joint of the Buddha's body, there is the strength of Nārāyaṇa;
that tangible power is even greater than seven times that of an elephant and so forth. (Abhidharmadīpa 505)
The strength called Nārāyaṇa is spoken of;
and that exists in every vital point (*marman*) of the Blessed One.
Furthermore, the joints of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Cakravartins are, respectively, like the *nāgagranthi*, the *śaṅkalā*, and the *śaṅku* knots.
What, then, is the measure of that Nārāyaṇa strength?
Indeed, the strength of ten ordinary elephants is equal to the strength of one scent-elephant (gandhahastin).
In this manner, by increasing tenfold at each step, the strengths of the Mahānagna, Praskandin, Varāṅga, Cāṇūra, and Nārāyaṇa should be described.
Others say it is equal to a thousand Airāvaṇas;

for at the time of a procession to the celestial gardens, he manifests himself with thirty-three heads and departs, carrying away as many divine palaces—each accompanied by thousands of attendants—as if they were birch-bark leaves, displaying those most wonderful and variegated gardens. Such is the extent of his power.
Thus they describe it: the physical power of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is infinite, just like their mental power.
Furthermore, that physical power is comprised within the sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
They explain that strength is comprised by its heaviness, while weakness is comprised by its lightness.
The four forms of fearlessness arise from the complete attainment of one's own and others' welfare;
two have the nature of the first and last powers, while two are the functions of the [first] two knowledges.
It is stated in the Sūtra: “While I am indeed a perfectly awakened one (*samyaksambuddha*), these dharmas have not been fully realized by you,” and so forth.
For here, by means of the first and second [statements], the Blessed One has manifested the perfection of his own welfare (*svārthasaṃpat*);
by the former, the perfection of knowledge (*jñānasaṃpat*).
By the second [verse], the perfection of abandonment is shown;
by the other two, the perfection of the welfare of others is indicated through the manifestation of purification and defilement.
Furthermore, what is fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), and how many types of knowledge does it consist of? This is explained as follows:
The first [power] consists of the power regarding what is possible and what is impossible;
the second consists of the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows; the third is the power of the knowledge that beings are the owners of their own karma.

The fourth ground of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) is the power of knowledge regarding the path leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*). Just as these powers have the nature of knowledge, so too should the four grounds of self-confidence be understood as having that same nature, respectively.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "There are these three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) which the Noble One cultivates," and so forth.
Furthermore, their characteristic is as follows:
the threefold application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthiti) depends upon the threefold perfection of the listener;
its specific characteristic is clear comprehension (saṃprajanya) whose capacity is established through recollection (saṃsmāra).

The classification of those to be trained (*vineya*) into three types is established based on the distinction between those who desire to listen (*śuśrūṣaka*), those who do not desire to listen, and so forth;
this is intended according to the three groups beginning with those who desire to listen.

Furthermore, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), which have as their nature the triad of mindfulness distinguished by clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*).

For, due to the Blessed One’s distinguished mindfulness and clear comprehension, he feels neither joy nor resentment toward the assembly of disciples—whether they are listening to him, not listening, or both.
Furthermore, because great compassion (mahākaruṇā) consists of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), it follows for a long duration;
because it functions equally toward all [beings] and so forth, it is "great pity" (mahākṛpā) precisely for one who is still bound [to cyclic existence].
If compassion exists even in the Śrāvaka and even in the Pratyekabuddha, why is it said that Great Compassion belongs to the Buddha alone?

Because this [Great Compassion] has the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) for the Śrāvakas and others, whereas for the Buddha it has the nature of non-hatred (*adveṣa*); furthermore, it persists over a long period of time, follows after subtle [objects], proceeds toward the gathering of all sentient beings, and pervades everywhere, residing in a body illuminated by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
And it is embraced by the ten powers;
therefore, it is called the "Great Compassion" of the Blessed Buddha alone.
Thus have been explained the uncommon qualities.
Those shared with the Śrāvakas are said to be:
absence of conflict (*araṇā*), knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
These five, however, belong to the continuum of an Arhat and are of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*).
Other qualities common to them as well, such as heedfulness and so forth—
listen, for I shall describe the characteristics of these as they have been taught.
In that regard, first:
Non-contention (araṇā) is conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), born from a human being, based on the final dhyāna; it arises within the continuum of an Ārya and perceives the causes of defilement.
In this case, a certain Arhat of unshakable nature, having experienced the supreme bliss of immortality through the abandonment of all afflictions, generates this thought:
"How might others also not give rise to afflictions by taking my mental continuum as an object, and how might they not experience that undesirable result?

Having attained the fourth dhyāna, which has reached the pinnacle of its development, he acts in such a way that no one gives rise to an affliction within his mental continuum while he is moving about or dwelling in his abode.
The knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*) is likewise supported by all phenomena;
it is taught for one of unshakable nature (*akopyadharman*), and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are exactly the same.

The knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*) also has the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), because it is attained through the fourth dhyāna at its ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*); for whatever an Arhat resolves upon, he knows that very thing, since the knowledge resulting from resolve has all phenomena as its object.
Furthermore, the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are indeed that which dispels confusion regarding the names associated with the intended meaning.
It should be known that the first [analytical knowledge] is manifested by the others, while the latter is the investigation of knowledge.
The third is the refinement of words, which destroys delusion regarding knowledge;
the fourth, however, is the continuous discourse, which is oriented toward the production of meditative concentration and so forth.

Among those things comprised within the twelvefold scriptural teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) which are intended to be explained and connected with the meanings to be set forth—the sets of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth—that irreversible knowledge is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*). That irreversible knowledge regarding the collections of conventional meanings for the sake of others, which are expressed by those [names] and related to human or non-human [authorship], is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*). That irreversible knowledge regarding the words of speech that denote the sets of names and so forth, which are connected with gender, number, case-role, action, tense, person, and suffix—that is the analytical knowledge of etymology (*niruktipratisaṃvid*).

The irreversible knowledge regarding the phenomena, their meanings, and their definitions, as well as the clear manifestation of mastery over the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments—that is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
These six qualities are called "the ultimate limit" (*prāntakoṭika*).
Furthermore, as for these analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), which stages (*bhūmi*) do they belong to, and which consist of how many types of knowledge (*jñāna*)? This is now elucidated:
The one called "meaning" (*arthapratisaṃvid*) exists everywhere; it consists of six knowledges, or alternatively, nine.

The analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) exists in all stages, from the desire realm up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*); its nature consists of nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), because Nirvana alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and [excluding] the knowledges of others' minds, suffering, origin, and the path. Likewise, that which is called the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*) consists of ten knowledges. *Abhidharmadīpa* 515.
The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) in all stages consists of the ten knowledges;
therein,
that called "dharma" exists in the desire realm and the meditations, while the others exist in the first meditation and the desire realm.

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid) exists in the desire realm and in the four meditative absorptions (dhyānas); the analytical knowledge of language (niruktipratisaṃvid) exists in the desire realm and in the first meditative absorption.
These two analytical knowledges consist of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna). (Abhidh-d 516)
Both of these, the analytical knowledges of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) and of expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid), have conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) as their intrinsic nature.
The third quarter of the seventh chapter in the Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti is completed.
The fourth quarter of the seventh chapter:
Now, the qualities such as the superknowledges (abhijñā), which are shared with ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana), must be discussed.
These are called:

the supernormal power of psychic transformation, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of past lives, the knowledge of death and rebirth, and the knowledge of the destruction [of the outflows].
These six supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) are either wisdom (dhī) or the direct realization of knowledge on the path to liberation.
The direct realization of knowledge is indeed called the supernormal power (abhijñā) comprised within the path of liberation.
Of which qualities, then, is this the direct realization of knowledge? That is now explained.

The direct realization of knowledge regarding the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), knowledge of the minds of others (*cetaḥparyāya*), recollection of former abodes (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛti*), knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda*), and the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).
It is called *abhijñā* because one knows directly (*abhijānāti*) by means of it, or because it is known through it.

Why, then, is only the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) considered supernormal knowledge—just like the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*)—and not those paths whose nature is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*)?

Because the knowledge of others' minds is excluded from the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), and because it would follow that some Arhats—upon relinquishing the path of uninterrupted transition for the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)—would lack the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, among these [supernormal knowledges], four are conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); the knowledge of others' minds (*cittadhī*) consists of five knowledges;
and the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of all outflows (*sarvāsravakṣayābhijñā*) consists of six knowledges, or alternatively, ten.
Excluding the supernormal powers of knowing the minds of others (*cetaḥparyāya*) and the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*):

the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others consists of five knowledges—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya*), the knowledge of the path (*mārga*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta*).

The supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows consists of six knowledges, or ten; that is, it consists of [the six] excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya*), and the knowledge of the path—or alternatively, it consists of all ten.
The sixth [superknowledge] exists everywhere; the other five exist in the fundamental stages of dhyāna;
the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows exists in all stages;
and the remaining ones exist in the four fundamental stages of dhyāna.
They are obtained through effort and detachment; they have as their objects the spheres of their own level and lower levels.

All superknowledges (*abhijñā*) are obtained through effort and through detachment (*vairāgya*). Among these, those not previously practiced are obtained through effort, while those already practiced are obtained through detachment.
Indeed, the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) practiced in previous lives are obtained through detachment (*vairāgya*);
those that are exceptional are obtained through effort.
Furthermore, these have as their objects their own level and lower levels.
By means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), one goes to one's own level and to lower levels;
the same applies to the creation of emanations (*nirmita-nirmāṇa*).
By means of the superknowledge of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*), one also hears sounds belonging to one's own level and to lower levels.
In this way, one knows the minds of others and the knowledge of recollecting past lives;
furthermore, by means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of death and rebirth, one knows the forms belonging to one's own level and lower levels.
Furthermore, among these [supernormal powers], which ones correspond to how many applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)?
It is held that the three [powers] consisting of the knowledge of the course of others' minds (*cetaḥparyāya-dhī*) are applications of mindfulness;
as for the supernormal powers of psychic transformation (*ṛddhi*), the ear (*śrotra*), and the eye (*akṣi*), they consist of the first application of mindfulness.
The supernormal knowledge of others' minds consists of three applications of mindfulness, excluding the application of mindfulness to the body;
for it has mind and mental factors as its object.
The supernormal knowledges of psychic power, the divine ear, and the divine eye consist of the application of mindfulness to the body, because they have form as their object.
Supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) indeed has the four external sense-bases as its object;
the divine ear and eye have, respectively, the sense-base of sound and the sense-base of form as their objects.
However, according to the distinctions of wholesome and so forth—
The divine ear and eye, as well as other pure [powers], are considered neutral (*avyākṛta*).
It is said that the divine ear and eye are indeed neutral,
but that is not so.

Because the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) have the nature of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and because visual and auditory consciousnesses are non-conceptual (*avikalpa*), the knowledge of liberation (*vimuktijñāna*) does not arise [in them].

However, within the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), there exists a specific excellence of wisdom (*prajñāviśeṣa*) which has as its fruit the elements belonging to its own level; through the manifestation of this wisdom, the eye and ear belonging to that same level come into manifestation.
Since that [wisdom] serves as the support for visual and auditory consciousness, the wisdom associated with those two consciousnesses is not called a supernormal power (*abhijñā*).

But how, then, is the term "superknowledge" (abhijñā) applied to these two? It is said: Superknowledge is the state of being the fruit of superknowledge, [attained] through mental consciousness and wisdom.
In this context, the term "higher knowledge" (*abhijñā*) refers to the fruit of higher knowledge;
however, one knows through the wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
That very wisdom is called "higher knowledge" because it is that which discerns.
Furthermore, how many of these are knowledges (*vidyā*)?
Three are considered knowledges for the sake of dispelling delusion regarding the three times;
one is a knowledge by its very nature, being beyond training (*aśaikṣī*), while two arise from having a basis that is beyond training.

The three direct realizations consisting of the knowledge of former abodes, the knowledge of death and rebirth, and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows are indeed called the "knowledges of one beyond training" (*aśaikṣī vidyā*).
Why are only these [three]?
Because these alone are the knowledges by which the three types of ignorance (*avidyā*) are turned back.
Through the knowledge of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, delusion regarding the past is eliminated;
through the supernormal power of the knowledge of death and rebirth, delusion regarding the future is eliminated;
and through the supernormal power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, delusion regarding the intermediate state is eliminated.

And although all three are indeed beyond training (aśaikṣa), nevertheless, "one is beyond training by its own nature, while two are beyond training because they arise from a basis that is beyond training.
Alternatively, the last one is beyond training both by its own nature and by way of its continuum (santāna);
the first two, however, are called "beyond training" because they belong to the continuum of one who is beyond training.
Furthermore, how many among these are the miracles?

The three miracles are known as the supernormal power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhi*), the supernormal power of the mind (*cetaḥparyāya*), and the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
One carries away two from the Kuśāstṛs; one carries away the supreme from the Māras.

Indeed, by means of the miracle of supernormal power and the miracle of mind-reading, he draws the minds of those to be trained away from the teachers of false doctrines—such as Kapila, Ulūka, Akṣapāda, and others—and establishes them in the Buddha, the Blessed One, the teacher of ultimate truth;
and by means of the miracle of instruction, he draws them away from the Māras and establishes them in the Supreme Guide, the All-Knowing One.

What, then, is this supernatural power (*ṛddhi*)? It is said that "supernatural power" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while its fruit is eightfold sovereignty. This is twofold: movement and transformation; of these, movement is held to be threefold. *Abhidharmadīpa* 524.

Supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is indeed of the nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); however, because it is the fruit of that concentration, it is called "supernormal power" in the Sūtra as a miraculous manifestation (*prātihārya*).
When concentration is embraced by its constituent factors, all this miraculous manifestation succeeds.
Therefore, meditative concentration itself is supernormal power.

Its fruit is the eightfold sovereignty, beginning with *aṇimā*, which is taught in the Sūtra as the ability to abide in one or many forms according to one's wish, and so forth. Furthermore, this fruit of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is twofold: movement (*gati*) and emanation (*nirmāṇa*).
Movement, moreover, is threefold. Among these:
The mind-made movement of the Teacher proceeds from his mere wish;
for others, it is produced by resolute conviction and thus carries along the body.
The supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) that is as swift as thought belongs to the Buddha alone;
its speed is like that of the mind.
In the same amount of time that visual consciousness perceives the color blue, in that same amount of time the Blessed One [traverses the distance] with his body.

For the Blessed Buddhas possess bodies of infinite miraculous power (*ṛddhi*) that pervade all intermediate spaces of the world, because they accomplish their intended purposes effortlessly and according to their wish;
however, for the Śrāvakas and others, movement involves the physical carrying of the body, as is the case with gods or birds.
Furthermore, through resolute intention (*ādhimokṣika*), even that which is distant becomes near by means of resolute conviction;
and with merely an extension of the arm, one appears upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. Thus has the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) been explained.
The emanation of movement must now be discussed;
it is of two kinds: belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
Regarding these, first—
In the desire realm, emanation is held to consist of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility;
in the form realm, it is considered to consist of visible form and tangibility, whether within one's own body or externally.
Indeed, the four external sense bases belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) are emanated;
it is not otherwise, for that would entail the undesirable consequence of accepting the doctrine of a creator God (*īśvara*).
However, only two sense bases belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) are emanated there, because of the absence of odor and taste.
Furthermore, this should be observed both in one's own body and in the bodies of others.
These four types of emanation are to be understood as such in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and likewise in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
thus, there are eight types of emanation.

Is it indeed by means of the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) itself that the emanation (*nirmāṇa*) is created? What then? It is by means of the mind that is the fruit of the supernormal power. Those [minds] are fourteen;
two are the fruits of the first dhyāna, and from those, they increase one by one for each higher stage. (Abhidh-d 527)
Indeed, within the mind of transformation that is the fruit of the first dhyāna, there are those belonging to the desire realm and those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna;
there are three that are the fruits of the second dhyāna,
and four that are the fruits of the third dhyāna.
The fruits of the fourth dhyāna are five.
How, then, are the minds of transformation obtained?
Their acquisition should be understood as being like that of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*);
for just as the meditative absorptions are obtained through detachment (*vairāgya*), through rebirth (*upapatti*), and through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), so too are the minds of transformation.
How, then, does that arise? It arises from the pure [dhyāna] and from itself.
Immediately after the pure dhyāna, the mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta) arises; or it arises from the mind of transformation itself, and not from anything else.

Furthermore, immediately after a mind of emanation (nirmāṇacitta), both a pure dhyāna (śuddhakadhyāna) and a mind of emanation arise, and nothing else. Moreover, every emanation is produced by a mind belonging to its own level; however, speech may also be produced by a mind of a lower level.

Indeed, an emanation belonging to one level is not produced by an emanation-mind belonging to another level; however, speech [is produced] by a mind of its own level or of a lower level. For an emanation belonging to the desire realm or the first dhyāna speaks by means of a mind belonging to its own level alone.
However, those belonging to the higher stages [are perceived] by means of that which belongs to the stage of the first dhyāna,
because the mind that originates informative action exists precisely there.
Furthermore, does the speech of the emanation and the emanator occur sequentially or simultaneously? To this it is said:
"Except for the Sugata, these speak together with the emanator.
For it has been stated:
“When one speaks, all the emanations speak;
when one becomes silent, they all become silent.
However, by the will of the Blessed One, the emanations speak either before, after, or simultaneously [with him].
Furthermore, when one among them speaks, all the emanations speak simultaneously.
"But having empowered the emanation, they speak with another mind.
"Having empowered the emanation" means having established it.
Furthermore, because one initiates speech by means of another mind known as the "producer of intimation," there is no fault regarding the disappearance of an emanation.
Moreover, this sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) does not belong to the living alone; rather, sustaining power exists even for the dead, but only for a stable object. (Abhidh-d 530)

Through the empowerment of the noble Mahākāśyapa, upon hearing of that location where the skeleton was situated, the characteristic of the bone—which is stable—remained, while that of the flesh, blood, and so forth, did not.
Furthermore, does one create a single emanation with a single mind, or many?
One who has not yet attained mastery creates one with many; for those who have attained mastery, it is the reverse.
Through numerous initial productions of emanation-minds, one creates a single emanation that possesses a basis of appropriation (*sopādāna*).

When supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) has been mastered, however, by the will of the creator, one produces even many [emanations] with a single state of mind, and even those that are without a basis (*nirupādāna*).

Furthermore, that emanation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) is of two kinds: consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) and acquired at birth (*upapattiprātilambhika*). Among these, that which arises from supernormal knowledge is neutral (*avyākṛta*); however, that which arises from birth is of three types. (Abhidh-d 531)
Indeed, that emanation-mind which is the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*) is neutral (*avyākṛta*);
however, that which is acquired at birth (*upapatti-prātilambhika*) is of three kinds, such as wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth.
That fruit of birth is endowed with ten excellences (*atiśaya*).
This tenfold sovereignty of the Arhats arises from their possession of both the knowledge of the destruction of all outflows and liberation.
This tenfold bliss of sovereignty, beginning with *aṇimā* and ending with mastery over the *śaikṣas*, which is endowed with excellence, arises only for Arhats.
If, then, this sovereignty is common to these three types of Arhats, what then is the distinction between the Teacher and the disciple?
To this it is taught:
"Even though this aforementioned sovereignty is equal for both the Teacher and the disciple,"
The very great interval of the Teacher that was previously mentioned.

Regarding the contemplation of the ten powers and other unique qualities of a Buddha, one should understand the distinction [between them] through the four conditions and the analogies of the scent-elephant, the dog, and the hare while crossing a river.
The fourth quarter of the seventh chapter in the *Abhidharmapradīpa*, in the commentary known as the *Vibhāṣāprabhā*.
And thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Analysis of Knowledge."
The Eighth Chapter. First Section.
For the detailed exposition of insight has indeed been explained.
Now, calm abiding (śamatha) must be explained.

This calm abiding is indeed comprised within the four dhyānas and the formless attainments (ārūpya). In that context, however, dhyāna is the stability of mind together with its factors; it is fourfold according to the distinction of its factors.

Tranquility (śamatha), which is indeed wholesome one-pointedness of mind accompanied by its factors, is called meditative absorption (dhyāna). That mental factor among the mental states and processes (citta-caitta), by virtue of being embraced by these factors and through its intensity, causes them not to proceed toward another object, is designated as concentration (samādhi).

We shall explain that it is fourfold according to its constituent parts. Furthermore, regarding that stability of mind, the term "dhyāna" (meditative absorption) is used in its primary sense; it is used figuratively for those factors that coexist with it.
In the ultimate sense, meditation has the nature of concentration (*samādhi*);
however, when taken together with its retinue, it has the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
By way of figurative designation, the same term is applied even to those factors that coexist with it.
In brief, this fourfold class of meditative absorption (dhyāna) has been explained:
namely, the first, second, third, and fourth absorptions.
I shall now describe its distinctions in terms of substantial entities according to the scriptures.
I shall now briefly explain the distinction between the substances of the fourfold class of meditations and the same number of classes of attainments.

In that regard, there are eight kinds of meditative attainments (samāpatti), including the four formless [attainments]. This is because they are taught as groups consisting of four or five aggregates (skandha). Abhidh-d_536 //
When the five aggregates are grouped together, meditative absorption (dhyāna-samāpatti) is designated;
when there are four or five [aggregates], the formless attainment (ārūpya-samāpatti) is designated.
When distinguished by their individual types, however, the actual entities of the meditative attainments (samāpatti-dravya) are seventeen:
ten [fundamental dhyānas] together with the eight preparatory stages (sāmantaka) and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntarika).

Indeed, for the eight stages of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-bhūmi*) and the eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka-dravya*) themselves, there are the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntarika*) included within the first dhyāna as the means for entering them.
These seventeen, when divided according to their relative grossness, become seventeen; therefore it is said:
"These other divisions of them shall also be explained as enjoined by the treatise."
Furthermore, other distinctions of meditative attainments (samāpatti) mentioned in the Sūtras and Abhidharma, which are included therein, will also be explained;
yet all of them truly come within the range of the Buddha’s cognition.

For the Blessed One alone possesses direct cognitive engagement regarding the various distinctions such as the attainment of the first dhyāna, as well as their infinite natures, powers, activities, and fruits.
How are these meditations (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya) of three kinds?
That is now undertaken:
the fundamental meditations are of three types, according to the distinctions of being "tasted" (sāsvāda) and so forth.
In the same way, there are three formless realms; however, the peak of existence is considered to be of two kinds.
In that regard, first, the fundamental dhyānas are of three kinds, distinguished as being associated with tasting (*āsvādana*), pure (*śuddhaka*), or untainted (*anāsrava*).
Likewise, there are three fundamental formless attainments (*ārūpya*);
however, the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is not untainted.
Because the desire realm and the peak of existence are the roots of existence.
The neighboring [attainments] are of two kinds, seven in number; however, the first is considered to be of three kinds.
The intermediate dhyāna is likewise of three kinds; moreover, that which is undefiled has its support in a lower realm.

Excluding the preliminary stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna, the other seven preliminary stages are of two types, with the exception of the untainted (*anāsrava*). However, the preliminary stage of the first dhyāna is of three types;
some, however, do not accept that which is associated with relish (*āsvādana*).
In the same way, the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntarika) is threefold;
that which is there non-defiled is a substance belonging to a lower basis.

Furthermore, what are the characteristics of these three [types of concentration] associated with relishing and so forth? It is said: That which is worldly and accompanied by faith is considered to possess relishing and craving; that which is below it is destroyed [by the path], while that which is supramundane is untainted (*anāsrava*). *Abhidharmadīpa* 541.
That which is accompanied by craving is said to be "associated with relishing," because craving is a synonym for relishing. Furthermore,
that which is not associated [with craving] is also said to be "possessing relishing" because it coexists with craving and shares the same fruit as craving.
That wholesome attainment-substance which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called "pure" (*śuddhaka*),
because it is untainted by the stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and is conjoined with white dharmas such as non-greed (*alobha*).
This very pure state is the object of relish for that attainment which is not associated with relishing.
Therefore, that which has just passed away immediately after it is tasted.
One who tastes has entered into that by which one tastes, and one has emerged from that which is tasted.
For, through their mutual association, there is the manifestation of craving and meditative absorption.
The relishing of meditative concentration due to the power of craving is called "concentration," while the state of craving due to the power of concentration is called "meditation" (dhyāna);
otherwise, it would be a contradiction.
For no one enters into craving,
nor does one relish through meditative concentration;
however, the substance of supramundane attainment is called "untainted" (anāsrava).
Furthermore, among these attainments (*samāpatti*), only the dhyānas possess constituent members (*aṅga*), not the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Now, how many members belong to which dhyāna? This is set forth as follows:

In the first wholesome [dhyāna], there are five factors: applied thought (vitarka), mental subtlety (cittasūkṣmatā), joy (prīti), bliss (sukha), and meditative concentration (samādhāna). The afflicted [dhyāna] is devoid of bliss.
First, in the first pure dhyāna, there are five factors: applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), joy (prīti), bliss (sukha), and concentration (samādhi).
In the defiled [first dhyāna], there are four, excluding bliss.
In the second [dhyāna], there are four factors: internal serenity, bliss, joy, and concentration; however, when it is defiled, faith is absent, as is bliss.
In the second wholesome dhyāna, there are four factors:
internal clarity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind; in the defiled [second dhyāna], there are two, excluding faith and bliss.
In the third [dhyāna], there is wisdom; in the fifth [dhyāna], mindfulness, equanimity, bliss, and stability.
However, in the defiled [dhyānas], it should be known that there are only two factors: concentration and the bliss of sensation.
In the third pure dhyāna, there are equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, bliss, and concentration;
however, in the defiled [third dhyāna], there are two [factors]: non-concentration and the bliss of feeling.
In the last [dhyāna], there are four factors: two are equanimity, one is concentration, and one is mindfulness alone.
In the defiled fourth dhyāna, however, there are two factors: feeling and stability.
In the fourth meditative absorption (dhyāna), which is pure, there are four factors:
neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, equanimity, purity of mindfulness, and concentration.
In the defiled [fourth dhyāna], however, there are two: feeling and stability.
Furthermore, how many of these exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*) and how many exist nominally (*nāmataḥ*)?
Substantially there are eleven, while nominally there are eight and ten;
these are called the limbs (*aṅga*), and for this reason they are remembered as forming four categories (*catuṣkoṭi*).
In substance, there are indeed eleven factors.
In the first dhyāna, there are five factors;
in the second, internal serenity increases.
In the third [dhyāna], the factors excluding concentration increase;
in the fourth, however, there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*).
But is it not the case that what was called "pleasure" (*sukha*) in the third dhyāna is likewise present in the first and second?
The first quarter of the eighth chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti* is completed.
The second quarter of the eighth chapter; and [the section] on calm abiding (*śamatha*).
In the preparatory stages of the dhyānas and in the formless attainments, there is no fixed establishment of the factors (aṅga).
In the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), insight (*vidarśanā*) is predominant while calm (*śamatha*) is deficient.
In the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), calm functions more extensively everywhere, while insight is even more deficient.
Because of the statement, "for one who sees by means of insight, [this occurs] in perception" (*saṃjñāyām*), there is also a subsequent mention of the possessor of the factors (*aṅgin*).
Thereupon, insight is accomplished.
Since all four meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are indeed immovable with respect to their maturation (vipāka), why is only the fourth called "unshakable" (ānejya)?
To this it is replied: because of the destruction of applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra) and the cessation of inhalation and exhalation (praśvāsa-āśvāsa).
Because of the absence of both equanimity and feeling, the last [dhyāna] is called "imperturbable" (ānejya).
Furthermore, the Blessed One has stated that the first three dhyānas are "shaken" because they are associated with the eight defects, beginning with applied thought (*vitarka*).

These eight defects are: applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), and mental grief (*daurmanasya*).
It is stated in the Abhidharma that because it is free from these, the fourth dhyāna is "unshakable."

The fourth [dhyāna] is described in the Sūtra as "imperturbable" (*āneñja*) because it cannot be shaken by applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), or pleasure (*sukha*).
The teaching in the Sūtra is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), whereas in the Abhidharma it is defined according to its specific characteristics (*lākṣaṇika*).
For it is said: "By the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and through the disappearance of previous joy and dejection, one enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna."
In the Abhidharma, it is precisely initial inquiry (vitarka), sustained investigation (vicāra), joy (prīti), and bliss (sukha) that constitute "movement" (iñjita).
This must now be explained:
here, regarding the meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) is said to exist in the first and second dhyānas because of the mention of joy (*prīti*).
For joy is indeed mental pleasure.
In the third [dhyāna] there is pleasure (*sukha*), and in the fourth there is equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Is this the same restriction regarding feeling (*vedanā*) even in the dhyānas of rebirth?
No, it is said. What then?
In the first [dhyāna], there are joy, pleasure, and equanimity; in the second, however, with the exception of pleasure;
in the third, there are pleasure and equanimity; and in the last, only equanimity is recognized.
In the rebirth of the first dhyāna, there are indeed three feelings:
pleasure belonging to the three groups of consciousness, mental joy belonging to the mental level, and equanimity belonging to the four groups of consciousness.
In rebirth in the second dhyāna, there are two feelings—mental joy and equanimity—which belong to the mental level;
there is no [bodily] pleasure here because of the absence of the five groups of sensory consciousness.
In rebirth in the third dhyāna, there are two feelings which belong to the mental level.
In the rebirth of the fourth dhyāna, only equanimity exists as feeling.
But surely, in the second and subsequent dhyānas, there exist perceptions of visible forms, sounds, and tangibles, as well as the mind that originates informative action (*vijñapti*).
How then can it be said that there is no feeling belonging to the three groups of consciousness, nor initial and sustained mental application (*vitarka-vicāra*) therein?
This is not a fault,
because it is a negation of [the consciousness] belonging to its own level.
But then, by what means are form and so forth cognized, and how is non-informative action (avijñapti) produced?
That is explained as follows:

Visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses, which likewise produce informative intimation (*vijñapti*), belong to that level which is without investigation (*avicārā*); moreover, they are neutral (*avyākṛta*) from the very beginning. *Abhidharmadīpa* 550.

Indeed, those born in the second dhyāna who desire to perceive forms, sounds, and tangibles, and who wish to go [to them], bring forth the three consciousnesses—visual consciousness and the others—which belong to the level of the first dhyāna, as well as the consciousness that originates informative action (*vijñapti*). Like a mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*), they perceive and move by means of these.

Furthermore, they bring forth only a neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind belonging to the level of the first dhyāna; they do not bring forth a wholesome one because it is inferior and lacks the necessary esteem, nor do they bring forth an afflicted one because they are free from passion (*vītarāga*).
It is, for example, like a certain lord who went to the house of a poor friend;

invited by that friend with the offering of all his possessions, he—out of deference to his friend's intent—set aside things both inferior and superior and took whatever was at hand. In this same way, the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) have been explained in their essential nature.
The formless attainments (ārūpyas) must now be explained. This is commenced:
"Drawn by the grasping of the sign of space, it is called the mental application of the infinite."
The formless realm (ārūpya) is of various forms; it is designated as "infinite space" (ākāśānantya).

The apprehension of the sign of infinite space is the cause for the arising of the designation [“infinite space”]. Subsequently, however, mental orientations (*manaskāra*)—which have as their objects the four aggregates, or one of those other than that, or other phenomena—come into manifestation.

For it was said by the Blessed One: “By completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [one perceives] ‘space is infinite,’ and thus, having attained the sphere of infinite space...”
"...dwells.
But what, then, is the distinction between these three perceptions of form and so forth?
Here, the distinction should be understood by way of the perceptions of the manifold forms of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Therefore, according to this scripture, the various aggregates of form and formlessness are subsumed therein.

Among them, those characterized by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) are dissociated from the morality that follows the mind, while the remainder are dissociated from the morality of rebirth (*upapatti*).
These formless states (*ārūpya*), excluding the preliminary stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first formless realm, are those in which the perception of form has been transcended (*vibhūta-rūpa-saṃjñā*).
However, because the first preparatory stage (sāmantaka) has a mode of activity that is not yet free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, it is a tight bond;
therefore, it alone does not receive the designation "having transcended the perception of form" (vibhūta-rūpa-saṃjñā).
How, then, is it determined that there is no form in the formless realms (ārūpya)?
This is established both through scripture and through reasoning.

First, as for scripture: this has been revealed [in the sūtras] such as, "By completely transcending perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*). Furthermore, there is another authoritative statement: "There are beings who are formless (*arūpin*)."
If it is argued that [form] is non-material because it possesses only a slight degree of form— just as a girl is called "thin-waisted" [even if she has some small amount of flesh]— we say no;
for it is designated as being "entirely" [without form],
and because its departure [from the world] is spoken of.
For it has been said: "The formless realms are the escape from forms.
Just as it is said, "Whatever is conditioned and whatever is experienced, the cessation of that is the escape," for indeed, in cessation, the dissociation from all conditioned phenomena is accepted.
For liberation is not characterized by a formal body or physical form, because that would obstruct its own manifestation.

This is also logical: having discarded the basis of form and so forth, it arises through the gateway of its own internal agitation, because it takes recourse in its own basis—just as one who has been plundered by bandits takes refuge in a place separated from them.

It has thus been stated that for those being reborn in the realms of form from the formless realms, form arises by the power of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, because name-and-form (nāmarūpa) are mutually causal, their status as causes is established: for both exist as homogeneous (sabhāga) and ripening (vipāka) causes therein; because consciousness is seen to arise with form as its condition; and because the production of specific states of mind is seen to result in the arising of form, such as the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the translucent matter of the sense faculties (indriyaprasāda). Thus, their mutual causality is proven.
The first formless attainment of application has been explained;
the second is now described: likewise, for one who perceives the mastery of mind, it is characterized by the infinity of consciousness.

Averse to the perception of the infinity of space, with a mind directed toward the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in the infinity of consciousness that takes that [space] as its object, one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Here too, mental applications (*manaskāra*) subsequently arise that take the four aggregates as their object, those that take other aggregates as their object, and those that take eternal phenomena as their object;
this is designated as "distraction from that."
Furthermore, there is the one who hates the infinity of consciousness, and the one called "nothingness."

That yogi, indeed, being averse to the perception of the infinity of consciousness, enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*) because of his perception of nothingness there. Alternatively, the sphere of nothingness is so called because it is the perfection of the application of equanimity toward "nothing whatsoever.
For, through seclusion from that [preceding state], the liberation of perception proceeds by viewing [the sphere of nothingness] as coarse in its infinite aspect.
For this very reason, the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*) is called supreme equanimity;
because therein the non-intentionality regarding infinite aspects and the effortless state of the mind (*anābhogatā*) are established.
Fearing the annihilation of that consciousness, he does not dwell in the state called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Indeed, regarding even that contracted perception as a "thorn of perception," he abandons it—however slight it may be—because its form is clearly discerned; and fearing annihilation, he attains the state that is neither with perception nor without perception, which possesses a clear form.
Therefore, one does not enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
nor the cessation of perception and feeling, nor even the distinct perception of the previous meditative attainment;
this applies to all the formless attainments.
Because it was applied in that manner at the outset, it is designated by that name.
However, it has already been demonstrated previously that the formless realms (ārūpya) are not merely designated by those names alone.
Thus, the eight fundamental substances of meditative attainment have been explained.
Furthermore, regarding the preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*), what is the nature of the first dhyāna preliminary known as the *anāgamya*? That is explained as follows:
it is that which possesses vitarka and vicāra, which is dependent, and which is accompanied by a subsequent flow.
The mind, whether of the noble or the non-noble type, is then called "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya).

That which is indeed the mind serving as the means for entering the first fundamental dhyāna—possessing applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā-saṃprayukta*), accompanied by its attendants (*sānuparivartaka*)—[is as described].
The second quarter of the eighth chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.
[End of] the eighth chapter.
The third quarter: ... [they] enter the leap-meditative attainment (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*); that is now explained—
Four types of meditators are proclaimed based on their insight into the four dhyānas;
they are those who understand the side of decline and so forth regarding the perception of prosperity and adversity.
For four types of meditators were spoken of by the Blessed One:
"Of them, one perceives attainment as misfortune; the second perceives misfortune as attainment."
"The third perceives prosperity as prosperity, and the fourth perceives adversity as adversity.

Thus, there are four [types of practitioners] due to the application of seeing the distinctions and excellences in the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) regarding decline, stability, distinction, and progress.
Who, then, is this meditator, and what are the meditation, the object of meditation, and the fruit of meditation?
That is now being revealed:
The meditator has been described, as well as the object of meditation, the meditation itself, and likewise the fruit of meditation.
All of this fourfold [set] has already been explained in detail previously.
However, for you,
because it is unestablished and because of the aforementioned faults, the fourfold set beginning with the self does not exist.

For this fourfold set is not established for you; the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the fruit of knowledge as postulated by the followers of the Upaniṣads, the Sāṃkhyas, the Vaiśeṣikas, and others, have already been shown to be subject to the aforementioned defects.
Furthermore, does liberation arise from the performance of ritual action, or rather from the practice of knowledge?
To this, we reply:
Liberation comes from the performance of ritual action as well as from the practice of knowledge;
for it exists when there is activity, and also upon the realization of the true nature of reality.

Indeed, by practicing the three types of action known as generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation, and by practicing the ten knowledges which serve as the antidotes to delusion regarding the specific and general characteristics of phenomena, one attains the supreme Brahman and not otherwise.
This is now being revealed:
In this context, action (karma) should be understood as twofold: meritorious and non-meritorious activity, and non-activity.
Among these, meritorious activity is said to be threefold, and abstention from such [non-meritorious] acts is likewise taught.
In the investigation of karma and so forth.
But the ultimate knowledge should be understood as it was previously illustrated;
he who resorts to anything other than this chews upon the bit [of worldly existence]. (Abhidharmadīpa 559)

But he who thinks that liberation occurs through ritual acts such as the immolation of animals and so forth, or through the thorough knowledge of the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, should be told: "He is chewing on a bit of bridle. For, because they involve activity directed toward harming others, killing, greed, falsehood, and the like should be known as causes for the miserable states (apāya), obstructing the gateway to the highest good.
For faults such as violence, falsehood, and greed are causes for going to an evil rebirth; they are not means for attaining heaven or liberation.
If it is argued that violence enjoined by the scriptures is not unrighteousness (*adharma*), we say no, because of a lack of thorough understanding of the defining characteristics of the scriptures.
How so?
Because it provides instruction on the meaning that is logically consistent, because it protects from suffering, and because it teaches regarding faults;
therefore it is called a "treatise" (śāstra). Anything else spoken by Vātika should be known as such.
Indeed, that speech which does not contradict the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
which protects by restraining one from evil deeds that cause rebirth in miserable states,
and which instructs regarding passion, hatred, and delusion— that is [true] speech. (Jaini_418)
It is said that only this is the treatise (śāstra) and nothing else;
therefore, anything other than this is the speech of one who is untrustworthy. No.
Because the capacity of Vedic mantras to neutralize poison is observed through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),

and because direct perception is the most powerful means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the two [other] means of valid cognition based upon it— namely those expressed as the Dharma of the Three Vedas (*trayī*)— are also authoritative. To this, the following is replied:
In some cases, the power of Pārasīka and other mantras is seen to be superior even to poison, yet this is not the case for all of them, because they do not avert misfortune (*ariṣṭa*) and the like.
For the efficacy of even the mantras of the Pārasīkas, Śabarakas, Kāpālikas, and others is indeed observed; yet you do not admit that those mantras destroy sin,
nor do they pacify all calamities,
since death is seen to occur due to misfortune (ariṣṭa) and the like associated with them.
If violence enjoined by the scriptures becomes an auxiliary to dharma through the power of mantras, why does one not kill the animal by the power of the mantra alone?
What is the use of performing procedures such as striking with a weapon or repeatedly cutting the throat?

Furthermore, let the manifestation of the *apūrva*—the cause for ascending to heaven—occur from the power of the mantra itself in the case of sacrificial cakes made of flour; enough with the slaughter of animals and the like!
The efficacy of mantras in neutralizing poison is indeed observed, yet they lack the power to alleviate hunger, thirst, and the like without food, drink, and so forth.
Likewise, let there be efficacy for mantras in neutralizing poison;
let it not be that they possess the power to destroy evil.

As for what you say—that only Brahmins who perform Vedic sacrifices are entitled to the path of liberation, and not those of other castes—that too appears to the wise as nothing more than the talk of children. For it is said:
"The mind is defiled by passion and the like, and it is purified by faith and the like."
Therefore, even for a Brahmin, it is only the one possessed of virtues who is liberated.
Just as medicine produces health only for one whose internal organs are pure, and not for one whose humors such as wind are aggravated,
so too even a potter who is of a fortunate disposition and whose self is refined by qualities such as faith is qualified for the path to liberation;
whereas one who possesses the four Vedas but whose mental ground is seized by defects such as passion, hatred, and delusion is not.
Let us not pursue this digression further; let the subject at hand be introduced.
This is now commenced: "The pure [attainment] is fourfold, beginning with that conducive to decline, in due order."
For that [attainment] conforms to what is inferior, equal in strength, superior, stainless, or concordant.

Indeed, the pure [attainment] is of four kinds: partaking of decline, partaking of stability, partaking of distinction, and partaking of penetration; the same applies to the formless attainments, except for the Peak of Existence, which is of three kinds, excluding that which partakes of distinction.
What, then, is their definition?

It is that which conforms to the afflictions, to its own level, to a higher level, or to the stainless state, respectively. Indeed, that which is conducive to the arising of afflictions is "partaking of decline" (*hānabhāgīya*).

That which conforms to its own level is conducive to stability (*sthitibhāgīya*); that which conforms to a higher level is conducive to distinction (*viśeṣabhāgīya*); and that which conforms to the untainted (*anāsrava*) is conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
From that [last one], the untainted arises.
Now, among these four, how many arise immediately after which?
Two, three, three, or two [minds] arise immediately after those belonging to the side of decline and so forth.
Immediately after a state conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*), two states arise: one conducive to decline and one conducive to stability (*sthitibhāgīya*).
After a state conducive to stability, three arise, excluding that which is conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
After a state conducive to distinction (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), three also arise, excluding that which is conducive to decline.
Immediately after the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), that same [path] is one.
The leap-over attainment belongs only to the Arhat of immovable nature.
Indeed, this [attainment] belongs only to the Arhat of immovable nature because of his freedom from defilements and his mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Although one who has attained through vision possesses mastery over concentration due to having sharp faculties, his mental continuum is not free from defilements.
Although one liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) is free from afflictions, he lacks mastery over meditative concentration (samādhi).
How, then, is this [mastery] produced?
Its preparation is twofold: having gone to a stage, it is undertaken with the desire to conquer what has not yet been conquered.
By skipping stages of the dharma-planes, one attains the eight [levels] from the so-called pure [state] to the untainted;
from the pure, the third [level] of its own [plane]; and from the pure, the ultimate stainless [state].
"Having gone" means having attained the eight stages in forward order;
"having come" means having attained them in reverse order;
"twofold" means both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
"Desiring to conquer" means wishing to achieve victory by transcending the stages of the dharma;
[it refers to] "from the pure, the untainted," and "from the pure, the third of its own [kind].
"The culmination," however, is from the pure to the untainted.
Having thus conquered the seven untainted [attainments], he subsequently enters from the tainted first dhyāna into the tainted third dhyāna;

from there, into the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana); and from there, into the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcanyāyatana). Having likewise conquered them again in reverse order, he enters the untainted attainments as well, skipping one at a time, both in forward and reverse order. This is the preparatory practice for the leap-meditation (vyutkrāntakasamāpatti).

But when one enters the first impure dhyāna, then the third pure dhyāna, then the impure sphere of infinite space, and from that the pure sphere of nothingness— in this way, proceeding again in reverse order—
then it becomes fully accomplished through the transition to a third substance of a different category.
Because it is too remote, one does not enter the fourth.
And he enters that [meditative attainment] in the three continents.
The pure states of existence belonging to the meditations and the formless realms arise only from their own level and from above;
however, one abiding at the peak of existence, having no other alternative, takes the stainless as its object at the beginning.

The peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is manifested both at the peak of existence and below, down to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Likewise, the remaining [attainments] are manifested in their own level and below.
One born in a higher realm does not manifest an attainment belonging to a lower realm, because it would be useless.
For there is no untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) therein, because that [realm] is the root of *saṃsāra*.
Nor can the afflictions belonging to that realm be destroyed without the untainted path.
If it is argued that detachment from that [realm] occurs by taking the person (*puruṣa*), whose nature is consciousness (*caitanya*), as its object, we say: no.

Because your person possesses activity, because the existence of both plurality and unity is established, and because it is logically possible for it to be a substratum in relation [to others]—just like cognition—and because consciousness and knowledge are perceived...
[omission]. Now, by the attainment of which meditation is what cultivated? That is set forth in sequence:
When an ordinary person attains the first dhyāna for the first time,
only the mundane [path] is cultivated for him in its future state.
This is also the case when the intermediate dhyāna has not been attained, excluding the stages of "heat" (ūṣmagata) and so forth.
For one in their final existence (*caramabhavika*), it is inappropriate [to cultivate] the [path] excluding heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth.
In that case, within the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), only the contaminated (*sāsrava*) [path] is cultivated first;
however, in the appropriate [stages], it is not cultivated because it has already been attained through detachment (*vairāgya*).
However, in the stages beginning with "heat" (ūṣmagata), it is not cultivated;
rather, those very [factors] included within the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara) are cultivated first, not the threshold concentration (anāgamya).

For one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), when the preliminary stage (*pūrvasāmantaka*) has not been previously attained, it is cultivated first even if it is unaccustomed; likewise, for one free from passion, even if the threshold state (*anāgamya*) has not been attained and is unaccustomed, it is cultivated first. [The pure factors] included in the threshold state are cultivated because they resemble the first noble path (*āryamārga*).
However, for one who was previously detached, only the stainless (*nirmala*) ones are cultivated.

For a noble one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), however, in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—excluding the moments at the end of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika*)—only the untainted (*anāsrava*) is cultivated. And for a learner (*śaikṣa*), during the increase of faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*) by means of two moments, and at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) in the seventeen [moments], likewise in the penetration of the immovable state (*akopyaprativedha*) through its ninefold nature and whatever follows it, whatever consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) that he brings face-to-face and has not previously obtained, therein only the untainted is first cultivated; thus, it is not called "cultivation of both."
In the subsequent knowledge of the path of certainty (*nyāmamārga*), in the increase of the faculties of one in training (*śaikṣa*),
in the path called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*), and in the path of seeing (*dṛṅmārga*), there are twelve moments.
And in the case of detachment from the peak of existence (bhavāgra), excluding the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna), [one attains] the immovable [arhatship]... // Abhidh-d_572 //
In the noble one’s detachment from the desire realm, on the final path of liberation,
in the three knowledges known as the "threefold," and in the application of attention excluding the preparatory stage (anāgamya).
For a learner (śaikṣa) who still possesses attachment, when increasing the faculties (indriya) belonging to the three lower realms,
as well as those born of the desire realm and the dhyānas, during the paths of preparation (prayoga-mārga) and liberation (vimukti-mārga).
In the attainment of the two types of arhatship on the final path of liberation,
and for those learners who are detached in the conquest of the other three realms without distraction.
The cultivation of both [types]—
namely, that of the first dhyāna which is both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*)— takes place;
however, there is no cultivation of both together.
The entry into the state of certainty (nyāma) occurs based on the preparatory stage (anāgamya), as well as through the arising of its factors conducive [to penetration] and so forth.

If one who relies on the *anāgamya* enters into the determination of correctness (*niyāma*), it is only the *anāgamya* that is cultivated for him, and not even the slightest portion of the first dhyāna.

Indeed, when he produces the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) based on the *anāgamya*, it is cultivated through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and not the first dhyāna; this has been made clear because of its similarity to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

In the second and subsequent [moments], one should infer by means of this very same method through reasoning; thus, the cultivation of future knowledge regarding the principles of the Abhidharma is to be understood.

Indeed, regarding the second and subsequent meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), one who follows the logic therein according to the treatise (*tantra*) by means of this very method of cultivation pertaining to the first absorption... [as follows]:
"Whose meditation is it, and what is its object? To answer this, the following is set forth in sequence:
"The pure (*śubha*) meditation accompanied by relish (*sāsvāda*) has its own nature as its object; the all-seeing [meditation] is likewise."
The fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not take the lower worlds as their object.
Associated with relishing (*āsvādana*), it takes as its object existence belonging to its own level—that is to say, a contaminated (*sāsrava*) thing.

It does not take a lower level as its object because of the absence of passion (*vītarāgatva*) for it; nor does it take a higher level as its object because of being delimited by craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Nor does it take an uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) thing as its object, for that would entail the consequence of it being wholesome (*kuśala*).

Wholesome meditative absorption (dhyāna), whether pure (śuddhaka) or untainted (anāsrava), has everything as its object— whatever exists, whether conditioned (saṃskṛta) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). However,
for the fundamental wholesome formless absorptions (ārūpya), a tainted entity belonging to a lower stage is not an object,
because they take as their objects only their own stage and higher stages.

However, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) object of focus consists of all categories of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), but not the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), nor the cessation (*nirodha*) of a lower stage.
For the preparatory (*sāmantaka*) and uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) paths, however, the lower stage is the object of focus.
Furthermore, among these three types of meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya),
the mental impurities are abandoned by means of the stainless (anāsrava) dhyānas and ārūpyas; however,
those of the lower stages are acquired even through the pure (śuddhaka) preparatory stages (sāmantaka).

Defilements are abandoned only by means of untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyāna and formless attainments (*ārūpya*), not by means of the wholesome; how much less so by the afflicted? Like one who is free from passion, they are not abandoned by what is below, because that [lower state] is not an antidote to it.
Not on its own level, because it is not more distinguished; nor above, because [the higher levels] are superior.

Defilements are abandoned even by the pure (*śuddhaka*) preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the dhyānas and formless attainments, because these serve as the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to the lower levels.
Furthermore: Having summarized all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), three types of concentration are taught in the Sūtra:
"Three concentrations, beginning with those accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), have been proclaimed.
That cessation (*nirodha*) exists in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*); it is dual in two [other] cases, and non-dual elsewhere. (Abhidharmadīpa 580)

“Concentration with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*).
Among these, first, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only;
everything below it is concentration with both applied thought and sustained thought.
But that which is subsequent is without vitarka and without vicāra.
Furthermore,

there are three other types of concentrations— those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*)— which pertain to eleven stages and illuminate the aspects (*ākāra*) of the noble ones, beginning with emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The meditative concentration whose object is emptiness, as well as the wishless and the signless, are the third.

Furthermore, by which [factors] are these noble aspects [constituted]? ... Because [it is said], "by sixteen aspects," therefore all three are illuminations of the sixteen aspects beginning with impermanence.
However, individually, ten are considered the aspects of the wishless (*apraṇihita*), and two are considered those of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The signless [samādhi] proceeds by means of the four aspects of the deathless.

The wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) is indeed associated with the two aspects of impermanence and suffering, with the four aspects of origin, and with the four aspects of the path... [it is] associated with the two aspects of selflessness.
The signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) is associated with the four aspects of cessation, beginning with the aspect of cessation.
Furthermore, for the sake of attaining the two kinds of liberation,
those same three stainless [factors] are revealed by the term "gateways to liberation" (vimokṣamukha).
Through the fading away of passion, there is liberation of mind; through the fading away of ignorance, there is liberation by wisdom.
These two forms of liberation... [are] manifested therein.
Among them, the concentration associated with emptiness is the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
It is called "wishless" (*apraṇihita*) because one does not direct a wish toward existence (*bhava*).

It is "signless" (*animitta*) due to the departure of the ten signs; the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that has that as its object is the signless concentration. Furthermore, there are three other concentrations known as "emptiness-of-emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) and so forth.
In order to demonstrate the means for relinquishing those three concentrations, three concentrations—namely emptiness-of-emptiness and so forth—are taught in the Abhidharma:
