"The two [concentrations] take as their object the state beyond training (aśaikṣa), [viewing it] as empty and likewise as impermanent. (Abhidh-d 584)

The last [of the three] takes as its object the cessation known as "non-analytical" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), perceiving it as peaceful. Because it has emptiness and so forth as its objects, it is given that name. Two other concentrations take the concentration of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) as their object:
the "emptiness-of-emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā) takes the aśaikṣa concentration of emptiness as its object by way of the aspect of emptiness (śūnyākāra).
The wishless [samādhi] that takes the wishless as its object is also the wishless [samādhi] of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), by way of the aspect of impermanence.
It does not take it as suffering, nor as cause and so forth, because that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) does not possess those characteristics.
Nor does it take it by way of the aspects of the path, because [the wishless samādhi] is subject to revulsion.
Because it is the signless among the signless, the concentration of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) takes as its object the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) of the signless;
this is because there is no analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) for that which is untainted (anāsrava), since it is characterized by peace.

It does not take it as an object through the aspects of cessation, excellence, or escape, because [analytical cessation] would be common to the cessation of impermanence, because it is neutral (avyākṛta), and because it is not a dissociation (avisaṃyoga).
Furthermore, these concentrations belong to all eleven stages; they are all with-outflows (sāsrava) and do not exist among the gods.
Among those, the contaminated [attainments] arise among humans because they are averse to the Noble Path.

For an unshakable Arhat, they arise in the other eleven stages—excluding the seven preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the eleven stages—namely, in the desire realm, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna, the [four] dhyānas, and the [four] formless attainments (ārūpya).
Furthermore...
The cultivation of concentration through meditative absorption is the first virtuous [practice] for the sake of happiness;
the supernormal power of the eye is said to be for the sake of vision; and those [practices] involving effort are for the sake of the differentiation of wisdom.
“There are indeed four cultivations of concentration (*samādhibhāvanā*).
There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to dwelling in the present life,” and so forth.
This is indeed wholesome (*kuśala*).
The cultivation of concentration for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life consists of the first dhyāna, whether it be pure (*śuddhaka*) or untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because this is the primary case, other [dhyānas] should also be understood in the same way;
however, they do not necessarily lead to dwelling in happiness in future lives.
One who has fallen away from a higher rebirth does not possess it because of having passed into final nirvana (*parinirvita*).

The cultivation of concentration for the sake of seeing with the supernormal power of the divine eye is indeed the cultivation of all qualities born of application— whether belonging to the three realms or untainted— for the purpose of the differentiation of wisdom.
That which is the final [moment] in the diamond-like meditation (*vajropama-dhyāna*) for the destruction of all afflictions—
that which is the diamond-like concentration (*samādhi*) in the fourth meditation— is the cultivation of concentration for the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava*).
And this Sūtra was proclaimed by the Buddha as applicable to himself.
Therefore, it is said that only the fourth dhyāna is [the one] described.
The third quarter of the eighth chapter in the *Abhidharmapradīpa*, in the commentary known as the *Vibhāṣāprabhā*, is completed.
The fourth quarter of the eighth chapter:
The meditative absorptions have been explained.
Hereafter, the qualities based upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are explained.
There are four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*): loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

They are called "immeasurable" because they function by taking sentient beings as their objective support, because they bring about immeasurable merit, and because they serve as the cause for immeasurable fruits.
Now, what is the intrinsic nature of the immeasurables?
It is held that for the four immeasurables, loving-kindness is non-hatred, compassion is likewise [non-hatred], sympathetic joy is gladness, and equanimity is non-greed. *Abhidharmadīpa* 588.
Loving-kindness has non-hatred as its intrinsic nature;
likewise, compassion has non-hatred as its intrinsic nature.
What, then, is the distinction between these two immeasurables?
Although both consist in the absence of hatred, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the antidote to hatred that persists in not abandoning sentient beings and functions with the aspect of joy;
compassion (*karuṇā*) is the antidote to hatred that persists in the intention to strike or harm and functions with the aspect of sorrow.
Thus, there is a distinction between them.
"The ancient masters [state] that sympathetic joy (muditā) has the nature of mental happiness (somanasya).
Equanimity (upekṣā), too, has non-attachment (alobha) as its essence. This is the intrinsic nature of the immeasurables (apramāṇa)."

Why are there exactly four, neither fewer nor more? This is declared to be the antidote for ill-will, harmfulness, lack of joy, thirst, and hatred, for the purpose of taming one's own mind. (Abhidh-d 589)
It is said in the Sūtra: "Loving-kindness, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed, leads to the abandonment of ill-will;
compassion leads to the abandonment of cruelty;
sympathetic joy leads to the abandonment of discontent; and equanimity leads to the abandonment of sensual desire and ill-will."
Furthermore, the commentary should be consulted:

"Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is pleasant when establishing happiness; compassion (*kṛpā*) is oriented toward the destruction of suffering; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is inclined toward rejoicing; and the last [equanimity] is directed toward these very beings. (Abhidharmadīpa 590)
Their conduct is to be observed,
but how, moreover, is their physical form to be recognized?
That is now explained:
By means of the aspects of "happy" and so forth:
reflecting in one's mind, "May beings indeed be happy," one enters into loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
reflecting, "Alas, beings are suffering," one enters into compassion (*karuṇā*).
Thinking, "May beings indeed rejoice," one enters the meditative absorption of sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
Thinking simply "beings," one enters the meditative absorption of equanimity (*upekṣā*) due to impartiality.
By means of even one of these [four immeasurables], however, one attains union with Brahmā (*brahmasāyujya*).
From among these immeasurables, by cultivating even one, the state of Brahmā is attained.
It is explained as follows: what are the objects of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and how many stages (*bhūmi*) do they possess?
Those called "joy" (*muditā*) have humans as their object and belong to two dhyānas; those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have [beings of] the desire realm as their object.
Some maintain that those others belong to six levels within the seven [stages].
The three—loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*)—have sentient beings of the desire realm as their object;
equanimity (*upekṣā*) is indeterminate.

For those for whom these [three] consist of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) and for whom sympathetic joy is the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*), sympathetic joy exists in the first and second dhyānas.

Above that, because of the absence of the faculty of mental gladness (*saumanasyendriya*), the other three immeasurables exist in six stages: the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four dhyānas.
Furthermore, according to some, these are also produced by reflection (*cintāmaya*); and since joy (*pramodya*) is a distinct factor from rapture (*prīti*), for them they belong to seven stages.
Because joy is associated with two types of feeling,
the immeasurables have been explained.
Now, how many liberations (vimokṣa) are there?
Eight liberations have been taught; among them, two consist of the nature of the foul (aśubha).
These two occur in the first and last dhyānas. The third is characterized by non-greed (alobha).
"One possessing form sees forms" is the first liberation.
"Being internally percipient of the formless, one sees forms externally" is the second liberation.
"Having personally realized the beautiful liberation with the body and having attained it, one dwells therein" is the third.

Among these, the first two have the nature of the unwholesome because they take that as their aspect; and by way of their level, they exist in the first and second dhyānas along with their preliminary stages (sāmantaka), as well as in the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
The wholesome liberation exists in the fourth dhyāna along with its preliminary stage;
furthermore, it has non-attachment (alobha) as its very nature and does not consist of the unwholesome.
Because they proceed with a virtuous aspect,
these, together with their attendants, have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
The four wholesome formless states are called liberations when they are in a state of meditative concentration;
the attainment known as cessation is declared to be the eighth liberation.
The other four liberations (vimokṣa) should be understood as being exclusively wholesome and concentrated states of the formless realm (ārūpya).
The eighth liberation, however, is the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha).
For the meaning of "liberation" (vimokṣa) is indeed the sense of turning away (vaimukhya).
The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
because it is turned away from all functioning that has an object of perception.
Its manifestation occurs immediately after the extremely subtle [state].
For the mind belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is of three kinds, distinguished by the names "gross," "subtle," and "extremely subtle.
These are, respectively, gross, subtle, and extremely subtle.
Therefore, immediately after the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they enter that attainment known as the "subtle-subtle" (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma*).
For those who have thus entered it, even the mind of emergence from this state is its own pure and stainless [state], belonging to the level below. (Abhidh-d 595)
Because it is both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*):
if the mind emerging from that [attainment] emerges by means of a mind with-outflows, it is by means of one belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);
if it emerges by means of a mind without-outflows, it is by means of one belonging to the stage of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*).
Now, what are the objects of these liberations?
The first three liberations have as their objects visible things belonging to the desire realm;
the object of these [three] is the form realm and the desire realm, respectively, according to the case, by way of the unattractive and the attractive.
Others, however, [belong] to the category of those possessing subsequent cognition (anvayajñāna), as they observe the suffering and so forth of the higher realms.
The objects of the formless liberations (ārūpyavimokṣa) are the suffering belonging to their own level and the higher levels, as well as the causes and the cessation thereof.
In all cases, the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) is comprised of both higher and lower levels,
as is non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha).
The liberations have been explained.
In the Sūtra, an octad of sense-bases called the "perceptions of mastery" is taught;
this, by way of its function as an addition to the liberations, demonstrates sovereignty over the mind.

In the Sūtra, the Blessed One has taught the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*): "Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally—whether beautiful or ugly—and having mastered those forms, one knows them;
having mastered them, one sees them."
Having such a perception, this is the first *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery).
Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, whether beautiful or ugly; the detailed description continues up to what is the second *abhibhvāyatana*.
Likewise, perceiving no forms internally, one sees external forms—both limited and immeasurable; thus there are four.
And one who is internally percipient of the formless sees external forms—blue, yellow, red, white...
[as before] ...In the *Abhidharmadīpa*, in the commentary known as the *Vibhāṣāprabhā*, the fourth quarter of the eighth chapter is completed.
The eighth chapter is completed.
The Abhidharmadīpa with the Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti commentary is completed.
